1: ## Vinaya Piṭaka ## Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā ## Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ## 5. Pācittiya Section ## 1. Musāvāda Vagga ## 1. Commentary on the Musāvāda Training Rule These ninety-two (minor) training rules are well-collected into nine chapters. Now, this commentary on those training rules will be presented. Among those ninety-two training rules, in the first training rule of the Musāvāda Vagga, 'Hatthaka' is the name of that Elder. 'Sakyaputta' means a son of the Sakyans. In the time of the Buddha, it is said that eighty thousand men from the Sakyan clan went forth; the Venerable Hatthaka was one among them. 'Vādakkhitta' means one who is sent or dispatched to opponents with the thought, 'I will engage in debate.' Or it means one whose mind is cast into debate (one whose mind is focused only on debate). Because he is seen wherever there is a debate, he is also called 'Vādakkhitta.' 'Avajānitvā avajānāti' means when he sees some fault in his own argument, he denies it saying, 'This is not my argument,' and then, while speaking further, when he perceives it to be faultless, he acknowledges it saying, 'This is indeed my argument.' 'Paṭijānitvā avajānāti' means when he sees an advantage in some statement, he acknowledges it saying, 'This is my argument,' and then, while speaking further, [seeing] a fault in that statement...
2:
...noticing [a fault], he denies it saying, "This is not my view." "Aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati" means covering, concealing, or overshadowing one reason with another reason. For example, after saying "Form is impermanent because it is to be known," he then changes and says, "because it is of the nature of birth," and so on. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is said, "He speaks many other things for the sake of concealing that point." The meaning of that passage is that to conceal the admission or denial, he speaks much, such as "Who said it? What was said? Where was it said?" and so forth. Furthermore, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated, "Admitting after denying, and denying after admitting, is also called concealing one thing with another (aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati)."

"Sampajānamusā bhāsati" means speaking a lie knowingly. "Saṅketaṃ katvā visaṃvādeti" (deceiving by making an appointment) means making an appointment in the morning or such, saying "Let there be a debate at such a time and in such a place," and then going either before or after the appointed time and saying, "Look, sirs, the sectarians have not come and are defeated," and then departing.

"Sampajānamusāvāde" is because of knowing beforehand that one will speak a lie and also knowing it at the moment of speaking. "Visaṃvādana-purekkharassa" (of one who intends to deceive) refers to the volition (cetanā) of one who speaks with the intention to deceive as the priority. "Vācā" is the volition that originates speech included in wrong speech. By the term "Girā", the sound originated by that volition is shown. "Byappatho" is the path of speech; indeed, speech itself is called "byappatho" because it is like a path for others who follow it. "Vacībhedo" is the breaking of speech, which is called "vaci"; speech that has reached differentiation is so called. "Vācasikā viññatti" is verbal intimation (vaci-viññatti). Thus, it should be understood that by the first term (vācā), pure volition is "spoken"; by the middle three (girā, byappatho, vacībhedo), volition accompanied by the sound originated by it; and by the last term (viññatti), volition accompanied by intimation. "Anariyavohārā" means the expressions of the ignoble, the foolish worldlings.

Having thus shown the "sampajānamusāvāda" (deliberate lying), he now says "adiṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ me" (I saw what was not seen), etc., wishing to show the characteristics of the ignoble expressions known as deliberate lying mentioned at the end. Therein, the speech of one who says "I saw what was not seen," or the volition that originates that speech, is one ignoble expression; the meaning should be understood in this manner for the rest. Furthermore, herein, an object not perceived by the eye is "adiṭṭha" (unseen); that not perceived by the ear is "asuta" (unheard); that not perceived by the three senses of nose, tongue, and body, as if binding them into one, is "amuta" (unsensed); and that not perceived other than by the five senses (i.e., by the mind) is "aviññāta" (unknown).
3:
An object that is not grasped by the five doors but only by the pure mind-consciousness should be understood as 'unperceived' (aviññāta). In the Pali text, however, the teaching is given in this obvious way: 'What is called unseen is that which is not seen with the eye.' Among the seen and so forth, what is seen by oneself or by another is indeed 'seen' (diṭṭha). The same applies to what is heard (suta), sensed (muta), and cognized (viññāta). This is one method (pariyāya). Another method: What is seen by oneself is 'seen'. This same method applies to 'heard' and so forth. However, what is seen by another stands in the place of 'heard' (suta) for oneself. The same applies to 'sensed' and so forth.

Now, wishing to show the offense based on those ignoble modes of speech (anariya-vohāra), he said 'tīhākārehi' (by three modes) and so forth. Its meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the commentary on the fourth Pārajika, such as: 'For a monk who, knowing [the truth], speaks a deliberate lie saying he has attained the first jhāna by three modes, there is an offense of Pārajika.' Indeed, in that Pārajika it says 'attained the first jhāna', while in this training rule it says 'I see what is unseen'. There, it says 'an offense of Pārajika', while here it says 'an offense of Pācittiya'. Thus, there is a difference only in the matter (vatthu) and the offense; the remaining characteristics are the same.

The meaning of 'one who is doubtful about what is seen by three modes' and so forth should also be understood in the same way as stated in the commentary on the Duṭṭhadosa training rule, such as: 'One who commits a Pārajika offense regarding what is seen is one who is doubtful about what is seen.' In these two training rules, only the Pali text differs, but in the meaning, including the Theravāda tradition, there is no difference at all.

'Sahasa bhaṇati' means speaking 'I did not see' even regarding what was seen, quickly without investigating or reflecting. 'Aññaṃ bhaṇiဿāmīti aññaṃ bhaṇati' means speaking something else due to dullness or stupidity, such as speaking 'cīra' and so forth when 'cīvara' should be said, due to a slip of the tongue. If a monk, when asked by a novice, 'Venerable sir, did you see my preceptor?', wishing to play a joke, says, 'Your preceptor must have gone yoking a wood-cart,' or upon hearing the sound of a jackal and being asked, 'Venerable sir, what sound is this?', says, 'That is the sound of those pulling out a wheel stuck in the mud while your mother was traveling by carriage'—if he speaks such other things, neither in jest nor in play, he indeed falls into an offense.

There is also what is called 'pūraṇakathā' (exaggerated speech). For example, a monk who obtained a little oil in the village and, upon returning to the monastery, says to a novice, 'Where did you go today? The whole village was nothing but oil!' or having obtained a piece of cake kept in a small basket, says, 'Today they are distributing cakes by the basketful in the village.' Such speech is indeed a lie (musāvāda). The rest of the explanation is clear.

This training rule has three origins (samuṭṭhāna): body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It is an act (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), an action of body, an action of speech, with unwholesome consciousness, and involving the three feelings. The first Musāvāda training rule is finished.
4:
...having obtained (a piece of cake) and saying 'Today they are distributing cakes by the basketful in the village' is indeed a lie. The rest of the meaning is clear.

This training rule has three origins: it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an act (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), an action of body, an action of speech, with unwholesome consciousness, and involving the three feelings.

## The First Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvāda).

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Insulting Speech (Omasavāda).

In the second training rule, 'omasanti' means they pierce with the spear of the tongue. 'Khuṃsenti' means they revile. 'Vambhenti' means they disparage and destroy.

The Lord brought this story 'bhūtapubbaṃ' (once upon a time) to criticize insulting speech. 'Nandivisāla' is the name: 'Nandi' was the name of that bull, and because his horns (visāṇa) were large (visāla), he was called 'Nandivisāla'. At that time, the Bodhisatta was the bull named Nandivisāla. A brahmin raised that bull very well with gruel, rice, and so forth. Then, the bull, out of compassion for the brahmin, said, 'Go you,' and so forth. 'He stood right there' means that even in a birth as an animal with rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi), he recognized the insulting of others as unpleasant; therefore, wishing to show the brahmin's fault, he stood still. 'He made a hundred carts tied together move' means that having arranged them in a row, tied them together with wooden beams underneath to make them a single unit, he made the hundred carts filled with green gram, black gram, sand, and so forth move. Although it is said to move when a point on the rim of a wheel previously established reaches that point again, the Bodhisatta made them move over a distance equal to a hundred carts so that the last cart would stand where the first cart had been. For Bodhisattas, there is no such thing as doing something slackly. 'Because of that, he was delighted' means that Nandivisāla was delighted because of the brahmin's gain of wealth and because of his own deed.
5:
In the phrase beginning with "akkosenapi"—because the author later wishes to distinguish between two types of insults, namely "low insult and high insult," he does not say "they disparage with a low insult" as said previously, but simply says "with an insult."

"Vena-jāti" refers to the carpenter caste; some also say it is the bamboo-worker caste. "Nesāda-jāti" refers to the caste of hunters and the like. "Rathakāra-jāti" refers to the leather-worker (or cobbler) caste. "Pukkusa-jāti" refers to the caste of flower-scavengers (refuse-cleaners). Names such as "Avakaṇṇaka" are names of slaves, and are therefore low names. "Oñāta" means a name recognized as low; it is also read as "uñāta." "Avañāta" means a name known with contempt. "Hīḷita" means a loathed name. "Paribhūta" means a name that is overpowered or humiliated, as in "What use is there for this person?" "Acittīkata" means a name that is not treated with respect.

"Koṭṭhakakamma" refers to the work of carpenters (or stone-masons). "Muddā" is the art of calculation by bending the fingers. "Gaṇanā" refers to other types of calculation such as "acchindaka." "Lekhā" is the art of writing letters. The disease "madhumeha" (diabetes) is called an "exalted disease" because of the absence of acute pain. "Pāṭikaṅkhā" means that which is desired. Insulting with the letter "ya" or "ba" means insulting by joining the letters "ya" and "ba." In the phrase "kāṭakoṭacikāya vā," "kāṭa" refers to the male organ and "koṭacikā" refers to the female organ; insulting with these is called a low insult.

Now, wishing to show the offense by way of the distinctions of those castes and so forth, the author says "upasampanno upasampannaṃ" and so on. In that context, one who "desires to disparage, desires to despise, desires to shame" means one who desires to insult, desires to oppress, desires to blame, or desires to deprive of dignity. "Calling a low person by a low term" (hīneena hīnaṃ) means addressing a person of low caste with words referring to a low caste. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all remaining terms.

In this context, a monk who addresses a low monk with low words, even if he speaks the truth, incurs a Pācittiya offense for every word because of the desire to disparage. A monk who addresses a low monk with high words (ironically), even if he speaks a falsehood, incurs a Pācittiya offense only by this training rule because of the desire to disparage; he does not incur an offense by the previous training rule (on lying). If a monk says, "You are an extreme Caṇḍāla, you are an extreme Brahmin, you are a corrupt Caṇḍāla, you are a corrupt Brahmin," and so forth, he should also be dealt with according to the offense.
6:
In the section "santi idhekacce," a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred because the statement is made evasively, avoiding direct speech. The same method applies to the sections "ye nūna...pe... na mayaṃ." When speaking to an unordained person (anupasampanna), only a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred in all four sections. In statements such as "You are a thief, you are a burglar," a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred in all sections, whether the person is ordained or unordained. However, if one speaks with the desire to jest (davakamyatā), a Dubbhāsita offense is incurred in all sections, whether the person is ordained or unordained. "Davakamyatā" means the state of desiring to play or laugh. In this training rule, excluding monks, all beings such as bhikkhunīs and others are to be understood as being in the position of the unordained.

In the terms "atthapurekkhārassa" and so forth, one who explains the meaning of the Pali text is known as "atthapurekkhāra" (one who aims at the meaning). One who teaches the Pali text is known as "dhammapurekkhāra" (one who aims at the Dhamma). One who, established in the role of admonishing, speaks in this manner: "Even now you are a Caṇḍāla; do not do evil; do not be one who goes from darkness to darkness," and so forth, is known as "anusāsanīpurekkhāra" (one who aims at instruction). The rest is clear.

This training rule arises from three origins (samuṭṭhāna): body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It is associated with: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), intentionality (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling. The Dubbhāsita offense, however, arises from speech and mind. It is associated with: action, release through perception, intentionality, unwholesome mind, and two feelings (pleasant and neutral).

## Second Training Rule on Insulting Speech (Omasavāda).

## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Slander (Pesunña)

In the third training rule, "bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ" means those for whom a quarrel has arisen. "Bhaṇḍana" is the preliminary stage of a quarrel, such as the consultation within one's own party: "This person and that person have done this; if they say this, we will say that," and so forth. "Kalaha" is the transgression of body and speech that leads to an offense. "Vivāda" is contentious speech. Those who have entered into such a dispute are called "vivādāpannānaṃ." "Pesunña" means slanderous speech (pisunā vācā); it means speech that makes one empty of the state of being loved.
7:
“Bhikkhupesuñña” means slandering monks. It means conveying slanderous speech heard from one monk to another monk.

“Dvīhākārehi” means by two reasons. “Piyakamyassa vā” means because of a person desiring to be loved, thinking, “By speaking thus, I will become dear to this person.” “Bhedādhippāyassa vā” means because of a person desiring division, thinking, “By speaking thus, this person will be divided from that person” (slander occurs). All expressions such as “jātitopi” etc., follow the method already stated in the previous training rule. In this training rule also, starting from bhikkhunīs, all are called “anupasampanna” (unordained).

“Na piyakamyassa na bhedādhippāyassa” means seeing one monk abusing and another monk enduring, and thinking, “Oh, how shameless! He thinks he should abuse this noble person who is so patient again,” and speaking with the intention of censuring the wicked person without the desire to be loved or to cause division—there is no offense for such a monk. The remaining words have clear meanings. This training rule has 3 origins (samuṭṭhāna): it arises from body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It is endowed with kiriya, saññāvimokkha, sacittaka, lokavajja, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and the 3 feelings.

## Pesuñña-sikkhāpada, the Third.

## 4. Padasodhamma-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule: “Appatissā” means those who are disrespectful. It means they do not even want to listen to the word “Upāsaka” and are disregardful. Or it means those who have no humble behavior because they have no reliance. “Asabhāgavuttikā” means they have a dissimilar livelihood; they do not practice as monks should practice.

“Padaso dhammaṃ vāceyya” means teaching the Dhamma word by word together, or teaching it group by group. Since that word named “koṭṭhāsa” (group) is of four kinds, to show that, the padabhājanī (word-analysis) is stated as “Pada, Anupada, Anvakkhara, Anubyañjana.” Among them, “Pada” means one line (pāda) of a verse (gāthā). “Anupada” means the second line. “Anvakkhara” means each individual syllable (akkhara). “Anubyañjana” means a subsequent consonant similar to the preceding consonant. Or, any single syllable is called “anvakkhara,” a collection of syllables is called “anubyañjana,” and a collection of syllables and anubyañjana is called “pada.” The first word is just pada, and the second is anupada; thus the distinction should be understood.
8:
Now, “Pada” means starting together and finishing together. A teacher who teaches Dhamma composed in verse starts each line of the verse, such as “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā,” together with the novice (sāmaṇera) and finishes it together. For a teacher who teaches thus, a pācittiya offense should be known according to the number of words (lines of verse). “Anupada” means starting separately and finishing together. When the elder says “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā,” the novice, without reaching that line, recites the second line “Manoseṭṭhā manomayā” together (with the teacher). This starting separately and finishing together is called anupada. For a teacher who teaches thus also, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of anupada. “Anvakkhara” (syllable by syllable) means when making one say “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ,” reciting only the syllable “Rū” together. When it is said, “Novices, say ‘Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ’,” they recite only the syllable “Rū” together and stop. For a teacher who teaches thus also, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of syllables. This method also applies to Dhamma composed in verse.

“Anubyañjana” means when making one say “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ,” uttering the sound “Vedanā aniccā.” When teaching this sutta, “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā,” while the elder says “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ,” the novice, being of quick wisdom, utters the words by reciting this anicca-pada “Vedanā aniccā” together with the elder’s anicca-pada “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ.” For a teacher who teaches thus also, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of anubyañjana. The summary here is: among these pada etc., whatever text is recited together, one falls into an offense by that text.

“Buddhabhāsita” (spoken by the Buddha) refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, Abhidhamma Piṭaka, Dhammapada, Cariyāpiṭaka, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, and suttas such as the Brahmajāla Sutta. “Sāvakabhāsita” (spoken by disciples) refers to suttas spoken by disciples included in the four assemblies, such as the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Anumāna Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, and Mahāvedalla Sutta. “Isibhāsita” (spoken by sages) refers to the entire Paribbājaka-vagga spoken by external wanderers, such as the questions of the sixteen brahmins who were disciples of the brahmin Bāvarī. “Devatābhāsita” (spoken by deities) refers to the Dhamma requested by deities, which should be understood by way of the Devatā-saṃyutta, Devaputta-saṃyutta, Māra-saṃyutta, Brahma-saṃyutta, Sakka-saṃyutta, etc.

“Atthūpasañhita” (connected with meaning) refers to Dhamma based on the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). “Dhammūpasañhita” (connected with Dhamma) refers to Dhamma based on the Pali Text (Pāḷi). By both of these, it means only the Dhamma based on Nibbāna, which is the cause for liberation from the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). Even if it is Dhamma based on Nibbāna, for a teacher who teaches only the Dhamma included in the three Councils (Saṅgīti) word by word...
9:
(An offense is committed by a monk who teaches the Dhamma approved in the Councils word-by-word.) Even if it is a teaching leading to Nibbāna, there is no offense if it is composed in languages other than Māgadhi, such as in the form of verses (Gāthā) or stanzas (Siloka). Even if they have not been included in the three Councils, an offense is indeed committed for teaching suttas such as the Kulumbo Sutta, Rājovāda Sutta, Tikkhindriya, Catu-parivaṭṭa, and Nandopananda. It is also stated that an offense is committed for the Apalāladamana. However, it is prohibited in the Mahāpaccari. Regarding the Meṇḍakapañhā and Milindapañhā, there is no offense for the words of the Elder Nāgasena which are his own intellectual insights; however, an offense is committed for the words he brought forth and spoke from the Pāḷi and Commentaries to make the King understand. It is stated that the Vaṇṇapiṭaka, Aṅgulimālapiṭaka, Raṭṭhapālagazzita, Āḷavakagazzita, Guḷhamagga, Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhavinaya, and Vedallapiṭaka are certainly not the words of the Buddha. Some say the Sīlūpadesa was spoken by the General of the Dhamma, Ven. Sāriputta; an offense is indeed committed for that text. There are other texts such as the Maggakathā, Ārammaṇakathā, Buddhika, Daṇḍaka, Ñāṇavatthu, and Asubhakathā; in those texts, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are analyzed, and in the Dhutaṅgapañhā, the practice (paṭipadā) is analyzed; therefore, it is stated in the ancient commentaries that an offense is committed for those texts. In the Mahāpaccari and others, however, it is stated that an offense is committed only for the Rājovāda, Tikkhindriya, Catu-parivaṭṭa, Nandopananda, and Kulumbo Sutta which were not included in the Councils; for the remaining suttas, only the words brought forth from the Buddha's teachings are grounds for an offense, not other words—this is the determined meaning.

'Ekatō uddisāpentō' means that even if one is learning the Pāḷi together with an unordained person, there is no offense if they recite it simultaneously.

In this matter, the decision is as follows: A monk and an unordained person sit and have the Pāḷi recited to them. If the teacher, intending to recite for those sitting, recites simultaneously with them, the teacher commits an offense. For the monk who is learning together with the unordained person, there is no offense. If both are standing while learning, the same rule applies. If a junior monk is sitting and a novice (Sāmaṇera) is standing, there is no offense for the teacher who recites with the intention of reciting for the sitting junior monk. If the junior monk is standing and the other (novice) is sitting, there is no offense for the teacher who recites with the intention of reciting for the standing junior monk. If a novice is sitting among many monks, an acittaka (unintentional) offense is committed by the teacher who teaches the Dhamma word-by-word while that novice is sitting there. If the novice is standing or sitting outside the twelve-cubit precinct (upacāra), it is called an 'escaping text' (palāyanakagantha) because he is not included among those being taught, and thus there is no offense. A monk who performs communal recitation (sajjhāya) together with an unordained person, if he performs communal recitation together with an unordained person...
10:
...if he recites together with him, there is no offense. Even for a monk who learns the Pāḷi in the presence of an unordained person, if he recites simultaneously with him, there is no offense. This is because such simultaneous recitation is also reckoned as "performing communal recitation together."

Regarding prompting one who is reciting a text that is mostly mastered (yebhuyyena paguṇa): if one foot (pāda) of a verse does not come to mind but the remaining three feet do, this text is called "mostly mastered." This method should also be understood for the Sutta Pāḷi. There is no offense for one who, while prompting the person reciting that mastered text to reach the end, says "recite it like this" and recites together with him. While having the Pāḷi recited, there is no offense for one who says "speak it like this" and speaks together with a novice who is hesitant in the midst of the assembly. In commentaries such as the Mahāpaccari, it is stated that if one recites together even after being told "Do not recite with me," there is "no offense"; however, that statement is not found in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Its absence is indeed appropriate. Why? Because this training rule is action-based (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna). Otherwise, it would become a matter of both action and non-action (kiriyākiriya). The remaining words are clear in meaning.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the Padaso Dhamma training rule: it arises from speech, and from speech and mind. It is action-based (kiriya). It is not a release through perception (saññā-vimokkha). It is unintentional (acittaka). It is a breach of a conventional regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja). It is a vocal act (vacī-kamma). It is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## Fourth: Padaso Dhamma Training Rule.

## 5. Sahasayya Training Rule Commentary

In the fifth training rule: "muṭṭhassatī asampajānā" (losing mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension) is stated because of the failure to maintain mindfulness and clear comprehension in the period prior to falling asleep. When one has descended into the subconscious (bhavaṅga) and is asleep, how could there be mindfulness and clear comprehension? "Vikūjamānā" means talking or moaning in one's sleep. "Kākacchamānā" means emitting a meaningless sound (snoring) from the nose like the cawing of a crow. "Upāsakā" refers to lay devotees who wake up earlier than the monks.

"Etadavocuṃ" means: "Friends, the Blessed One has prescribed a training rule for Rāhula," the monks said this out of respect for the training rule. By nature, those monks, out of respect for the Blessed One and because of the Venerable Rāhula's desire for training, would prepare whatever was available—whether a small couch (cūḷamañcaka) or a leaning board—for the Venerable Rāhula when he came to their dwelling, and would give him a double-layered robe or an upper robe to use as a pillow.
11:
The monks gave Venerable Rāhula a small couch or a bolster. This story is an example of that Venerable Rāhula's desire for training (sikkhākāmatā). It is said that when the monks saw Venerable Rāhula coming from afar, they would throw a hand-broom and a dust-basket outside. Then, when other monks asked, "Friends, who dropped this broom and basket?", some would say, "Venerable sirs, Rāhula was wandering in this area; it might have been dropped by him." That Venerable Rāhula, without even once protesting, "Venerable sirs, this is not my doing," would put away the broom and basket, ask for forgiveness from the monks, and then depart.

Regarding the statement that he slept in the latrine (vacca-kuṭi), while further cultivating that same desire for training, he did not go to the presence of the great elders such as the Marshal of the Dhamma Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, or Venerable Ānanda, but instead slept in the latrine used by the Blessed One. That latrine, it is said, was fitted with door-panels, perfumed with scents, and had garlands of flowers hanging down, standing like a shrine (cetiya), and was not for the use of others.

## 51. Uttari-diratta-tirattaṃ
The Blessed One allowed the practice of sleeping together for three nights for the sake of supporting the novices (sāmaṇeras). This is because it is not proper to ordain sons of good families into the Dispensation and then not support them. "Sahaseyya" means sleeping together. The term "seyyā" refers to both the act of sleeping, known as stretching out the body, and the lodging or place where one sleeps. Among these two, to show the lodging or sleeping place, the words beginning with "Seyyā nāma sabbacchannā" were spoken. To show the stretching out of the body, the words beginning with "Anupasampanne nipanne bhikkhu nipajjati" were spoken. Therefore, the meaning here is: "Having entered the lodging known as the sleeping place, one performs, arranges, or accomplishes the sleep known as stretching out the body."

With the words beginning with "Sabbacchannā," the characteristics of that lodging known as the sleeping place are stated. Therefore, a lodging that is entirely covered from above by any of the five types of roofing or by any other kind of roof is called a "sabbacchannā" sleeping place. In the Commentaries, however, taking the common usage, it is recited by heart as "sabbacchannā means covered by the five types of roofing." Even though it is said so, a monk living in a small hut covered with cloth cannot remain free from offense. Therefore, in this context, anything capable of covering, whether it be a roof or a screen, should be understood. If only the five types of roofing were taken, then sleeping together in a lodging roofed with wooden planks would not constitute an offense.

A lodging that is enclosed from the ground up to the roof by a wall or any other screen, even at the minimum by a cloth, is called a "sabbaparicchannā" sleeping place. The Kurundī Commentary states that even if it does not reach the roof, if it is enclosed by a wall or similar structure at least one and a half cubits (1.5 cubits) in height, it is still "sabbaparicchannā." If a lodging has a roof over most of its area and only a small part is unroofed, or if it has screens around most of it and only a small part is unscreened, that lodging is called "yebhuyyacchannā" (mostly roofed) or "yebhuyyaparicchannā" (mostly enclosed). A lodging endowed with these characteristics, even if it be a seven-storied mansion, because it has a single precinct (ekūpacāra)...
12:
...if most of the surroundings are enclosed and only a small part is not enclosed, this place is called 'mostly enclosed' (yebhuyyena paricchanna). If it is endowed with this characteristic, whether it be a seven-storied mansion, a monastery with a hundred rooms, or a long building with four sides, it must be regarded as having a single precinct (ekūpacāra) and falls under the category of a single-roofed, single-enclosed sleeping place. Referring to such a place, it was said: 'When the sun has set on the fourth day, if a monk lies down while an unordained person is lying down, there is an offense of Pācittiya,' and so forth.

In that Pali text, the Pācittiya offense is incurred merely by lying down. If there are many novices and one monk, there are as many Pācittiya offenses as there are novices. If those novices get up and lie down repeatedly, the monk incurs an offense for each action (payoga) of the novices' lying down. In the case of the monk himself getting up and lying down repeatedly, the monk incurs an offense due to his own action. If there are many monks and one novice, that single novice can cause all the monks to incur an offense. Even by that novice getting up and lying down repeatedly, the monks incur offenses. The same method applies when both monks and novices are many.

Furthermore, in this training rule, the fourfold (catukka) beginning with 'single dwelling' (ekāvāsa) should be understood. A monk who sleeps together with the same unordained person in a single dwelling for three nights incurs an offense daily starting from the fourth day. A monk who sleeps together with various unordained persons in a single dwelling for three nights also incurs it. A monk who sleeps together with the same unordained person in various dwellings for three nights also incurs it. A monk who sleeps together with various unordained persons in various dwellings, even after traveling a hundred yojanas, also incurs an offense daily starting from the fourth day.

This offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya), because of the statement in the Pali, 'Excepting a monk, the rest are called unordained (anupasampanna),' can also occur by sleeping with an animal. The definition of such animals should be understood according to the method stated in the offense of sexual intercourse (methunadhamma). Therefore, if any animal such as a monitor lizard, a cat, or a mongoose enters and sleeps in a monk's dwelling within the same precinct (ekūpacāra), it constitutes sleeping together (sahaseyya).

If, in a mansion built upon pillars with walls not connected to the upper floor, an animal enters through the hollow at the top of a joist (tulā) above the lower wall, sleeps inside the joist, and then leaves through that same hollow...
13:
There is no offense for a monk sleeping on the lower floor of a mansion (pāsāda). If there is a hole in the roof and one enters through that hole, stays inside the roof, and departs through that same hole, an offense is committed by a monk sleeping inside the upper roof in a dwelling with separate precincts (upacāra), but there is no offense for a monk sleeping on the lower floor. If all floors are used by ascending from within the mansion, they constitute a single precinct; in such a case, an offense is committed by one who sleeps anywhere on those floors.

In a dwelling with half-walls built in the style of a market hall, if animals such as pigeons enter and sleep on the rafters where lion-figures and the like are installed, it is indeed an offense. If they sleep within the eaves that extend outside the enclosure, there is no offense. Even if a dwelling has a hundred rooms under a single roof, whether circular or square, if it can be entered through a single common door and all rooms are accessible without separate enclosures for their precincts, then if an unordained person (anupasampanna) sleeps in even one room, an offense is committed by the monks sleeping in all the rooms.

If the rooms are provided with a porch (pamukha), and even if there is a high platform (jagati) without a roof above the porch, a person sleeping on the porch does not cause an offense for the monks sleeping in the rooms. However, if the roof of the porch is connected to the roof of the rooms, a person sleeping on that porch causes an offense for all the monks. Why? Because it is all under one roof and all fully enclosed, for the enclosure of the rooms is indeed the enclosure of that porch. In this same manner, it is stated in the Commentaries that an offense is committed in the four gatehouses of the enclosure of the Lohapāsāda.

As for the statement in the Andhaka Commentary that 'there is no offense in a porch without an enclosure,' this was said in reference to a porch situated on the ground without a platform (jagati). It was said in reference to rows of rooms under a single roof that exist separately in that Andhaka region. The statement in that Andhaka Commentary, 'on the ground without a platform,' does not exist in the ancient Commentaries, nor does it agree with the Pāḷi. Even a platform ten cubits high does not count as an enclosure. Therefore, the statement in that Andhaka Commentary regarding the second training rule, which gives the measurement of a platform and says, 'this is called an enclosure of a single precinct,' should not be accepted. In great mansions (mahāpāsāda) built as single-wing, two-wing, three-wing, or four-wing structures, if it is possible to go everywhere after washing one's feet at a single place and entering, one is not exempt from the offense of communal sleeping (sahaseyya) in those mansions. If the precincts are partitioned in various places, an offense is committed only in the place that shares a single precinct.
14:
If a partition is made in the middle of a plastered pavilion (maṇḍapa) with two doors, and an unordained person sleeps in one section after entering through one door while a monk sleeps in the other section, there is no offense. Even if there is a hole in the partition just large enough for animals like monitor lizards to enter, and monitor lizards sleep in one section, there is no offense. This is because a house does not become a single precinct (ekūpacāra) merely by having a hole.

If a door is installed by cutting through the middle of the partition, it becomes an offense because it is a single precinct. Even if they sleep after closing that door with a door-leaf (kavāṭa), it is still an offense. This is because a house does not become a separate precinct (nānūpacāra) merely by closing a door; a door does not cease to be a door. A door-leaf is made for the purpose of use as desired by closing and opening, not for the purpose of cutting off use. However, if that door is closed again with bricks, it ceases to be a door and remains in the state of having separate precincts as before. There may be a Cetiya hall (cetiyaghara) with a long porch. If there is one door-leaf inside and one outside, and an unordained person is between the two doors while a monk sleeps inside the Cetiya hall, it causes an offense because it is a single precinct.

Regarding such an offense, someone might raise this objection: "This matter of being a single precinct or separate precincts was stated in the Udossita (Kathina) training rule. But in this training rule, it is only stated that 'a sleeping place (seyyā) means fully roofed and fully enclosed, or mostly roofed and mostly enclosed.' A room with a closed door is indeed fully enclosed. Therefore, an offense should only occur when sleeping together inside that room, and there should be no offense when sleeping outside."

That person should be asked: "But why is there an offense for one sleeping outside in a monastery where the door is not closed?" If he replies, "Because the porch is fully roofed along with the room," then he should be asked, "When the room is closed, is the roof destroyed?" He will reply, "It is not destroyed, but the state of the porch being fully enclosed along with the room no longer exists." If asked, "Is the enclosure destroyed?" he will certainly say, "It is not destroyed; the precinct is merely partitioned by the door-leaf." Thus, even after going far in argument, he will eventually return to the state of single precinct and separate precincts.

Furthermore, if the meaning were easily understood by the literal words alone, then because of the words 'fully roofed,' only a dwelling roofed with one of the five types of roofing would be a 'sleeping place,' and not any other. If that were so, there would be no offense in dwellings roofed with wooden planks and the like. Then the very purpose for which the training rule was laid down would be lost. Whether the purpose is lost or not, if one asks, "How can what is not stated be accepted?" who says, "What is not stated should be accepted"? For this was indeed stated in the Aniyata training rules: "A concealed seat means one concealed by a wall or by a door-leaf..."
15:
"It is covered by a mat, or by a curtain, or by a tree, or by a pillar, or by a wall, or by any kind of screen." Therefore, just as in those Aniyata training rules, a place covered by any screen is taken as 'covered', so it should be taken here as well. Thus, whether the dwelling is small or large, connected or unconnected to another dwelling, long, round, square, single-storied, or multi-storied—in all such dwellings sharing a single precinct—it should be understood that an offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya) occurs in a dwelling that is entirely roofed and entirely enclosed, or mostly roofed and mostly enclosed.

Regarding the statement, "In a dwelling half-roofed and half-enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that in cases such as being entirely roofed but only half-enclosed, it is also only an offense of dukkaṭa. However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: "There is a pācittiya offense in a dwelling entirely roofed and mostly enclosed, entirely roofed and half-enclosed, mostly roofed and half-enclosed, entirely enclosed and mostly roofed, entirely enclosed and half-roofed, and mostly enclosed and half-roofed. Together with the pācittiya mentioned in the Pāḷi text, there are seven pācittiya offenses." It is also stated: "There is a dukkaṭa offense in a dwelling entirely roofed and slightly enclosed, mostly roofed and slightly enclosed, entirely enclosed and slightly roofed, and mostly enclosed and slightly roofed. Together with the dukkaṭa mentioned in the Pāḷi text, there are five dukkaṭa offenses."

It is further stated: "There is no offense in a dwelling half-roofed and slightly enclosed, half-enclosed and slightly roofed, or slightly roofed and slightly enclosed. In a dwelling that is entirely roofed but not enclosed at all, it is like the form of a senamba pavilion." By this statement, it should be understood that: "In whatever way the ground base does not count as an enclosure, that way should be noted." The remaining text is clear in its meaning.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the Eḷakaloma training rule: It arises from the body, and from the body and mind; it is an action (kiriya); there is no release through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is a breach of a regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is a bodily action (kāyakamma); it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Fifth Sahaseyya Training Rule.

## 6. Commentary on the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule
In the second Sahaseyya training rule: 'Āvasathāgāraṃ' means a dwelling for guests (a rest house). 'Paññattaṃ hoti' means it has been built and prepared by one desiring merit. 'Yena sā itthī tenupasaṅkami' means she went there after hearing from people that there was a rest house prepared in such and such a place. 'Gandhagandhinī' means she is called 'fragrant' because she possesses the scent of perfumes such as aloeswood and saffron. 'Sāṭakaṃ nikkhipitvā' means she did this thinking, 'Perhaps lust might arise in this monk upon seeing this state of disarray.' 'Okkhipitvā' means casting the eyes downward. 'Accayo' means a fault or offense. 'Maṃ accagamā' means it has overcome and surpassed me (meaning, the offense has been committed). The rest of the explanation should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first training rule. This is the only distinction: in the first training rule, the offense occurs on the fourth day, but in this rule, it occurs even on the first day. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) if one sleeps together with a female yakkha or peta who has a visible form, or with a female animal that is a base for sexual intercourse. With other females, there is no offense. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are the same as the first rule.

## The Sixth Sahaseyya Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Dhamma-desanā Training Rule
In the seventh training rule: 'Gharaṇī' means the mistress of the house. 'Nivesanadvāre' means at the main door of the house. 'Gharasuṇhā' means the daughter-in-law in that house. 'Āvasathadvāre' means at the door of the room. 'Vissaṭṭhena' means with a voice that is well-emitted. 'Vivaṭena' means with a voice that is well-manifested and open, not concealed. 'Dhammo desetabbō' means should not this Dhamma, consisting of the Refuges, the Precepts, and so on, be taught? 'Aññātuṃ' means for the sake of understanding. 'Viññunā purisavigghena' means by a wise man, one who is a real human being, not a yakkha, a peta, or an animal.

There is no offense for one who teaches much Dhamma to a woman who is staying with a wise man. 'Cha-pañca-vācāhi' means there is no offense for one who teaches with five or six sentences. In this context, one line (pāda) of a verse is considered one sentence (vācā); the measure of speech should be understood in this way throughout. If one wishes to teach the Commentary, the Dhammapada, or stories such as the Jātakas, only five or six sentences...
17:
It should be taught. A monk teaching along with the Pali text should teach no more than six words: one word from the Pali and five from the Commentary. All the various details mentioned in the Padasodhamma training rule are the same in this training rule as well. The phrase 'teaches at that moment' means he teaches at that very instant. Alternatively, the locative case 'tasmiṃ' is used in the sense of the dative (sampadāna), meaning 'he teaches to her.' 'To another woman' means teaching one woman and then teaching another who arrives later. In this way, sitting in a single seat, he can teach even a hundred thousand women.

In the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, it is stated: 'If he says to women sitting together, "I will teach each of you one verse; listen to that," and then teaches, there is no offense.' One should intend and inform them beforehand that he will teach each person one verse; it should not be done after teaching. Regarding 'asking a question and answering when asked': if a woman asks, 'Venerable sir, what meaning does the Dīgha Nikāya show?' and the monk, being thus asked, teaches the entire Dīgha Nikāya, there is no offense. The remaining terms are clear in meaning.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the Padasodhamma training rule: it arises from speech, and from speech and mind; it is action and non-action (kiriya-akiriya); it is not perception-release (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is a breach of a man-made rule (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Seventh Training Rule on Teaching Dhamma (Dhamma-desanā-sikkhāpada).

## 8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Telling the Truth (Bhūtārocana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

Regarding the story of the eighth training rule, everything to be said is according to the method already stated in the commentary on the fourth Pārājika. The difference is this: there, they reported what was false; here, they report what is true (bhūta). Even though it was true, only worldlings (puthujjanas) reported it, not Noble Ones (ariyas). For Noble Ones, there is no speech connected with requisites and gains. When worldlings spoke of their virtues, other Noble Ones did not forbid them, and they enjoyed the requisites that arose from such talk, not knowing they arose for that reason.

In the passage beginning 'Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,' it should be understood that the monks who spoke of the excellence of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) reported it. When asked, 'Monks, is it true?' they all—both worldlings and Noble Ones—acknowledged, 'It is true, Blessed One.' This is because the true superhuman state exists not only in Noble Ones but also in worldlings. Then...
18:
Because Noble Ones (ariyas) were mixed among them, the Blessed One did not say 'worthless men' (mogha-purisā), but said, 'Monks, how can you...' and spoke the words beginning with 'for the sake of the belly' (udara-kāraṇā). In that passage, the meaning is: because the Noble Ones, hearing the words of others such as 'Venerable sir, we hear that this noble one is a stream-enterer,' were asked by faithful people, and since the training rule had not yet been laid down, they did not see any fault. With pure hearts, they acknowledged their own and others' special attainments. While they acknowledged this, other worldlings (puthujjanas) spoke of the excellence of superhuman states for the sake of the belly to obtain alms-food. Although the Noble Ones enjoyed that food with pure hearts, it was as if the excellence of superhuman states was spoken for the sake of the belly. Therefore, using a method that includes everyone, he said, 'Monks, how can you speak to laypeople of one another’s excellence of superhuman states for the sake of the belly?' The rest is just like the story of the fourth Pārājika.

In the word-analysis (vibhaṅga) of the training rule, the only difference is that in the fourth Pārājika, it is a Pārājika and a Thullaccaya, whereas here, because it is true, it is a Pācittiya and a Dukkaṭa. The rest is as previously stated.

'Tells the truth to one who is ordained' is said with reference only to superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). At the time of approaching Parinibbāna, or in the interval before Parinibbāna, it is allowable for a monk who is being strongly urged to tell the truth to an ordained person. However, it is allowable to tell even an unordained person (anupasampanna) about the virtues of learning (suta), study (pariyatti), and virtue (sīla). There is no offense for the first offender (ādikammika). The phrase 'to an insane person' is not mentioned here. Why? Because for those who have attained right view (Noble Ones), there is no insanity or mental derangement. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is analyzed: 'A jhāna-attainer might become insane when the jhāna is lost; even for such a person, it should not be said that there is no offense for telling the truth, because the true superhuman state no longer exists.' The rest is clear.

This Bhūtārocana (telling the truth) arises from three origins not mentioned before: from the body, from speech, and from both body and speech. It is action (kiriya); it is not perception-release (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is a breach of a man-made rule (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is bodily action and verbal action; it involves two types of consciousness (wholesome and indeterminate) and two types of feeling (pleasant and neutral).

## The Eighth Training Rule on Telling the Truth (Bhūtārocana-sikkhāpada).

## 9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reporting Gross Offenses

In the ninth training rule, regarding the Pali passage, "Gross offenses (duṭṭhullā) are the four Pārājikas and the thirteen Saṅghādisesas," the Commentaries (Atthakathās) state that the Pārājikas are mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word 'gross' (for the purpose of extracting all possible meanings), but in this training rule, only the Saṅghādisesa is intended. In this regard, there is this investigation of the Pali and the Commentary—if a Pācittiya offense did not occur for a monk who reports a Pārājika, then just as the word "ordained" (upasampanna) is common to both monks and nuns, yet in a training rule where nuns are not intended, those other than monks are called "unordained" (anupasampanna); similarly, although the word "gross" (duṭṭhulla) is common to both Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa in this training rule, if Pārājika were not intended, it should have been taught only as "Gross offenses are the thirteen Saṅghādisesas."

If it were taught in that way, the thought might arise: "A person who has fallen into a Pārājika has fallen away from monkhood; therefore, a monk who reports his offense incurs a Dukkhaṭa (wrongdoing)." If this were the case, a monk who reviles him would also incur a Dukkhaṭa, but in fact, he incurs only a Pācittiya. For it is said: "A person is impure having committed one or another Pārājika offense; if another, knowing him to be impure, obtains permission and speaks with the intention to revile, he incurs an offense of Omasavāda Pācittiya" (Pārājika, 389). When the Pali is investigated in this way, it is seen that a monk who reports a Pārājika also incurs only a Pācittiya. Even if it is so seen, because it is stated in all Commentaries, only the Teachers of the Commentaries (Atthakathācariyas) are the authority here; no other investigation is an authority. As was said previously: "The Buddha taught the Dhamma and Vinaya; his sons knew them exactly as they were," and so on. Only the Teachers of the Commentaries know the intention of the Buddha.

This point should also be understood by this method. It is said, "except with the authorization (sammuti) of the monks." The Buddha allowed reporting with the authorization of the monks for the sake of future restraint, so that such an offense would not be committed again. It was not allowed for the sake of merely exposing the monk's faults (avaṇṇa), nor for the sake of prohibiting his standing in the Sasana. For a monk who has already fallen into a Pārājika, there is no such thing as monkhood to be maintained by not falling into such an offense again. Therefore, what is said in the Commentaries—"Pārājikas are mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word 'gross', but in this training rule, only the Saṅghādisesa is intended"—is indeed well said.
20:
Regarding the Pali passages such as "There is a monk's authorization (bhikkhu-sammuti) ending with the offense," this monk's authorization does not appear in any other Pali text. However, because it is mentioned in this training rule, it should be understood that when a monk is seen to frequently fall into offenses, the Sangha, out of a desire for that monk's welfare, thinking, "This monk, through shame and fear of others, will practice restraint in the future," performs the act by requesting three times (through an apalokana-kamma).

In the phrase "If he reports a non-gross offense, he incurs a Dukkhaṭa," a monk who reports any of the five groups of offenses incurs a Dukkhaṭa. In the Mahāpaccari Commentary, however, it is said that a monk who reports a Pārājika offense also incurs only a Dukkhaṭa. Regarding the "misconduct" (ajjhācāra), whether gross or non-gross, of an unordained person (anupasampanna), the first five training rules are called gross misconduct; the remaining training rules are called non-gross misconduct. However, it is said that only his emission of semen, physical contact, gross speech, and desiring sexual intimacy are called misconduct (ajjhācāra).

"Reports the basis (vatthu)" means there is no offense for a monk who speaks thus: "This person has reached the emission of semen, has reached gross conduct, has reached the desire for sexual intimacy, has reached physical contact." In the phrase "reports the offense (āpatti)," if he says, "This person has reached a Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkhaṭa, or Dubbhāsita offense," there is no offense. However, an offense occurs only for a monk who reports the offense in connection with the basis, in the manner: "This person, having caused the emission of semen, has reached a Saṅghādisesa offense," and so on. The rest of the text is clear.

Three origins (samuṭṭhāna): it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, or from body, speech, and mind. It is an action (kiriya), it is a release through perception (saññāvimokkha), it is with intention (sacittaka), it is worldly fault (lokavajja), it is bodily action (kāyakamma), it is verbal action (vacīkamma), it is unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and it has painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## Ninth: Training Rule on Reporting Gross Offenses.

## 10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Digging the Soil

In the tenth training rule, the terms "natural soil (jātā pathavī) and unnatural soil (ajātā pathavī)" show natural earth and non-natural earth. In the terms such as "appapāsāṇa" (few stones), the meaning should be understood as "in this soil, stones are few." Among those terms like appapāsāṇa, stones larger than the size of a fist should be known as "pāsāṇa" (stones). Stones the size of a fist should be known as "sakkharā" (gravel). "Kathalā" refers to pieces of potshards.
21:
Stones larger than the size of a fist should be known as '*pāsāṇa*'. Stones the size of a fist should be known as '*sakkharā*' (gravel). '*Kathalā*' refers to pieces of broken potsherds. '*Marumbā*' refers to grit (crushed stone) often found on mats. '*Vālikā*' is simply sand. '*Yebuyyena paṃsukā*' (mostly dusty earth) refers to earth where two out of three parts are dust and one part is stones and so on.

'*Adaḍḍhāpi*' (unburnt earth) refers to earth that has not been burnt by such means as placing on a tripod, firing alms-bowls, or the firing process of potters. This earth does not exist separately but should be understood as one of the types such as *suddhapaṃsu* (pure dust/soil). '*Yebuyyena sakkharā*' refers to earth that is mostly gravel. It is heard that in the region of Hatthikucchi, having ordered a basketful of earth to be brought and washed in a basin, and knowing that the earth was mostly gravel, the monks themselves dug a pond. The two terms in the middle, '*appapaṃsu appamattikā*', are included within the group of five beginning with *pāsāṇa*. This group of five merely shows the distinction between those two.

In the context of 'If one digs oneself, one commits a *pācittiya* offense,' it should be understood that a *pācittiya* offense is committed with every stroke of the hoe. If a person is commanded once and digs the whole day, only one *pācittiya* offense is committed by the one who gave the command. However, if the person commanded is lazy and must be commanded repeatedly, a *pācittiya* offense is committed by the monk who gives the command for every word spoken to make him dig. This is the commentary on the Pali text.

This is the decision outside the Pali text (*pāḷimuttakavinicchaya*): To say "Dig a pond" is permissible. Since it is called a 'pond' only after it has been dug, this is a permissible expression (*kappiyavohāra*). The same method applies to saying "Dig a reservoir, a tank, or a pit." However, it is not permissible to specify the location by saying "Dig this spot" or "Dig a pond at this spot." To say "Dig a tuber" or "Dig a root" without specifying is permissible. To say "Dig this vine" or "Dig a tuber or a root at this spot" is not permissible.

For monks cleaning a pond, it is permissible to remove thin mud that can be scooped up with pots. It is not permissible to remove thick mud. In mud that is dried and cracked due to the sun's heat, it is permissible to remove only that mud which is detached from the ground below. If a water film (*udakappappaṭaka*) forms where water flows and it moves due to the wind, it is permissible to remove it.

If the bank of a pond etc. breaks and falls near the water, if it is a period of less than four months since it was rained upon, it is permissible to cut or break it. If it exceeds four months...
22:
...it is not permissible. However, if it falls into the water itself, it is permissible because the rain falls only on the water surface, even if it has rained for more than four months. Monks dig a cistern (*soṇḍi*) on a rock surface; if fine dust first falls there and that dust is rained upon, it becomes classified as *akappiyapaṭhavī* (*jātapaṭhavī*) after the lapse of four months. When the water is exhausted, monks cleaning the cistern must not destroy that earth. If it is first filled with water and dust falls later, it is permissible to destroy that earth. This is because even if it rains on that water-filled cistern, the rain falls only on the water. If there is fine dust on a rock surface and it sticks due to a drizzle, it is not permissible to destroy that dust after the lapse of four months.

If an anthill has arisen in an unworked cave, it is permissible to destroy it as one pleases. If it arises in the open, it is permissible only if it has been rained upon for less than four months. The same method applies to termite-mud found on trees and so on. The same method also applies to worm castings, earth from mouse holes, mud in cow tracks, and so on.

'*Gokaṇṭaka*' refers to mud cut by the hooves of cows. If it is connected to the ground at the bottom, it is not permissible even if it has been there for only one day. The same method applies to one who takes a clod of earth cut by a ploughshare in a ploughed area. There is an old dwelling that is either roofless or has a ruined roof; if it has been rained upon for more than four months, it becomes classified as *jātapaṭhavī*. Other remaining materials such as roofing tiles or rafters etc. may be taken with the perception: "I am taking a tile, I am taking a rafter, a wall-base, a plank, or a stone pillar." If soil falls along with those tiles etc., there is no offense. But for one who takes wall-soil, there is an offense. If one takes soil that has not been rained upon, there is no offense.

There is a heap of earth inside a house; after that heap has been rained upon for even one day, they roof the house. If the whole heap is wet, it becomes *jātapaṭhavī* after the lapse of four months. If only the upper part is wet and the inside is not wet, it is permissible to have the wet part removed by *kappiyakārakas* using permissible speech, and then use the remaining earth as one pleases. Only earth that has become a single mass by being wetted with water is *jātapaṭhavī*; other earth is not *jātapaṭhavī*.
23:
In the open, there may be a clay wall; if it has been rained upon for more than four months, it is reckoned as natural earth (jātapathavī). It is allowable to touch and take the dust clinging to that clay wall with a wet hand. If it is a brick wall, it mostly stands in the place of potsherds; therefore, it is allowable to break it as one pleases. It is not allowable to take a pavilion post standing in the open by shaking it this way and that, thereby breaking the earth; it is only allowable to pull it straight up. This same rule applies to a monk taking other dry trees or dry stumps. For the sake of construction work (navakamma), monks go about lifting stones or logs with sticks and rolling them; in such rolling, the earth is broken. If they roll them with a pure mind, there is no offense. However, if they have the intention to break the earth under that pretext, there is an offense. This same rule applies to monks dragging branches etc., and to monks splitting wood on the ground.

It is not allowable to strike or insert anything such as bones, needles, or thorns into the earth. It is also not allowable to urinate with the thought, "I will break the earth with the force of the stream of urine"; if it breaks while doing so, there is an offense. It is not allowable to scrub with a broom with the thought, "I will make the uneven ground level"; one must sweep only for the sake of performing the duty (vatta). Some strike the ground with a staff, or scratch it with the big toe, or walk back and forth repeatedly breaking the earth with the thought, "I will show the place for the walking meditation"; all such actions are not allowable. However, it is allowable to walk with a pure mind while performing the recluse's practice to arouse energy. Some rub their hands on the ground with the thought, "I will wash my hands"; this is not allowable. Without rubbing, it is allowable to place a wet hand on the ground to take dust. Some monks with itchy skin or scabies rub their limbs against broken banks etc.; this is not allowable.

"Digs or causes to dig" means digging oneself or causing another to dig, even with the big toe or a broomstick. "Breaks or causes to break" means breaking oneself or causing another to break, even by pouring water. "Burns or causes to burn" means burning oneself or causing another to burn, even while baking a bowl. In as many places as one gives fire or causes fire to be given, there are that many Pācittiya offenses. Even a monk baking a bowl should bake it only in a place where it was baked before. It is not allowable to place fire on earth that has not been burnt. However, it is allowable to place fire on top of the shard used for baking a bowl. On top of the wood...
24:
(If one) places (fire on firewood), and that fire, while burning that wood, goes and burns the earth, it is not allowable. This same rule applies to brick shards etc. Even in that case, it is only allowable to place (fire) on top of the bricks etc. Why? Because those bricks etc. are not fuel (anupādāna). Indeed, they do not come under the designation of fuel for fire. It is also not allowable to give fire to dry stumps, dry trees, etc. However, if one gives it with the thought, 'I will extinguish it before it reaches the earth,' it is allowable. If later one is unable to extinguish it, it is no offense because it is beyond one's power. A monk carrying a grass torch who drops it on the ground when his hand is burnt commits no offense. It is stated in the Mahāpaccari that it is allowable to make a fire by giving fuel only at the spot where the fire fell. It is also stated therein that it is allowable to destroy all the ground that has been reached by the heat of the burnt earth. If a monk who does not know how to make fire produces fire with a fire-drill and, lifting it with his hand, asks, 'What should I do?', he should be told, 'Make it flame.' If he says, 'My hand is burning,' he should be told, 'Do it in such a way that your hand does not burn.' He should not be told, 'Drop it on the ground.' If he drops it because his hand is burning, there is no offense because he did not drop it with the thought, 'I will burn the earth.' It is stated in the Kurundī that it is allowable to make a fire at the spot where the fire fell.

In the phrases 'no offense for one who knows this' (anāpatti imaṃ jānāti) etc., the meaning should be understood thus: 'Know the hole for this pillar,' 'Know the large clay lump,' 'Know the clay mixed with chaff,' 'Give the large clay lump,' 'Give the clay mixed with chaff,' 'Bring the clay,' 'Bring the dust,' 'There is a need for clay,' 'There is a need for dust,' 'Make the hole for this pillar allowable (kappiya),' 'Make this clay allowable,' 'Make this dust allowable'—thus should the meaning be understood.

'Unintentional' (asañcicca) means if the earth is broken while rolling stones, logs, etc., or while going along striking with a staff; because it was not destroyed with the perception and volition 'I will break it with that staff etc.', it is called unintentional breaking. For a monk who breaks it unintentionally in this way, there is no offense. 'Unmindful' (asatiyā) means if one stands scratching the earth with a big toe or a staff while one's mind is on another object, speaking about something with someone; for a monk who scratches or breaks it unmindfully in this way, there is no offense. 'Not knowing' (ajānantassa) means if one destroys earth that has been rained on and covered inside a house, not knowing it is 'unallowable earth' (akappiya-pathavī) but perceiving it as 'allowable earth' (kappiya-pathavī); or if one does not (know) 'I am digging, breaking, or burning'...
25:
He knows (that he is destroying the earth); or he places a spade and so forth merely for the sake of securing it; or while his hand is burning, he drops the fire; for one who does not know in this way, there is no offense. The rest of the words are clear.

This training rule arises from three origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is endowed with action (kiriya), release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), consciousness (sacittaka), being a breach of a regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāya-kamma), verbal action (vacī-kamma), three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Tenth Training Rule on Digging the Earth is finished.

## The First Chapter on Lying is finished in its explanatory order.

## 2. Bhūtagāma Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Bhūtagāma Training Rule

In the first training rule of the Bhūtagāma Chapter—"Anādiyanto" means not paying attention to her words (and continuing to cut).

"Dārakassa bāhuṃ ākoṭesi" means that being unable to restrain the raised axe from striking, he cut the arm of the young deity at the very base of the shoulder while the child was sleeping in the divine mansion situated in the tree, which was obtained from the Great King Vessavaṇa and was beyond the range of human vision.

In the passage beginning with "Na kho metaṃ patirūpaṃ," this is the summary of the commentary: It is said that on the full-moon and new-moon days in the Himālaya mountains, there is an assembly of deities. In that assembly, they ask about the tree-duty (rukkhadhamma): "Do you abide in the tree-duty or not?" What is called tree-duty is the absence of anger in the mind of a tree deity while the tree is being cut. In that assembly, a deity who does not abide in the tree-duty is not allowed to enter. Thus, that deity saw this disadvantage caused by not abiding in the tree-duty, and in accordance with the Dhamma teaching previously heard in the presence of the Blessed One, she recollected the former conduct of the Tathāgata during his time as the Chaddanta elephant and so forth. Because of that, the thought occurred to her: "This is not proper for me... I should not deprive (the monk of life)."

As for the thought, "What if I were to inform the Blessed One of this matter?"—it occurred to that deity as she reflected: "This monk has a father (the Buddha); surely the Blessed One, having heard of this transgression of his, will establish a boundary and prescribe a training rule."

"Sacajja tvaṃ devate" means "Deity, if you today (had killed that monk)."

"Pasaveyyāsi" means you would have produced or generated (demerit). Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, in order to make that deity understand, said:

As a charioteer restrains a moving chariot from going where it should not,
He who can truly restrain arisen anger,
That person I call a charioteer;
Others who cannot restrain anger are merely holders of the reins.

At the end of the verse, that deity was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Then, the Blessed One, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the assembled audience, spoke this verse: "Yo uppatitaṃ... purāṇaṃ."

As a snake-doctor removes spreading snake venom with medicines,
That monk who can remove arisen anger,
As a snake sheds its old skin,
That monk can abandon the five lower fetters.

Of those two verses, the first verse is recorded in the Dhammapada. The second verse is recorded in the Sutta Nipāta. The background story, however, should be noted as being recorded in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Then, while the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma, he reflected on the dwelling place for that deity and, seeing a suitable place, said, "Deity, go..."
26:
"Whoever restrains arisen anger like a rolling chariot,
That person I call a charioteer; other people are merely holders of the reins."
(Dhammapada 222). He spoke this verse. At the end of the verse, that deity was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Again, the Blessed One, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the assembled audience, said—

"That monk who removes arisen anger as one removes spreading snake venom with medicines,
That monk abandons the 'hither and the farther shore' (the fetters), as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin."
(Sutta Nipāta 1). He spoke this verse.

Of those two verses, the first verse was recited in the Dhammapada, and the second in the Sutta Nipāta; the story, however, was recited in the Vinaya Piṭaka. After that, while the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma, he reflected on the dwelling place of that deity and, seeing a suitable place, said: "Deity, go; in such and such a place there is a vacant tree; go to that tree." That tree, it is said, was not in the region of Āḷavī, but was a tree within the enclosure of the Jetavana monastery. The deity who had possessed that tree had passed away (cuta); therefore, it was called a "vacant tree."

From that time on, that deity, having received protection and honor from the Fully Enlightened One, became an attendant of the Buddha. When there was an assembly of deities, if powerful deities arrived, other deities of lesser power had to retreat as far as the Great Ocean and the Cakravāḷa mountains. This deity, however, could listen to the Dhamma while sitting in her own dwelling place. Even when monks asked questions in the first watch of the night, and deities asked questions in the middle watch, she could hear all of that while sitting in that very place. Even the Four Great Kings, when coming to attend upon the Blessed One and then leaving, would only depart after seeing and greeting that deity.

In the term "Bhūtagāma-pātabyatāya":
They are called "bhūta" because they have come into being and have grown; the meaning is that they are "bhūta" because of the senses of being born, growing, having been born, and having been grown. "Gāma" means a heap or a collection. Because it is a collection of living beings (plants), it is called "bhūtagāma." Or, the living beings themselves are the collection, thus "bhūtagāma." This is a designation for green grass, trees, and so forth that are established in the earth. "Pātabyatā" is the state of being used; the meaning is the state of being used as one pleases by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth. In that term "bhūtagāma-pātabyatāya," the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimittattha); the meaning is that a pācittiya offense is incurred because of the cause of cutting and so forth of living plants (bhūtagāma).
27:
Now, wishing to show the classification of that bhūtagāma, he said: "Bhūtagāmo nāma pañca bījazātāni" and so forth. In that Pali, "as to bhūtagāma" means that when there is a seed, bhūtagāma exists; to show that seed, the Commentaries say he said "five kinds of seeds." Even so, this does not agree with the Pali passage "whatever others there are that grow from the root," etc. For root-seeds and so forth do not grow in the roots; rather, those plants arising in the roots are said to be produced from seeds. Therefore, the explanation here should be understood thus: "Bhūtagāmo nāma" is the term to be analyzed. "Pañca" is the delimitation of its classification. "Bījazātāni" is the indication of the delimited states. Its meaning is: "born from seeds, thus bījazāta"; this is a designation for trees and so forth. Alternatively: they are both seeds and things produced (having sprouted leaves and roots), thus bījazāta. By this method, ginger (siṅgivera) and so forth, which have sprouted leaves and roots and are placed in moist sand, etc., are included.

Now, to show those seeds from which trees and so forth are born and thus called bījazāta, he said "mūlabījaṃ" and so forth. The list of them is clear. In the detailed explanation, in the passage "whatever others there are that grow from the root, arise from the root," the seed is shown by the plant produced from the seed. Therefore, the meaning here should be seen thus: whatever thickets, creepers, trees, etc., grow and arise in roots such as the roots of potatoes (āluva), water chestnuts (seruka), red lotuses (rattuppala), blue lotuses (kuvalaya), white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), white water-lilies (kumuda), kanda, trumpet flowers (pāṭali), etc.; both the root in which those thickets, creepers, and trees grow and arise, and the turmeric (haliddā), etc., directly mentioned in the Pali—all this is called root-seed (mūlabīja). This same method applies to stem-seeds (khandhabīja) and so forth. Herein, among the "whatever others" stem-seeds, the ambaṭaka, indasāla, nuhī, pālibhaddaka, kaṇikāra, etc., are stem-seeds. The amūlavallī, caturassavallī, kaṇavīra, etc., are joint-seeds (phalubīja). The makaci, sumana, jayasumana, etc., are bud-seeds (aggabīja). Mango (amba), rose-apple (jambu), jackfruit (panasa), sixty-day rice (saṭṭhika), etc., are to be understood as seed-seeds (bījabīja).

Now, regarding the training rule stated as "There is a pācittiya for the destruction of vegetation (bhūtagāma)," wishing to show the distinction between offense and non-offense according to perception, and the distinction of destruction (pātabyatā), he said "bīje bījasaññī" and so forth. Therein, just as in passages like "he eats the boiled rice of sāli rice," the rice of sāli grains is called "sāli rice," so too, the bhūtagāma produced from a seed is called "seed" (bīja).
28:
As for what is stated in the Sutta passages such as "He refrains from the destruction of seeds and vegetation (bījagāma-bhūtagāma)," a seed that has been made free from bhūtagāma (by picking from a tree, etc.) is an object for an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Or alternatively, connecting it with the opening term of the word-analysis (vibhaṅga) of the training rule, "bhūtagāmo nāma," the meaning should be understood thus: whatever seed is called bhūtagāma, if one, perceiving that bhūtagāma-seed as a seed, cuts it himself or has another cut it with a knife, etc.; or breaks it himself or has another break it with a stone, etc.; or burns it himself or has another burn it by applying fire—there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, taking the meaning as it is literally stated, one should not say there is a pācittiya for the destruction, such as cutting, of a seed that is dissociated from bhūtagāma (it is only a dukkaṭa).

This is the decision herein: For one who destroys bhūtagāma, there is a pācittiya. For one who destroys the five kinds of bījagāma that are dissociated from bhūtagāma, there is a dukkaṭa. This bījagāma-bhūtagāma exists as water-based and land-based types. Among those two, the water-based type includes all kinds of moss (sevāla), whether with leaves or without leaves, such as mustard-seed sized moss and sesame-seed sized moss, down to the water-crust (udakapappaṭaka); these should be known as "bhūtagāma." The water-crust is hard and rough-colored on top, and soft and blue-colored underneath. Among those mosses, if the root of a moss descends and is established in the earth, its location is the earth. If it moves on the water, its location is the water.

If one destroys moss established in the earth in any place, or uproots it and moves it to another place, there is a pācittiya. For moss moving on the water, there is a pācittiya only if one destroys it. However, it is allowable to push it aside with the hands here and there in order to bathe, because the entire water is its location. Therefore, by merely doing this, it is not considered moved to another location. But it is not allowable to intentionally lift it out of the water without water; it is allowable to lift it out with water and put it back into the water. If it comes out through the hole of a water-filter, one should use that water only after making it allowable (kappiya). For one who pulls water-creepers or grasses such as blue lotuses and red lotuses out of the water, or destroys them right there, there is a pācittiya. If one destroys creepers or grasses uprooted by others, there is a dukkaṭa. For those uprooted things are included under bījagāma. Even moss the size of a sesame or mustard seed, if lifted from the water and not yet withered, is included under bud-seeds (aggabīja).
29:
In the commentaries such as the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "Waterweeds called ananta, water-sesame (kantilaba) the size of a sesame seed, water-scum (udakapappaṭaka), etc., are grounds for an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." In that statement, the reason is not seen. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated: "Because it is not a complete bhūtagāma, it is a dukkaṭa." That statement also does not agree with the Pāḷi and the Commentaries. The reason is that it is taught that for bhūtagāma there is a pācittiya offence, and for bījagāma there is a dukkaṭa offence. A third category called "incomplete bhūtagāma" (asampunnabhūtagāma) appears neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentaries.
