If it is said that this incomplete bhūtagāma is included in bījagāma, that statement is also inappropriate. This is because such a bījagāma is not the root of a bhūtagāma. Furthermore, this characteristic: "Between a heavy offence (garuka) and a light offence (lahuka), one should stand on the side of the heavy," is a characteristic of the Vinaya.

## Regarding Bījagāma and Bhūtagāma situated on land -
There are green stumps remaining from trees that have been cut. Among those stumps, the stumps of trees such as the kakudha, karañja, piyaṅgu, and panasa (jackfruit) grow upwards; such a stump is included under bhūtagāma. The stumps of trees such as the palmyra palm and coconut do not grow upwards; such a stump is included under bījagāma. However, the stump of a banana tree that has not yet fruited is included under bhūtagāma, while the stump of a banana tree that has fruited is included under bījagāma. As long as a fruited banana tree still has green leaves, it is included only under bhūtagāma; the same applies to a fruited bamboo. When it starts to dry up from the tip, then it falls under the category of bījagāma. Under which bījagāma is it included? It is included under phalubījagāma (propagation by joints). What grows from that dried banana or bamboo? Nothing grows. If something were to grow, it would be included only under bhūtagāma. Trees such as the indasāla are cut and made into a pile. Even if branches the size of a cubit (ratana) emerge from the logs in the pile, they are included only under bījagāma. If those logs are planted in the ground for the purpose of a pavilion post, a fence, or for climbing vines, and both roots and leaves emerge, they once again come under the designation of bhūtagāma. However, if only roots or only leaves emerge, they are included only under bījagāma.

Any seeds whatsoever, whether placed in the ground, kept watered, or placed in moist soil in a potsherd etc.—all those seeds, even after only roots or only leaves have emerged, are still just seeds (bīja). Even if roots and a sprout above have emerged, as long as the sprout is not yet green, they are still just seeds. When the leaves of beans etc. have emerged, or when the sprout of grain etc. becomes green and takes on the color of a dark green leaf, they are included under bhūtagāma. In the case of palmyra seeds etc., first a root like a boar's tusk emerges. Even after that root has emerged, as long as the leaf-bud above has not yet emerged, it is still just bījagāma. Having pierced the husk of a coconut, a sprout like an ivory pin...
30:
The root of palm seeds and the like first emerges like a pig's tusk. Even after the root has emerged, as long as the leaf-bud (shoot) has not yet appeared above, it is still considered bījagāma (seed-group). When a sprout emerges from a coconut shell like an ivory pin, as long as the dark leaf-bud resembling a deer's horn has not yet formed, it is still bījagāma. If such a leaf-bud has appeared even before the root has emerged, it is included under rootless bhūtagāma (plant-group).

Mango seeds and the like should be determined in the same way as grain plants. Whether it is a parasitic plant (vandākā) or any other unspecified plant growing on and covering a tree, that tree is the base for those parasites. If one destroys those parasites or removes them from that tree, one commits a pācittiya offense. There is a type of rootless creeper that winds around forest bushes like a ring; the same judgment applies to this creeper.

Dark algae or moss often grow on house porches, walls, and pagodas. As long as two or three leaves have not yet appeared, it is included under aggabīja (propagation by top-growth). Once leaves have appeared, it becomes a basis for a pācittiya offense. Therefore, it is not proper to apply plaster in such places. However, it is allowable to apply a coat of oil (paint) over plaster applied by an unordained person (anupasampanna). If dry moss remains during the summer, it is allowable to rub and remove it with a broom or similar tool. Moss on the outside of water pots and the like is a basis for a dukkaṭa offense. Moss on the inside is negligible (abbohārika). Mold on tooth-sticks, cakes, etc., is also negligible. Thus it was said: "If a wall treated with red ochre becomes moldy, it should be wiped gently with a cloth moistened and wrung out."

Stone-scum, stone-moss, stone-lichen, and the like, which lack a green color and have no leaves, are bases for dukkaṭa offenses. A mushroom is a basis for a dukkaṭa offense as long as it is in the bud stage. From the time it blooms, it is negligible. However, a monk who takes a mushroom from a living tree commits a pācittiya offense because it involves damaging the tree bark. The same rule applies to peeling off the outer bark of a tree. There is no offense for a monk who takes the bark of trees like the indasāla or kudha that has already detached from the tree. It is allowable to take resin (niyyāsa) that has detached from the tree or is stuck to a dry tree. It is not allowable to take it from a living tree. The same rule applies to lacquer (lākhā). A monk who shakes a tree to make yellow leaves or mature flowers like the kaṇikāra fall commits a pācittiya offense. The same rule applies to a monk who, out of playfulness, carves letters on the soft trunks of trees like the indasāla or nuhī, or on the palm leaves growing on those trees.

It is allowable to bend a branch for novices (sāmaṇeras) while they are picking flowers. However, one should not scent drinking water with flowers obtained by such bending. A monk who wishes to scent drinking water should encourage a novice to pick them. One should not bend a branch with fruit for oneself to eat. One should encourage a novice to take the fruit. It is not allowable to pull a bush or creeper together with novices who are uprooting it. However, to encourage them, it is allowable to hold the tip as if pulling, without actually pulling. If one takes a branch of a tree capable of sprouting for the purpose of a fly-whisk etc. without having it made allowable (kappiya), or if one scratches the bark or leaf even with a fingernail, one commits a dukkaṭa offense. The same rule applies to fresh ginger and the like. If roots emerge from ginger that has been made allowable and kept in a cool place, it is allowable to cut the upper part.
31:
It is allowable to bend a branch for novices (sāmaṇeras) while they are picking flowers. However, one should not scent drinking water with those flowers (obtained by bending the branch for oneself). A monk who wishes to scent drinking water must encourage a novice to pick them. One must not bend a branch with fruit for oneself to eat. One must encourage a novice to take the fruit. It is not allowable to pull any bush or creeper together with novices who are uprooting it. However, to encourage them, it is allowable to hold the tip as if pulling, without actually pulling, as if showing them how to pull.

If one takes a branch of a tree capable of sprouting for the purpose of a fly-whisk etc. without having it made allowable (kappiya), a monk who scratches the bark or leaf of that tree even with a fingernail commits a dukkaṭa offense. The same rule applies to fresh ginger (singivera) and the like. If roots emerge from ginger that has been made allowable and kept in a cool place, it is allowable to cut the upper part. If a sprout emerges, it is allowable to cut the lower part. If both roots and sprouts have emerged, it is no longer allowable to cut.

Regarding "cuts or causes to be cut," this includes cutting grass oneself or causing another to cut it while sweeping the ground, even with a broomstick, with the intention to cut the grass. Regarding "breaks or causes to be broken," this includes intentionally breaking creepers or grass with one's feet while walking on a path, thinking "let what is to be cut be cut, let what is to be broken be broken, I will show the walking path," or causing another to break them. If a grass or creeper breaks while one is making a knot, even making the knot is not allowable.

Monks should not hammer wooden brackets (dārumakkaṭaka) or tie thorns to palm trees etc. to prevent thieves from climbing. If the wooden bracket merely touches the tree without pressing against it, it is allowable. It is allowable to speak without specification, saying "Cut the tree, cut the creeper, uproot the tuber or the root." However, it is not allowable to speak with specification, saying "Cut this tree," etc. Even using a name, such as "Cut, break, or uproot the mango tree, the square-creeper, the potato tuber, the muñja grass, or the bark of such-and-forth tree," is considered non-specific and is thus allowable. Only a statement like "this mango tree," which points it out, is called specific; such a statement is not allowable.

Regarding "cooks or causes to be cooked," this includes cooking oneself or causing another to cook by intentionally placing fire on top of grass etc., wishing to bake an alms-bowl.
32:
The entire discussion on "let [him] cook" should be understood according to the method already stated in the training rule on digging the earth (Pathavīkhaṇana-sikkhāpada). However, without specifying [particular items], it is allowable to say, "Cook mung beans, cook black grams," and so forth. It is not allowable to say, "Cook these mung beans, cook these black grams," in such a [specific] manner.

In the sections on non-offence (anāpatti-vāra) such as "know this root-medicine," the meaning should be understood as follows: "Know this root-medicine; give this root or leaf; bring this tree or vine; there is a need for this flower, fruit, or leaf; make this tree, vine, or fruit allowable (kappiya)." By saying this much, one has effected the release from the state of living plants (bhūtagāma-parimocana). However, a monk who wishes to consume it must again have it made allowable for the sake of release from the state of seeds (bījagāma-parimocana).

In this context, the making of what is allowable (kappiya-karaṇa) should be understood according to the sequence of this scriptural text: "Bhikkhus, I allow fruit to be consumed by five means of ascetic-allowance: [fruit] damaged by fire, [fruit] damaged by a tool, [fruit] damaged by a fingernail, [fruit] that is seedless, and fifthly, [fruit] from which the seeds have been removed." Among these five, "aggi-parijita" means fruit that is damaged, overcome, burnt, or touched by fire. "Sattha-parijita" means fruit that is damaged, overcome, cut, or pierced by a tool. This same method applies to "nakha-parijita" (damaged by a fingernail). Seedless fruits and fruits from which seeds have been removed are naturally allowable.

One who makes [an item] allowable by fire should do so with any kind of fire, such as a wood fire or a cow-dung fire, or at the very least, with a glowing piece of iron. While doing so, one must touch a portion of it and say, "Kappiya" (Allowable). One who makes [an item] allowable with a tool should do so with any tool made of iron, at the very least with the tip or edge of a needle or a nail-cutter, showing the act of cutting or piercing while saying, "Kappiya." One who makes [an item] allowable with a fingernail should not do so with a decayed nail. The fingernails of humans, lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and so forth, as well as the claws of birds, are sharp; it is allowable to make [items] allowable with those. The hooves of horses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, cattle, and so forth are not sharp; one should not use them, and even if used, it is as if it were not done. The nails of elephants, however, are not hooves; it is allowable to use them. For those [nails] which are allowable to use, whether they are still attached to the creature or have been removed, one should show the act of cutting or piercing while saying, "Kappiya."

In making [items] allowable, if there is a mountain-like pile of seeds, or if a thousand trees have been cut and joined together, or if sugarcane is tied into a large bundle, if one makes a single seed, a single branch, or a single stalk of sugarcane allowable, then the whole is considered made allowable. When sugarcane and wood are tied together, [intending] "I will make the sugarcane allowable"...
33:
...and one happens to pierce the wood, it is still allowable. If sugarcane pieces are brought in a full basket, making one piece allowable makes the whole basket allowable. When alms-food is brought mixed with ripe chilies and so forth, and it is said, "Make it allowable," even if one pierces a grain of rice, it is still allowable. The same method applies to sesame, husked rice, and so forth. However, items put into gruel (yāgu) do not remain connected; therefore, in that case, one must pierce each item individually to make it allowable. If the inner pulp of a wood-apple (kapittha) or similar fruit has detached from the shell and moves about, one must have it broken to make it allowable. If it is still attached, making the shell allowable is also proper.

"Unintentionally" (asañcicca) refers to instances where grass is severed while rolling stones or logs, while pulling a branch, or while walking and striking the ground with a staff. Because one does not cut with the intention, "I will cut that grass," it is called cutting unintentionally. There is no offence for a monk who cuts unintentionally in this way.

"Inattentively" (asatiyā) refers to standing and cutting grass or a vine with one's big toe or hand while one's mind is elsewhere, such as when talking to someone. There is no offence for a monk who cuts inattentively in this way.

"Unknowingly" (ajānantassa) refers to not knowing that there are seeds (bījagāma) or living plants (bhūtagāma) within [an area], or not knowing "I am cutting." It also includes placing a chisel, a crowbar, or a hoe in a fence or a straw pile for safekeeping, or dropping fire from a burning hand, whereby grass is severed or burnt in that place; in such cases, there is no offence. However, in all the commentaries explaining the Pārājika on human beings (Manussaviggaha-pārājika), it is stated: "If a monk is pinned down by a tree or has fallen into a pit, even if he is able to escape by cutting the tree or digging the earth, he should not do so himself even for the sake of his life. However, it is allowable for another monk to dig the earth, cut the tree, or cut a stick from a green tree to roll that tree away and help him escape; there is no offence." No reason is seen for this [restriction]. Only this one scriptural text is found: "Bhikkhus, I allow the setting of a counter-fire or the making of a firebreak when a forest fire is burning." (Cullavagga 283). If, in accordance with this text, [it is thought] "It is not allowable for oneself, but for another..."
34:
It is not possible to obtain this distinction of "it is allowable." One who acts for one's own benefit does so only with an unwholesome mind of self-love, whereas another acts out of compassion; therefore, if it is said there is no offense, this reason is also invalid. This is because one can fall into this offense even with a wholesome mind. However, since it is stated in all the Commentaries, it cannot be prohibited. A suitable reason should be sought here. Or else, a decision should be made based on faith in the teachers of the Commentaries. The rest is clear.

There are three origins (samuṭṭhāna): it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It involves action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), consciousness (sacittaka), conventional fault (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## First Training Rule on Bhūtagāma.
## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Evasive Speech

In the second training rule: "Anācāraṃ ācaritvā" means having committed an improper act and having fallen into an offense through the doors of body and speech. "Aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati" means covering, blocking, or overwhelming the question asked with a speech other than the one required for the answer. Now, wishing to show the method of such covering, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with "Ko āpanno." In this context, the connection of words is as follows: That monk, having seen some transgression, when questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding the offense, "Friend, you have fallen into an offense," says, "Who has fallen into an offense?" When it is said, "You have," he says, "What offense have I fallen into?" Then, when it is said, "Either a pācittiya or a dukkaṭa," he, wishing to ask about the basis (vatthu), says, "On account of what basis have I fallen into an offense?" Then, when it is said, "On account of such and such a basis," he asks, "How have I fallen into it? By doing what have I fallen into it?" Then, when it is said, "By doing such and such an act," he says, "Whom are you talking about?" Then, when it is said, "We are talking about you," he says, "What are you saying?"

Furthermore, there is also a method of evasive speech (aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇa) not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text: If monks say, "A coin (kahāpaṇa) was seen in your bag; why do you do such an improper thing?" and he says, "Venerable sirs, it was well seen, but this is not a coin; it is just a small lead disc or a small tin disc." Or if they say, "You were seen drinking intoxicants; why do you do this?"...
35:
...and he says, "Venerable sirs, it was well seen, but this is not an intoxicant; it is ariṭṭha liquid prepared for medicinal purposes." Or when it is said, "You were seen sitting with a woman in a concealed place; why do you do such an improper thing?" and he says, "The one who saw it saw it well, but there was a second wise companion here; why was that person not seen?" Or when asked, "Did you see anything like this?" and he says, "I do not hear," while bringing his ear forward, or brings his eye forward to those questioning at the ear-door—such a person should be known as one who covers one matter with another (aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati). "Aññavādakaṃ ropetu" means "let him be charged with the act of evasive speech" or "let it be established." The same method applies to the phrase "vihesakaṃ ropetu" (let him be charged with the act of annoying).

In this training rule, "Aññavādake vihesake pācittiyaṃ": because he speaks something other than the matter asked, he is called "aññavādaka" (one who speaks evasively). This is the name for speech that covers one matter with another. Because he causes annoyance, he is called "vihesaka" (one who annoys). This is the name for remaining silent. Regarding these acts of evasive speech and annoying, two pācittiya offenses are taught due to the two bases.

"Aropite aññavādake" refers to the time before the charge of evasive speech has been formally laid by the legal procedure (kammavācā). The same method applies to the phrase "aropite vihesake."

In the phrases beginning with "Dhammakamme dhammakammasaññī": if the formal act of charging with evasive speech or annoying is performed, and that act is a lawful act (dhammakamma), and the monk perceives it as a lawful act yet still commits the act of evasive speech or annoying, then he incurs a pācittiya offense for that evasive speech and for that annoying. The meaning should be understood in this way.

"Ajānanto pucchati" means asking, "Venerable sirs, what are you saying? I do not know," without knowing that he has fallen into an offense. "Gilāno vā na katheti" means having a disease of the mouth that prevents him from speaking. In the phrases beginning with "Saṅghassa bhaṇḍanaṃ vā": it means not answering while thinking, "If I answer in the midst of the Saṅgha, it will lead to quarreling, strife, or contention within the Saṅgha; let that not happen." The meaning should be understood in this way. The rest is clear.

Three origins (samuṭṭhāna): the origin is from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. Sometimes it is an act of commission (kiriya), sometimes an act of omission (akiriya). This is true for the monk who covers one speech with another.
36: It is the performance of an act of transgression that should not be done, or the non-performance of a duty that should be fulfilled for one who harasses by remaining silent. It involves Saññāvimokkha (liberation through perception), being with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling. ## Second: Aññavādaka Training Rule. ## 3. Commentary on the Ujjhāpanaka Training Rule In the third training rule—'the monks caused Dabba Mallaputta to be criticized'—means that by saying things such as 'Venerable Dabba Mallaputta acts according to his own desire (bias),' they cause that Venerable to be looked upon as inferior by those monks, or they cause them to think of him as low without saying it explicitly, or they cause him to be perceived as a base person. In this context, the characteristic should be understood according to the science of grammar. There is also a variant reading 'Ojjhāpenti,' which has the same meaning. 'Chandāya' means that due to favoritism through desire, he assigns excellent lodgings to those who are close to him. 'Khiyyanti' means they manifest the fault by saying things such as 'Venerable Dabba acts according to his desire.' In the phrase 'Ujjhāpanake khiyyanake pācittiyaṃ,' the words by which they cause criticism are called 'ujjhāpanaka.' The words by which they complain are called 'khiyyanaka.' In these two cases of ujjhāpanaka and khiyyanaka, it means there are two Pācittiya offenses due to the two bases. The terms 'Ujjhāpanakaṃ nāma upasampannaṃ saṅghena sammataṃ senāsanapaññāpakaṃ vā... appamattakavissajjanakaṃ vā' should be connected with the phrase 'maṅkukatukāmo' (desiring to make him feel dispirited). By virtue of the phrases 'avaṇṇaṃ kattukāmo' (desiring to speak dispraise) and 'ayasaṃ kattukāmo' (desiring to cause ill-repute), the case ending in 'upasampannaṃ' etc. should be changed to 'upasampannassa' to interpret the meaning. In the phrase 'ujjhāpeti vā khiyyati vā āpatti pācittiyassa,' although the matrix term 'khiyyanakaṃ nāma' is extracted, it should be understood that because it is described according to the same detailed analysis (vibhaṅga) as shown for the term 'ujjhāpanakaṃ nāma,' and because there is no other distinction as in the Aññavādaka training rule, that 'khiyyanaka' is not extracted separately or analyzed in detail, but the conclusion is made together. In the phrases 'dhammakamme dhammakammasaññī' etc., if the formal act of authorization (sammutikamma) performed for that monk is indeed a lawful act (dhammakamma), and that monk, perceiving it as a lawful act, causes criticism or complains, then he incurs a Pācittiya offense for that criticism and complaint. The meaning should be understood in this manner.
37:
In the phrase "anupasampannaṃ ujjhāpeti vā khiyyati vā," it means causing a layperson or a novice to look down upon a monk authorized by the Saṅgha, or grumbling about that monk in the presence of that layperson or novice. "Upasampannaṃ saṅghena asammataṃ" refers to a person who has not been authorized by a formal act (kammavācā) but has been assigned a duty by the Saṅgha saying, "This burden is your responsibility," or a person who voluntarily carries out that duty for the comfortable living of the monks, or a person who performs such a duty in a monastery where two or three monks reside.

In the phrase "anupasampannaṃ saṅghena sammataṃ vā asammataṃ vā," although it is not appropriate to give the thirteen types of authorizations (sammuti) to a layperson or a novice, the term "authorized by the Saṅgha" refers to one who received authorization while a monk but later became a layperson or a novice. The term "not authorized" refers to a novice skilled in the Vinaya who has been assigned a duty by the Saṅgha or by an authorized monk saying, "You do this work." The rest of the words are clear.

This training rule arises from three origins (samuṭṭhāna): body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It involves commission (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññāvimokkha), being with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.

## The Third Training Rule on Complaining (Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada).

## 4. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Lodgings (Paṭhamasenāsana Sikkhāpada)

In the fourth training rule, "hemantike kāle" means during the winter season, at the time of snowfall. "Kāyaṃ otāpentā" means warming the body by sitting in the sun on couches, stools, etc. "Kāle ārocite" means when a certain time for congee, rice, etc., has been announced. "Ovaṭṭhaṃ hoti" means it becomes wet from snow or rain.

"Avassikasaṅkete" refers to the eight months—the four months of winter and the four months of summer—which are not designated as the rainy months. "Maṇḍape vā" means in a pavilion made of branches or a pavilion made of planks. At the foot of a tree...
38:
Under any tree (one is permitted to place beds and benches). In a tree where crows or hawks do not habitually live and build nests, and thus do not drop dung on that lodging—under such a tree, he permits (beds and benches) to be placed. Therefore, under a tree where birds returning from their feeding grounds rest briefly and then leave, it is proper to place (beds and benches). However, under a tree where they habitually live and build nests, they should not be placed. Because of the statement 'for eight months,' even in regions where it does not rain during the rainy season, it is not proper to place them (during the four months of the rains). Because of the statement 'where there is a sign of no rain,' even in the winter, in regions where it rains during the winter, it is not proper to place them in the open. In the summer, however, in all places, the sky is clear and free of clouds; at such a time, it is proper to place beds and benches in the open for some necessary business.

A monk who habitually lives in the open (abbhokāsika) should also know the duties. If that monk has a personal bed, he should sleep only on that bed. If taking a communal (saṅghika) bed, a small bed woven with rattan or bark should be taken. If that is not available, an old bed should be taken. If even that is not available, a newly woven bed or one covered with leather should be taken. Having taken it, it is not proper to spread it and lie down in the open or under a tree at an inappropriate time without even making a small robe-shelter, saying, 'I am a pre-eminent tree-root dweller, a pre-eminent open-air dweller.' If a small shelter made even with a fourfold robe cannot protect (the bed and bench) from getting wet, and there are seven-day rain spells and so on, it is proper (even if it gets wet) because it follows the monk's own body.

People who are inspired by the perfection of virtue of monks living in leaf-huts in the forest often donate new beds and benches, saying, 'Please use these as communal property (saṅghika).' Monks who are leaving after staying there should send them to fellow (sabhāga) monks in a nearby monastery before going. If there are no fellow monks, they should be placed in a spot where the rain does not fall before going. If there is no spot where the rain does not fall, they should be hung on a tree before going. Having taken a broom at the courtyard of a Cetiya and having swept and washed either the courtyard of the dining hall, the courtyard of the Uposatha hall, the precincts, the day-quarters, or the fire-room, etc., the broom should be placed back only in the broom-shed. The same method applies to a monk who takes a broom from one place, such as the Uposatha hall, and sweeps the remaining areas like the dining hall courtyard.
39:
A monk who wishes to go while sweeping the path for alms-round should, after sweeping, leave the broom in a rest-house if there is one on the way. If there is no rest-house, and if he notices that no clouds are rising and knows "it will not rain until I return from the village," he may leave it in any unmarked place and return it to its original place upon his return. If he leaves it in the open knowing it will rain, it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If brooms are already placed in various spots for sweeping, he may return them to those same spots after sweeping. A monk sweeping a sitting hall must know the duties. The duty is: starting from the center, sand should be removed towards the place where feet are placed. Rubbish should be picked up by hand and thrown outside.

A *masāraka* is a bed made by piercing the legs and inserting the frame-rails into the holes. A *bundikābaddha* is a bed made in the form of a couch by joining the legs with the frame-rails. A *kuḷīrapādaka* (crab-legged) is a bed made with legs like those of a horse, a ram, etc.; or any bed with curved legs is called *kuḷīrapādaka*. Regarding the *āhaccapādaka*, since it is stated later in the Pali text itself that "a bed called *āhaccapādaka* is made by piercing the members," it should be understood as a bed made by piercing the frame-rails, inserting the tips of the legs into those holes, and securing them with a pin from above. The same applies to benches (pīṭha). The phrase "bound by wrapping inside" (*anto saṃveṭhetvā baddhaṃ*) means it is made in the shape of a drum, wide at the top and bottom and narrow in the middle, and then bound. They also make it by covering the middle with lion or tiger skin. Here, there is no such thing as an unallowable skin. Since a resting place is allowable even if made of gold, such a covering is of great value. If a monk has a layperson or a novice spread the bedding, the responsibility (palibodha) lies with the monk who gave the order. The statement "an offense of pācittiya for a monk who goes beyond the distance of a stone's throw (leḍḍupāta)" means a pācittiya offense is incurred by a monk who goes beyond the distance of a stone's throw of a man of average strength.

The decision here is: a senior monk (thera), having finished his meal in the dining hall, orders a junior monk, "Go and spread the bed and bench at the daytime resting place." The junior monk does as ordered and sits there. After the senior monk has wandered as he pleases and goes there, if he places his bag or upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) there, from that moment on, the responsibility lies only with the senior monk. If, after sitting, he goes away in the evening without putting it away himself or having someone else put it away, and goes beyond the distance of a stone's throw, he commits a pācittiya offense. If the senior monk does not place his bag or upper robe there but merely walks up and down and says to the junior monk, "You may go," then the junior monk must remind him, "Venerable sir, this bed and bench are still here."
40:
Even when going oneself, if one neither removes [the bed or chair] nor has it removed, and passes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw, there is a Pācittiya offense. However, if a Thera, without leaving his bag or upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) at that place, is merely walking to and fro and says to a junior monk (dahara), "You may go," then that junior monk should say, "Venerable sir, here is a bed and chair (mañca-pīṭha)." If the Thera knows the protocol (vatta), he should say, "You go, I will attend to it as usual (pākatika)." If the Thera is ignorant and has not learned the protocol, and threatens the junior monk, saying, "Go, do not stand here; I will not give you permission to sit or lie down," then the junior monk, having obtained permission by saying, "Venerable sir, may you sleep comfortably," should pay respects and depart. After that junior monk has left, the responsibility lies solely with the Thera. It should be understood that the Thera incurs the offense according to the previous method.

Furthermore, if at the very moment of being commanded, the junior monk says, "Venerable sir, I have some duties to perform, such as washing my belongings," and the Thera says, "Go after you have set [the seat] in order," and then the Thera leaves the dining hall for another place, he should be made to account for an offense at every step. If he goes to that place and sits down, he incurs an offense when he passes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw, as in the previous method. If the Thera commands a novice (sāmaṇera), and even if the novice remains sitting after setting the bed and chair in order, if the Thera goes elsewhere from the dining hall, he should be made to account for an offense at every step. If he goes and sits, and then leaves again, he should be made to account for a Pācittiya offense when he passes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw. However, if at the time of commanding, he says, "Set the bed and chair in order and remain sitting right there," then he has the right to come and go as he pleases. For one who goes without personally attending to it as usual, there is a Pācittiya offense upon passing beyond the distance of a stone’s throw. Monks who are sitting on beds and chairs set out in occasional assemblies should, when departing, say to the monastery attendants (ārāmika), "Please put these away." If they leave without saying so, they incur an offense when they pass beyond the distance of a stone’s throw.

When there is a great Dhamma assembly, beds and chairs are brought and set out from the Uposatha hall and the dining hall. In that case, the responsibility lies only with the resident monks (āvāsika). If visiting monks (āgantuka) take them, saying, "This is for our preceptor (upajjhāya), this is for our teacher (ācariya)," then from that moment on, the responsibility lies only with those visiting monks. When departing, if they pass beyond the distance of a stone’s throw without attending to them as usual, they incur an offense. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated again: "As long as others have not yet sat down, the burden lies with those who prepared [the seats]. Once others have come and sat down, the burden lies with those who are sitting. If they depart without removing them or having them removed, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Why? Because they were set out without being commanded." When a Dhamma seat (dhammāsana) is prepared, as long as the reciter (ussāraka) or the Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) has not arrived, the responsibility lies with those who prepared it. Once he has arrived and sat down...
41:
...or as long as the Dhamma preacher has not arrived, it is the responsibility of the monks who set it out; however, when that Dhamma preacher arrives and sits, it is his responsibility alone. If a Dhamma assembly (Dhamma-hearing) lasts for a whole day and night, and one reciter (ussāraka) or Dhamma preacher rises and another sits, the burden lies with each person who comes and sits. However, the monk who rises should depart after saying, "This seat is your responsibility." Even if the first monk who was sitting rises and departs before the other monk has arrived, if the other monk arrives and sits while the first monk is still within the precincts (upacāra), the monk who rose and departed should not be made to account for an offense. But if the first monk who was sitting rises from the seat and passes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw before the other monk has arrived, he should be made to account for an offense. In all cases, the method stated in the Mahāpaccariya is: "In passing beyond the distance of a stone’s throw, there is a dukkaṭa offense at the first step, and a pācittiya offense at the second step."

In the phrases beginning with "cimilikāṃ vā," a cimilikā is a covering made to protect the color of a floor treated with plaster and such; they spread this covering below and spread a mat (kaṭasāraka) on top. An uttarattharaṇa is an upper covering to be spread on top of beds and chairs. A bhūmattharaṇa is various kinds of mats, such as kaṭasāraka, to be spread on the ground. A taṭṭikā is a mat made of palm leaves or bark. A cammakhaṇḍa is any kind of skin among the skins of lions, tigers, leopards, and other wild animals. Indeed, in the commentaries, one does not find skins mentioned as forbidden for use as monastery requisites; therefore, the prohibition should be understood as applying only to the carrying of lion skins and such [as personal belongings]. A pādapuñchanī (foot-wiper) is an item made of cords or rags for the purpose of wiping the feet. A phalakapīṭha is a chair made of planks. Alternatively, it refers to both a plank and a wooden chair; by this term, all wooden items and such are included. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated in detail: "If one goes away after leaving any wooden item in the open—such as a bowl-rest (ādhāraka), a bowl-lid, a foot-stool, a palm-leaf fan, or a circular fan, down to even a water ladle or a water conch—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, this method is shown in the second training rule. After boiling dye in the open, everything—the dye-pot, dye-ladle, and dye-trough—should be stored in the fire-hall (aggisālā). If there is no fire-hall, they should be kept in a mountain cleft where they will not get wet by rain. If even such a place does not exist, it is allowable to go after placing them in a spot where monks can see them when they look.
42:
Regarding another's personal property, if taking it through trust (vissāsa) is not established, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed by a monk who departs without putting it away or moving it. However, if trust is established with that person, their property is as if it were one's own personal property; thus it is stated in the Mahāpaccari and other commentaries.

Going after asking permission means: if a monk, novice, or monastery attendant is conscientious (lajjī) and regards the lodging as his own responsibility, there is no offense for a monk who goes after asking such a person. Going while drying items in the sun means: he goes with the intention, 'I will put it away when I return after drying it in the sun'; for one who goes thus, there is no offense. Disturbed by someone means the lodging is troubled by someone. If a senior monk makes him get up and takes the place, or if a yakkha or a peta comes and sits there, or if some ruler comes and takes it, the lodging is said to be disturbed. Even if lions, tigers, and so on come and stay in that place, the lodging is indeed disturbed. For one who goes without putting things away when thus disturbed, there is no offense. In case of dangers means when there are dangers to life or to the holy life (brahmacariya). The rest of the words are clear.

This training rule has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Kathina training rule: it arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind. It is an offense of action or inaction, not released by perception, without specific intent, a breach of regulation, a bodily action, a vocal action, involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The First Training Rule on Lodgings, the Fourth.

## 5. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lodgings

In the second training rule on lodgings: bhisi means a bolster for a couch or a bolster for a chair. Bedding such as cimilikā (mats) are of the same types as mentioned in the previous training rule. Nisīdana (sitting cloth) should be understood as a mat with a border. Paccattharaṇa (bedspread) means only a cloak or a carpet. Tiṇasanthāra (grass mat) is a mat made of any kind of grass. The same applies to paṇṇasanthāra (leaf mat). Regarding 'one who crosses the boundary': if he crosses the first step, it is a dukkaṭa; if he crosses the second step, it is a pācittiya offense. The precinct (upacāra) of an unfenced monastery is the distance of two stone-throws from the outermost dwelling.
43:
In the phrase 'or should go without asking permission' (anāpucchā vā gaccheyya): if a monk is present, he should be asked. If no monk is present, a novice; if no novice, a monastery attendant; if no monastery attendant, the donor who built and offered the monastery, or anyone from that donor's family should be asked. If these people are also not present, he should place a couch on four stones, stack the remaining couches and chairs on that couch, pile the ten kinds of bedding such as bolsters on top, store away the wooden and clay items, close the doors and windows, fulfill the duties of a departing monk, and then go.

If the monastery leaks, and if grass or bricks have been brought for roofing, he should roof it if he is able. If he is unable, he should place the couches, chairs, etc., in a place that does not leak and then go. If the entire monastery leaks, he should, if able, place them in the house of lay followers (upāsakas) in the village. If those lay followers do not accept, saying, 'Venerable sir, communal property (saṅghika) is a heavy responsibility; we fear fire and so on,' he should place the couch on stones even in an open space, stack the rest as previously mentioned, cover them with grass and leaves, and then it is proper to go. For if even a part of the bedding remains there, it will be of use to other monks who arrive at that place.

In the terms 'in the precinct of the monastery' (vihārassa upacāre) and so on: the precinct of the monastery means the courtyard (pariveṇa). 'Assembly hall' (upaṭṭhānassālā) means the refectory within the courtyard. 'Pavilion' (maṇḍapa) means the pavilion within the courtyard. 'Foot of a tree' (rukkhamūla) means the foot of a tree within the courtyard. This is the method stated in the Kurundī Commentary. Although it is so stated, 'monastery' (vihāra) should be understood as an inner room or any other fully roofed and secure lodging. 'In the precinct of the monastery' means the area outside and near that monastery. 'In the assembly hall' means in the refectory. 'In the pavilion' means in a pavilion where many assemble, whether it is enclosed or not. Regarding the foot of a tree, there is nothing special to explain.

In the phrase 'an offense of wrongdoing' (āpatti dukkaṭassa): for a monk who goes after spreading the aforementioned ten kinds of bedding in a secure place like an inner room, the Buddha declared a pācittiya offense because both the bedding and the lodging could be destroyed by termites, becoming nothing but a mound of earth. However, if he goes after spreading them in an external place like an assembly hall, only the bedding might be destroyed because the place is not secure, but the lodging itself would not be destroyed due to the lack of security; therefore...
44:
Because the place is not secure, the dwelling is not secure; therefore, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated here. Regarding the couch or the chair, since termites cannot immediately eat through a couch or chair, an offense of wrong-doing is stated for a monk who goes away leaving them spread out even in the monastery. However, within the precincts of the monastery, monks making their rounds of the monastery will see them and put them away.

## 118. In the phrase "goes away after putting them away," a monk who goes away after putting them away should remove all the cords, cloth, or rattan used for binding the small couches and chairs, fold them, and hang them on the robe-rail before leaving. A monk who comes later to reside there must also do the same when he leaves after having spread out and slept on the couch or chair again. A monk who lives by spreading his bedding outside the wall from within the wall must, when leaving, put it away in the same place from which it was taken. This same method applies to a monk who stays on the lower floor after bringing things down from the upper floor of a pāsāda. Even if one stays by spreading a couch or chair in night-quarters or day-quarters, when leaving, they must be placed back in the same place from which they were taken.

In the phrase "goes away after asking permission," this is the decision on whether one should or should not ask permission. Whether it be a long hall or a leaf-roofed hut built on the ground, or a dwelling built on wooden pillars where termites are likely to emerge, a monk departing from such a monastery must depart only after asking permission. This is because if such a monastery is left untended for even a few days, termite mounds may even form. However, for a monk departing from a monastery built on a rock surface or on stone pillars, a mountain cave, or a plastered monastery where there is no suspicion of termites, it is allowable to go either after asking permission or without asking; however, asking permission is the proper conduct (vatta). Even in such a monastery, if termites are climbing up from one side, he must go only after asking permission. If a visiting monk (āgantuka) stays with a monk who has taken a communal (saṅghika) dwelling but does not take a dwelling for himself, as long as he does not take it, that dwelling remains the responsibility (palibodha) of the former monk. From the time the visiting monk takes the dwelling and stays there as its master, it becomes the responsibility of the visiting monk. If both divide and take it, it is the responsibility of both. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said: "If two or three people spread [their bedding] and stay together, all must ask permission when leaving. Among those monks, if the one who goes first leaves with the thought, 'The monk remaining behind will look after it,' it is allowable. For the last remaining monk, there is no release from the offense merely by such a thought. If many monks send one monk to spread [the bedding], when leaving, either all of them or the one monk who was sent must ask permission."
45:
One must ask permission, or send one monk to ask permission. Even if one brings beds, stools, etc., from another dwelling and resides elsewhere, they must be returned to the original place when leaving. If a senior monk arrives while one is residing with items brought from another place, one should not prevent him, but should say, "Venerable sir, I brought this from another dwelling; please use it as it was." If that senior monk accepts, saying, "I will do so," it is allowable for the other junior monk to go. In this way, if one uses communal property by bringing it elsewhere and it is lost, worn out, or stolen by thieves, one is not liable for compensation. However, if one uses it as personal (puggalika) property, one is liable for compensation. If another person's bed or stool is lost while being used either as communal or personal property, one is certainly liable for compensation.

"There is some obstruction" means the dwelling is obstructed by any cause such as a senior monk, an authority, an ogre, a lion, a beast of prey, or a cobra. If one goes away with concern, thinking, "I will return today and look after it," and while standing at a place where the intention to travel further arises—such as the other side of a river or another village—one sends someone to ask permission; or if one is oppressed by dangers such as a flooded river, kings, or thieves and is unable to return, there is no offense for such a monk. The rest of the procedure, including the origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., is the same as the method stated in the first training rule.

## The Second Lodging Training Rule, the Fifth.

## 6. Explanation of the Encroaching Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, "they obstruct" means they go first and stand blocking the way by bringing their bowls and robes forward. "They make senior monks get up" means they make them get up by saying according to seniority, "Friends, this place belongs to us." "They make their bed by encroaching (anupakhajja)" means they approach closely and spread out beds and stools, sitting, lying down, or reciting texts, saying, "Venerable sirs, only the space for the bed belongs to you, not the whole dwelling; now this place belongs to us."

"Knowing 'this monk is one who should not be made to get up'"—because of this meaning, it is stated in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of that term, "He knows he is senior," and so on. For a senior monk, because of his seniority...
46:
A sick monk is one who should not be made to rise from his bed because of his illness. The Saṅgha, recognizing the great service and special qualities of monks such as the treasurer, the Dhamma preacher, the Vinaya expert, and so on, or the teacher who instructs the group, designates and gives a dwelling for their permanent residence. Therefore, such a monk who has been given a dwelling by the Saṅgha is also one who should not be made to rise from his bed. In this context, the Saṅgha indeed gives a suitable bed and lodging even to a sick monk. However, it is specifically stated to show that even if a sick monk has a bed and lodging not formally given by the Saṅgha after a request, he should not be harassed but should be treated with compassion and cared for.

In this context, the 'precincts' (upacāra) of beds and benches are as follows: in a large monastery, the area of one and a half cubits (one cubit and four finger-breadths) all around is called the precincts. In a small monastery, wherever there is enough space, one and a half cubits from that point is the precincts. For one who enters after washing his feet or one who goes out to urinate, the path with a width of one and a half cubits leading from the foot-washing stone placed at the door or from the place of urination to the bed or bench is called the precincts. If a monk, wishing to sleep, encroaches upon the precincts of another monk who is standing, entering, or leaving the precincts of that bed or bench, and spreads a bed himself or has it spread, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Regarding the terms 'sits down' or 'lies down': by merely sitting down or merely lying down, he commits an offense of confession (pācittiya). If he does both, he commits two offenses of confession. For a monk who repeatedly gets up and sits or lies down, he commits an offense of confession for every effort (payoga).

In this section on the offense of wrong-doing regarding 'spreading a bed or having it spread while leaving out the precincts,' and in the subsequent sections on the offense of wrong-doing such as 'in the precincts of the monastery,' just as the various offenses of confession were taught here based on merely sitting, merely lying, doing both, and the different efforts, so too should the various offenses of wrong-doing be understood. Indeed, there is no benefit in living in the same dwelling or the same enclosure with such an incompatible person (visabhāga-puggala). Therefore, his residing in any place is forbidden. Regarding 'in the private [dwelling] of another': here too, the private property of an intimate friend is just like one's own private property; there is no offense in that case.
47:
If he does both sitting and lying down, then offenses of confession (pācittiya) are committed. For a monk who repeatedly gets up and sits or lies down, he commits an offense of confession for every effort.

122. In this section on the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) starting with 'precincts' (upacāra), and in all subsequent sections on the offense of wrong-doing such as 'in the precincts of the monastery' (vihārassa upacāre), just as the various offenses of confession were taught in this section on confession based on merely sitting, merely lying, doing both, and the different efforts, so too should the various offenses of wrong-doing be understood. The reason is that there is no benefit in living in the same dwelling or the same enclosure with such an incompatible person (visabhāga-puggala). Therefore, the residence of that incompatible monk is forbidden in all places. 'The private property of another' means that in this training rule as well, the private bed and lodging of an intimate person is just like one's own private bed and lodging. There is no offense in the bed and lodging of such an intimate person.

123. 'In emergencies' (āpadāsu) means if there is a danger to life or a danger to the holy life (brahmacariya) for a monk staying outside, and a monk enters because of such dangers, there is no offense for him. The rest of the explanation is clear. It has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the first Pārājika; it is an action (kiriya); it is released by perception (saññā-vimokkha); it is intentional (sacittaka); it is a worldly fault (lokavajja); it is a bodily action (kāyakamma); it involves unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta); and it has painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Sixth Training Rule on Encroaching (Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada).

## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Ejection (Nikkaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada)

126. In the seventh training rule, 'if he passes through many doors with a single effort' refers to those mansions (pāsāda) with four or five stories, or those four-sided long dwellings (catussālā) with six or seven gateways. In such dwellings, if he takes [another monk] by the hands or by the neck and makes him pass through without stopping in between with a single effort, he commits a single offense of confession (pācittiya). For a monk who makes him pass through by stopping repeatedly with various efforts, he commits offenses of confession according to the number of doors. For a monk who ejects him by speech, saying 'Get out!' without touching him with the hand, the method is the same. (This means if he speaks once, he commits one offense of confession; if he has to speak repeatedly, he commits many offenses of confession according to the number of utterances.)

In the phrase 'if he commands another,' by the mere command 'Eject this monk,' he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If the monk who is commanded makes him pass through many doors having been commanded once, he commits one offense of confession. However, if he is commanded with a limit, such as 'Eject him through this many doors' or 'Eject him as far as the main gate,' he commits offenses of confession according to the number of doors.

'His requisites' (tassa parikkhāraṃ) refers to any of his belongings such as the bowl, robes, water-strainer, water-filter (dhammakaraṇa), bed, bench, mattress, pillow, and so on, down to even a piece of dyeing bark; if a monk himself ejects them or has another eject them, he commits offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) according to the number of items. However, in the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated that if the requisites are tied together firmly, only a single offense is committed.

127. 'The private property of another' means that in this training rule as well, the requisites of an intimate person are just like one's own private requisites. Just as in this training rule the private requisites of an intimate person are like one's own, so too in all training rules, the requisites of an intimate person are just like one's own private requisites. Where there is a distinction, we shall mention it in that training rule.

128. In the words 'if he ejects a shameless monk' (alajjiṃ nikkaḍḍhati) and so on, only a person who is a maker of quarrels and a maker of strife may be ejected from the entire monastery grounds (saṅghārāma). The reason is that such a monk might gain a faction and even cause a schism in the Saṅgha. Shameless monks and others, however, should be ejected only from one's own place; it is not proper to eject them from the entire monastery grounds. There is no offense for a monk who is himself insane. The rest of the explanation is clear. The seventh training rule on ejection is finished.

The statement that it is not proper to eject from the entire monastery grounds is said because it is unsuitable. In the Vimati, it is said that if a monk who censures evil ejects someone with a mind free from anger, there is no offense under this training rule, because it is stated [in the rule] 'being angry and displeased'.
48:
It can also cause a split in the Saṅgha. Shameless (alajji) monks and the like, however, should only be expelled from their own place of residence; it is not proper to expel them from the entire Saṅghārāma. "Unmattakassa" means there is no offense for a monk who is himself insane. The rest is clear.

Threefold origination: This training rule arises from three causes: body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It involves action (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññā-vimokkha), consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusala-citta), and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Seventh Training Rule on Expulsion (Nikkaddhana Sikkhāpada).

## 8. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Upper-room Hut (Vehāsakuṭi Sikkhāpada).

In the eighth training rule, "upari vehāsakuṭiyā" refers to a two-storied hut or a three-storied hut, etc., which has a roofed floor above. "Mañcaṃ sahasā abhinisīdi" means sitting down suddenly, overpowering and pressing upon the couch. Here, the accusative case "mañcaṃ" is used in the sense of the locative case, meaning "sits on the couch". The word "abhi" is merely a prefix used for linguistic elegance. "Nippatitvā" means either falling or coming out. Since the peg (āṇī) had not yet been driven into the top of that couch, it came out of the couch. "Vissaramakāsi" means making the distorted sound of a person in pain.

A "vehāsakuṭi" (upper-room hut) is a hut where the head of a man of average height does not strike [the ceiling]. If a hut is such that the head of a man of average height does not strike the lowest beams, that hut is shown here as the intended "vehāsakuṭi". This is not the actual definition of a vehāsakuṭi. Any two-storied or three-storied hut, etc., with a roofed floor above is called a "vehāsakuṭi". However, in this context, a hut where the head does not strike is intended. Regarding sitting down (abhinisīdana) and so forth, the classification of offenses should be understood according to the effort (payoga) as previously mentioned.

"Avehāsakuṭiyā" means there is no offense in leaf-huts and the like built on the ground (even if one sits or lies down there). This is because it is not possible to cause harm to another in such a hut. "Sīsaghaṭṭāyā" means there is also no offense in a hut where the head strikes [the ceiling]. This is because it is not possible to move about in the lower floor of such a building without stooping; therefore, since it is not a place for moving about, causing harm to another is not possible.
49:
(Harm to another) will not occur. "If it is not in use below" means if the hut is not in use because building materials such as timber and bamboo are stored beneath it, there is no offense in such a hut (even if one sits or lies down on a couch or stool). "If it is spread with planks" means if the upper floor of the hut is solidly spread with wooden planks or finished with plaster and so forth, there is no offense in that hut. "If a peg is driven" means if a peg (or nail) is driven into the tips of the legs of the couches or stools, so that the legs do not fall out even when one sits down; there is no offense for one sitting on such a couch or stool. "Standing on that couch" means standing on a couch or stool with legs fitted into the frame, and taking a robe or anything else hanging on an elephant-tusk peg (nāgadantaka) above, or hanging another item; there is no offense for that monk. The rest is clear. The origination of the Sheep's Wool (Eḷakaloma) training rule: it arises from the body and from the body and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is not liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without consciousness (acittaka); it is a conventional fault (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is bodily action (kāyakamma); it has three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Eighth Training Rule on the Upper-room Hut (Vehāsakuṭi Sikkhāpada).

## 9. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Large Dwelling (Mahallakavihāra Sikkhāpada).

In the ninth training rule: in the phrase "as far as the door-frame (yāva dvārakosā)", "door-frame (dvārakosa)" refers to the space around the door-post (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa) equal to the width of the door-leaf. In the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, however, it is said to be "one and a half cubits (1.5 cubits) starting from the door-post". In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said to be "the size of the door-leaf on both sides of the door". In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated that "a door-leaf may be one and a half cubits, two cubits, or two and a half cubits"; that statement is well-said. Intending that very measure of two and a half cubits, the Blessed One also gave this supreme description: "the reach (hatthapāsa) around the door-post". "To make the door-leaf and door-frame firm" means for the purpose of making the door-frame along with the door-leaf stable. This word-analysis (padabhājanī), "to make the door firm", is also spoken with this same purpose of stability in mind. The intended meaning here is: a door-leaf turns quickly and strikes the wall when opening, and strikes the door-frame when closing. Due to that striking, the wall shakes, and from that, the fine earth (plaster) moves, becoming loose or falling off. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "as far as the door-frame, to make the door firm". In this regard, although it is not directly stated in either the Matika or the Word-analysis (Padabhājanī) that "such and such a task must be done", because it is mentioned in the origin story (aṭṭhuppatti) that "he had it roofed again and again, he had it plastered again and again", the meaning should be understood as: one should personally apply plaster or have it applied again and again around the door-frame so that the door-leaf and door-frame do not shake.
50:
Regarding the statement in the *Padabhājanī*, "within a *hatthapāsa* (two and a half cubits) around the doorframe," I shall explain. In that context, if it is a dwelling with a door in the middle and a high wall above the door, the area within a *hatthapāsa* on three sides—the two sides and above—is the *upacāra* (precinct). If it is a small dwelling (with no space above), the *upacāra* is only on the two sides. Even in such a small dwelling, when the door leaf is opened, the wall it strikes might not reach the full *upacāra* of two and a half cubits. However, as a maximum limit, plastering is permitted within a *hatthapāsa* on three sides to ensure the door is firmly fixed. If there is space for plastering below the door as well, it is proper to plaster there too. In the phrase "for the preparation of the light-vent (*ālokasandhi*)," *ālokasandhi* refers to small window shutters. These small shutters, when opened, strike the wall at a distance of about a span (*vidatthi*) or more. For these light-vents, the *upacāra* is available on all four sides. Therefore, on all four sides, an area the width of the shutter should be plastered by oneself or caused to be plastered by another to ensure the light-vent is firm; this is the meaning here.

The words beginning with "white-washing" (*setavaṇṇa*) are not from the *Padabhājanī* of the *Mātikā*. It has already been permitted in the *Padabhājanī* itself that there is no fault (burden) in the dwelling (*vihāra*) due to such white-washing. Therefore, one may perform white-washing and so on as one pleases.

After showing what should be done regarding plastering, the words beginning with "of two or three layers of roofing" (*dwatticchadanassa*) are spoken to show what should be done regarding roofing. In that context, "a sequence of two or three layers of roofing" (*dwatticchadanassa pariyāyaṃ*) means roofing two or three layers all around. *Pariyāya* means encircling (*parikkhepa*). It means two or three layers of roofing should be arranged. "Standing on non-green ground" (*appaharite ṭhitena*) means one should supervise while standing in a place where there are no green crops. Here, "green" (*harita*) refers to the seven kinds of grain (*pubbaṇṇa*) and pulses such as green gram, black gram, sesame, kidney beans, gourds, and pumpkins (*aparaṇṇa*). That is why it is said, "Green means *pubbaṇṇa* and *aparaṇṇa*."

Regarding the statement that an offence of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is committed if one supervises while standing on green plants: even if seeds sown in a field have not yet sprouted, if they will sprout when it rains, they are still counted as "green" (*harita*). Therefore, one should not supervise while standing in such a field, but only while standing in a place where there are no green plants. Even when standing in a place without green plants, this is the limit: one should stand in a place where a person sitting beside the ridge-pole, or at the junction of the pinnacle, or beside the upper finial, can see the monk standing on the ground when looking down from the edge of the roof, and where the monk standing on the ground can also see the person sitting above.
51:
One should supervise while standing in such a place where they can see each other. One is not allowed to stand and supervise within that area, even if it is a place without green crops. Why? Because if the dwelling were to accidentally collapse, this is the area where it would fall.

In the phrase "roofing by way of a path" (*maggena chādentassa*), roofing by way of a path means roofing straight without encircling. Such roofing can be done with bricks, stones, or plaster. If two rows are poorly roofed, they may be removed and re-roofed repeatedly. Therefore, after supervising two rows as one wishes, one should command for the third row, "Now roof it in this way," and then depart. *Pariyāyena* means encircling. Such roofing can be done with grass or leaves. Therefore, in roofing by this *pariyāya* as well, after supervising two rounds as one wishes, one should command for the third round, "Now roof it in this way," and then depart. If one does not wish to depart yet, one should remain standing in silence. All this roofing should be understood as layers upon layers of roofing. People roof in layers thinking that a dwelling roofed in layers will not leak for a long time. "Beyond that" means the fourth row or round above the three rows or rounds.

"*Karaḷe karaḷe*" means for every handful of grass. The remaining words are clear. The origination (*samuṭṭhāna*) of this training rule is sixfold: action, not being released by perception (*nosanyāvimokkha*), lack of intention (*acittaka*), breach of a regulation (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Ninth Training Rule on Large Dwellings (Mahallakavihāra Sikkhāpadaṃ).

## 10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada)

In the tenth training rule: "*jānaṃ sappāṇakaṃ*" means knowing in some way that "this water contains living beings." "*Siñceyya vā siñcāpeyya vā*" means pouring it oneself or commanding another to pour it. The meaning of words in the Pali such as "*siñceyya* means pouring oneself" should be understood according to the method previously mentioned.

In that training rule, for a monk who pours without breaking the stream of water, there is only one offence per pot of water. This same method applies to all vessels. If the stream is broken while pouring, an offence is committed for every effort (*payoga*). If one directs a channel of water containing living beings towards one's desired direction, even if it flows all day, there is only one offence. If one blocks it at various places and carries it elsewhere, an offence is committed for every effort. If one throws a cartload of grass into the water all at once, one offence is committed. If one throws grass or leaves one by one, an offence is committed for every effort. The same method applies to fine earth, firewood, cow dung, and so on. However, it should be understood that these words do not refer to a large body of water. They refer only to a small amount of water that could dry up, become turbid, or where small insects could die if grass or fine earth were added. The remaining words are clear. The tenth training rule on water with living beings is finished. The Chapter on Living Plants (Bhūtagāma Vagga) is finished.
52:
The way an offense is committed is as follows: If one directs a drain containing living beings towards a desired direction, even if it flows all day, there is only one offense. If one blocks it at various places and diverts it elsewhere, there is an offense for every effort (payoga). If one throws grass equivalent to a cartload into the water with a single effort, there is only one offense. For a monk who throws grass or leaves one by one, there is an offense for every effort. The same rule applies to fine clay, wood, cow dung, and so forth. This statement is not made with reference to a large body of water. It should be understood that it refers only to such water that becomes depleted or turbid when grass or fine clay is added, where small insects might die. The remaining words here are clear.

This training rule arises from three origins (samuṭṭhāna): body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It involves action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), being with intention (sacittaka), an offense by convention (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of mind, and three types of feeling.

## The Tenth Training Rule: Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada.

## The Second Chapter: Senāsana Vagga, explained in order, is finished.

## 3. Ovāda Vagga

## 1. Explanation of the Ovāda Sikkhāpada

141-144. In the first training rule of the Bhikkhunī Vagga, regarding the words 'they are recipients of gains,' the nuns do not give to those elders themselves, nor do they cause others to give. However, women of high families who have gone forth as nuns, when asked by their visiting relatives, 'Venerable ladies, from which elder do you receive exhortation (ovāda), the recitation of the Pāḷi (uddesa), and the questioning of the commentary (paripucchā)?', they point to the eighty great disciples (mahāsāvaka) and speak of their existing virtues such as their virtue (sīla), learning (suta), conduct (ācāra), birth (jāti), and lineage (gotta), according to the course of the conversation. It is proper to speak of such existing virtues. Because of such talk, people with confident hearts brought great gains and offerings, such as robes, to the elders. Therefore, it is said: 'They are recipients of robes... and other requisites.'
53:
## Explanation of the Ovāda Sikkhāpada in the Ovāda Vagga. 'Bhikkhuniyo upasaṅkamitvā' means that not even a single one of those nuns came to the Chabbaggiya monks. However, with hearts pulled by craving for gains, they went to the nuns' quarters. With reference to that going, it is said: 'Bhikkhuniyo upasaṅkamitvā.' Those nuns also, due to their unsteady minds, followed the words of those Chabbaggiya monks. Therefore, it is said: 'Then those nuns... sat down.' 'Tiracchānakathā' (animal talk) refers to various kinds of useless talk, such as talk about kings (rājakathā), which is contrary even to the path to heaven. 'Iddho' means prosperous, connected with meaning, deep, having much flavor, and connected with the penetration of characteristics.

145-147. Regarding the words 'I allow, O monks,' because those Chabbaggiya monks, if told 'Monks, do not exhort the nuns,' might bear ill-will towards the Blessed One as they have not yet seen the Four Noble Truths and might thus go to the states of deprivation (apāya). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to prevent them from going to the states of deprivation, desired to exclude those monks from exhorting the nuns by another means, and thus it should be understood that He allowed this authorization to exhort nuns (bhikkhunovādakasammuti). Having allowed it in this first instance with the desire to exclude them, He later said: 'I allow, O monks, one endowed with eight factors,' and so forth. These eight factors had never occurred to the Chabbaggiya monks even in their dreams.

In that context, one is 'virtuous' (sīlavā) because of having virtue. Now, wishing to show what kind of virtue that is and how it exists in that monk, He said 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' (pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto), and so forth. In that phrase, the Pātimokkha itself is the restraint, thus it is called Pātimokkhasamvara. One who has body and speech restrained by the Pātimokkhasamvara is called 'pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto.' 'Viharati' means he dwells or lives. In the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, it is said:

'Pātimokkha means virtue, the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the closure, the foremost and noble Dhamma for the attainment of wholesome states. Restraint (samvara) means non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, and non-transgression by both body and speech. Restrained (samvuto) means being endowed with, possessed of, approached by, attained to, accomplished in, and gifted with this Pātimokkha restraint; therefore, it is called "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha." Dwells (viharati) means he moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, wanders, and dwells; therefore, it is called "viharati."' (Vibhaṅga 511-512).
54:
"Ācāragocarasampanno" means being endowed with good conduct, not by improper conduct (ācāra) such as giving bamboo and so forth which is prohibited as wrong livelihood, but truly by good conduct; and being endowed with proper resort (gocara) by abandoning improper resorts (agocara) such as prostitutes and so forth, and instead frequenting proper resorts such as families endowed with faith and so forth. "Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī" means having the habit of seeing danger in even the slightest faults. It means one who is accustomed to seeing those faults as a peril. "Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu" means properly undertaking, correctly accepting, and practicing without abandoning each of those training rules, which are established in three ways by way of the higher virtue (adhisīla) and so forth. This is the summary here. Those who desire the detailed explanation should take it from the Visuddhimagga.

One is called "Bahussuta" (learned) because of having much hearing (suta). One is called "Sutadhara" (bearer of learning) because of being able to bear that learning. His great learning is not merely hearing, but actually being able to bear it. One is called "Sutasaunnicayo" (accumulator of learning) because of accumulating learning in that monk like treasures in a chest. By this term "Sutasaunnicayo," it shows that the learning borne by that monk does not perish for a long time, like treasures securely kept in a chest. Now, wishing to show that learning in its essence, he said "Ye te dhammā" and so forth. That is in the same manner as stated in the Verañjakaṇḍa. The conclusion here is: because of having heard such teachings much, he is called "Bahussuta." Because of bearing them, he is called "Sutadhara." Because of being familiarized by speech, pondered by mind, and well-penetrated by wisdom, he is called "Sutasaunnicayo." Therein, "vacasā paricitā" means being thoroughly familiarized by speech. "Manasānupekkhitā" means being repeatedly reflected upon by the mind, so that when reflecting, it becomes as clear as if illuminated by a thousand lamps. "Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā" means being well-penetrated and realized by wisdom, both in terms of meaning and cause.

This learned person is of three types: nissayamuccanaka (one free from dependence), parisupaṭṭhāpaka (one who looks after a group), and bhikkhunovādaka (one who exhorts nuns). Therein, a person free from dependence (nissayamuccanaka) must have at least five years (vassa) since ordination and must have mastered and memorized the two Mātikās. For the purpose of hearing the Dhamma on the Uposatha days of the waxing and waning moon, four bhāṇavāras (recitation sections) from the Suttas; for the purpose of preaching to the arriving audience, one course of discourse similar to the Andhakavinda Sutta, Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, or Ambaṭṭha Sutta; for the purpose of expressing appreciation (anumodanā) at Saṅgha meals or auspicious and inauspicious ceremonies, three appreciation discourses; and for the purpose of knowing the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā etc...
55:
...decisions on minor and major legal acts (kamma), and one meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) ending in Arahantship, either by way of concentration (samādhi) or by way of insight (vipassanā) for the purpose of practicing the recluse's Dhamma—this much learning should be acquired. Indeed, with this much learning, this monk becomes a learned one capable of traveling in the four directions (cātuddiso), and he gains the right to live by his own authority (without dependence) in any place he chooses.

A monk who can look after a group (parisupaṭṭhāpaka) must have at least ten years (vassa) since ordination and, to discipline his group in the higher Vinaya, must have mastered and memorized the two Vibhaṅgas. If unable to memorize them, he should make himself capable of reciting them together with three other persons. He should also learn the minor and major legal acts and the duties mentioned in the Khandhakas. For the purpose of teaching Abhidhamma (the discernment of mind and matter) to the group, if he is a reciter of the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhima-bhāṇaka), he should learn the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka. A reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya should learn the Mahāvagga. A reciter of the Saṃyutta Nikāya should learn the lower three vaggas or the Mahāvagga. A reciter of the Aṅguttara Nikāya should learn half of the Nikāya from either the lower or upper part. If unable to learn half, it is also proper to learn from the Tikanipāta downwards. In the Mahāpaccarī Commentary, it is said: "A monk learning one Nipāta should take either the Catukkanipāta or the Pañcakanipāta." A reciter of the Jātakas (Jātaka-bhāṇaka) should learn the Jātakas together with the commentary; less than that is not proper. It is stated in the Mahāpaccarī that it is also proper to learn the Dhammapada along with its stories. To the question of whether it is proper or not to learn just the equivalent of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka by collecting from various Suttas, it is rejected in the Kurundī Commentary as "not proper," while in other commentaries there is no such investigation. Regarding Abhidhamma, it is not stated that any specific part must be learned. However, if a monk is proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka along with their commentaries but lacks the aforementioned texts from the Suttas, he does not get the right to look after a group. If a monk has learned the prescribed amount of texts from both the Suttas and the Vinaya, he becomes a learned one who can look after a group, is prominent in all directions, can go wherever he wishes, and gains the right to look after a group.

A monk who exhorts the bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka) must learn the three Piṭakas along with their commentaries. If unable to do so, he should master the commentary of one of the four Nikāyas. This is because, through one Nikāya, he will be able to answer questions in the remaining Nikāyas as well. Among the seven books of the Abhidhamma, he should master the commentaries of four books; through the method obtained in those four books, he will be able to answer questions in the remaining books. As for the Vinaya Piṭaka, because it has various meanings and various origins, he must master it along with its commentary. With this much learning, a monk is called a learned exhorter of nuns (bhikkhunovādaka).
56:
