In the phrase beginning with "ubhayāni kho panassa," although one may have great learning in the entire ninefold dispensation, it is not appropriate to exhort without the Vinaya Piṭaka together with its commentary; therefore, the Vinaya is mentioned separately. In that context, "extensively" means together with both Vibhaṅgas. "Well-mastered" (svāgatāni) means well-mastered in the mouth (memorized). To show how they are well-mastered, the phrase beginning with "well-analyzed" (suvibhattāni) is stated. Therein, "well-analyzed" means well-analyzed by being free from the faults of repeating previous words or mixing up words. "Well-rehearsed" (suppavattīni) means being able to recite fluently by heart. "Well-determined according to the Suttas" (suvinicchitāni suttato) means well-determined by way of the Suttas brought from the Khandhaka and Parivāra. "By way of syllables" (anubyañjanaso) means well-determined by the completeness of letters and words, and by having letters that are unbroken and not distorted. By this, the Commentary is indicated. This is because this determination comes from the Commentary.

"One who has pleasant speech" (kalyāṇavāco) is one endowed with speech that is polite, free from phlegm and saliva, and capable of making the meaning known, with rounded words and syllables by reciting letters such as lax (sithila) and tense (dhanita) according to the rules. "One who has pleasant delivery" (kalyāṇavākkaraṇo) means one with a sweet voice. This is because women delight in the perfection of voice; therefore, they despise even speech with perfect words and syllables if it lacks the perfection of voice. In the phrase "generally dear and pleasing to the bhikkhunīs," although it is difficult to be loved by everyone, he is dear and pleasing to many wise bhikkhunīs because of his perfection in virtue and conduct, and he is one who gladdens the mind. "One who is competent to exhort the bhikkhunīs" means one who is able to teach such Dhamma to exhort the bhikkhunīs by threatening them with the danger of saṃsāra, showing the Suttas and the reasons. "In one wearing saffron robes" means in a bhikkhunī wearing saffron robes. "Heavy rule" (garudhamma) means he must be one who has never previously committed physical contact with a bhikkhunī or sexual intercourse with a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī during his time as a layman. This is because women, remembering past deeds, do not have respect even for the Dhamma teaching of an elder who is restrained, but rather their minds incline toward that very unrighteousness. "One of twenty years" means one who has twenty years or more since his higher ordination. Such an elder, even if he repeatedly encounters contrary objects, does not suddenly reach the destruction of virtue like a young monk, but is able to dispel desire and lust in inappropriate places by reflecting on his own age; therefore, it is said, "he is of twenty years or more than twenty years."
57:
Among these (eight factors of a nun-exhorter), the phrase beginning with "sīlavā" is the first factor; the phrase beginning with "bahussuto hoti" is the second factor; the phrase beginning with "ubhayāni kho panassa" is the third factor; the phrase "kalyāṇavāco hoti kalyāṇavākkaraṇo" is the fourth factor; the phrase "yebhuyyena bhikkhunīnaṃ piyo hoti manāpo" is the fifth factor; the phrase "paṭibalo hoti bhikkhuniyo ovadituṃ" is the sixth factor; the phrase beginning with "na kho panetaṃ" is the seventh factor; and the phrase beginning with "vīsativasso" is to be understood as the eighth factor.

148. The word "ñatticatutthena" (by a motion and three proclamations) is just as in the story mentioned previously. "By the heavy rules" (garudhammehi) means exhorting by way of the rules that should be respected. These are called heavy rules (garudhammas) because they must be accepted by the bhikkhunīs with respect and honor. In the phrase "ekatoupasampannāya" (ordained on one side), if a monk exhorts or teaches the heavy rules to a bhikkhunī who has received higher ordination only from the community of bhikkhunīs, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, in exhorting a bhikkhunī who has received higher ordination also from the community of bhikkhus, it is only an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the story.

"Having swept the precinct" (pariveṇaṃ sammajjitvā) means one should sweep a place that has not been swept in the early morning, or a place that, though swept, has become messy again with grass, leaves, or rubbish, or where sand has been scattered due to footprints. If they see that messy place, those bhikkhunīs might become unwilling to listen to the Dhamma, thinking, "The venerable one does not even urge his own resident young monks in the major and minor duties, but only preaches the Dhamma." Therefore, it is said, "having swept the precinct." Bhikkhunīs coming from within the village are thirsty and tired, and they desire drinking water and water for washing hands, feet, and face. If those waters are not available, they may also become unwilling to listen, having developed disrespect in the same manner as before. Therefore, it is said, "having provided drinking water and water for use."

"A seat" (āsanaṃ) means arranging a place, thinking, "This will be the seat for those bhikkhunīs," using anything from a low stool, a wooden board, a mat, or a reed mat, down to even a branch of a tree. To be free from the offense regarding Dhamma teaching, a second companion is desired. Therefore, it is said, "one should sit having taken a second [companion]." "One should sit" (nisīditabbaṃ) means one should not sit at the edge of the monastery, but rather in the middle of the monastery, at a place where everyone assembles, such as the door of the Uposatha hall or the refectory. "Are you all assembled?" (samaggāttha) means "Have all those who were to come arrived?" "They are proceeding" (vattantī) means "They are coming" (they have mastered it by heart). "Should be handed over" (niyyādetabbo) means "should be entrusted" (should be concluded). "Should be recited" (osāretabbo) means the Pali (the Pali of the heavy rules) should be recited. The phrase beginning with "vassasatūpasampannāya" shows the Pali that should be recited.
58:
Among those (Garudhammas), 'proper conduct' (sāmīcikamma) refers to appropriate duties such as making way, fanning, and inquiring about or offering drinking water. In this context, a bhikkhunī must perform the act of salutation (abhivādana) to a bhikkhu whether in a village, outside a village, inside a monastery, outside a monastery, inside a house, or on a main road. This must be done even at the minimum when the road is being cleared for a royal procession, when it is raining, when the ground is muddy, when she is holding an umbrella and an alms-bowl in her hands, or even when being pursued by elephants, horses, and so on. If she sees monks entering for alms-food in a continuous line, she should pay homage in one place, saying, 'I pay homage, Venerable Sirs.' If they are walking with a distance of about twelve cubits between them, she must pay homage to each one separately. If they are seated in a large assembly, she should pay homage in one place. This same method applies to the act of raising joined palms (añjalikamma). However, a bhikkhunī who is seated anywhere must rise (paccuṭṭhāna) [upon seeing a monk]. She must perform each respective duty at the place and time appropriate to that particular act of proper conduct (sāmīcikamma).

'Sakkattvā' means acting in such a way that the deed is well-done. 'Garukatvā' means generating reverence in that act of salutation and so on. 'Mānetvā' means acting with mental endearment. 'Pūjetvā' means honoring by performing these three types of actions (sakkāra, garukāra, mānanā). 'Anatikkamanīyo' means that which must not be transgressed.

Regarding the term 'abhikkhuke āvāse' (in a residence without monks), if there are no monks who can give exhortation (ovāda) living within half a yojana of the bhikkhunī's residence, it is called a 'residence without monks' (abhikkhuka āvāsa). One must not spend the rains retreat (vassa) in such a residence. For it was said (in the Pācittiya Pāḷi): 'A residence called "without monks" is one where it is not possible to go for exhortation or for communion (uposatha and pavāraṇā).' Furthermore, it is not possible to go beyond that half-yojana distance after the meal, listen to the Dhamma, and return. If bhikkhunīs who do not wish to spend the rains retreat there are told by relatives or supporters, 'Venerable ladies, please stay; we will invite and bring monks here,' then it is proper to stay. If monks who wish to spend the rains retreat within the stated distance arrive and have stayed even for a single night in a pavilion roofed with branches—provided they are those who intend to stay and are not just those who wish to leave after being invited for a meal—by this much it becomes a 'residence with monks' (sabhikkhuka āvāsa), and it is proper to enter the rains retreat there. Those entering the retreat must request the monks on the thirteenth day of the fortnight, saying, 'Venerable Sirs, we shall stay under your exhortation.' However, if there is a residence of monks at a distance of half a yojana by a straight path, but traveling by that path poses a danger to life or a danger to the holy life (brahmacariya), and by another path...
59:
...if traveling by another path results in a distance exceeding half a yojana, this residence remains categorized as a 'residence without monks.' However, if there is another bhikkhunī residence in a safe place about one gāvuta away from that residence, those bhikkhunīs should request the bhikkhunīs of that other residence and then go again to the monks and request: 'Venerable Sirs, there is danger on our straight path, and by another path, the distance exceeds half a yojana. However, there is another bhikkhunī residence about one gāvuta from our residence on the way; we shall stay there under the exhortation that comes from the presence of the Venerable Sirs.' Those monks must accept. Then, those bhikkhunīs must come to that bhikkhunī residence and perform the Uposatha; or, having met those bhikkhunīs, it is also proper to return to their own residence to perform it.

If monks who wish to enter the rains retreat arrive at the monastery on the fourteenth day, and being asked by the bhikkhunīs, 'Venerable Sirs, will you spend the rains retreat here?' they reply, 'Yes.' After the bhikkhunīs have said, 'In that case, Venerable Sirs, we too shall stay depending on your exhortation,' if on the second day the monks do not see an abundance of alms-food in the village and depart thinking, 'It is not possible to stay here,' what should be done if the bhikkhunīs go to the monastery on the Uposatha day and do not find the monks? They must go to where the monks are living and enter the later rains retreat (pacchimikā vassa). Or, with the intention that 'monks will come to enter the later rains retreat,' they should stay under the exhortation of the monks who arrive. 

If no monks arrive even for the later rains retreat, and there is danger from kings, danger from thieves, or famine on the journey, an offense is incurred by the bhikkhunī who stays in the residence without monks, and an offense is also incurred by the bhikkhunī who goes after breaking the rains retreat; that offense must be guarded against. However, it is taught that in times of danger, there is no offense for a bhikkhunī staying in a residence without monks. If monks arrive and enter the rains retreat but then depart for some reason, the bhikkhunīs must simply continue to stay. For it was said: 'There is no offense if the monks who entered the rains retreat have departed, or have disrobed, or have passed away, or have joined another faction, or in times of danger, or for a mad bhikkhunī, or for the first-offender.' As for the bhikkhunī performing Pavāraṇā, she must go to where the monks are and perform Pavāraṇā.

'Anvaddhamāsaṃ' means every half-month. 'Dve dhammā paccāsīsitabbā' means two things (practices) should be desired. 'Uposathapucchakaṃ' means asking about the Uposatha day. In that regard, for the Uposatha on the fifteenth day, one goes on the fourteenth day of the fortnight; for the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, one goes on the thirteenth day...
60:
The Uposatha day should be inquired about. In the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, however, it is stated: "One should go only on the thirteenth day of the fortnight and ask, 'Is this Uposatha on the fourteenth or the fifteenth?'" One should approach for the purpose of receiving exhortation (ovāda) on the Uposatha day. From the first day of the waxing (or waning) moon onwards, one should go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. In this way, the Blessed One, without giving opportunity for other work, prescribed for the bhikkhunīs only the constant going to the presence of the bhikkhus. Why? Because women (mātugāma) have tender wisdom (mandapaññā). Since women have tender wisdom, constant hearing of the Dhamma is of great benefit. When hearing the Dhamma in this way, they will not be conceited, thinking, 'The venerable ones know only what we know,' and by attending upon the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, they will be able to make their renunciation fruitful; therefore, the Blessed One arranged it thus. The bhikkhunīs also, saying 'We will practice as we have been instructed,' all of them constantly approached the monastery.

Regarding this matter, it is said: "At that time, the entire Bhikkhunī Saṅgha went to receive exhortation. People complained, grumbled, and spread rumors, saying, 'These are the wives of these [monks], these are the mistresses of these [monks]; now these [monks] will delight with these [nuns].' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [He said:] 'Monks, the entire Bhikkhunī Saṅgha should not go to receive exhortation. If they go, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Monks, I allow four or five bhikkhunīs to go to receive exhortation.' Again, they complained in the same way. Again, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I allow two or three bhikkhunīs to go to receive exhortation.'"

Therefore, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha should request and send two or three bhikkhunīs, instructing them: "Go, sisters, and request the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the approach for exhortation. The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha requests the venerable ones... [pe]... for the approach for exhortation." Those bhikkhunīs should go to the monastery. Then, having approached and paid homage to a monk who will receive the request for exhortation, one bhikkhunī should address that monk thus: "Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests the approach for exhortation. May the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha receive the approach for exhortation." That monk should approach the monk who recites the Pātimokkha and address him thus: "Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests the approach for exhortation. May the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha receive the approach for exhortation." The Pātimokkha reciter should ask: "Is there any monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka)?" If there is someone...
61:
If there is a monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka), the Pātimokkha reciter should say: "The monk named so-and-so is appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approach that monk."

If there is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs, the Pātimokkha reciter should ask: "Which venerable one is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs?" If a certain monk is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs and is endowed with the eight qualities, after appointing him, [the reciter] should say: "The monk named so-and-so is appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approach that monk."

However, if no monk at all is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs, the Pātimokkha reciter should say: "There is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha strive for perfection [in the three trainings] with a graceful manner." By this much speech alone, the Dispensation (Sāsana), which is summarized in the three trainings (sikkhā-ttaya), is declared. That monk [the messenger], having accepted saying "Very well," should inform the bhikkhunīs on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada). The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha should also send those bhikkhunīs, instructing them: "Go, sisters, and ask, 'Venerable sir, does the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha receive the approach for exhortation?'" Having accepted saying "Very well, sister," they go to the monastery, approach that monk, and should speak thus: "Venerable sir, does the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha receive the approach for exhortation?" He should say: "There is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha strive for perfection with a graceful manner." They should accept saying "Very well, venerable sir." This [plural] speech is said with reference to the bhikkhunīs who come together. In fact, among those bhikkhunīs, only one should do the requesting and the accepting; the other bhikkhunīs are merely her companions.

Furthermore, if the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha or the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is not complete (in number), or if on both sides there is only a small group (gaṇa) or just individuals, or if one bhikkhunī is sent from many nunneries for the purpose of exhortation, in such a case, this is the sequence of words: "Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request the approach for exhortation. May the bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation." [Or if it is one nun:] "Venerable sir, I pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request the approach for exhortation. May I receive the approach for exhortation."
62:
“Venerable sirs, the community of bhikkhunīs pays homage to the feet of the venerable ones and requests to approach for exhortation. Venerable sirs, may the community of bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated. “Venerable sirs, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the venerable ones and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sirs, may the bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated. “Venerable sirs, I pay homage to the feet of the venerable ones and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sirs, may I receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

“Venerable sir, the community of bhikkhunīs pays homage to the feet of the venerable one and requests to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the community of bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated. “Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the venerable one and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated. “Venerable sir, I pay homage to the feet of the venerable one and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may I receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

“Venerable sirs, the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha (or) the venerable ones (or) the venerable one, and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sirs, may the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

That monk who receives the exhortation should also speak thus at the time of the Uposatha: “Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the bhikkhunīs receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated. “Venerable sir, the bhikkhunī pays homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the bhikkhunī receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

“Venerable sir, the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī pay homage to the feet of the venerable ones and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the bhikkhunī receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

“Venerable sir, the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the venerable ones, and request to approach for exhortation. Venerable sir, may the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī receive the approach for exhortation.” It should be stated.

If there is an authorized monk, the monk who recites the Pātimokkha should also say, according to the previous method: “Let the bhikkhunīs approach that monk,” “Let the bhikkhunī approach that monk,” “Let the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī approach that monk.” If there is no [authorized monk]...
63:
The monk who inspires confidence should say: “May the community of bhikkhunīs, the bhikkhunīs, and the bhikkhunī be successful (sampādetu).” The monk who accepts the exhortation should bring it back on the day of Paṭipadā and speak in the same manner. Regarding the exhortation, except for the ignorant monk (bāla), the sick monk (gilāna), and the traveling monk (gamika), other monks, even if they are forest-dwellers (āraññaka), are not allowed to refuse to accept it. For it was said by the Blessed One:
“I allow, monks, the remaining monks, except for the ignorant, the sick, and those going on a journey, to receive the exhortation” (Cūḷavagga 414).

Among those, a monk who wishes to travel on the Uposatha days of the 14th or 15th, or on the day of Paṭipadā, is called a traveler (gamika). Even if that monk is to depart on the second day of the fortnight, he is not allowed to not receive the exhortation. He commits an offense as it was said: “Monks, the exhortation must not be not received. Whoever should not receive it, commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” (Cūḷavagga 414). Having received the exhortation, it is not proper to not announce it in the Uposatha hall or to not bring it back to the bhikkhunīs on the day of Paṭipadā. For it was said:
“Monks, the exhortation must not be not announced. Whoever should not announce it, commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Cūḷavagga 415).
It was also said elsewhere:
“Monks, the exhortation must not be not brought back. Whoever should not bring it back, commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Cūḷavagga 415).

Among those who accept the exhortation, the forest-dwelling monk should make an appointment for the purpose of bringing back the exhortation. For it was said: “I allow, monks, a forest-dwelling monk to receive the exhortation and to make an appointment, saying ‘I will bring it back here’.” Therefore, if a forest-dwelling monk obtains alms in the village where the bhikkhunīs reside, he should wander for alms there, and upon seeing the bhikkhunīs, he should depart after announcing the exhortation. If alms are difficult to obtain in that village, he should wander for alms in a nearby village and then come to the bhikkhunīs' village and act in the same way. If he must go to a distant place, an appointment should be made: “I will come to such-and-such a rest-house, pavilion, or the foot of a tree at your village gate; come to that place.”
64:
"Come," (is the appointment). The bhikkhunīs must go to that appointed place; they are not allowed not to go. For it has been said: "Monks, a bhikkhunī should not fail to go to an appointment. For one who does not go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." (Cūḷavagga, 415).

In the statement "Invitation (pavāraṇā) should be made in both assemblies," the bhikkhunīs, having performed pavāraṇā among themselves on the fourteenth day, should perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha on the Uposatha day. For it has been said: "Monks, I allow [them] to perform pavāraṇā today (the 14th) and to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha on the following day (the 15th, Uposatha day)." (Cūḷavagga, 427).

The decision here should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka. For it has been said:

"At that time, the entire Bhikkhunī Saṅgha made a great noise while performing pavāraṇā. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [He said:] 'Monks, I allow a wise and competent bhikkhunī to be appointed to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the sake of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. And thus, monks, she should be appointed. First, the bhikkhunī should be requested. Having requested her, a wise and competent bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha:

'Venerable Ladies of the Saṅgha, please listen to me. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint bhikkhunī so-and-so to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the sake of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. This is the motion (ñatti).

'Venerable Ladies of the Saṅgha, please listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints bhikkhunī so-and-so to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the sake of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. Whichever venerable lady approves of the appointment of bhikkhunī so-and-so to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the sake of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, let her be silent. Whichever lady does not approve, let her speak.

'Bhikkhunī so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha to perform pavāraṇā before the Bhikkhu Saṅgha for the sake of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record it.'" (Cūḷavagga, 427).
65:
That appointed bhikkhunī, taking the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha with her, should approach the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, and with hands joined in salutation, should speak thus: "Venerable Sirs, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites the Bhikkhu Saṅgha—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sirs, let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends. Venerable Sirs, for a second time... Venerable Sirs, for a third time, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha... will make amends."

If the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha is not complete (a full quorum): "Venerable Sirs, these bhikkhunīs invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sirs, let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha speak to these bhikkhunīs out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends." And: "Venerable Sir, I invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sir, let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha speak to me out of compassion; seeing [an offense], I will make amends." Thus it should be said three times.

If the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is not complete: "Venerable Sirs (to a group), the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sirs, speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends." And: "Venerable Sir (to an individual), the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sir, speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends." Thus it should be said three times.

If both sides are not complete: "Venerable Sirs, these bhikkhunīs invite you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sirs, speak to these bhikkhunīs out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends." And: "Venerable Sir, these bhikkhunīs invite you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sir, speak to these bhikkhunīs out of compassion; seeing [an offense], they will make amends." And: "Venerable Sirs, I invite you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sirs, speak to me out of compassion; seeing [an offense], I will make amends." And: "Venerable Sir, I invite you—by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable Sir, speak to me out of compassion; seeing [an offense], I will make amends." Thus it should be said three times.

The practice of mānatta and the seeking of higher ordination (upasampadā) will also be clear in their respective places [in the Pali text].
66:
A bhikkhunī should not, by any means, or by the ten grounds for abuse, or by any other means, abuse, revile, or threaten a bhikkhu with danger. 'Ovaṭa' means obstructed, forbidden, or rejected. 'Vacanapatha' means speech itself. 'Anovaṭa' means unobstructed, not forbidden, or not rejected. Therefore, a bhikkhunī, standing in a position of authority or seniority, should not instruct or admonish a bhikkhu by any means, such as saying, "Go forward like this, go back like this, dress in the inner robe like this, dress in the upper robe like this."

However, upon seeing a fault, it is proper to point out an existing fault in this manner: "In the past, the great elders did not go forward like this, did not go back like this, did not dress in the inner robe like this, did not dress in the upper robe like this, did not wear such dyed robes, and did not anoint their eyes like this," and so on. Monks, however, may instruct or admonish a bhikkhunī as they wish, saying, "This old nun dresses in the inner robe like this, dresses in the upper robe like this; do not dress in the inner robe like this, do not dress in the upper robe like this; do not perform tasks such as rubbing with sesame oil or picking vegetables."

Teaching another Dhamma to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha who says, "Venerable sirs, we are in harmony," means teaching another Suttanta or Abhidhamma. Indeed, by the words "We are in harmony," they expect the exhortation (ovāda); therefore, for a monk who teaches another Dhamma instead of the exhortation, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). "Without handing over the exhortation" means without saying, "Sisters, this is the exhortation."

In the words beginning with "adhammakamma," the act of formal appointment of a monk as an exhorter (bhikkhunovādaka-sammuti-kamma) should be understood as the "act" (kamma). In that unlawful act (adhammakamma), by way of the two groups of nine (navaka), eighteen pācittiya offenses occur. In a lawful act (dhammakamma), there is no offense (anāpatti) in the final clause of the second group of nine; in the remaining clauses, seventeen dukkaṭa offenses occur.

"Giving the recitation (uddesa)" means reciting the Pali text of the eight heavy rules (garudhammas). "Giving the explanation (paripucchā)" means explaining the commentary of that very Pali text of the eight heavy rules which has been mastered. Reciting when requested, "Venerable sir, please recite and chant," means reciting the Pali text of the eight heavy rules. Thus, for a monk who gives the recitation, gives the explanation, or recites the eight heavy rules when requested, there is no pācittiya offense. For one who teaches another Dhamma, there is no dukkaṭa offense. If a bhikkhunī asks a question concerning the heavy rules or concerning the aggregates (khandhas), etc., and a monk answers that question,
67:
for that monk also, there is no offense. "Teaching for the sake of others" means that while a monk is teaching the Dhamma to the fourfold assembly, bhikkhunīs approach and listen; in that case too, there is no offense for the monk. "To probationary nuns (sikkhamānās) and novice nuns (sāmaṇerīs)" means there is no offense for a monk who teaches (the garudhammas) to these probationary nuns and novice nuns. The remaining words are clear in meaning.

The origin of the Padasodhamma training rule arises from speech, and from speech and mind; it is an action (kiriya); there is no release from offense by perception (no saññāvimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is a breach of a conventional rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is a vocal act (vacīkamma); it has three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The First Ovāda Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Atthaṅgata Training Rule

In the second training rule, "pariyāyena" means by turn, or in order. "Adhicetaso" means one with a superior mind, one endowed with the fruit of Arahantship which is superior to all types of consciousness. "Appamajjato" means one who is not negligent, meaning one endowed with the constant performance of wholesome states through heedfulness (appamāda). "Munino" refers to the verse: "He who knows both worlds is called a sage (muni) for that reason" (Dhp. 269); thus, he is called a muni because of knowing both worlds, or because he is endowed with knowledge called "mona," an Arahant is called a muni; to that muni. "Monapathesu sikkhato" means training in the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammas) which are the paths of mona (knowledge of Arahantship), or training in the three trainings (sikkhās). This is said by taking the practice of the preliminary stage. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: to the muni who, having practiced in the preliminary stage, has reached the state of a muni through this practice.

"Sokā na bhavanti tādino" means that within such a Khīṇāsava sage, there are no sorrows caused by separation from loved objects and so on. Or, "tādino" means for a muni of such a nature who is endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi-lakkhaṇa), sorrows do not occur; this is the meaning here. "Upasantassa" means for one who is calmed by the subsiding of lust and other defilements. "Sadā satīmato" means for one who is never without mindfulness because of having reached the fullness of mindfulness. "Ākāse antalikkhe" means in the sky known as the firmament; it is not the space obtained by removing a kasina (kasiṇugghāṭima), nor is it the space that delimits material form (rūpapariiccheda). "Caṅkamatipi tiṭṭhatipi" means of those bhikkhunīs...
68:
Hearing such words, [he thought], "These bhikkhunīs underestimate me, thinking 'This venerable one knows only this much.' Well then, I shall now show them my power." Having aroused great appreciation for the Dhamma, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā). Emerging from it, he performed such a miracle of psychic power as "walking in the air... disappearing." In that context, "disappearing" means reaching the state of being invisible. That elder recited that inspired utterance (udāna) as well as many other words of the Buddha (Buddhavacana). It is said that the elder, in the presence of his elder brother—

"Behold the radiant Aṅgīrasa,
Shining like the sun in the sky,
Like a fragrant Kokanuda lotus,
Blooming in the morning with its scent unfaded."

Having been assigned this verse, he recited it for four months but could not master it. Therefore, his elder brother, saying "You are not worthy of this Dispensation (Sāsana)," expelled him from the monastery. He stood at the gateway weeping. Then the Blessed One, surveying beings to be tamed with his Buddha-eye, saw him. As if wandering through the monastery, He approached him and asked, "Cūḷapanthaka, why are you weeping?" He reported the matter. Then the Blessed One gave him a piece of clean cloth and said, "Rub this, saying 'Removal of impurity, removal of impurity' (rajo-haraṇaṃ)." He accepted it, saying "Very well, Bhante," and sat in his place. As he rubbed one end of the cloth, the place he rubbed became black. He gained a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "Even such a pure cloth has become soiled because of this body (attabhāva)," and began to practice insight (vipassanā). Then the Blessed One, knowing his effort was aroused, spoke this verse of radiance beginning with "Adhicetaso." At the end of the verse, the elder attained Arahantship. Therefore, the elder naturally cherishes this verse; to make known his cherishing of it, he recites that very verse. He also brought forth and recited many other words of the Buddha in between. Thus it is said: "He recited that inspired utterance as well as many other words of the Buddha."

"Ordained by one side" (ekato upasampannāya) refers to a bhikkhunī who has received ordination in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. However, for a monk who instructs a bhikkhunī who received ordination in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The rest of the words are clear. This training rule also has its origin in the same way as the Padaso-dhamma rule. The second training rule, the Atthaṅgata Sikkhāpada, is finished. In the explanation of the third training rule, the Bhikkhunupassaya Sikkhāpada: In the words beginning with "Aññatra... pācittiyassa," it should be understood that a pācittiya offense is incurred only when instructing with the eight heavy rules (garudhammas). If instructing with other teachings, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred. "Ordained by one side" refers to one who has received ordination in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. For a monk who instructs one who received ordination in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, only a pācittiya offense is incurred. Hereafter, wherever "ekato upasampannā" is mentioned, this meaning should be understood. The rest of the words are clear. The third training rule, the Bhikkhunupassaya Sikkhāpada, is finished. In this training rule, the miscellaneous decision mentioned in the Mahāpaccariya is: If an unauthorized monk, after sunset, [goes] to the bhikkhunīs' quarters...
69:
"One who is ordained on one side" refers to a bhikkhunī who has received ordination in the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha; for a monk who instructs a bhikkhunī who has received ordination in the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The rest of the words here are clear. This rule also has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Padasodhamma rule.

## Atthaṅgata-sikkhāpada, the Second.

## 3. Explanation of the Bhikkhunupassaya Training Rule

In the third training rule, among the words beginning with "Instructing except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation," it should be understood that there is an offense of expiation only for a monk who instructs with the eight Weighty Rules (Garudhammas); if he instructs with other Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "One who is ordained on one side" refers to a bhikkhunī who has received ordination in the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha; however, for one who instructs a bhikkhunī who has received ordination in the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, there is only an offense of expiation. Hereafter, wherever "ekato-upasampannā" is mentioned, this same meaning should be understood. The rest is clear. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of this training rule is like the Kaṭhina-samuṭṭhāna: it arises from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya), not released by perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a breach of a regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), a vocal action (vacīkamma), involving three types of consciousness (ti-citta), and three types of feeling (ti-vedana).

## Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada, the Third.

The miscellaneous decision stated in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary regarding this training rule is: If an unauthorized monk approaches a nunnery after sunset and instructs with the eight Weighty Rules, there are three offenses of expiation. If he instructs with other Dhamma, there are two offenses of wrong-doing and one offense of expiation. How? One wrong-doing due to being unauthorized; one wrong-doing due to going to the nunnery and instructing with other Dhamma; and one expiation due to instructing after sunset. For an authorized monk who goes there after sunset and instructs with the eight Weighty Rules, there is one non-offense (anāpatti) and two offenses of expiation. How? A non-offense because he is authorized; one expiation due to instructing after sunset; and one expiation due to going and instructing with the Weighty Rules—thus two offenses of expiation. If that same authorized monk instructs with other Dhamma, there is one non-offense, one wrong-doing, and one expiation. How? A non-offense because he is authorized; one wrong-doing due to going and instructing with other Dhamma; and one expiation due to instructing after sunset.
70:
One should know the remaining offenses and non-offenses, excluding the single pācittiya offense based on teaching at night, for an authorized or unauthorized monk who goes and teaches during the day.

## The miscellaneous discussion is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Āmisa Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, "na bahukatā" means they are not highly esteemed; the meaning is that they do not teach out of great respect for the Dhamma. The meaning of the words beginning with "bhikkhunovādakaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kattukāmo" should be understood in the same way as stated in the Ujjhāpanaka training rule.

In the phrase "upasampannaṃ saṅghena asammataṃ", "asammata" (unauthorized) should be understood as a monk who has been assigned a duty by an authorized monk or by the Saṅgha. In the phrase "anupasampannaṃ sammataṃ vā asammataṃ vā", one who received the authorization to teach nuns (bhikkhunovādaka-sammuti) while a monk but now remains in the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) is called "sammata" (authorized). A learned novice who has been assigned a duty by an authorized monk or by the Saṅgha should be understood as "asammata" (unauthorized). The rest is clear as it follows the method already mentioned.

This training rule has three origins (samuṭṭhāna). It arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action (kiriya). It is released by perception (saññā-vimokkha). It is intentional (sacittaka). It is a worldly fault (lokavajja). It is bodily action and vocal action. It involves unwholesome consciousness and painful feeling.

## The fourth, the Āmisa Training Rule, is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Cīvaradāna Training Rule

In the fifth training rule, "visikhāya" means in the street. "Piṇḍāya carati" means wandering frequently by way of regular wandering for alms. "Sandiṭṭhā" means they were acquaintances (seen friends). The remaining words in this rule are clear in meaning. Regarding the decision, it should be understood together with the origins and so forth in the same way as stated in the Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇa training rule. In that Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇa training rule, the monk is the recipient, but in this training rule, the nun is the recipient. This is the distinction. The rest is just like that training rule.

## The fifth, the Cīvaradāna Training Rule, is finished.
71:
## 6. Commentary on the Cīvarasibbana Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, "Udāyī" refers to the frivolous Lāḷudāyī. "Paṭṭha" means capable, having subtle wisdom, and being skillful. "Aññatarā bhikkhunī" refers to the former wife of that same Lāḷudāyī. "Paṭibhānacitta" refers to an artistic figure made by one's own ingenuity. It is heard that after dyeing the robe, Lāḷudāyī made figures of a man and a woman in the middle of that robe with various colored threads, depicting unfinished sexual intercourse. Therefore, it is said, "having caused an artistic figure to appear in the middle." "Yathāsaṃhaṭa" means just as it was folded.

"Cīvara" (robe) refers to a cloth that can be worn or draped. This is stated in the commentaries such as the Mahāpaccari. In the phrase "sews it himself," a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a monk who plans and arranges, saying "I will sew," as well as by a monk who cuts the cloth. For a monk who sews, however, there is a pācittiya offense. "For every needle path" (ārapatha) means in the act of inserting and withdrawing the needle repeatedly. If, however, one does not withdraw the entire needle but pierces and withdraws it even a hundred times for the purpose of inserting a long thread, only one pācittiya is incurred. "Once commanded" means being told once, "Sew the robe." Even if one sews much, finishing all the needlework and completing the robe, only one pācittiya is incurred. Otherwise, if one says, "The work to be done on this robe is your responsibility," and the monk does it, a single pācittiya is incurred for every needle path by the commanded monk. For the commanding monk, many pācittiyas are incurred with a single word. In the case of repeated commands, there is no need to even mention it.

If, while teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya) are sewing a robe for their own relative nuns, their dependents sew it, thinking "We are performing the duty for the teacher and preceptor" or "We are performing the Kathina duty," offenses are incurred by those dependents according to the number of needle paths. If teachers and preceptors have their resident pupils sew a robe for their (the teachers') relatives, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the teachers and preceptors, and a pācittiya offense by the pupils. The same method applies when pupils have their teachers and preceptors sew a robe for their (the pupils') relatives. If it is a robe of a nun who is a relative of both the pupils and the teachers and preceptors, but the teachers and preceptors deceive the pupils into sewing it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by both. Why? Because the pupils sew it thinking she is not a relative, and the others (the teachers) have urged them in what is not allowable. Therefore, one should have it sewn only after explaining, "This is a robe for your mother" or "This is a robe for your sister."
72:
"Other requisites" refers to any requisite such as a sandal bag and so forth. The rest of the words are clear in meaning. This training rule has six origins (samuṭṭhāna): action, not released by perception, without thought, worldly fault (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## Sixth Training Rule on Sewing Robes (Cīvarasibbana-sikkhāpada).

## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Arranging [a Journey] (Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the seventh training rule, "thieves robbed the bhikkhunīs who were following behind" means thieves took the bowls and robes of the bhikkhunīs who were following behind. "Assaulted" means the thieves violated those bhikkhunīs, causing the destruction of their virtue (sīla).

182-183. "Having arranged" (saṃvidhāya) means having planned well, making an appointment regarding the time and place at the time of departure. In the term "kukkuṭasampāda" (a cock's walk), a village where a cock can go from one village to another just by walking is called a kukkuṭasampāda. The word-meaning is: they can go well here, thus it is sampāda. Who can go? Cocks. Since it is the place where cocks go, it is kukkuṭasampāda. Alternatively, sampāda means going; since there is the going of cocks, it is kukkuṭasampāda. There is also a reading "kukkuṭasampāta" (a cock's flight); in that case, a village where a cock flies up from the roof of one house and lands on the roof of another house is called kukkuṭasampāta. The word-meaning should be understood in the same way as mentioned before. Both types of villages mentioned are so close that the village precinct (upacāra) cannot be distinguished. In a country full of such villages where the sound of a cock crowing at dawn in one village can be heard in the adjacent village, it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that a Pācittiya offense is incurred for every interval between villages [if traveling by arrangement]. Even though it is so stated, according to the word "a Pācittiya offense for every interval between villages," even if the villages are separated by only one cubit (ratana), an offense is incurred for the monk who enters the precinct of that village as designated by people.

The decision regarding the offense is as follows: If at the time of arranging, both [the monk and the nun] are standing in a bhikkhunī's quarters, or a monastery within a village, or a refectory, or a dwelling of non-Buddhists (titthiya-seyyā), and they arrange it, there is no offense because these are allowable grounds (kappiya-bhūmi). Therefore, in this case...
73:
...they do not say it is a Dukkaṭa offense due to the arrangement; for the one who goes, the offense is according to the object [i.e., Pācittiya]. However, if they arrange it inside a village, at the gate of a bhikkhunī's quarters, on a carriage road, or in other places such as a crossroads, a junction of three roads, or an elephant stable, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the monk. Having arranged thus, they depart from the village; there is no offense in departing. However, when entering the precinct (upacāra) of the adjacent village, a Pācittiya offense is incurred by the monk. Regarding that, it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that "there is a Dukkaṭa on the first step, and a Pācittiya on the second step." After departing from the village, as long as they have not yet entered the precinct of the adjacent village, even if they arrange it in that interval, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the monk; when entering the precinct of the adjacent village, the offense is incurred as in the previous method. If they wish to go a long distance, an offense is incurred for every entry into a village precinct according to the number of village precincts; however, there is no offense when passing through those villages.

If a bhikkhunī intends to go to a certain village and leaves her quarters, and a monk also intends to go to that same village and leaves his monastery, and then both meet at the village gate and [the nun] asks, "Where are you going, Bhante?" and he replies, "I am going to such-and-such a village," and he asks, "Where are you going?" and they reply, "We are also going there," and they arrange it saying, "Come now, let us go," and they go together, there is no offense. Why? Because it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that they had already intended to go before arranging. That statement does not agree with the Pāḷi nor with the other Commentaries.

"At every half-yojana" (addhayojane addhayojane) means for a monk crossing each half-yojana, when it is time to say "now he will cross," there is a Dukkaṭa on the first step and a Pācittiya on the second step. In this method, an offense is incurred upon crossing, but there is no offense upon entering the precinct.

"The monk arranges" means seeing a bhikkhunī at a city gate or on a carriage road and asking, "Have you ever been to such-and-such a village?" If she replies, "I have never been there, Bhante," he says, "Come, let us go," or "I will go tomorrow, you should come too." "The bhikkhunī arranges" means seeing a monk leaving a village to pay homage to a shrine in another village and asking, "Where are you going, Bhante?" He says, "To such-and-such a village to pay homage to a shrine." She says, "I will also come, Bhante." In this way, only the bhikkhunī arranges, not the monk.

Regarding "by breaking the appointment" (visaṅketena), if they say "we will go before the meal" but go after the meal, or if they say "we will go today" but go tomorrow. In this way...
74:
There is no offense only in the case of a mistake in the appointed time; however, if there is a mistake in the appointed gate or a mistake in the appointed path, there is indeed an offense. "Āpadāsu" refers to times of danger such as when a country is in turmoil and the inhabitants of the countryside travel about having mounted carts; in such dangers, there is no offense. The rest of the text is clear.

(This training rule) has 4 origins (samuṭṭhāna): it arises through the body, through body and speech, through body and mind, and through body, speech, and mind. It is an action (kiriya); it is not released by perception (no saññāvimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is a prescribed wrong (paṇṇattivajja); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with 3 types of consciousness and 3 types of feeling.

## The Seventh Training Rule on Making Arrangements is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Boarding a Boat

In the eighth training rule, "saṃvidhāya" means having made an arrangement with the aim of enjoyment through the power of worldly friendship. "Uddhaṃgāminiṃ" refers to a boat going upstream against the current of a river. Since a monk who plays with a boat called ujjavanikā due to its speed going upstream is said to "board a boat going upstream," therefore, to show only the meaning of that term in the word-analysis (padabhājana), it is said "ujjavanikāya." "Adhogāminiṃ" refers to a boat going downstream with the current. Since a monk who plays with a boat called ojavanikā due to its speed going downstream is said to "board a boat going downstream," therefore, to show the meaning of that term also in the word-analysis, it is said "ojavanikāya." Among those boats, there is no offense in being carried upstream or downstream for the purpose of reaching a landing place (tittha). In the phrase "tiriyaṃ taraṇāya," the ablative case (of taraṇāya) is used in the sense of the accusative case.

In the phrase "gāmantare gāmantare," if one bank of a river is crowded without gaps with villages within a cock's flight of each other, and the other bank is a forest without villages, when traveling along the side of the bank with villages, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every village passed; when traveling along the side of the bank without villages, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every half-league (addha-yojana). If the river is one league wide, it should be understood that pācittiya offenses are incurred for every half-league even when traveling through the middle of that river. Regarding the exception "for crossing across" (tiriyaṃ taraṇāya), there is no offense not only in crossing a river, but also for a monk who goes from a great landing port to Tāmalitti or Suvaṇṇabhūmi. This is because in all commentaries, the offense is examined only regarding rivers, not regarding the ocean.
75:
In the term "visanketena," in this training rule also, there is no offense only due to a mistake in the appointed time; however, for one going with a mistake in the appointed landing place or a mistake in the appointed boat, there is indeed an offense. The rest of the passage is just like the first training rule, along with the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on.

## The Eighth Training Rule on Boarding a Boat.

## 9. Explanation of the Training Rule on Food Caused to be Prepared

In the ninth training rule—the phrase "mahānāge tiṭṭhamāne" uses the accusative case in the sense of the locative case, meaning "while the Great Serpents (Great Elders) were present." Alternatively, the remaining word "adissā" (not seeing) should be inserted and considered here as "without seeing that the Great Serpents were present." Otherwise, the meaning would not be appropriate. "Antarākathā" refers to a talk that has reached the middle between the beginning and the end, without having reached the conclusion. "Vippakatā" means being spoken. The words "Truly, householder, by you the Great Serpents..." and so on were spoken by that nun after she looked askance and saw the elders entering, and knowing that they had heard.

"Bhikkhuniparipācitaṃ" means alms-food prepared by a nun, brought to completion by praising qualities, or made to be obtained. In the word-analysis (padabhājana), however, to show that nun and the manner of her preparation, it is said: "A nun is one ordained in both Saṅghas; 'preparing' means for those who were previously unwilling to give..." and so on. In the phrase "pubbe gihisamārambhā," "pubbe" means beforehand (before the nun's preparation). "Samārambho" refers to alms-food that has been well-prepared; it is a designation for prepared alms-food. The exertion of laypeople is called "gihisamārambha." It means that for a monk who, setting aside the alms-food prepared by laypeople beforehand before the nun's preparation, eats other alms-food, there is an offense; but if he eats that prepared alms-food, there is no offense. In the word-analysis, however, since alms-food, even if not specifically prepared for a monk by relatives or those who have given an invitation, is effectively already prepared because it can be requested as desired, therefore, disregarding the literal expression and wishing to show only the meaning, it is said: "What is called gihisamārambha refers to relatives or those who have given an invitation."
76:
"Pakatipatiyattaṃ" means it has been prepared naturally for the benefit of that monk, with the intention, "We shall offer it to the Elder." In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is stated generally without distinction, not saying "for that monk" or "for another monk," but rather "it is prepared with the thought, 'We shall offer it to the monks.'"

"Excluding the five kinds of meals, there is no offense in all cases" means that in all cases involving gruel, hard food, small fruits, and large fruits, there is no offense even if prepared by a bhikkhunī. The remaining words are clear. Like the origin of the first Pārājika, it originates from body and mind; it is an action (kiriya), it is released by perception (saññāvimokkha), it is intentional (sacittaka), it is a violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), it is a bodily action (kāyakamma), and it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Ninth Training Rule on Having Food Cooked (Paripācita) is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting in Private (Rahonisajja)

In the tenth training rule, the entire meaning of the Pali text and the decision should be understood in the same manner as stated in the second Aniyata. This is because this training rule is identical to the second Aniyata training rule and the fourth training rule of Upananda in the Acelaka Chapter above. However, it was laid down separately by way of the origin of the story.

## The Tenth Training Rule on Sitting in Private is finished.

## The Third Chapter on Bhikkhunīs (Bhikkhunīvagga) is finished according to the commentary order.

## 4. The Chapter on Meals (Bhojanavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Public Alms-food (Āvasathapiṇḍa)

In the first training rule of the Bhojanavagga, "āvasathapiṇḍa" refers to alms-food (rice) established at a rest-house or similar dwelling. Having built a rest-house that is enclosed, provided with couches and stools as appropriate for travelers, the sick, pregnant women, and ascetics, and consisting of many rooms and a porch, those desiring merit establish alms-food there. The meaning is that all consumables such as gruel, rice, and medicine are placed there for the purpose of being offered to various travelers, the sick, and so on. "Yesterday also" means "tomorrow also."
77:
"Apasakkanti" means they move away. When people do not see the non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas) and ask, "Where have the titthiyas gone?" and hear, "They moved away upon seeing these monks," their subsequent criticism is what is meant by "manussā ujjhāyanti." "Kukkuccāyanto" means feeling remorse and giving rise to the perception of it being unallowable.

"Sakkoti" means being able to travel half a league (yojana) or a full league to depart from that rest-house. "Na sakkoti" means being unable to travel even that far. "Anodissa" means it is established for everyone without specifying only for these people or only for this many people, or for any particular sect (pāsaṇḍa). "Yāvadattho" means it is established so that one may eat as much as desired without limiting the meal to a certain amount. "Sakiṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ" means it should be eaten only once (for one day); if one accepts it starting from the second day, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and for every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

The decision in this matter is as follows: Whether by a single family or by many families together, if alms-food is established at one place or at various places without specifying the location, such as "today at one place, tomorrow at another," then after eating for one day at one place, it is not allowable to eat at that same place or another place on the second day. However, if various families establish alms-food at various places, after eating for one day at one place, it is allowable to eat at another place on the second day. But it is stated in the Mahāpaccari that it is not allowable to eat starting from the beginning again after the sequence of turns has ended. The same method applies to one or many donor groups (pūga), and one or many villages. Even if the alms-food established by a single family or many families together is interrupted occasionally due to the lack of rice and so on, that alms-food should not be eaten. If they stop, saying "We can no longer give," but later, a wholesome mind arises and they strive to give again, it is stated in the Mahāpaccari that it is allowable to eat that alms-food for one more day.

"Anāpatti gilānassa" means there is no offense for a monk who is ill (gilāna), even if he stays and eats daily. "Gacchanto vā" means there is no offense for a monk who is traveling, even if he eats for one day on the journey and for one day at the destination. The same applies to a monk who is returning. A monk who has gone and returned also has the right to eat for one day on the journey and for one day at the destination. If, after eating with the intention "I will go," he turns back while departing because the river is in flood or there is danger from thieves, and then goes when he knows it is safe, he has the right to eat for one more day. All of this is stated in the commentaries such as the Mahāpaccari.
78:
If, after having planned and eaten, a monk encounters a full river or danger from robbers while departing, and returns to wait until it is safe, the commentaries such as the Mahāpaccari state that he is allowed to eat for another day. 'Odissa paññatto' means a rule prescribed specifically for the benefit of monks. 'Na yāvadattho' means it is not prescribed for as much as one desires; rather, it is permissible to eat small amounts of such alms-food regularly. 'Excepting the five kinds of meals, in all cases' means there is no offense regarding all types of food such as gruel, snacks, and various fruits. It is permissible to eat gruel and such regularly. The rest is clear. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the offense concerning sheep's wool arises from the body, and from both body and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is not a release through perception (no-saññāvimokkha); it is without consciousness (acittaka); it is a breach of a conventional rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is a bodily action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The First Avasathapiṇḍa Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule

In the second training rule, 'one whose gain and honor have declined' refers to Devadatta. It is said that although he had King Ajātasattu kill King Bimbisāra, sent assassins to kill the Buddha, and caused the Buddha to bleed, these acts remained hidden and his guilt was not public. However, when he sent the elephant Dhanapālaka in broad daylight, his guilt became manifest. When the talk arose, 'Why did Devadatta send the elephant?', it became public knowledge: 'He not only sent the elephant, but also had the King killed, sent assassins, and rolled down a rock; Devadatta is truly wicked.' When asked, 'With whom did he do this?', they said, 'With King Ajātasattu.' Then the citizens rose up, saying, 'How can the King go about keeping such a rebel and a thorn in the Dispensation?' Knowing the city's turmoil, the King expelled Devadatta. From then on, the five hundred pots of rice sent daily for Devadatta were cut off, and the King no longer went to attend on him. Other people also considered that nothing should be given or done for Devadatta. Therefore, it is said, 'one whose gain and honor have declined.' 'He eats by begging from houses' means that, thinking 'May my group not break up,' and wishing to support his followers, he begged from houses with his group, saying, 'You, give a meal for one monk; you, give for two.'

'Robes arise sparingly' means that because people do not offer robes to monks who do not accept meals, robes become scarce.
79:
'They invite monks who are making robes with a meal' means that seeing the monks taking a long time to finish making robes because they have to go for alms in the village, people invite them with a desire for merit, thinking, 'May they finish quickly and be able to use the robes.'

'Nānāverajjake' means those who have come from various other countries. There is also a reading 'nānāvirajjake', but the meaning is the same.

217-8. 'Gaṇabhojane' means eating a meal in a group. Here, 'group' (gaṇa) refers to four or more monks. Therefore, to show the lowest limit, it was said: 'Where four monks... this is called a group meal.' That group meal arises in two ways: through invitation or through request.

How does it arise through invitation? Approaching four monks and saying, 'Venerables, I invite you with rice; please accept my rice, desire it, look upon it, consent to it, or welcome it,' or using any such synonym or other language, one invites them by mentioning the name of one of the five kinds of meals. Having been invited together in this way, if they go together, accept together, and eat together at the appointed time, whether today or tomorrow, it is a group meal, and there is an offense for all. If, having been invited together, they go together or separately, but accept together and eat separately, there is still an offense. For here, the acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) is the standard. If, having been invited together, they go together or separately, but accept separately and then eat together or separately, there is no offense.

Whether one goes to four precincts or four monasteries and invites them separately, or if, while the monks are standing in one place, one is invited by the son and another by the father, etc.—even if they are invited separately—if they go together or separately, and eat together or separately, but accept together, it is a group meal and there is an offense for all. This is how it arises through invitation.

How does it arise through request? If four monks, while standing or sitting together, see a lay follower and request, 'Give a meal for all four of us,' or if, seeing him separately, they request, 'Give to me, give to me,' whether they request together or separately, and whether they go together or separately, and after receiving the meal, whether they eat together or separately—if they accept together, it is a group meal and there is an offense for all. This is how it arises through request.
80:
The phrase "the feet are cracked" means that they are so severely cracked that the flesh can be seen from within, like seeing the flesh from the inner side of a large hide. Being so, even a mere touch by sand or gravel causes suffering, and one is unable to wander for alms within the village. When such an illness exists, it should be considered as *gilānasamaya* (the time of illness) and a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*) may be eaten; one should not make it allowable by a mere trivial pretext.

Regarding the phrase "when a robe is being made," this refers to the time when, having obtained cloth and thread, a robe is being made; there is no separate time designated as robe-making time. Therefore, anyone who performs any task that must be done for that robe (the *Mahāpaccari* states this even for one who merely threads a needle) should consider it as *cīvarakārasamaya* (robe-making time) and may eat. In the *Kurundī*, it is stated in detail: one who arranges the robe, cuts it, lays the basting thread, lays the additional layer (*āgantukapaṭṭa*), sews it back, binds the additional layer, cuts the border, rubs/smooths it, places it on top, sews it back on top, makes the thread, twists the thread, sharpens the small knife, or makes the thread-winding tool—all these are called robe-makers. However, a monk who sits nearby and recites a Jātaka or the Dhammapada is not a robe-maker. Excluding such a monk, there is no offense in a group meal for the remaining monks.

"Half a league" (*addhayojana*) means for a monk who intends to travel this much distance. For a monk who intends to travel a long distance, there is no need to even mention it (it is certainly allowed). A monk who is currently traveling is allowed to eat even within a distance of one *gāvuta* (a quarter league) within the half-league. A monk who has arrived should eat for the duration of one day. The same principle applies to boarding a boat. There is this distinction: the *Mahāpaccari* states that a monk who has boarded a boat may eat as long as he has not yet disembarked, even if he has reached his desired destination. "When a fourth monk has arrived" refers to the final limit; when a fourth monk arrives and the food is insufficient, that is a *mahāsamaya* (great occasion). In a situation where a hundred or a thousand monks assemble, there is no need to even mention it is a *mahāsamaya*. Therefore, at such a time, one should resolve it as a *mahāsamaya* and eat. "Any wanderer" (*paribbājaka*) refers to either a fellow practitioner or one of the outside ascetics; when a meal is prepared by any of these, it should be considered as *samaṇabhattasamaya* (the time of a meal for ascetics) and may be eaten.

"There is no offense during the time" means there is no offense during any one of the seven times (*samaya*). "Two or three together" means that even if monks accept an improper invitation and eat together in groups of two or three, there is no offense for them.
81:
Regarding that group meal, the decision should be understood by way of five types of 'fourth monks' (*catukka*): the uninvited fourth, the alms-food seeker fourth, the unordained fourth, the bowl-sending fourth, and the sick fourth. How? In this case, someone invites four monks, saying, "Please accept a meal." Among them, three go, and one does not. The lay devotee asks, "Venerable sir, where is the other elder?" They reply, "Lay devotee, he did not come." That lay devotee then invites any other monk who happens to arrive at that moment, saying, "Come, venerable sir," and gives food to all four. There is no offense for any of them. Why? Because the fourth monk who completes the group was not invited. Only three were invited and accepted the meal there; the group is not completed by those three, and the one who completes the group is uninvited, thus the group is broken. This is called the 'uninvited fourth monk.'

In the case of the 'alms-food seeker fourth'—at the time of invitation, one monk is an alms-food seeker (*piṇḍapātika*) and does not accept. However, at the time of going, when told, "Come, venerable sir, you will get alms-food here," they take him along even though he did not formally accept. That monk breaks the group. Therefore, there is no offense for all of them.

In the case of the 'unordained fourth'—they are invited together with a novice (*sāmaṇera*); that novice also breaks the group.

In the case of the 'bowl-sending fourth'—one monk does not go himself but sends his bowl. In this way too, the group is broken. Therefore, there is no offense for all of them.

In the case of the 'sick fourth'—they are invited together with a sick monk. In that case, only the sick monk has no offense; for the others, that sick monk is one who completes the group. The group is not broken by a sick monk. Therefore, there is an offense for those monks. However, in the *Mahāpaccari*, it is stated generally without distinction.

A monk who has obtained a valid excuse (*samaya*) is personally freed from offense, but for the remaining monks, he becomes one who completes the group and thus causes an offense. Therefore, the 'fourth monks' should also be understood by way of those who have obtained the robe-giving time (*cīvaradānasamaya*), etc. If, however, four monks have accepted and gone, but one wise monk says, "I will break the group for you; accept the invitation," and after the gruel and snacks are finished, when the lay devotees are taking the bowls for the main meal, he does not give his bowl but sits there saying, "Feed these monks first and let them go; I will follow later after performing the *anumodanā* (blessing)." When those monks have eaten and left, the lay devotee says, "Venerable sir, please give your bowl," and taking the bowl, he offers the meal. After eating and performing the *anumodanā*, the monk departs. In such a case, there is no offense for all of them. This is because, by way of the five kinds of food, there is no flaw in the group meal. Being invited with rice...
82:
Having given the blessing (anumodanā), he departs; there is no offense for any of the monks. This is because, regarding a group meal (gaṇabhojana), there is no discrepancy only by way of the five kinds of food. Even if they are invited for alms-food, if they accept barley-gruel (kummāsa), they incur an offense. And those foods were not taken by them together. However, in the case of rice-gruel (yāgu) and so forth, a discrepancy occurs; those were taken by them together. In this way, one wise monk can make it so that there is no offense for other monks as well.

Therefore, if a lay devotee wishing to offer a Sangha-meal (saṅghabhatta) is sent to invite [monks] and comes to the monastery, and instead of saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept alms-food (bhikkhā) at our house tomorrow," he says, "Please accept a meal (bhatta)," or "Please accept a Sangha-meal," or "May the Sangha accept a meal," the meal-allocator (bhattuddesaka) must be wise. He must free the monks who accept the invitation from the offense of group-meal (gaṇabhojana) and free the alms-food-eater (piṇḍapātika) dhutaṅga-practitioners from the breaking of their dhutaṅga.

How should he free them? First, he should say: "Lay devotee, it is not possible to go tomorrow." If he asks, "What about the day after, Bhante?", he should say, "It is not possible on the day after either." In this way, having delayed for up to half a month (15 days), he should ask again, "Lay devotee, what did you say?"

If he says again, "Please accept a Sangha-meal," then he should distract him by saying, "Lay devotee, please make this flower allowable (kappiya), please make this grass allowable," and then ask again, "What did you say?"

If he says the same thing again, he should say, "Friend lay devotee, you will not get the alms-food-eater dhutaṅga-practitioners or the Great Elders; you will only get novices (sāmaṇeras)." If he asks, "Bhante, in such and such villages, they get to feed the venerable ones, why don't I?", he should say, "They know how to invite; you do not." If he asks, "Bhante, how do they invite?", he should say, "They say, 'Venerable sirs, please accept our alms-food (bhikkhā).'"

If that lay devotee also says the same, it is allowable. Otherwise, if he says again, "Please accept a meal (bhatta)," he should say, "Lay devotee, now you will not get many monks; you will get only three." If he asks, "Bhante, in such and such villages, they get to feed the entire Sangha of monks, why don't I?", he should say, "Because you do not know how to invite." If he asks, "How do they invite?", he should say, "They say, 'Please accept alms-food (bhikkhā).'"

If that lay devotee also says, "Please accept alms-food," it is allowable. Otherwise, if he still says "only a meal," then he should say, "Go, we have no need for your meal; this village is our regular alms-resort, we will wander for alms in this village."

When that lay devotee says, "Venerable sirs, please wander [for alms]," and returns, people ask him, "Hey man, did you get the monks?" He says, "What is the use of this question? There is much to say here. The Elders have said, 'We will wander for alms tomorrow.' Now, do not be negligent."

On the second day, to the monks who are standing after performing the duties at the shrine (cetiya-vatta), the Sangha Elder should say: "Friends, there is a Sangha-meal in the nearby alms-village, but an ignorant person came to invite us. Let us go; we will wander for alms in the nearby alms-village."

The monks should follow the Elder's words; they should not be difficult to speak to. They should wander for alms without stopping at the village gate. If those lay devotees take the bowls, have them sit, and then feed them, it is proper to eat. If they have placed the food in the refectory and while [the monks] are wandering in the streets, they say, "Venerable sirs, please accept the food in the refectory," it is not allowable. Otherwise, if they bring the food and go to various places saying, "Please accept the alms-food," or if they had brought it to the monastery early on, placed it in a suitable spot, and offered it to all the monks who came...
83:
The elder of the Saṅgha should say: "Friends, although there is a Saṅgha-meal in the main village nearby, an ignorant person has come (to invite us). Let us go; we shall wander for alms in that village." The monks should follow the elder's words; they should not be difficult to admonish. They should wander for alms without stopping at the village gate. If the donors take the bowls, seat the monks, and serve them, they may eat. If they place the food in the alms-hall and wander the streets saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept the food at the alms-hall," it is not allowable.

Otherwise, if they take the food, go here and there, and say, "Please accept the food," or if they bring it to the monastery beforehand, place it in a suitable spot, and give it to whoever comes, this is called "brought-forward alms" (abhihaṭabhikkhā) and is allowable. If they prepare the gift in the alms-hall and send word to various monastic cells (pariveṇa) saying, "Please accept the food at the alms-hall," it is not allowable. However, those who see monks wandering for alms, sweep the alms-hall, seat them there, and serve them, should not be refused. If people see monks leaving the village without having received alms and say, "Venerable sirs, please accept food," they should be refused, or (if not refused) one should not turn back.

If they say, "Venerable sirs, please turn back and accept food," it is allowable to turn back according to the word "turn back." If they say, "Venerable sirs, please turn back; food is prepared at the house, food is prepared in the village," it is allowable to turn back, reflecting that food in a house or village could be for anyone. If they say it as a connected phrase, "Turn back and accept food," it is not allowable to turn back. The same method applies when they see monks leaving the alms-hall to wander for alms and say, "Venerable sirs, please sit and accept food." "Niccabhatta" means a permanent meal (dhuvabhatta). If they say, "Please accept the permanent meal," it is allowable to accept it even for many monks together. The same method applies to ticket-food (salākabhatta) and so on. The rest of the words here are very clear.

(This training rule) has its origin like the Eḷakaloma training rule, arising from action, not exempt by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, a bodily action, and involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada

In the third training rule: "It should be known that these people prepare the meal with great care according to a certain sign; because of that sign, this Dispensation and this offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha will certainly not be inferior (meager)." In the word "Kirapatika", the name "Kira" is the name of that clansman. He is called "Kirapatika" because of the sense of being a chief. He is named Kira and is a master; therefore, he is Kirapati. That Kirapatika, being a master (chief), would give wages according to the sign of the month, season, or year and make the laborers work. The phrase "Jujubes have been prepared" is understood by way of conventional usage (metonymy). Even though other foods and snacks were prepared besides jujubes, he announced it by using jujubes as a sign, according to the method of implication (upalakkhaṇa), saying, "Jujubes have been prepared."
84:
