People prepare the meal with great care. By that sign, it is known: "In this Dispensation, this gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha will not be inferior; it will certainly not be small or poor." In the term "Kirapatika", "Kira" is the name of that clansman. He is called "Kirapatika" in the sense of being a chief. That Kirapatika was a master and chief who employed laborers by giving wages based on the sign of the month, season, or year. "Jujubes have been prepared" is said by way of conventional usage. "Mixed with jujubes" means food mixed with jujube syrup.

"Brought late in the day" means brought when the sun was very high.

"I give my expectation of receiving a meal to such-and-such a monk"—this is called the assignment (vikappanā) of a meal, and it is allowable both in the presence and in the absence (of the recipient). If seen in person, one should say, "I assign it to you," and then eat. If not seen, one should say among the five classes of co-religionists, "I assign it to such-and-such a monk," and then eat. In the Mahāpaccari and other commentaries, only assignment in absence is mentioned. Since this assignment is included in Vinaya procedures, it is not allowable to assign it to the Blessed One. The reason is that whether the Blessed One is staying in the Gandhakuṭi chamber or sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, when the Saṅgha takes enough monks to form a group (quorum) and performs a particular Vinaya act, it is well-performed. The Blessed One neither invalidates the act nor completes it. He does not invalidate it because He is the Lord of Dhamma; He does not complete it because He is not one who fills a group (for legal quorum).

"He eats two or three invitations together" means putting food from two or three invitations into a single bowl, mixing them, and eating them as one. If two or three families invite and seat the monks in one place, and bring food and curries from here and there and pour them in, so that they become mixed as one, the Mahāpaccari states there is no offense in eating that. However, if the food from the original invitation is at the bottom and the food from subsequent invitations is on top, an offense is incurred for a monk who eats starting from the top. But if he puts his hand inside, takes out even a single morsel from the first invitation and eats it, from that time onwards, there is no offense regardless of how he eats. If they pour milk or broth into that food so that the covered food becomes of a single taste, the Mahāpaccari states there is no offense for a monk who eats starting from the edge. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: "If one who is seated having received milk-rice or broth-rice has others pour more milk-rice or broth-rice into it, there is no offense for one who drinks the milk or broth. But for one who eats, he must first take a piece of meat or a morsel of food received earlier..."
85:
It is allowable to eat a lump of rice by putting it in the mouth and starting from the edge. The same method applies to ghee-rice (sappipāyāsa).

A great lay devotee invites a monk; when the monk arrives at the house, the devotee, as well as his son, wife, brother, sister, and others, bring their own portions and put them in the bowl. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated that there is no offense (anāpatti) for a monk who eats the food received later without first eating the food given by the lay devotee. However, in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā, it is said to be allowable. In the Mahāpaccarī, it is stated: "If they cook separately and give by bringing from their own cooked rice, then for the monk who eats the food brought later first, there is a Pācittiya offense. If, however, there is only one cooking for everyone, it does not constitute a consecutive meal (paramparabhojana)." When a great lay devotee invites and has the monk sit, if another person takes the bowl, it should not be given. If asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not give it?", one should say, "Lay devotee, have you not invited us?" If the host says, "Let it be, venerable sir, please eat whatever you have received," then it is allowable to eat. It is stated in the Kurundī that it is allowable to eat food brought and offered by another person after asking permission from the original inviter.

When all invite a monk who is departing after giving a blessing (anumodanā), saying, "Venerable sir, please come tomorrow as well," because they wish to hear the Dhamma, it is allowable to come the next day and eat whatever is received. Why? Because he was invited by everyone. A monk wandering for alms receives food; another lay devotee invites him and has him sit in the house, but the food is not yet ready. If that monk eats the food he received from wandering for alms, it is an offense. If he sits without eating and is asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not eat?", and he replies, "Because I have been invited by you," and is then told, "Venerable sir, please eat whatever you have received," then it is allowable to eat.

"By the whole village" means that if the whole village invites together, there is no offense for a monk eating anywhere. The same method applies to a guild (pūga). "Being invited, he says he will take alms" means when invited with "Please accept a meal," he says, "I have no need for your meal, I will take alms." Regarding this, Mahāpaduma Thera said: "A monk speaking thus can make it not an invited meal (nimantana) in this training rule, but because the opportunity was made for the purpose of eating, he is not exempt from group-meal (gaṇabhojana) or from conduct (cāritta)." Mahāsuma Thera, however, said: "To the extent that he can make it not an invited meal, to that extent it is neither a group-meal nor conduct." The rest of the text is clear.
86:
The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the Kathina training rule arises from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind. In this training rule, eating the meal is an action (kiriyā), and not performing the formal assignment (avikappana) is an inaction (akiriyā). It is not an offense released by perception (saññāvimokkha); it is unintentional (acittaka); it is a transgression of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja); it occurs through bodily action, vocal action, the three minds, and the three feelings.

## The Third Training Rule on Consecutive Meals (Paramparabhojana) is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Kāṇamātā Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, "Kāṇamātā" means the mother of Kāṇā. It is heard that her daughter was extremely beautiful; whoever saw her became as if blind through lust; the meaning is they were blinded by lust. Therefore, because she caused others to become blind, she became known as "Kāṇā". On account of that daughter, her mother also became famous as "Kāṇamātā". "Āgataṃ" refers to the coming. "Kismiṃ viya" means "like what?"; the meaning is it is like something shameful. "Rittahattaṃ gantuṃ" means that going empty-handed in this way is like something shameful. "Parikkhayaṃ agamāsi" means that the laywoman, who was a noble disciple (ariyasāvikā), could not refrain from giving whatever she had upon seeing the monks, and thus she gave until all the cakes were exhausted. Regarding "dhammiyā kathāyā", here Kāṇā also listened to the Dhamma being preached for her mother and became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) at the conclusion of the teaching. "Uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi" means he [the Buddha] rose from the seat and departed. That man [the husband], having heard that "The Teacher has gone to Kāṇamātā's house," brought Kāṇā back and placed her in her original position as the chief wife.

Just as this story arose, even before the training rule was prescribed, the matter of provisions for a journey (pātheyyavatthu) arose; therefore, to show this immediately after, "Tena kho pana samayena" etc., was said. And that lay devotee, being a noble disciple, gave everything. Therefore, it was said: "Parikkhayaṃ agamāsi".

Whatever is prepared for the purpose of a gift—any kind of delicious cake (atirasaka), long cake (layā), twisted cake (mva-kywet-kyit), etc.—all are included here under the name "pūva" (cake).
87:
Whatever is prepared for consumption on the journey for those traveling—whether bound or unbound, such as cakes, flour, sesame, rice, etc.—all are reckoned as 'mantha' (flour/provisions) in this training rule. If one accepts a third bowlful beyond those two bowls, making it heaped up, an offense of Pācittiya is committed according to the number of cakes.

Accepting two or three bowlfuls means accepting bowls filled up to the lower rim of the bowl's edge. If I have accepted two bowlfuls at that house, I must say, 'I have accepted two bowlfuls at this house; Venerable Sir, please accept only one bowlful.' That second monk, upon seeing another monk, must also say, 'The monk who came first accepted two bowlfuls, and I have accepted one; Venerable Sir, do not accept any more.' Even if the first monk accepted only one bowlful, the same method applies in the successive informing. However, if a monk himself has accepted three bowlfuls, upon seeing another monk, he should simply say, 'Do not accept [anything] at this house.' Taking it to the refectory means taking it to the āsanasālā (sitting hall). A monk going to the āsanasālā should not go to a hall abandoned by many monks. He should go only to a hall where a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus resides. In the Mahāpaccari Commentary, however, it is stated: 'One should go to the āsanasālā nearest to the place where the food was obtained. One is not allowed to go to another place with the intention of giving it to one's acquaintances, friends, or those of the same Nikāya. However, if that monk has a regular sitting place, it is permissible to go even to a distant place.'

'Should be shared' means: if three bowlfuls were accepted, one should keep one for oneself and give two to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. If two bowlfuls were accepted, one should keep one for oneself and give one to the Saṅgha. It is not permitted to give them just because of friendship. A monk who accepted only one bowlful does not need to give anything if he does not wish to; he may do as he pleases.

'When the journey has subsided' means the travel plans are cancelled, either because of seeing danger on the way or because of not wanting to go, thinking, 'We will not send [it] now, we will not go.' There is no offense for a monk who accepts even a large amount from relatives or those who have invited him. However, in the Commentaries, it is said: 'Even for them, if it is food prepared as provisions for a journey or as a gift, only the specified amount is allowable.' The rest of the words are clear.

This training rule has 6 origins (samuṭṭhāna): action (kiriya), not-perception-exemption (no-saññā-vimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), transgression of a regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāya-kamma), verbal action (vacī-kamma), three types of consciousness (ti-citta), and three types of feeling (ti-vedana).

## The Fourth Training Rule: Kāṇamātā.
88:
## 5. Commentary on the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule

In the fifth training rule, 'bhikkhū bhuttāvī pavāritā' refers to monks who have been invited by a brahmin saying, 'Venerable sirs, please take as much as you wish' (yāvadattha-pavāraṇā), and who have also refused by saying, 'Enough, friend, give only a little' (paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā).

'Paṭivissake' means those living in nearby houses (neighbors).

'Kākoravasaddaṃ' means the sound of crows cawing together in a flock. In the phrase 'alametaṃ sabbaṃ', it is proper to say only 'alametaṃ sabbaṃ' without adding the syllable 'ti'.

238-9. 'Bhuttāvī' means one who has eaten. In this context, if a monk has swallowed even a single grain of rice, whether well-chewed or not, he is counted as 'bhuttāvī' (one who has eaten). Therefore, in the Word Analysis (Padabhājanī), it is said: 'Bhuttāvī nāma pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ', etc. 'Pavārito' means one who has performed the refusal (pavāraṇā). This is not achieved merely by refusal, but only when endowed with five factors. Therefore, in the Word Analysis, it is said: 'Pavārito nāma asanaṃ paññāyati', etc. Among those five factors, by the words 'asanaṃ paññāyati', it refers to one who has food that is being eaten (not yet finished). One who is still eating has eaten some and not yet eaten some; thus, in reference to what has been eaten, he can also be called 'bhuttāvī'. Therefore, we do not see any distinct or special meaning in the word 'bhuttāvī' [separately]. Just like the words 'diratta', etc., in 'dirattatirattaṃ, chappañcavācāhi', etc., it should be understood that this word 'bhuttāvī' is mentioned as an accompaniment to the word 'pavārita' and for the sake of euphony (byañjanasiliṭṭhatā).

In the words 'asanaṃ paññāyati', etc., the food being eaten is seen; it means this person is currently eating. 'Bhojanaṃ paññāyati' means food sufficient for pavāraṇā is seen. It means there is food that should be refused among the five types of food such as odana (boiled rice), etc. 'Hatthapāse ṭhito' means the donor, holding food sufficient for pavāraṇā, is within a distance of two and a half cubits (or less than three cubits). 'Abhiharati' means the donor brings that meal toward the monk with his body. 'Paṭikkhepo paññāyati' means the refusal is evident. It means the monk refuses that meal brought toward him either by body or by speech. Thus, by virtue of these five factors, one is called 'pavārita' (one who has refused). This has also been stated—
89:
“Upāli, through five factors, pavāraṇā (refusal of a further meal) is known: eating is known, the food is known, [the donor] stands within the hatthapāsa (forearm's length), [the donor] offers, and the refusal is known,” thus it is stated (in the Parivāra). 

In this matter, this is the decision: Regarding 'asana' (eating) and so forth, first, whatever food is being eaten, and whatever food offered by one standing within the hatthapāsa is refused, that food should be understood as one of these five types of bhojana (staple food): odana (cooked rice), kummāsa (barley bread/gruel), sattu (flour/confection), fish, and meat. Among these five types of food, odana refers to cooked rice made from the grains of the seven types of cereals: sāli (fine rice), vīhi (rice), yava (barley), godhuma (wheat), kaṅgu (millet), varaka (bean/wild grain), and kudrūsaka (rye/grass grain). Among these seven, sāli refers to all varieties of fine rice, starting from nīvāra at the lowest. Vīhi refers to all varieties of ordinary rice. There is no distinction between yava and godhuma. Kaṅgu refers to all varieties of millet, including white, red, and black. Varaka refers to all white varieties of beans/wild grains, starting from varakacoraka at the lowest. Kudrūsaka refers to all varieties of grass grains, including black sāmāka and others.

Among these grains, it is said that nīvāra and varakacoraka are 'grain-like.' Whether they are grains or grain-like, if one takes the rice of these seven types of grains and cooks them with the intention of making 'cooked rice' (bhatta), or 'gruel' (yāgu), or 'sour milk rice' (ambilapāyāsa), or any other dish; if, while eating it hot or cold, a distinct mark (odhi) [such as a spoon or hand mark] is visible at every place where it is taken, it is classified as odana and causes pavāraṇā. If a distinct mark is not visible, it is classified as yāgu and does not cause pavāraṇā.

If milk rice (pāyāsa) or sour gruel mixed with leaves, fruits, and sprouts is steaming hot just after being removed from the stove, and can be drunk by tilting [the bowl], and does not show a distinct mark even when taken by hand, it does not cause pavāraṇā. However, if it thickens after the steam has gone and it has cooled down, and thus shows a distinct mark, it causes pavāraṇā again. The initial thinness does not prevent [the later state] from causing pavāraṇā. Even if curd, whey, etc., are placed on the stove and many leaves, fruits, and sprouts are added, and even if only a handful of rice is included, if a distinct mark is visible during eating, it causes pavāraṇā. In an invitation where gruel is not included, if one intends to 'give gruel' and pours water, vinegar, milk, etc., into cooked rice and offers it saying 'Please accept this gruel,' even if that gruel is thin, it...
90:
...causes pavāraṇā indeed. However, if [rice] is added to boiling water and cooked before being offered, it is classified only as yāgu. Even if it is classified as yāgu, if fish or meat is added to that liquid or any other liquid, and a piece of fish or meat or a tendon even the size of a mustard seed is visible, it causes pavāraṇā.

However, pure meat broth or gruel made of meat broth does not cause pavāraṇā. Excluding the aforementioned grains, rice made from other things such as bamboo seeds, or from tubers, roots, and fruits, does not cause pavāraṇā; how much less so if it is thick gruel (ghana-yāgu). But if fish or meat is added to this [bamboo seed rice, etc.], it causes pavāraṇā. In the Mahāpaccarī, it is stated: 'Rice made for the purpose of pupphi (puffed grain snacks) also causes pavāraṇā.' Rice made for pupphi refers to rice that has been boiled in boiling water for the purpose of making pupphi snacks. If those rice grains are dried and eaten, it is allowable; they are classified neither as sattu (flour) nor as bhatta (rice). Furthermore, rice made again from those [dried] grains causes pavāraṇā indeed. If those grains are cooked in ghee, oil, etc., or made into cakes (pūva), they do not cause pavāraṇā. Flattened rice (puthuka) or flour and rice made from such flattened rice also do not cause pavāraṇā.

Kummāsa refers to kummāsa made from barley (yava). However, kummāsa made from other beans like mung beans does not cause pavāraṇā. Sattu refers to flour made from sāli, vīhi, or yava grains. The heads of kaṅgu, varaka, and kudrūsaka are also roasted, lightly pounded to remove the husks, and then pounded vigorously again to make powder. Even if that powder sticks together because it is wet, it is still classified as sattu. If the rice of well-roasted vīhi is pounded and offered, that powder also is classified as sattu. However, rice of vīhi that is only moderately roasted, or empty vīhi grains, or just roasted rice grains themselves do not cause pavāraṇā. But the powder of such rice grains does cause pavāraṇā. Broken rice from well-roasted vīhi also causes pavāraṇā. However, broken rice from moderately roasted or sun-dried grains does not cause pavāraṇā. Puffed rice (lāja) or rice and flour made from puffed rice do not cause pavāraṇā. Roasted flour or any kind of pure snack (khajjaka) does not cause pavāraṇā. However, a snack filled with fish or meat, or a sattu-modaka (flour ball), causes pavāraṇā. Fish and meat are clearly [bhojana].

This is the distinction: if a monk who is drinking gruel is offered two pieces of fish or meat, each only the size of a grain of rice, in a single vessel or in different vessels, and without yet eating those pieces of fish or meat, [he refuses] any other thing capable of causing pavāraṇā...
91:
(To a monk drinking gruel, when pieces of fish or meat the size of a grain of rice are offered in a single vessel or various vessels, if he refuses other food before eating those pieces of meat,) he does not incur pavāraṇā. If he has eaten one of those two pieces of meat and refuses other food while the other piece is still in his hand or bowl, he incurs pavāraṇā. If he has eaten both pieces and not even a mustard seed's worth remains in his mouth, he does not incur pavāraṇā even if he refuses other food.

If he refuses allowable meat while eating allowable meat, he incurs pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable meat while eating allowable meat, he does not incur pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is not the basis for pavāraṇā. This is because pavāraṇā is incurred only when a monk refuses allowable meat (kappiya-maṃsa) that is fit to be eaten. Whether he refuses this unallowable meat knowing it is unallowable or without knowing, it is still something that ought to be refused, so he does not incur pavāraṇā. However, if he refuses allowable meat while eating unallowable meat, he incurs pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is the basis for pavāraṇā. This is because the object the monk refused is the basis for pavāraṇā. Although the unallowable meat he is eating is something that ought to be refused, it does not lose its nature as meat while being eaten; therefore, he incurs pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable meat while eating unallowable meat, he does not incur pavāraṇā, following the previous method.

If he refuses any of the five kinds of allowable food while eating either allowable or unallowable meat, he incurs pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable food (akappiya-bhojana) that is rebuked by the Buddha and obtained through wrong livelihood (anesanā)—such as corrupting families, practicing medicine, claiming superhuman states, or accepting gold and silver—he does not incur pavāraṇā. While eating allowable or unallowable food, if he refuses allowable food, he incurs pavāraṇā; if he refuses unallowable food, he does not incur pavāraṇā. The reason should be understood in all cases according to the method already stated.

Thus, having understood how pavāraṇā is incurred by refusing food brought by someone standing within the hatthapāsa while eating food such as "asana," the following decision is stated to clarify how pavāraṇā is incurred: In the context of "asanaṃ bhojanaṃ," first, for a monk who has swallowed even a single morsel, if he refuses any of the five kinds of food while any of the five kinds of food is present in his bowl, mouth, or hand, he incurs pavāraṇā. If there is no food in any of those places and only the smell is apparent, he does not incur pavāraṇā. If there is no food in his mouth or hand but there is food in his bowl, yet he does not wish to eat it there but wishes to enter the monastery and eat it, or wishes to give it to another, and he refuses food in the meantime, he does not incur pavāraṇā. Why? Because the state of the meal being in progress has been interrupted. If he wishes to go elsewhere to eat and has food in his mouth...
92:
It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary that if a monk swallows his rice and takes the remainder while traveling, and refuses other food on the way, he also does not incur pavāraṇā. As it is with the bowl, so it is with the hand. Furthermore, if he does not wish to swallow the food present in his mouth and refuses other food at that moment, he does not incur pavāraṇā. This is because the characteristic stated for one term should be understood for all. Indeed, this method is already shown in the Kurundī Commentary. It is stated there: "If rice in the mouth has been swallowed, and he wishes to give the rice in his hand to a scavenger (vighāsāda), or wishes to give the rice in his bowl to another monk, and if he refuses [other food] at that moment, he does not incur pavāraṇā."

Regarding "one standing within the hatthapāsa": if the monk is sitting, it should be measured from the back edge of his seat; if he is standing, from the edge of his heels; if he is lying down, from the outer edge of the side on which he is lying. Excluding the donor's outstretched hand whether they are sitting, standing, or lying down, the distance of two and a half cubits (two cubits and a span) measured from the inner edge of the donor's nearest limb is to be known as the "hatthapāsa." Pavāraṇā occurs only for one who refuses food brought forward while standing within that hatthapāsa, not beyond it.

"Brings forward" (abhiharati) means to incline or bring it close so that the person within the hatthapāsa can receive it. However, even if a monk sitting nearby says, "Take the rice," without bringing forward the bowl that is in his hand, on his lap, or on a bowl-stand, the one who refuses it does not incur pavāraṇā. The same method applies when a basket of rice is brought and placed on the ground in front, and the person says, "Take it." But if they say, "Take it," while lifting it slightly or tilting it, and the monk refuses, then pavāraṇā is incurred. If a senior Elder sitting in his place sends a bowl to a junior monk sitting far away, saying, "Take rice from here," and the messenger who took it stands silently, and the junior monk refuses saying, "It is enough for me," he does not incur pavāraṇā. Why? Because of the Elder's distance and because the messenger did not bring it forward. However, if the monk who brought the bowl says, "Take this rice," and the other refuses, then pavāraṇā is incurred.

In the serving of a meal, if one person holds a rice basket with one hand and a ladle with the other and serves the monks, and another person comes and says, "I will hold the basket, you give the rice," and merely holds it while the server does not set the basket down, it is considered as being brought forward. Therefore, pavāraṇā is incurred for the monk who refuses while the server is scooping it out with the intention to give.
93:
Indeed, if the server is merely touching the food basket while another person is carrying it, the refusal by a monk while [the server] is intending to give and is scooping the food from that basket does not constitute pavāraṇā. However, in the case of food being scooped with a spoon, it does constitute pavāraṇā. This is because the act of bringing forward with a spoon is itself the act of offering. Even when the load is carried equally by two people, a monk who refuses it indeed incurs pavāraṇā; so it is stated in the Mahāpaccari. While food is being served to a nearby monk, if another monk covers his bowl with his hands, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is a refusal of food that is being offered to another.
Regarding the phrase 'refusal is evident,' a monk who refuses food offered verbally does not incur pavāraṇā. However, it should be understood that a monk who refuses food offered physically, whether by body or by speech, does incur pavāraṇā. 
Therein, physical refusal means moving a finger, a hand, a fly-whisk, or the edge of a robe; making a sign with the eyebrows; or looking with anger. Verbal refusal means saying 'Enough,' 'I will not take it,' 'Do not pour,' or 'Go away.' Thus, if one refuses by any such means, whether by body or by speech, it constitutes pavāraṇā. 
One monk, fearing he might incur pavāraṇā when food was being offered, removed his hand and said to the donor who was repeatedly pouring rice into the bowl, 'Pour, pour! Press it down and fill it up!' How is it in this case? The Elder Mahāsumma said, 'Since it was said with the intention that [the donor] should not pour, it constitutes pavāraṇā.' However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, 'Where is it said that pavāraṇā applies to one who says "Pour, fill it up"?' and thus held that it does not constitute pavāraṇā. Another monk, seeing a monk bringing food, said, 'Friend, will you take anything more from this? I wish to give you something.' In that case too, the Elder Mahāsumma said, 'Since it was said with the thought "In this way he will not come [forward]," it constitutes pavāraṇā.' But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, 'Where is it said that pavāraṇā applies to one who says "Will you take [more]"?' and thus held that it does not constitute pavāraṇā. 
A person brings broth containing pieces of meat and says, 'Please accept the broth.' For a monk who refuses upon hearing this, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. If it is refused when 'fish broth' or 'meat broth' is mentioned, it does constitute pavāraṇā. Even when it is offered as 'Please accept this' without naming it, it also constitutes pavāraṇā. If the meat is separated and one says, 'Please accept the meat broth,' and if therein there is a piece of meat even the size of a mustard seed...
94:
...is present, for one who refuses it, it constitutes pavāraṇā. However, if it has been strained, the Elder Abhaya said, 'It is allowable.' 
To one who invited him with meat broth, the Great Elder said, 'Wait a moment,' and then said, 'Friend, bring a bowl.' How is it in this case? The Elder Mahāsumma said, 'Since the movement of the one bringing [the food] was first interrupted, it constitutes pavāraṇā.' But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, 'Where is this donor going? What is his movement like? Can there be pavāraṇā even for one who is accepting [the food]?' and thus held that it does not constitute pavāraṇā. Meat is cooked mixed with bamboo shoots, jackfruit, etc. If one takes that curry and says, 'Please accept the bamboo shoot soup' or 'Please accept the jackfruit dish,' even if offered this way, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is offered by the name of something that does not lead to pavāraṇā. However, if it is offered as 'fish soup' or 'meat soup,' or as 'Please accept this,' it does constitute pavāraṇā. There is what is called maṃsakarambaka (food mixed with meat). Even if one wishes to give it, if he says, 'Please accept the karambaka,' it is allowable; it does not constitute pavāraṇā. But if he says 'meat karambaka' or 'this,' it does constitute pavāraṇā. This same principle applies to all things mixed with fish or meat. 
In an invitation, if a monk who is eating refuses meat brought to him, thinking it is 'meat specifically prepared for him' (udissakata), it indeed constitutes pavāraṇā; so it is stated in the Mahāpaccari. The discussion on mixtures (missakakathā), however, is well-stated in the Kurundī. In that Kurundī, it is stated thus: A monk wandering for alms brings gruel mixed with rice and says, 'Please accept the gruel'; it does not constitute pavāraṇā. If he says, 'Please accept the rice,' it does constitute pavāraṇā. Why? Because the rice with which he made the request is present. The meaning here is: when one says, 'Please accept the food mixed with gruel,' if the gruel is more or if they are equal, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. If the gruel is less and the rice is more, it does constitute pavāraṇā. Although this decision cannot be rejected because it is stated in all the Commentaries, the reason for it is difficult to see. If one says, 'Please accept the food mixed with rice,' whether the rice is much, equal, or less, it indeed constitutes pavāraṇā. If one says, 'Please accept the mixed food' without using the name of rice or gruel, if the rice is more or equal, it constitutes pavāraṇā. If it is less, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. This should not be considered the same as karambaka. For karambaka may be mixed with meat or not mixed with meat. Therefore, if one says 'karambaka,' there is no pavāraṇā. This [case], however, is specifically a mixture with rice. It constitutes pavāraṇā exactly according to the method stated here. In rice with much broth, [it is named] broth; in rice with much milk, [it is named] milk; in rice with much ghee...
95:
In the case of thick rice, if ghee is offered separately with the words "Please take some ghee," there is no pavāraṇā (refusal of further food) for the one who declines that ghee. A monk who becomes pavārita while walking is allowed to eat while walking. If he stops upon reaching mud or water, the atiritta procedure must be performed. If there is a river full of water on the way, he should eat while going around the bushes on the riverbank. Or if there is a boat or a bridge, he should eat while walking to and fro on that boat or bridge; he must not interrupt the posture (iriyāpatha) of walking. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting in a vehicle, or on the back of an elephant or horse, or in the orb of the moon or sun, must eat while sitting even as those vehicles etc. are moving, until noon. One who becomes pavārita while standing must eat only while standing; one who becomes pavārita while sitting must eat only while sitting. If one changes those respective postures, the atiritta procedure must be performed. One who becomes pavārita while sitting in a crouching position must eat while crouching. For that monk, a straw seat or some small seat should be provided below. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a small seat is allowed to eat while turning toward the four directions without moving from the sitting position. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a couch is not allowed to move this way or that. If that monk is carried to another place along with the couch, it is allowable. A monk who becomes pavārita while lying down must eat while lying down. If he turns his body, he must not exceed the position of the side on which he was lying.

Anatitritta means food that is not leftover or not in excess. That anatitritta is stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājana) as "akappiyakata" (not made allowable) etc., because it is not performed through the seven disciplinary procedures such as kappiyakata, or because it is not an excess for a sick person. Among those seven, akappiyakata means: fruits, tubers, or roots in that bowl or vessel that have not been made allowable by the five ways of making them allowable for monks; or it is unallowable meat or unallowable food—this is called akappiya (unallowable). Even if that unallowable food is made atiritta with the words "This is all enough," it should be known only as akappiyakata. Appaṭiggahitakata means making atiritta in the same manner as before with food that has not yet been formally received (accepted) by a monk. Anuccāritakata means the monk who comes to make it allowable does not lift it even slightly or does not cause it to be inclined. Ahatthapāse kata means it is performed while standing outside the reach of a hand (hatthapāsa) of the monk who comes to make it allowable. Abhuttāvinā kata means the disciplinary expert who makes it atiritta with the words "This is all enough" does so without having eaten food sufficient for pavāraṇā. The case of a monk who has eaten, is pavārita, and performs it after rising from his seat is very clear. It means not uttering the words "This is all enough." Thus...
96:
Food that has not been made allowable as leftover through these seven disciplinary procedures, and food that is not the leftover of a sick monk—both of these should be known as anatitritta (not made allowable). Atiritta (leftover made allowable) should be understood by the opposite method of that anatitritta. However, there is a slight distinction: in performing this atiritta, "performed by one who has eaten" means that even if one eats a single grain of rice or a piece of meat from the bowl of a fellow (sabhāga) monk sitting nearby and then performs it, it should be known as "performed by one who has eaten."

In the phrase "one who has not yet risen from the seat," the decision to avoid confusion is as follows: If two monks become pavārita while eating early in the morning, one monk must remain sitting in that same place. The other monk should bring the regular meal (niccabhatta) or meal-by-tickets (salākabhatta), pour half of it into the bowl of the sitting monk, wash his own hands, and then eat the remaining food after having that monk make it allowable (the atiritta procedure). Why? Because the food sticking to his hands is not included in the atiritta procedure and is therefore unallowable. If the monk who was sitting first takes it from the other's bowl with his own hand, there is no need to wash the hands.

If, while eating after having it made allowable in this way, they again pour some curry or edible food into the bowl, the disciplinary monk who first made it allowable is not allowed to do it again. Another monk who has not yet performed it must do so. The food that has not yet been made allowable must also be made allowable. "By one who has not yet performed it" means it must be done by another monk who did not perform it first. "The food that has not yet been made allowable" means that even the monk who first made it allowable can make allowable the food that has not yet been made so. However, he is not allowed to do it in the first vessel. For if it is done in that first vessel, it becomes done together with what was done first; therefore, the intention is that it is proper to do it in another vessel. Food made allowable in this way may be eaten by that monk together with the food made allowable first.

One who makes it allowable should do so not only in a bowl, but also in a pot, a basket, or any vessel placed in front and inclined. Even if a hundred monks are pavārita, they can all eat that food; those who are not pavārita can also eat it. However, it is not allowable for the disciplinary monk who performed the procedure. If a monk who has become pavārita enters for alms and is invited to sit at an auspicious invitation where he must eat, he should eat only after having the atiritta procedure performed. If there is no other monk there, he should send the bowl to the refectory or the monastery to have it performed. One who makes it allowable must not do so for food held in the hands of an unordained person (layperson or novice). If there is only an unskilled monk in the refectory, he should go himself, have it made allowable, bring it back, and eat.

In the phrase "gilānātiritta," it is not only the actual leftovers of a sick monk that are called gilānātiritta. In fact, all food brought for a sick monk to eat today, tomorrow, or whenever desired should be known as gilānātiritta. Among the types of nutriment such as yāmakālika, it is preached that for every swallow of food not mixed with solid food (āmisa), an offense of dukkaṭa is incurred. If it is mixed with solid food like rice, for a monk who accepts and swallows it for the sake of nutriment, or even if not for nutriment (but as medicine), only an offense of pācittiya is incurred.

241. "When there is a reason" means when there is hunger and thirst, for the sake of cutting off that hunger and thirst with yāmakālika; and when there is an illness that should be cured by those respective medicines with sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika...
97:
In the term "gilānātiritta" (leftovers of the sick), it is not only the food left over after a sick person has eaten that is considered "gilānātiritta." In fact, all food brought with the intention for a sick person to eat today, tomorrow, or whenever they wish, should also be known as "gilānātiritta." Regarding yāmakālika and other such items, the statement that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for every swallow refers to food that is not mixed with nutriment (āmisa) such as alms-food. If it is mixed with nutriment like alms-food, a pācittiya offense is incurred for a monk who accepts and swallows it, whether for the sake of nutriment or not.

"If there is a cause (sati paccaye)" means: for yāmakālika, if there is thirst, it is for the purpose of quenching thirst; for sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika, if there is an illness that should be appeased by those respective medicines, there is no offense for a monk who consumes them to appease that illness. The remaining meanings here are clear.

This training rule, which has the same origin as the Kathina (kathiṇasamuṭṭhāna), arises through body and speech, or through body, speech, and mind. It is [an offense of] action and non-action (kiriyākirya), not freed by perception (nosannāvimokkha), without [necessary] intention (acittaka), a violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), involving three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).

## The First Pavāraṇā Training Rule: The Fifth.

## 6. Commentary on the Second Pavāraṇā Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, "commits misconduct (anācāraṃ ācarati)" means committing a transgression of the regulation. "Bears a grudge (upanandhī)" means giving rise to enmity and binding one's anger toward that person; the meaning is that one repeatedly generates malice. "A monk who bears a grudge (upanaddho bhikkhu)" refers to a monk in whom such a grudge has arisen.

"Should invite by bringing [food] forward (abhibhaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya)" means having brought it, one should invite him saying, "Here, monk, chew or eat." However, in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana), without extracting words like "Here, monk," the meaning of "abhibhaṭṭhuṃ pavāraṇā" is shown generally as "Take as much as you want." "Knowing (jānanti)" means knowing the state of having already been invited (pavārita). Since that knowing occurs through three modes, it is stated in the padabhājana by the method "knows by himself," and so on. "Desiring to annoy (āsādanāpekkho)" means desiring to blame or to make the other person feel embarrassed (during the invitation).
98:
In the phrase "paṭiggaṇhāti āpatti dukkaṭassa" (he accepts, there is an offense of wrong-doing), when the monk for whom the food was brought forward accepts it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the monk who brought it. For the other monk (who was already pavārita), all the varieties of offenses should be understood as stated in the first training rule. In this training rule, however, it should be understood that all offenses apply only to the one who brings [the food]. The rest is clear as it follows the method stated in the first training rule.

This training rule arises from three origins (tisamuṭṭhāna): from body and mind, from speech and mind, or from body, speech, and mind. It is [an offense of] action (kiriya), freed by perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), involving unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Second Pavāraṇā Training Rule: The Sixth.

## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time

In the seventh training rule, "giraggasamajja" refers to an excellent festival held on a mountain, or a festival held on the summit of a mountain. It is said that a proclamation is made in the city that the festival will take place on the seventh day. Outside the city, in a level area in the shadow of the mountain, a great crowd of people gathers. Various kinds of dances and dramatic performances take place. To watch these, tiers of benches (viewing stands) are constructed. The group of seventeen monks (Sattarasavaggiya) were young monks at a time before the training rule regarding being under twenty years of age (ūnavīsativassa-sikkhāpada) had been laid down. Those monks consulted each other, saying, "Friends, let's go see the performances," and went to that festival. Then their relatives, being delighted and thinking, "Our young masters have come," bathed them, anointed them, fed them, and also gave other items like cakes and snacks into their hands. Referring to those relatives, the Elders who held the Council said, "manussā sattarasavaggiye bhikkhū passitvā" (the people, having seen the group of seventeen monks), and so on.

248-9. "At the wrong time (vikāle)" means at a time that is past (the afternoon). "Time (kāla)" refers to the eating time for monks; that time is defined at its very limit as midday (noon). The meaning is that this midday time has passed. Therefore, in the padabhājana of that term, it is said, "The wrong time means from the time midday has passed until sunrise." Even the moment when the sun is at its zenith (midday) is included within the [proper] time. From that point onwards, it is not possible to chew or eat. It might be possible to drink quickly, but a monk who is scrupulous (kukkuccaka) should not do so. To know the division of time, a time-post (gnomon/kālatthambha) should be employed. The business of the meal should be concluded only within the [proper] time.
99:
Regarding the phrase "remaining edibles" (khādanīya), first, there is no need to discuss edibles made from grains such as sakkhalimodaka and lyā cakes. There are also edibles similar to nutritive food (āmisa) consisting of forest roots and the like. These are: root-edibles, tuber-edibles, lotus-stalk-edibles, terminal-bud-edibles, stem-edibles, bark-edibles, leaf-edibles, flower-edibles, fruit-edibles, seed-edibles, flour-edibles, and resin-edibles. All these are also counted as "edibles" (khādanīya).

To distinguish those that are similar to nutritive food (āmisa), here is a brief explanation. Among root-edibles, the roots of leafy plants suitable for cooking, such as radish roots, bitter roots, hiṅkhalāpho roots, red-sorrel roots, hiṅsaṅkwe roots, kywet-hnā-paung roots, kin-peik roots, and hiṅkhā-pantu roots, are similar to nutritive food. Among these, the mature parts of kin-peik roots are cut and discarded; those mature parts are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). Other similar mature parts should be understood in the same way. It is also stated that the mature parts of radish roots, bitter roots, and hiṅkhā-pantu roots are also similar to nutritive food.

In the Pāḷi Canon, it is stated:
'Monks, I allow roots as medicine: turmeric, ginger, orris root, white orris root, ativisa, black hellebore, usīra grass, nut-grass, or whatever other roots there are as medicine which do not serve the purpose of edibles (khādanīya) in the place of edibles, nor serve the purpose of soft foods (bhojanīya) in the place of soft foods.'

The roots mentioned here are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). If these roots are counted by methods such as the minor five roots (cūḷapañcamūla) or the major five roots (mahāpañcamūla), the counting would be endless. The characteristic of these lifelong medicines is simply that they do not serve the purpose of edibles or soft foods. Therefore, it should be understood that any root which serves as a regular food for people in various regions as an edible or soft food is a temporary edible (yāvakālika), while others are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). Although much is said about these roots, one should abide by this characteristic. Since mentioning many names might cause confusion for those who do not know them, the focus is placed on the characteristic rather than the names.

Just as explained for roots, the decision for tubers and others should also be understood by the power of the stated characteristic. It is also stated that the stems, bark, flowers, and fruits of the eight kinds of roots mentioned in the Pāḷi Canon, such as turmeric, are all lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika).
100:
In the category of tuber-edibles (kanda-khādanīya), tubers are of two types: long and short. Long tubers include lotus stalks (bhisa) and erythrina tubers (kiṃsuka-kanda). Round tubers include lotus tubers (uppala) and kaseruka tubers, which are also called "knots" (gaṇṭhi). Among these tuber-edibles, the decayed parts, old parts, bark, and fine roots of all tubers are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). However, the young and easily edible tubers such as the tubers of young sāla-kalyāṇī, young erythrina, young hog-plum, screw-pine tubers, kanyin tubers (khway-tauk-nwe), padumma lotus and puṇḍarīka lotus tubers (known as bhisa), satway tubers, yam tubers, and the like, as well as khīravallī tubers, peiñ tubers, drumstick tubers, palmyra tubers (or roots), and the tubers of blue lotus, red lotus, kumuda lotus, and sogandhika lotus, banana tubers, bamboo tubers, and kaseruka tubers—those tubers that serve as regular food for people in various regions as edibles or soft foods are temporary edibles (yāvakālika).

Khīravallī tubers are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika) if not washed (to remove the pungent taste), but become temporary edibles (yāvakālika) once washed. Tubers such as myauk-ngo, orchids, onions, and garlic are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). In the Pāḷi Canon, these tubers are included in the category of medicinal roots (mūlabhesajja) with the phrase: "or whatever other roots there are as medicine."

In the category of stalk-edibles (muḷāla-khādanīya), the stalk of the padumma lotus is similar to that of the puṇḍarīka lotus. Stalks such as peik-swe and white lotus stalks, which serve as regular food for people in various regions as edibles or soft foods, are temporary edibles (yāvakālika). The stalks of turmeric, ginger, thin-pan, lotus-creeper (four-angled creeper), screw-pine, palmyra, danon, min-baw, coconut, and betel nut trees are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika). All these stalks are also included in the category of medicinal roots in the Pāḷi Canon.

In the category of terminal-bud-edibles (matthaka-khādanīya), the terminal buds (known as kaḷīra) of palmyra, danon, min-baw, screw-pine, coconut, betel nut, thin-paung, rattan, hmeik, and banana trees, as well as bamboo shoots, reed shoots, sugar cane shoots, radish shoots, mustard shoots, sugar cane tip shoots, and the shoots of the seven types of grain—the terminal buds of trees and creepers that serve as regular food for people in various regions as edibles or soft foods are temporary edibles (yāvakālika). The shoots of turmeric, ginger, orris root, thin-pan, and garlic, as well as the mature knots cut and dropped from the terminal buds of palmyra, danon, min, and coconut, are lifelong medicines (yāvajīvika).
101:
Regarding edible stems: Among the stems of the Salakalyāṇī (napè) that grow underground, sugarcane stems, and the stems of the blue lotus (nīluppala), red lotus (rattuppala), kumuda lotus, and sogandhika lotus, etc., the stems that are used as ordinary food for the purpose of snacks and meals by people in various regions are yāvakālika (temporary). The leaf-stalks of the uppala lotus species, all the flower-stalks and leaf-stalks of the paduma lotus species, the stalks of the kāravindaka (hinyè) plant, and all other remaining stems are yāvajīvika (lifelong).

Regarding edible barks: Only sugarcane bark is yāvakālika, and that is only when it is with its juice. All other barks besides sugarcane bark are yāvajīvika. It should be understood that these three—sprouts, stems, and barks—are included under astringent medicines (kasāva-bhesajja) in the Pali. For the Blessed One said: "Monks, I allow astringent medicines: astringent of neem (nimba), astringent of kuṭaja, astringent of paṭola, astringent of phaggava, astringent of nattamāla, or whatever other astringent medicines there are that do not serve as food among snacks, nor serve as food among meals." (Mahāvagga). In this Pali passage, the inclusion of these sprouts, stems, and barks is established. It should be understood that all the aforementioned astringent medicines are entirely allowable.

Regarding edible leaves: The leaves of radish (mūlaka), khāraka, caccu, tambaka, taṇḍuleyyaka, papunnāga, vatthuleyyaka, vajakalī, jajjharī, sellu, siggu, kāsamardaka, ummā, cīnamugga, māsa, rājamāsa, and excluding the large nipphāva bean, the remaining nipphāva beans, aggimantha, sunisannaka, setavaraṇa, nāḷikā, and ground-moss (lonī) that grows on the earth—the leaves of these and other such plants which are used as ordinary food for the purpose of snacks and meals by people in various regions are strictly yāvakālika. However, the leaf of the ground-moss that is about the size of a fingernail and climbs on trees and bushes is yāvajīvika. The residents of the island (Sri Lanka) say that the brahmī leaf is yāvakālika. Mango shoots are yāvakālika, while asoka shoots are yāvajīvika. As for others in the Pali: "Monks, I allow medicinal leaves: neem leaf, kuṭaja leaf, paṭola leaf, sulasi leaf, cotton (kappāsaka) leaf, or whatever other..."
102:
"...there are leaves that are medicinal which do not serve the purpose of solid food in solid food, nor the purpose of soft food in soft food" (Mahāvagga, 263). These are stated to be yāvajīvika. Not only the leaves of those trees like neem, but also their flowers, fruits, etc., are yāvajīvika. Among leaves, there is no end to the count, such as phaggava leaf, white basil (ajjuaka) leaf, wild basil (phanijjaka) leaf, paṭola leaf, betel (tambūla) leaf, and paduma lotus leaf.

Regarding flowers as edible items (pupphakhādanīya): The flowers of radish, khāraka, caccu, tambaka, vajakali, jajjharī, small nipphāva, large nipphāva, kaseruka, the young flowers of coconut, palmyra, and ketaka, the flowers of setavaraṇa, drumstick (siggu), flowers of the uppala and paduma lotus species, the flower of the flame-of-the-forest (kaṇṇika) which has only the calyx, the odorless flower (agandhika), the sprout flower (kaḷīra), and the jīvantī flower, etc.—those flowers that are used as regular food for the benefit of humans as solid or soft food in various regions are yāvakālika. However, the flowers of asoka, bakula, kuyyaka, punnāga, campaka, jāti, kaṇavīra, kaṇikāra, kunda, navamālikā, mallikā, etc., are yāvajīvika, and there is no end to their count. In the Pāḷi Canon, it should be understood that these flowers are included under astringent medicines (kasāva-bhesajja).

Regarding fruits as edible items (phalakhādanīya): The fruits of the village jackfruit, wild jackfruit, palmyra, coconut, mango, rose-apple, ambaṭaka, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, gourd, pumpkin, pussaphala (a type of cucumber), timbaru, saka, cucumber, eggplant, wild banana (coca), village banana (moca), madhuka, etc.—whatever fruits in the world are used as regular food for the benefit of humans as solid or soft food in various regions—all these are yāvakālika. It is not possible to show the limit of these by counting their names. As for those mentioned in the Pāḷi: "O monks, I allow fruits as medicine: vilanga, long pepper (pipphalī), black pepper (marica), yellow myrobalan (harītakī), beleric myrobalan (vibhītakī), emblic myrobalan (āmalakī), goṭṭhaphala, or whatever other fruits there are which do not serve the purpose of solid food in solid food, nor the purpose of soft food in soft food" (Mahāvagga, 263). These are stated to be yāvajīvika. Among those fruits, the unripe fruits of acchi, bimba, varaṇa, ketaka, kāsmari, etc., as well as nutmeg (jātiphala), kaṭukaphala, cardamom (eḷā), and takkola—it is not possible to show the limit of these by name.
103:
Among seed-edibles, the seeds of monkey jackfruit, jackfruit, hog plum, sal, dates, screwpine, and persimmon (when the fruits are young), tamarind seeds, bimba fruit seeds, and lotus seeds of the Uppala and Paduma varieties, etc., which are commonly used as food or snacks by people in various regions, are yāvakālika (temporary). The seeds of Madhuka, Punnāga, Harītakī, etc., and white mustard seeds, black mustard seeds, etc., are yāvajīvika (life-long). These seeds should be understood as being included under fruit-medicine (phalabhesajja) in the Pali texts.

Among powder-edibles, first, the powders of the seven kinds of grain, grains of similar types, and pulses, as well as jackfruit seed powder, monkey jackfruit seed powder, hog plum seed powder, sal seed powder, washed palmyra seed powder, and edible lily (umvun) powder, etc., which are commonly used as food or snacks by people in various regions, are yāvakālika. Unwashed palmyra seed powder, edible lily powder, and powders of winter cherry (assagandhā), etc., are yāvajīvika. These powders should be understood as being included under astringent-medicine, root-medicine, and fruit-medicine in the Pali texts.

Among resin-edibles, only sugarcane juice is sattāhakālika (seven-day). The remaining resins are yāvajīvika, as stated in the Pali: "Bhikkhus, I allow resins as medicine—asafoetida (hiṅgu), asafoetida-resin, asafoetida-shavings, lac (taka), lac-syrup, lac-shavings, and resin-wax, or whatever other resins there are as medicine." Resins such as mango resin and kanikāra resin, which are included by the term "yevāpanaka" (whatever others) in that Pali text, cannot be listed exhaustively by name. In this context, if any of these root-edibles, etc., are yāvakālika, they are all included under the term "the remaining edibles."

Regarding what is called "bhojanīya" (soft food), it is as already stated in the Pali beginning with "the five kinds of meals." If a monk, with the intention "I will chew, I will eat," accepts these hard foods (khādanīya) or soft foods (bhojanīya) at the wrong time (after noon), he commits a dukkaṭa offense for the act of accepting. The remaining words are clear.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the sheep's wool rule—it arises from the body, and from the body and mind; it is an action (kiriya); there is no release through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is unintentional (acittaka); it is a proscribed wrong (paṇṇattivajja); it is a bodily action (kāyakamma); it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Seventh Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time (Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada).
104: ## 8. Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Storing Food (Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada) In the eighth training rule, the Great Elder named Belaṭṭhasīsa was one of the thousand matted-hair ascetics (led by Uruvela Kassapa). When it is said that he lived in the forest, it means he resided in a meditation hut in a dwelling place near the Jetavana monastery. 'Sukkhakura' refers to plain rice without any soup or curry. It is said that after eating in the village, the Elder would go for alms again and bring back such plain rice; he did this out of the quality of fewness of wishes (appicchatā), not out of greed for requisites. It is said that the Elder would spend seven days in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and upon emerging from the attainment, he would moisten that dry rice with water and eat it. Then he would remain in the attainment again for another seven days. In this way, he would let two, three, or even four weeks pass before entering the village for alms. Therefore, it is said, 'He enters the village for alms after a long time.' The terms kāra, karaṇa, and kiriyā are identical in meaning. Edibles or nutriments that are stored are called sannidhikāra or sannidhikāraka. This name refers to edibles and nutriments that have been received and kept past one night. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī), it is stated: 'Sannidhikāraka means that which is received today and kept until the next day.' When it is said that receiving results in a dukkata offense, it means that when one takes any yāvakālika or yāmakālika that has been stored in this way with the intention to swallow it, a dukkata offense is first committed for the act of taking. However, for the act of swallowing, a pācittiya offense is committed for every swallow. If a bowl is not properly washed, and when rubbed with a finger, a finger-mark is clearly visible; or if oil or grease has entered the crevices of a lumpy bowl and leaks out when dried in the sun; or if grease becomes apparent when hot gruel is poured into it—a monk who eats from such a bowl the next day commits a pācittiya offense. Therefore, after washing the bowl, one should pour clear water into it or rub it with a finger to ensure it is free of grease. If grease appears in the water or a finger-mark is visible on the bowl, it is considered improperly washed. However, a finger-mark visible on a bowl that has the color of oil is not considered a factor for an offense. If monks give up edibles and nutriments to novices without any expectation, and the novices store them and then offer them back, it is all allowable. It is only the edibles and nutriments that one has received oneself and kept until the second day without giving them up that are not allowable. Swallowing even a single grain of such rice results in a pācittiya offense.
105:
Among unallowable meats, if one swallows human flesh, a pācittiya offense for storing food (sannidhi) is committed along with a thullaccaya offense. If one swallows other unallowable meats, a pācittiya offense is committed along with a dukkaṭa offense. For a monk who swallows a yāmakālika item when there is a reason (such as thirst), a pācittiya offense is committed. If he swallows it for the sake of nutriment, a pācittiya offense is committed along with a dukkaṭa offense. If a monk who has already refused further food (pavārita) swallows food that has not been made leftover (anatiritta), two pācittiya offenses are committed in the case of ordinary food (pakaṭi-āmisa). In the case of human flesh, two pācittiya offenses are committed along with a thullaccaya; in the case of other unallowable meats, two pācittiya offenses along with a dukkaṭa. If he swallows a yāmakālika item when there is a reason with a mouth that still contains food (sāmisa), two pācittiya offenses are committed; if the mouth is free of food (nirāmisa), only one pācittiya is committed. If he swallows it for the sake of nutriment, the dukkaṭa offense increases in both cases (with or without food in the mouth). If he swallows it at the wrong time (vikāla, after noon), two pācittiya offenses are committed in the case of ordinary food: one due to storing (sannidhi) and one due to eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana). In the case of unallowable meats, the thullaccaya and dukkaṭa offenses increase. For yāmakālika items, there is no offense due to the wrong time (vikāla); however, due to the reason of not being leftover (anatiritta), there is no offense in any case during the wrong time.

For a monk who formally accepts sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika items for the sake of nutriment, a dukkaṭa offense is first committed due to the act of acceptance. At the time of swallowing, if it is not mixed with food (nirāmisa), a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every swallow. If it was accepted while mixed with food (āmisa-saṃsaṭṭha), only a pācittiya offense is committed according to the nature of the object.

In the training rule on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) beginning with "Anāpatti yāvakālikaṃ," food (khādanīya and bhojanīya) is called 'yāvakālika' because it is to be eaten until the time of noon. The eight kinds of drinks, along with allowable drinks (anuloma-pāna), are called 'yāmakālika' because they are to be consumed until the last watch (yāma) of the night. The five kinds of medicine, such as ghee (sappi), are called 'sattāhakālika' because they may be stored for seven days. All other things except water are called 'yāvajīvika' because they may be carried for life and consumed when there is a reason.

Among these four types of kālika, for a monk who consumes yāvakālika accepted at dawn, even if stored a hundred times, as long as the time limit is not exceeded; yāmakālika for one day and night; sattāhakālika for seven days; and the remaining yāvajīvika for life when there is a reason, there is no offense. The remaining words here are clear. In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the discussion on drinks (pānakathā), the discussion on allowable substitutes (kappiyānulomakathā), the discussion beginning with "Is yāmakālika allowable with yāvakālika?", and the discussion on allowable grounds (kappiyabhūmikathā) are expanded in this place. We shall discuss those matters only where they directly occur.

## 9. Explanation of the Paṇītabhojana Training Rule
In the ninth training rule, "paṇီtabhojanāni" refers to foods mixed with excellent nutriment. "Who would not find food endowed with excellence to be pleasing?" "Sādu" means having a good taste.

In this ninth training rule, regarding the phrase "Yo pana ... bhuñjeyya," the decision should be understood thus: A monk who requests and eats pure ghee (sappi) etc., which are not mixed with other food, does not commit a pācittiya offense; however, he commits a sūpodanavinnatti-dukkaṭa offense (wrong-doing for requesting curry or rice) according to the Sekhiya rules. But if he requests and eats ghee etc., that are mixed with rice, he commits a pācittiya offense.
106:
It has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Eḷakaloma training rule—it arises from the body, and from both body and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is not a release by perception (no-saññāvimokkha); it is without consciousness (acittaka); it is a transgression of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja); it is a bodily action (kāyakamma); it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Eighth Training Rule on Storing Food (Sannidhikāraka) is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Paṇītabhojana Training Rule

In the ninth training rule—'paṇītabhojanāni' means foods mixed with superior nutriment. Who would not love food that is endowed with excellence? 'Sādu' means having a good flavor.

Regarding the words, "Whatever monk, being not sick, should request for his own sake and eat such superior foods..."—in this context, a monk who requests and eats pure ghee (sappi) and so on does not commit a pācittiya offense; he only commits a dukkaṭa offense for requesting curry or rice (sūpodanavinnatti) as mentioned in the Sekhiya rules. However, it should be understood that if he requests and eats ghee etc., mixed with rice, he commits a pācittiya offense. This is the intended meaning here. For this reason, the word 'paṇītabhojanāni' was used in the Sutta instead of just 'paṇītāni'. If 'paṇītāni' were said, it would refer only to ghee and so on, but when 'paṇītabhojanāni' is said, it is clear that it refers to foods produced from the seven types of grain mixed with superior ingredients.

Now, regarding the statements such as "a dukkaṭa in the effort of requesting," this is the decision: For a monk who requests saying, "Give me rice with ghee," "Give me rice after pouring ghee on it," "Give me rice mixed with ghee," "Give me rice together with ghee," or "Give me both ghee and rice," there is a dukkaṭa for the request, a dukkaṭa for the acceptance, and a pācittiya for the swallowing. However, if he says, "Give me ghee-rice," since there is no such thing as 'ghee-rice' in the same way there is 'sāli-rice' (fine grain rice), it should be understood as only a sūpodanavinnatti-dukkaṭa.

If, when he has requested saying "Give me rice with ghee," the donor gives the rice and then says, "Eat it by making it with ghee," and gives fresh butter (navanīta), milk (khīra), or curd (dadhi); or if the donor gives the price (kappiya-vatthu) saying, "Buy ghee with this and eat it," such giving follows the nature of the case (yathāvatthuka). If he requests saying, "Give me rice with cow's ghee," and the donor gives cow's ghee; or if cow's ghee is unavailable, the donor gives cow's butter etc., as in the previous method, or even gives the cow herself saying, "Eat with the ghee from this cow," such giving also follows the nature of the case.
107:
If a donor, requested for cow ghee (for rice), gives goat ghee etc., it is a mismatch (vissaṅketa). In this case, because one thing was requested and another was given, there is no offense. This same principle applies to requests such as "Give goat ghee," and so on. If it is said, "Give allowable ghee (from an allowable animal)," and one gives unallowable ghee, it is merely a mismatch. If it is said, "Give unallowable ghee," and one gives unallowable ghee, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) both in acceptance and in consumption. If unallowable ghee is not available, and one gives unallowable butter etc., saying "Make it into ghee and eat," it is considered as giving unallowable ghee. If it is said, "Give unallowable ghee," and one gives allowable ghee, it is a mismatch. If it is said, "Give ghee," and one gives any of the remaining fine foods such as butter, it is merely a mismatch. This same principle applies to requests such as "Give butter," and so on. For whatever fine food the request is made, if that fine food or its value is received, it is considered as having received that specific food. If they give another kind, whether mentioned in the Pali or not, it is a mismatch. A monk who requests other types of butter etc., setting aside those mentioned in the Pali, commits an offense of wrongdoing. Just as it is said that when "ghee-rice" is requested, since there is no such thing as "ghee-rice" distinct like Sāli rice, it is merely an offense of wrongdoing for requesting curry and rice; the same principle applies to requests such as "Give butter-rice," and so on. Even if each is explained in detail in order, only this meaning should be stated; that meaning can be understood in brief, so why expand on it? Therefore, it is said: "This same principle applies to requests such as Give butter, and so on."

If one requests all fine foods such as ghee, either in one place or in various places, and pours the received food into a single vessel, making it a single flavor, and then swallows even a drop placed on the tip of the tongue with the tip of a kusa grass, one incurs nine pācittiya offenses. This has also been stated in the Parivāra: "Bodily, not vocal, all having various objects, might be incurred simultaneously, not before or after; this question has been considered by the wise." In the phrase "one who is not ill but perceives himself as ill," if one perceives himself as ill and requests the five medicines for medicinal purposes, [he should be dealt with] by the Mahānāma training rule...
108:
...legal action should be taken. However, in the case of a monk requesting the nine types of fine foods, legal action should be taken according to this training rule. For bhikkhunīs, these (allowable ghee, etc.) are matters of pāṭidesanīya (confession). Regarding the request for curry and rice, for both [monks and nuns], it is only a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense as prescribed in the sekhiya rules. The remaining meaning here is quite clear.

## Catusamuṭṭhāna (Fourfold Origination) – It originates from the body, from the body and speech, from the body and mind, and from the body, speech, and mind. It is an action (kiriya), not a release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), it is without intent (acittaka), a breach of regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), a bodily action, a vocal action, involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Ninth Training Rule on Fine Foods is finished.

## 10. Dantapona-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Training Rule on Tooth-sticks)

In the tenth training rule: Among the four requisites, one who resolves that "even a tooth-stick, at the very least, shall be entirely from refuse-rags" is called a "total refuse-rag user" (sabba-paṁsukūlika). That monk, it is said, made a bowl out of a discarded vessel in a cemetery, made robes out of discarded rags in that same cemetery, and took and used only discarded couches and stools from that cemetery. "Ayyavosāṭitaka" means: here, "Ayya" refers to deceased relatives such as fathers and grandfathers. "Vosāṭitaka" refers to snacks and meals discarded in cemeteries and such for their sake. People, intending for their deceased relatives, take the snacks and meals that those relatives liked while alive, make them into lumps, and place them in cemeteries and such, saying, "May our relatives enjoy these." That monk picks them up and eats them; he does not desire other fine offerings even when given. Therefore, it is said: "He personally takes and consumes ayyavosāṭitaka discarded in cemeteries, at the foot of trees, or on thresholds." "Thera" means one with firm and solid flesh. "Vaṭhara" means one who is stout. This means this monk is stout and has a compact body. Regarding the phrase "I think he eats human flesh"—the people's intention was that those who eat human flesh tend to be stout and compact like this. Regarding "They became anxious about water and tooth-sticks"—those monks became anxious because they did not clearly grasp the meaning of the phrase "One should not take unoffered food into the mouth." The Blessed One, like a father making his young children understand, established the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) by explaining it to those monks according to the circumstances that had arisen.
109:
"Adinna" (not given) refers to nutriment that has not been given to a monk who receives it through one of the efforts—by the body, by something connected to the body, or by tossing. With reference to this "adinna," it is stated in the Padabhājanī: "'Not given' refers to what has not been formally accepted." However, in the Second Pārājika, it is stated: "'Not given' refers to what is possessed by another." This term "dinna" (given) is extracted in the Padabhājanī for the purpose of showing its characteristic as the opposite of that "adinna."

In the exposition (Niddesa) of "dinna," it says: "When [the giver] gives by the body, by something connected to the body, or by tossing..." If a monk, standing within the hatthapāsa, receives by the body or by something connected to the body even a minute particle of dust (rathareṇu) being so given, such a received nutriment is called "dinna" (formally accepted). Nutriment relinquished only by words such as "Take this," "Let this be yours," etc., is not called "dinna."

In that context, "by the body" means by any part of the body, such as the hands, or even by a toe; food or snacks given in this way are said to be "given by the body" (kāyena dinna). The same principle applies to the act of receiving. Food or snacks received by any part of the body are said to be "received by the body" (kāyena gahita). If a sick person receives medicine given by a nasal-applicator through the nostril or receives it by the mouth, it is still considered "received by the body" (kāyena gahita). This is because, in this act of acceptance, the mere intention to accept is the essential factor. This method is mentioned in the Mahāpaccari. "By something connected to the body" means food or snacks given by any utensil, such as a spoon; this is called "given by something connected to the body" (kāyapaṭibaddhena dinna). The same principle applies to the act of receiving. Food or snacks received by a bowl, a plate, etc., which are connected to the body, are said to be "received by something connected to the body" (kāyapaṭibaddhena gahita). "By tossing" means food or snacks that are released from the body or from something connected to the body and made to fall onto the body or onto something connected to the body of a person standing within the hatthapāsa; this is called "given by the effort of tossing" (nissaggiyena dinna). This concludes the commentary on the Pali text (Pāḷivaṇṇanā).

The decision not found in the Pali text (Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya) regarding this training rule is as follows: Acceptance is valid if it fulfills five factors: (1) The object must be of a size and weight that a man of average strength can lift; (2) the hatthapāsa must be evident; (3) the act of offering must be evident; (4) a deva, human, or animal gives by the body, by something connected to the body, or by tossing; (5) the monk receives that food or snack by the body or by something connected to the body. Only when these five factors are fulfilled is the acceptance valid.

Among these five factors, the hatthapāsa of one who is standing, sitting, or lying down should be understood according to the method stated in the Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada. If, however, one of the two—the giver or the receiver—is in the air,
110:
and the other is on the ground, the measurement of the forearm's length (hattha-pāsa) must be determined from the nearest limb, starting from the head of the person on the ground and the outstretched hand of the person in the air intended for giving or receiving. If one is in a pit and the other is on the edge of the pit, or if one is in a tree and the other is on the ground, the measurement of the forearm's length must be determined in the same manner as mentioned. If a bird gives a flower or fruit with its beak, or an elephant gives with its trunk while standing within such a forearm's length, the formal offering is valid. If a monk sitting on the shoulder of an elephant that is seven and a half cubits (entering the eighth cubit) high receives what is given by that elephant with its trunk, it is indeed allowable.

If a person comes near a monk carrying many dishes of rice and curry on their head and says while standing, "Please take some," the act of offering (abhīhāra) is not yet evident; therefore, it should not be accepted. However, if they tilt slightly, the monk should stretch out his hand and accept by touching even a part of the bottommost dish. By doing so, all the dishes are considered formally offered. After being offered in this way, it is allowable to take and consume whatever is desired, whether by setting them down or opening the lids. In the case of a single vessel such as a rice basket, there is no need to say more. If a person carrying rice with a shoulder pole gives it by tilting the pole, it is allowable. If a molasses jar is tied to one end of a thirty-cubit bamboo pole and a ghee jar to the other end, and that bamboo pole is formally accepted, then everything is considered accepted. If someone says, "Please take the juice," as it drips from the trough of a sugarcane press, it should not be accepted because the act of offering is not evident. However, if they remove the dregs and give it by scooping it up with their hand, it is allowable.

When many alms-bowls are placed on a couch, a bench, a mat, a trough, or a wooden plank, if the donor is within the forearm's length, then whether the monk is standing, sitting, or lying down, if he touches the couch etc. with a finger with the intention of receiving, everything poured into those bowls is considered formally offered. If he climbs onto the couch etc. and sits there with the intention of receiving, it is also allowable. If he holds the couch etc. with his hand and sits on it, there is no need to say more.

On the ground, however, even if the bowls are touching each other at their sides, only what is poured into the bowl that is touched with a finger or a stylus is considered formally offered. The statement that "formal offering is not valid for bowls placed on a large mat or a large floor covering" should be understood as referring to exceeding the forearm's length (hattha-pāsa).
111:
It should be understood that this is said with reference to an alms-bowl that has exceeded the hatthapāsa (forearm’s length). If it is within the hatthapāsa, except for leaves still attached to that tree, it is allowable to receive [food] in any other vessel or container.

It is not allowable to receive [food] on a lotus leaf or a kiṃsuka leaf, etc., that is still attached to that tree. This is because such a leaf does not count as being ‘connected to the body’ (kāyapaṭibaddha). Just as formal acceptance is not valid on a leaf attached to the tree, it is also not valid on a couch or similar item tied to a tree stump, nor on an immovable plank or a stone slab. This is because such planks and stone slabs are also included in the category of ‘grown in that place’ (tatthajātaka). Formal acceptance is also not valid on delicate leaves like tamarind leaves spread out on the ground. This is because such leaves are not capable of supporting the object being offered. However, formal acceptance is valid on large lotus leaves and the like (which have been detached from the plant).

If a donor standing beyond the hatthapāsa offers food using a long-handled ladle, the monk should say, “Please come closer and give.” If the donor, either not hearing those words or disregarding them, simply pours the food into the bowl, it must be formally accepted again. The same rule applies to a donor who stands at a distance and throws a lump of food or snacks.

If there is dye powder in a bowl that is being taken out of its bag, it should be washed if water is available. If there is no water, one should wipe away the dye powder or formally accept the bowl [as it is] and then go on the alms round. If dust falls into the bowl while wandering for alms, it must be formally accepted before receiving food. For a monk who receives food without formal acceptance, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, there is no offense for a monk who eats that food after formally accepting it again. If, despite being told, “Please give after I have formally accepted,” the donor—either not hearing or disregarding the words—pours the alms-food anyway, there is no offense of wrongdoing. One should formally accept again and receive other alms-food.
