If a strong wind blows dust from various directions making it impossible to receive alms-food, it is allowable to receive it with a pure mind, intending, “I will give this to an unordained person (anupasampanna).” After collecting alms in this way, having gone to the monastery or the refectory and given that food to an unordained person, it is allowable to eat it after formally accepting it again, either as food given by that person or through trust (vissāsa) in that person.

If, during the alms round, a monk gives a bowl containing dust to another monk, he should be told, “Formally accept this bowl and then receive alms-food or consume it.” That monk should act accordingly. If the dust is floating on the surface, one should pour off the sour gruel (kañjika) and eat the remainder. If the dust has gone inside, it must be formally accepted again. If no unordained person is present, without letting go of the bowl from the hand, one should carry the bowl to where an unordained person is...
112:
...and have it formally accepted. If dust falls into dry food, it is allowable to remove the dust and eat. If the dust is extremely fine, it should be removed along with the top layer of food, or it must be formally accepted again before eating. If drops of rice-gruel (yāgu) or soup splash up from the vessels of those stirring them in front and fall into the alms-bowl, the bowl must be formally accepted again.

When people are bringing food with a ladle to give, if drops from the ladle fall into the bowl before the main portion is served, such falling is considered 'well-fallen'; since it was brought for the purpose of offering, there is no fault. Even if charcoal or ash falls from a small pot while food is being poured from it, there is no fault because it was brought for the purpose of offering. If a snack being given to a nearby monk jumps from his bowl and falls into another monk's bowl, it is 'well-fallen.' This is because that food has already been formally accepted.

If, while breaking a branch of a sour fruit tree (such as a soap-pod) to give to one monk, drops from the branch fall into another monk's bowl, the bowl must be formally accepted again. If they fall into the bowl of the monk over whose bowl the branch is being broken, there is no fault, as it is endowed with the intention of bringing it to give. If people offer a bowl filled with milk-rice (pāyāsa) and it cannot be held from the bottom because it is hot, it is allowable to accept it by holding the rim of the bowl. If it still cannot be held that way, it should be received using a bowl-stand (ādhāraka).

If a monk sitting in the refectory holding his bowl falls asleep and does not know that food is being brought or given, the formal acceptance is not valid. However, if he is sitting with the intention to accept, it is valid. Even if that monk lets go of the bowl-stand with his hand and keeps it pressed down with his foot while nodding off, it is still valid. For a monk who is awake, receiving by treading on the bowl-stand with his foot is a disrespectful acceptance; therefore, it should not be done. Some teachers say that receiving with a bowl-stand in this manner is called 'receiving with an object connected to an object connected to the body,' and therefore it is not allowable. That is merely the opinion of those teachers. In terms of meaning, this entire bowl and bowl-stand are simply objects connected to the body. This method has already been shown in the Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpada as well. It is also allowable to personally pick up and consume a snack that falls while being given to a monk. Regarding such picking up and consuming, there is this scriptural text:

"Monks, I allow you to personally pick up and consume what falls while being given. Monks, that [food] has been relinquished by the donors." (Cullavagga, 273).
113:
This Sutta is of indirect meaning (neyyattha). Therefore, the intention here should be understood as follows: if food being offered slips from the donor's hand and falls onto clean ground, or onto a lotus leaf, cloth, mat, etc., it is allowable to pick it up oneself and consume it. If it falls on dusty ground, it should be consumed after wiping off the dust, washing it, or having it formally offered again. If it rolls near another monk, it is allowable for that monk to have it brought to him. If [the first monk] says to that monk, "You eat it yourself," it is allowable for him to eat it. However, without being told to do so, he should not pick it up. Even if not told, if he picks it up thinking, "I will give it to another monk," it is allowable—so it is stated in the Kurundī. Why is it not allowable for another monk to pick it up [for himself]? Because it has not been permitted by the Blessed One. For when the Blessed One said, "Pick it up yourself and consume it," He permitted the consumption of food that falls while being given to a specific monk, even if it has not yet been formally received (paṭiggahita) by him. By the words, "Monks, that [food] has been relinquished by the donors," He showed that it is no longer the property of another. Therefore, it is not allowable for another monk to pick it up and consume it himself, but it is allowable by the instruction of the [original] monk; this is said to be the intention here.

And because it is permitted on the grounds of not having been formally received, if that same food is left as it is, without being touched by hand, and is covered with something, it is allowable to consume it even on the second day; there is no offense due to storing (sannidhi). However, it must be formally received before consumption. His picking it up and consuming it himself was permitted only on the day it fell during the offering, not beyond that; this is also said to be the intention here.

Now, the method regarding the negligible (abbohārika) is stated: while eating, the teeth wear down, the nails wear down, the color of the bowl wears down—all this is negligible. When sugarcane and such are split with a small knife that has been formally received, if dirt is visible, this is called "newly arisen" (navasamuṭṭhita) and must be formally received before consumption. If the knife is washed and, when splitting, no dirt is visible but only the smell of iron remains, that is negligible. The same method applies when a knife is carried without being formally received and used for splitting. This is because it is not carried for the purpose of consumption. When grinding or pounding root medicines and such, the grindstone, the muller, the mortar, and the pestle wear down. If a knife that is being carried is heated and placed in buttermilk or milk for medicinal purposes, and a dark blue mark appears, the judgment is the same as stated for the small knife. However, one should not personally put it into raw buttermilk and such. If one does, one is not free from the [offense of] cooking for oneself (sāmapāka).
114:
While walking for alms in the rain, if dirty water from the monk's body or robes falls into the bowl, it must be formally received again. The same method applies if [rainwater] falls while eating at the foot of a tree and such. However, if it has been raining steadily for seven days and the water is clean, or if it falls directly from the open sky, it is allowable [without re-offering]. A monk giving rice to a novice should give it without touching the rice already in the novice's bowl. Or, the novice's bowl should be formally offered [to the monk]. If he touches the rice in a bowl that has not been formally offered and then takes rice from his own bowl again, he incurs the offense of taking what is not offered (uggahitaka).

If, with the desire to give, he says, "Novice, bring the bowl, take the rice," and the other refuses saying, "It is enough for me," and even if he says again, "I have relinquished this for you," the novice still says, "I have no need of this," even if he relinquishes it a hundred times, as long as it remains in his own hand, it is still considered formally received.

However, if he places it on a bowl-stand and says "Take it" without any lingering attachment, it must be formally received again. If he places the bowl on the stand with lingering attachment and tells the novice, "Take cake or rice from here," and the novice, having washed his hands, takes it even a hundred times without touching the food already in his own bowl, there is no need for re-offering. If he touches the rice in his own bowl and then takes from [the monk's bowl], it becomes mixed with the novice's property, and must be formally received again. Some teachers say, "If while being taken, it breaks and falls back there [into the monk's bowl], it must be formally received again." This should be understood as applying only when it is given with a specific limit, such as "Take one lump of rice," "Take one cake," or "Take this much portion of this lump of molasses." Here, however, there is no such limit. Therefore, only that which falls into the novice's bowl loses its status of being formally received [by the monk]. As for what is in the novice's hand, as long as the novice does not stop by saying "Enough," or the monk does not prevent him, it still belongs to the monk; therefore, it does not lose its status of being formally received.

If he puts rice into a pot used for cooking gruel for himself or for other monks for the sake of someone, he should say, "Novice, place your hand over the pot," and put it into his hand. For that which falls from his hand into the pot, having been relinquished, does not make the pot unallowable on the second day [due to sannidhi]. If he puts it in without doing this, the pot must be used only after being made free of food particles (nirāmisa), just like washing a bowl. When donors leave a large gruel pot and depart, if a young novice is unable to lift it to have it formally offered, the monk should tilt his bowl towards it, and the novice [should tilt] the neck of the pot [towards] the bowl...
115:
If a pot of gruel (yāgu) is placed on the rim of an alms bowl (even if it cannot be fully supported) and tilted, the gruel that enters the bowl is considered formally offered (paṭiggahita). Alternatively, if a monk places his hand on the ground and a novice rolls the pot of gruel and places it upon that hand, it is allowable (vaṭṭati). The same method applies to baskets of cakes, baskets of alms-food, loads of sugarcane, and so on.

If two or three novices together give a load that is capable of being formally offered, or if two or three monks together receive a load lifted and offered by one strong novice, it is allowable.

If pots of oil, molasses, or fresh butter are hung on the legs of a couch (mañca) or a chair (pīṭha), it is allowable for a monk to sit on that couch or chair. It is not considered 'taken without being offered' (uggahitaka).

If two oil pots are hung on a wall-peg (nāgadantaka) or a hook, where the upper one has been formally offered but the lower one has not, it is allowable to take the upper one. If the lower one has been formally offered but the upper one has not, for a monk who takes the upper one and then the lower one, the upper one becomes 'taken without being offered' (uggahitaka). If there is an unoffered oil bowl under a couch, and a monk who is sweeping hits that oil bowl with the broom, it is not 'taken without being offered'. If one intends to take a formally offered object but accidentally picks up an unoffered one, and upon realizing it, puts it back, it is not 'taken without being offered'. If one realizes it after taking it outside, one should not leave it outside but return it to its original place; there is no fault. However, if it was an open object before being taken, it should not be closed; it must be placed exactly as it was before. If it is left outside, it must not be touched again.

If one realizes [an item is unoffered] while descending to the lower floor of a multi-storied building and is in the middle of the stairs, since there is no space to place it, it should be carried up or down and then placed. If mold grows on offered oil or similar substances, or if thick dust settles on ginger and such, since these arise from the items themselves, there is no need for a second formal offering.

If a person who has climbed a palmyra or coconut tree lowers a cluster of fruit by a rope and says 'Please receive it' while still remaining above, it should not be received. But if another person standing on the ground takes the rope loop and lifts it to give, it is allowable. If a large branch with fruit is made allowable (kappiya) and then formally offered, the fruits are also considered formally offered; it is allowable to consume them as desired.

If someone standing inside a fence cuts the fence and gives sugarcane or timbarūsaka fruit, it is allowable if it is within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa). If one receives fruit that has come out without hitting the fence posts, it is allowable. Regarding fruit that comes out after being hit, no fault is shown in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathās). But we [teachers]...
116:
...consider that it is merely falling by itself from the place where it was struck. If it does not stop at the place where it was struck but continues moving, it is suitable (to be received), like goods that roll out from a customs house (suṅka-ghāta). If they give by passing over a fence or a wall, and if the wall is not thick and the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) between the person inside and the person outside is sufficient, it is allowable to catch fruit that comes from even a hundred cubits above.

A monk carries a sick novice on his shoulders; if that novice sees various fruits, takes them, and gives them while still sitting on the shoulders, it is allowable. If another person carrying a monk gives to the monk sitting on his shoulders, it is certainly allowable.

A monk travels holding a branch with fruit for the sake of shade; if the desire to eat the fruit arises, it is allowable to eat after having it formally offered. If he has it made allowable (kappiya) to ward off flies and then receives it, and if he then wishes to eat, the original formal offering is sufficient; there is no fault for the monk who eats it.

A monk travels after placing items suitable for formal offering on a vehicle belonging to laypeople; if the vehicle gets stuck in the mud and a young monk (dahara) takes the wheel and lifts it, it is allowable; it is not considered 'taken without being offered' (uggahitaka). If he places it on a boat and moves the boat with an oar or pulls it by hand, it is allowable. The same method applies to a raft. Even if placed in a large jar (cāṭi) or a rice pot, it is allowable to have an unordained person (anupasampanna) hold it and then cross [the water] by holding that person's arm. If such a jar is not available, it is allowable to have the unordained person take [the items] and cross by holding his arm.

Lay devotees give travel provisions of raw rice to monks who are going on a journey. The novices, carrying the monks' rice, are unable to carry their own rice; so the monks carry the novices' rice. When the rice carried by the novices is exhausted, they cook gruel (yāgu) with the other rice [carried by the monks], arrange all the monks' bowls in order, and pour the gruel. A wise novice takes his own bowl and gives it to the senior monk (thera), takes the senior monk's bowl and gives it to the next senior monk (anuthera), and thus exchanges all the bowls. In this way, all have eaten what belonged to the novice, and it is allowable.

Even if the novice is not wise (in Vinaya) and begins to drink the gruel in his own bowl by himself, if the senior monks request in order, saying, 'Friend novice, give your gruel to me,' and then drink it, it is allowable; all have consumed only what belonged to the novice.
117:
It is considered as eating only the property of the novice; no fault is incurred due to the reasons of uggahita (taken without being offered) or sannidhi (storing). In this matter, no distinction is seen between those who take oil and such for their parents, or branches and such for shade, and these monks. Therefore, the underlying cause should be investigated.

If a novice wishes to cook a meal and washes the rice but is unable to remove the dregs and impurities, the monk may receive the rice and the pot, wash the rice, and place the pot on the stove; however, he must not light the fire. When it is cooked, he should open it to know whether it is done. If it is undercooked, it is not proper to close it again for the purpose of further cooking. It is, however, proper to close it to prevent dust or ash from falling in. When it is cooked, it is proper to take it down and to eat it; there is no further need for the act of receiving it again.

If a novice is capable of cooking but has no free time and wishes to go somewhere, the monk, having received the pot together with the rice and water and placed it on the stove, should say, "Go (after lighting the fire)." Thereafter, it is proper to do everything according to the previous method.

If a monk places a clean pot for the purpose of gruel and heats the water, it is proper. If the novice puts rice into the hot water, from that point onwards, the monk must not light the fire. It is proper to receive the cooked gruel and drink it.

While a novice is cooking gruel, if a restless monk, out of playfulness, touches the pot, touches the lid, or removes the rising foam, it is not proper for that monk alone to drink it; this is called "badly handled" (durupaciṇṇa). However, if he takes a ladle or a spoon and stirs without lifting it, it is not proper for any of the monks; it is both "self-cooked" (sāmapāka) and "badly handled." If he lifts the pot, it also becomes uggahita.

When a monk has finished his alms round and placed his bowl on a bowl-stand, if another restless monk, out of playfulness, touches the bowl or the bowl-lid, it is not proper for that monk alone to eat the food obtained from it. If he lifts the bowl and puts it back, it is not proper for any of the monks. If one takes a branch or a vine and shakes the fruits on that tree, it is not proper for that monk alone to eat the fruit obtained from it, and he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for bad handling (durupaciṇṇa). However, leaning against a fruit tree or tying thorns to that tree is proper; it is stated in the Mahāpaccari that it does not constitute durupaciṇṇa.
118:
If one sees mangoes or other fruits fallen in the forest and thinks, "I will give them to the novice," it is proper to bring and give them. Even if one sees lion's leftovers and such, and thinks, "I will give them to the novice," it is proper to bring and give them, whether having received them or not. If one can clear the thought that "the novice will give it back to me," it is also proper to eat what is obtained from that novice. No fault is incurred due to the reason of receiving raw meat or fish, nor due to the reason of uggahita (handling without being offered).

If a monk who is carrying oil and such for his parents falls ill on the way, it is proper for him to receive and use whatever he desires from that oil and such. If it was already received from the beginning, there is no need for the act of receiving it again. If he brings rice and gives it to his parents, and those parents prepare gruel and such from that very rice and give it back to him, it is proper to use it. There is no fault due to the reason of storing (sannidhi) or uggahita.

If a monk heats water while keeping it covered (to prevent ash), it is proper to use it until it is exhausted. However, if ash falls into that hot water, it must be received again. If ash falls while cooking oil by holding the vessel with long tongs, he should continue cooking without letting go of it with his hand, and after taking it down, it must be received again. If embers or wood have already been received and kept, the original reception is sufficient.

While a monk is chewing sugarcane, a novice says, "Please give some to me too." If the monk says, "Cut and take from here," and the novice takes it, there is no need for the act of receiving the remaining part of the sugarcane again. The same method applies to one chewing a lump of jaggery. Indeed, the part remaining after being cut and taken from the specified place is considered as not having lost its status of being received.

When a monk, having received jaggery to distribute it, makes it into portions, and other monks or novices come and take one portion each in a single act of taking, the remainder of what was taken is still considered received. If a restless novice takes it and then puts it back, the remainder touched by that novice becomes "not received" (appatiggahita).

When a monk receives a medicinal cigarette and smokes it, even if the mouth and throat become as if coated with realgar (manosilā), it is proper to eat yāvakālika food. There is no fault in the mixing of yāvakālika items with yāvajīvika items.
119:
If smoke enters through the ears, nose, or mouth while baking a bowl or boiling dye, or if one smells a flower or fruit due to illness, it is allowable because it is *abbhohārika* (negligible). If food vomited due to belching or similar causes touches the palate and returns inside, it is allowable as it is beyond control. However, for a monk who swallows vomit that has entered the mouth during the afternoon, there is an offense. If the juice of food stuck between the teeth enters [the throat], it is indeed an offense. If the food is subtle and the taste is not apparent, it falls under the category of *abbhohārika*.

When the time of noon is near, if one has eaten in a place where there is no water, one should cough up phlegm, discard two or three lumps of saliva, and then go to a place where there is water to rinse the mouth. If sprouts emerge from ginger or other items that have already been formally accepted, there is no need for further acceptance. If salt is unavailable, it is allowable to use seawater for the purpose of salt. If salt water that has been formally accepted turns into salt, or if salt turns into water, or if sugarcane juice turns into molasses, or if molasses turns into liquid, it is allowable by the original acceptance alone. Snow and hail are of the same nature as water. If one clears water using the seeds of the *kataka* (clearing-nut) tree that have been brought, those seeds are *abbhohārika*, and it is allowable to drink the water along with the seeds. Water cleared with wood-apple fruits or similar items, which are of the nature of food (*āmisa*), is allowable only in the morning.

In ponds and similar places, even if the water is turbid, it is allowable. However, if it sticks to the mouth or hands, it is not allowable; it must be formally accepted before use. In places where fields are being ploughed, turbid water must be formally accepted. If it flows and enters streams or similar channels and fills a river, it is allowable. In pools such as those of the *kakudha* trees, where the water is covered by flowers fallen from trees, if the taste of the flowers is not apparent, there is no need for formal acceptance. If the water is little and the taste is apparent, it must be formally accepted. The same method applies to water in mountain clefts and similar places covered by dark-colored leaves.

If flowers with pollen or flowers with milky sap from the stems are placed in a drinking water pot, they must be formally accepted. Alternatively, the flowers should be formally accepted before being put in. If *pāṭali*, *campaka*, or *mallikā* flowers are placed and only the scent remains, that scent is *abbhohārika*, and it is allowable to drink it even on the second day along with food. If a *sāmaṇera* takes water from a drinking water pot scented with flowers that was formally accepted by a monk, and pours the remainder back into the pot, it must be formally accepted again. In lotus ponds and similar places, the pollen that lies spread over the water...
120:
...it is allowable to take water by pushing [the pollen] aside with a pot. If there is a tooth-stick that has been made allowable and formally accepted, and one wishes to drink its juice, the original acceptance is sufficient. A tooth-stick that has been kept without being formally accepted must be accepted [before use]. Even if the juice enters [the throat] unknowingly, it is still an offense. This is because this training rule is *acittaka* (an offense regardless of intention).

Regarding the Great Elements (*Mahābhūta*), what is allowable and what is not? Firstly, milk is allowable. Whether it is the milk of an animal whose flesh is allowable or an animal whose flesh is not allowable, there is no offense for the monk who drinks it. Tears, saliva, nasal mucus, urine, excrement, phlegm, tooth-grime, eye-wax, ear-wax, and salt produced on the body—all these are allowable. However, among these things belonging to the body, whatever moves from its place and falls into a bowl or onto the hand must be formally accepted. Whatever is still attached to the body is considered already accepted. If the sweat of a monk eating hot milk-rice flows down along his fingers and stays in contact with the milk-rice, or if while walking for alms, it flows from the hand or from the rim of the bowl down to the bottom of the bowl, there is no need for formal acceptance in these cases. Among the Great Elements that have been burnt, there is nothing that is said to be unallowable; however, that which is poorly burnt is not allowable. Even human bone that is well-burnt may be powdered and added to lickable medicine.

If there is no lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) to make them allowable, it is allowable to take and consume the four Great Filth Medicines (*Mahāvikaṭa*) by oneself. In this context, a person who is disobedient or incapable is considered the same as having no lay attendant. If there is no ash, one should burn dry wood and take the ash. If there is no dry wood, it is allowable even to cut green wood from a tree to make it. However, these four types of Great Filth Medicines are called *kālodissaṃ* (for a specific time) and are allowable only at the moment of a snake bite. The remaining matters are clear.

The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the *Eḷakaloma* training rule is: it arises from the body and from the body and mind; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is not a release by perception (*no saññāvimokkha*); it is *acittaka* (without specific intent); it is a transgression of a regulation (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is a bodily action (*kāyakamma*); it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Tenth Training Rule on Tooth-sticks.

## The Fourth Chapter on Food (Bhojanavagga) is complete according to the sequence of commentary.
121:
## 5. Acelaka Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Acelaka Training Rule
In the first training rule of the Acelaka Vagga— 'Parivesanaṃ' refers to the place where food is served. 'Paribbājakasamāpanno' refers to one who has well entered the practice of going to a hermitage, having abandoned worldly affairs. 'Deti āpatti pācittiyassa' means that if one gives a bowl of gruel filled to the brim with a single effort, one commits a Pācittiya offense. If one gives by repeatedly breaking the flow of the gruel, a Pācittiya is incurred for every effort. The same applies to cakes, rice, and so on. Even if one perceives a titthiya (non-Buddhist ascetic) as a non-titthiya, or if one's mother or father is practicing the Brahmin life among titthiyas and one gives to them with the perception of them being parents, it is still a Pācittiya. 'Dāpeti' means causing an unordained person (anupasampanna), such as a layperson or a novice, to give.

'Upanikkhipitvā detī' means placing food in a vessel suitable for giving to such titthiyas and putting that vessel on the ground near them, or having them put down their vessel and putting food into it. It is allowable to place the bowl on a bowl-stand or on the ground and say, "Take from this bowl." If a titthiya says, "This belongs to me; please pour it into this vessel," one may pour it. Since that property belongs to the titthiya, it does not constitute "giving with one's own hand" (sahatthā dāna). The remaining points in this training rule are clear.

This training rule has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Eḷakaloma training rule. It occurs through action (kiriya), no release by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), non-volitional (acittaka), breach of regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), three minds, and three feelings.
## First: Acelaka Training Rule.

## 2. Commentary on the Uyyojana Training Rule
In the second training rule— 'Paṭikkamanepi' means also in a village refectory. 'Bhattavissaggaṃ' refers to the act of eating. 'Na sambhāvesi' means not arriving or not catching up.

'Anācāraṃ' refers to misconduct of the body and speech doors other than what is directly taught in the Pali. In the phrase 'dassanūpacāraṃ vā savanūpacāraṃ vā vijahantassa', if one dismisses a monk while standing or sitting, and the dismissed monk leaves the range (upacāra) of sight or hearing, no offense is incurred by the monk who leaves. However, when he leaves, in effect, the other monk (who dismissed him) has also left the range. Therefore, this offense is incurred only by the monk who dismisses. In that dismissal...
122:
If one foot remains within the range (upacāra), it is a Dukkaṭa offense. If one crosses the boundary of the range, it is a Pācittiya offense. Here, the range of sight (dassanūpacāra) in an open space is twelve cubits (dvādasa-hattha) in measure; likewise for the range of hearing (savanūpacāra). However, if there are walls, doors, fences, etc., in between, being obscured by them constitutes crossing the range of sight; the offense should be understood by way of such crossing. There is no other reason except for the aforementioned various types of misconduct.

"Kalisāsanaṃ āropeti": "Kali" means anger; it means imposing the command of that anger, or imposing the authority of anger. By the power of anger, one points out faults in standing, sitting, etc., saying, "Look, sirs, at this monk's way of standing, sitting, looking ahead, and looking around. He stands still like a tree stump, sits like a dog, and looks here and there like a monkey." One says such unpleasant words thinking, "Perhaps he will depart, being harassed by these words." The rest is clear.

This training rule has three origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It occurs with action (kiriya), release by perception (saññāvimokkha), volitional (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusala-citta), and three feelings.

## Second: Uyyojana Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Sabhojana Training Rule

In the third training rule, "Sayanighare" means in the bedroom. "Yato ayyassa bhikkhā dinnā" means "Alms have been given for this reason; the monk has received what he should receive; therefore, please depart." "Pariyuṭṭhito" means overwhelmed by lust, meaning having a desire for sexual intercourse.

It is called "Sabhojana" because it involves two people, a husband and wife; in that family (is the meaning). Or, "Sabhojana" means "Sabhoga" (with enjoyment). For a man overwhelmed by lust, a woman is an object of enjoyment, and for a woman, a man is an object of enjoyment. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājana) of this term, it is said, "There is a woman and there is a man," and so on. "Mahallake ghare" means in a large bedroom. "Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā" means leaving the distance of a hand's reach from the doorframe of that bedroom chamber and sitting near the bed.
123:
It means "sitting in a place near the inner sleeping chamber." Such a sleeping chamber exists in large houses with four wings and so on. By the words "piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā," it shows the crossing of the middle part. Therefore, it should be understood that an offense is committed when crossing the middle of a small sleeping chamber constructed in any manner. The rest of the words here are clear.

The origin of the first Pārājika consists of: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and two feelings (dvivedanā).

## The Third Training Rule on Eating Together (Sabhojana Sikkhāpada).

Regarding the fourth and fifth training rules, whatever decision should be stated, all of it follows the method already stated in the two Aniyata training rules. Just as the Sabhojana training rule has the origin of the first Pārājika, these fourth and fifth training rules also have the origin of the first Pārājika.

## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Visiting (Cāritta Sikkhāpada)

In the sixth training rule, regarding the words "Friends, give the meal," it is said that the meal had already been brought forward; therefore, they spoke thus. However, in the case of a meal that has not been brought forward, one is not allowed to speak in this way; it would be "speech connected with requisites" (payuttavācā).

Regarding the words "Therefore, bhikkhus, having accepted it, set it aside," the Blessed One said this for the sake of protecting the faith of the family. If He had said "Divide it and eat it," there might be a change in the people's devotion (loss of faith). "Ussāriyittha" means it has been taken back; it means they took that food and went back to their house.

Regarding the words "a present monk" (santaṃ bhikkhuṃ), by what extent is a monk "present" and by what extent is he "not present"? Within the monastery, from the place where a monk stands and develops the intention to visit families, whatever monk he sees to his side or in front of him, whom he is able to inform with normal speech—this is called a "present" (santa) monk. There is no such thing as the duty of searching here and there to inform. A monk who must be searched for in such a way is indeed "not present" (asanta). Furthermore, if one sees a monk within the precincts (upacāra-sīmā) and goes there thinking "I will ask permission," and sees a monk there...
124:
That monk should be asked for permission. If he is not seen, one is said to have entered without asking a monk who is not present.

"Antarārāma" means there is a monastery within the village, and he goes to that monastery. "Bhattiyaghara" means the house where one is invited for a meal or the house of donors of ticket-food (salākabhatta) and so on. "Āpadāsu" means in the event of danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacariya), it is proper to go. The rest of the words here are very clear.

The origin is like that of the Kathina training rule. It arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind. It is [an offense of] action or non-action. It is not "release through perception" (saññāvimokkha). It is "without intention" (acittaka), meaning it can occur even without conscious intent. It is a "fault of regulation" (paṇṇattivajja). It is bodily action or vocal action. It has three types of mind and three types of feeling.

## 7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Mahānāma (Mahānāma Sikkhāpada)

In the seventh training rule, the one named Mahānāma was the son of the Blessed One's paternal uncle and was about one month older than the Blessed One. He was a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) established in the lower two fruits. "The medicine is abundant" means the ghee brought from the cow-pen and stored was very plentiful.

"Should be accepted" (sāditabbā) means at the time of the invitation, one should not refuse saying there is no illness yet; one should accept it with the thought, "I will ask for it when there is an illness." "I invite you with this much medicine" means inviting by name with two or three kinds among ghee, oil, etc., or inviting by measure such as a pattha, a nāḷi, or an āḷhaka. "He asks for other medicine" means being invited with ghee but asking for oil, or being invited with the measure of one nāḷi but asking for the measure of one doṇa. "No need for medicine" means if one can subsist even with mixed almsfood, then there is no need for medicine.

"For those who have invited" (pavāritānaṃ) means there is no offense in asking according to the invitation from donors who have made a specific personal invitation for oneself. However, in the case of those who have invited in connection with the Saṅgha, the measure must certainly be noted. The rest is clear.
125:
This training rule has six origins (samuṭṭhāna). It occurs through action (kiriya), not being released by perception (no saññāvimokkha), being unintentional (acittaka), being a prescriptive fault (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## Mahānāma Sikkhāpadaṃ Sattaṃ.

## 8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the eighth training rule: 'Abbhuyyāto' means setting out towards. It refers to leaving the city with the intention of going towards the opposing army. 'Uyyuttaṃ' means a mobilized army that has already departed from the village.

'Dvādasapuriso hatthī' (an elephant with twelve men) refers to an elephant carrying four riders and two foot guards for each of the four legs (eight guards), totaling twelve men. 'Tipuriso asso' (a horse with three men) refers to a horse with one rider and two foot guards, totaling three men. 'Caturpuriso ratho' (a chariot with four men) refers to a chariot with one driver, one warrior, and two axle guards (āṇirakkhaka), totaling four men. 'Cattāro purisā sarahatthā' refers to four men with bows in their hands. These mentioned above constitute a fourfold army (caturaṅgasenā) at its minimum limit. For a monk who goes to see such an army, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred for every step. 'Dassanūpacāraṃ vijahitvā' means that when the army is not visible because it is obscured by forests, mountains, etc., or because it has descended into a low-lying area, and the monk, thinking he cannot see from where he stands, moves to another place to watch, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every effort made.

'Ekam-ekaṃ' refers to any one of the four branches of the army, such as the elephants. Even going to see a single elephant with at least one rider, or a single man with a bow in his hand, incurs an offense. 'Anuyyuttā' refers to the type of army that accompanies a king when he goes to a park or a river. Such an army is called 'anuyyuttā' because it has not set out from the country for the purpose of war.

'Āpadāsu' means that in the event of danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacariya), there is no offense for a monk who goes there thinking he will be safe by entering the army. The remaining words are clear. This training rule has six origins like the Eḷakaloma training rule: it is an action (kiriya), not released by perception (no saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta), and three types of feeling.

## Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadaṃ Aṭṭhamaṃ.

## 9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth training rule, Senāvāsa: 'stays in the army when the sun has set' means whether he stands, sits, or lies down; even if he maintains any posture in the air through psychic power, it is still a pācittiya offense. 'The army is besieged by the opposing army' means it is blocked to the extent that movement is cut off. 'Palibuddho' means being obstructed by an enemy or a ruler. The remaining words are clear. This training rule has origins like the Eḷakaloma training rule: it is an action (kiriya), not released by perception (no saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a prescriptive fault (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## 10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the tenth training rule, Uyyodhika: 'they advance and fight here,' therefore it is called 'uyyodhika.' This is a designation for a battleground. 'They know the strength of the troops here,' therefore it is called 'balagga.' It means the place where the number of troops is counted. The specific arrangement of the army's assembly is called 'senābyūha.' This is a designation for the encampment of the army. 'Three elephants' refers to the elephant corps (hatthānīka) at the rear. ## 6. Surāpānavaggo

## 1. Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the first training rule of the Surāpāna Vagga: 'Bhaddavatikā' is the name of a village. It received this name because it was endowed with a beautiful fence. 'Pathāvino' means travelers. '(Subduing) the power of the Naga with his own psychic power.' 'Kāpotikā' refers to liquor that has a red color like the feet of a pigeon. 'Pasannā' means...
127:
The name 'pasannā' is the name for clear liquor. "Monks, it is not suitable for Sāgata" means that for Sāgata, who possessed the five supernormal powers (abhiññā), drinking intoxicants is not suitable.

Liquor made from the juice of flowers such as the Madhuka is called pupphāsava (flower-liquor). Liquor made by crushing fruits such as grapes and using their juice is called phalāsava (fruit-liquor). Liquor made from the natural juice of grapes is called madhvāsava; it is said that it is also made from honey. Liquor made from sugarcane juice and the like is called guḷāsava. Liquid made by adding yeast to flour-powder is called surā. Liquid made from the juice of coconuts and the like is also designated as surā. It is said that when the clear part of that surā made with yeast is taken, it is designated as meraya. "Even as much as a blade of grass" means that for a monk who drinks even a drop of this aforementioned surā or meraya, from the time of its inception, it is a Pācittiya offense. If one drinks a large amount with a single effort (payoga), only one offense is incurred. For a monk who drinks repeatedly, breaking the flow, there are as many offenses as there are efforts.

If it is not an intoxicant but has the color, smell, and taste of an intoxicant, such as loṇasovīraka (salted sour gruel) or sutta beverage, there is no offense. In cooking soup, if a small amount of liquor is added to make it fragrant, there is no offense in that soup. The same applies to cooking meat well. Oil is cooked with liquor as a medicine for wind ailments; if the liquor is not added excessively, there is no offense. If it is added excessively so that the color, smell, and taste of the liquor are apparent, an offense is indeed incurred. "Non-intoxicating ariṭṭha" means there is no offense in ariṭṭha medicinal liquid that is not an intoxicant. It is said that ariṭṭha is made from the juice of fruits like the emblic myrobalan (āmalaka); though it has the color, smell, and taste of liquor, it is not an intoxicant. This statement refers to such non-intoxicating ariṭṭha. However, ariṭṭha made by adding fermenting ingredients (sambhāra) is an intoxicant; that liquor is not allowable from the time of its inception.

The rest of the words here are clear. This training rule has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Eḷakaloma training rule: it is an action (kiriya), not exempt by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), without specific intent regarding the object (acittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and involves the three feelings (tivedana). In this training rule, it should be understood as acittaka because an offense is incurred even without knowing the object, and as lokavajja because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind.

## The First Training Rule on Drinking Intoxicants.
129:
For a monk who plays by taking even a mere drop of water and throwing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, it is allowable to write letters [on the water] to clarify a meaning. This is the decision on this matter. The rest of the words are clear.

Just like the origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the first Pārājika, it consists of: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and three feelings (tivedanā).

## 4. Anādariya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule—"kathāyaṃ nasseyya" means "How might this Dhamma, this lineage of tradition, perish?" (This is the intent). One acts with disrespect, not wishing to train in that rule. "Taṃ vā na sikkhitukāmo" means he does not wish to train in whatever training rule has been laid down and is being spoken of. "Apaññattena" means [speaking] with words of Dhamma that appear in the Suttas or the Abhidhamma.

In the phrase "This is the learning of our teachers," one should not accept the censurable learning of teachers; one should only accept the learning of teachers that has come down through the lineage. However, in the Kurundī, it is said: "The learning of teachers is not allowable in the case of worldly faults (lokavajja), but it is allowable in the case of faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja)." In the Mahāpaccari, it is said: "The learning of teachers who have studied the Pāḷi and the commentaries consistent with the Pāḷi is the standard; the words of those who do not know are not the standard." All those words meet in the view that has come down through the lineage. The rest of the words are clear.

It has three origins (tisamuṭṭhāna)—it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, or from body, speech, and mind. It consists of: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## 6. Joti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth training rule—Bhagga is the name of a country (janapada). Saṃsumāragira is the name of a city. Bhesakaḷāvana is the name of the forest near that city. Because that forest was given for the sake of the deer's comfortable living, it is called Migadāya (Deer Park). "Samādahitvā" means having kindled a fire. "Paripātesī" means he followed or chased.

"Padīpepi" means even in lighting a lamp. "Jotikepi" means in making a fire for such tasks as baking a bowl or sudation (sweating treatment). "Tathārūpapaccayā" means because of such reasons as lighting a lamp.

354-5. In the phrase "sayaṃ samādahati," from the time one sets up the fire-sticks (araṇi) with the desire to kindle a fire, as long as the flame has not yet arisen, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every effort (payoga). "Paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati" means he picks up a burning ember that has fallen from the hearth and places it back in its original position. For a monk who thus picks up an unextinguished ember and puts it back into the hearth, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for a monk who rekindles an ember that has already gone out, there is only a pācittiya offense.

"Tathārūpapaccayā" means that, excluding lighting a lamp and so forth, there is no offense (anāpatti) for a monk who kindles a fire for other such reasons. "Āpadāsu" refers to times of danger; that is, if danger arises from fierce wild animals or non-humans (amanussa), there is no offense for a monk who kindles a fire at that time. The rest of the words are clear. There are six origins: action (kiriya), no release through perception (no-saññāvimokkha), without intention (acittaka), fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of mind (ticitta), and three feelings (tivedanā).

## 7. Nahāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the seventh training rule—in the phrase "cuṇṇena vā mattikāya vā," from the time of preparing the soap powder or fine clay, there is a dukkaṭa offense for every effort (payoga).

In the phrase "pāraṃ gacchanto nhāyati," it is allowable to bathe even in small pits made by scraping the sand in a dried-up river. "Āpadāsu" means it is allowable to submerge in water when being chased by creatures such as bees. Here, the rest of the words are clear. According to the Eḷakalomā origin: action (kiriya), no release through perception (no-saññāvimokkha), without intention (acittaka), fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), three types of mind (ticitta), and three feelings (tivedanā).

## 8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Discoloring (Dubbaṇṇakaraṇa-sikkhāpada)

368-9. In the eighth training rule—regarding the phrase "navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhena": the word "labha" is used in the sense of "alabhi" (has obtained); "labha" itself is "lābha" (acquisition). What was obtained? A robe. Of what kind? A new one. Thus, although it should be said as "navacīvaralābhena" [with the nasal dropped], it is expressed as "navacīvaralābhena" without dropping the nasal (anunāsika/niggahīta); it means a monk who has obtained a new robe. The two words standing in the middle, "pana", are merely particles (nipāta). "Bhikkhunā" is an indication of the person who obtained it. In the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanī), however, without focusing on the literal syllables, the phrase "cīvaraṃ nāma channaṃ cīvarānaṃ" etc. is stated to show what was obtained. In this context, "cīvara" should be understood only as a robe that can be worn or draped. For this reason, "vikappanūpagapacchima" (the smallest robe suitable for assignment) was not mentioned.

"Kaṃsanīla" refers to the dark blue/black dye used by cobblers. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said, "The color of iron rust or bronze rust is called kaṃsanīla." "Palāsanīla" refers to any leaf-green color. "Dubbaṇṇakaraṇaṃ ādātabbaṃ" (a discoloring mark must be made) is said with reference to making this ritual mark (kappabindu); it does not mean discoloring the entire robe with blue dye and so on. A monk making that ritual mark, after dyeing the robe, should apply a mark the size of a peacock's eye-circle or the size of a bedbug's back at all four corners, or three, or two, or at just one corner. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said, "It is not proper on the border or on the knot-fastener." In the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said, "It is indeed proper." Since marks such as pālikappa (marking in lines) and kaṇṇikakappa (marking in the shape of a lotus) are forbidden in all commentaries, one must not make the ritual mark in any other peculiar form except for a single round circle (vaṭṭabindu).

Regarding the words "aggaḷe" (on a patch) etc., there is no need to perform the ritual marking again because these patches and so on are added later to a robe that has already been ritual-marked. The rest is clear. The origin of this training rule is like the Eḷakaloma rule—it is [classified as] action and non-action (kiriyākirya), no release by perception (nosanyāvimokkha), without thought (acittaka), a breach of a formal prescription (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), involving three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).

## The Eighth Training Rule on Discoloring is finished.

## 7. The Sapāṇaka Chapter (Sapāṇakavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Intentionally Killing (Sañciccapāṇa-sikkhāpada)

In the first training rule of the Sapāṇaka Chapter—"issāso hoti" means he was a teacher of archers during his time as a layman. "Jīvitā vorepitā" means deprived of the life-faculty.

In the training rule also, "vorepeyya" means would deprive (of the life-faculty). This is because this expression is merely a conventional usage (vohāramatta). In reality, just as when a head ornament is separated, the head remains, in the case of a living being deprived of life, there is no such thing as "life" that remains separately; rather...
133:
(The life-faculty) only reaches destruction; therefore, to show that meaning, it is stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājaniya) as "cuts off the life-faculty (jīvitindriya)," and so on. In this training rule, only an animal should be understood as a "living being" (pāṇa). Whether that animal is small or large, there is no difference in the offense for the one who kills it. However, in the case of a large being, because the effort is great, the unwholesome (akusala) is greater. While perceiving a living being as a living being, even when cleaning a bed or a chair, if one lacks compassion and crushes and removes even a bedbug egg while perceiving it as a living being, one commits a Pācittiya offense. Therefore, in such matters, one should arouse compassion and perform one's duties without negligence. The remaining decisions, along with the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Manussaviggaha Sikkhāpada.

## The First Training Rule on Intentionally Killing a Living Being is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings

In the second training rule—"containing living beings" (sappāṇaka) refers to water with small insects that would die through use. For a monk who uses such water knowing it contains insects, a Pācittiya offense is committed for every effort (payoga). If one drinks a full bowl of water in a single continuous effort without interruption, one offense is committed. If one rinses a bowl stained with food and so on with such water, or if one cools a hot bowl of rice gruel (yāgu) by dipping it into such water, or if one takes that water with the hand or a ladle to bathe, a Pācittiya offense is committed for every effort. If one enters a pool or a pond and causes waves to make the water flow out, an offense is committed. Monks cleaning a pool or a pond should pour the water taken from it back into the water itself. If there is no water nearby, one should pour about eight or ten pots of allowable (kappiya) water onto a place where water can settle well, and then pour it into that. One should not pour water onto a hot stone slab thinking, "It will roll down and fall into the water." It is proper to cool the stone slab with allowable water first and then pour it. The remaining meanings here are clear.

## Three origins: action, release by perception, with intention, fault by prescription (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

In this training rule, it should be understood as a fault by prescription (paṇṇattivajja) because it is used with the perception of water even though one knows there are insects, just as one lights a lamp knowing that moths might fall into it but with a pure mind.

## The Second Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings is Finished.
134:
## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Reopening

In the third training rule—"they reopen" (ukkoṭenti) means they go to various monks and say things like "the act was not properly done," thereby agitating them and not allowing the matter to remain settled as it was.

"According to the Dhamma" (yathādhammaṃ) means by whatever means of settling (samatha) that was stated for the purpose of calming that legal issue (adhikaraṇa). "A settled legal issue" (nihata-adhikaraṇaṃ) refers to a legal issue that has been suppressed; it means a legal issue that has been calmed by the very means of settling taught by the Teacher.

"Perceiving a legal act as a legal act" (dhammakamme dhammakammasaññī) means that the legal issue was calmed by a certain act, and while that act is indeed a legal act (dhammakamma), this monk also perceives it as a legal act, yet if he reopens it, he incurs a Pācittiya offense. In this manner, the remaining terms should also be understood. This is a summary here; the detail is taught in the Parivāra in the manner beginning with "Among these four legal issues, how many reopenings are there?" In the ancient commentaries, all of that was brought forward and the meaning of that legal issue was explained. However, we will explain that meaning where it directly occurs in the Parivāra. If it were brought and explained here, it might cause even greater confusion; therefore, we have not explained it. The remaining words here are very clear. This training rule has three origins: action, release by perception, with intention, worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, vocal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.

## The Third Training Rule on Reopening is Finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Grave Offenses

In the fourth training rule—"an offense known as a grave offense" (duṭṭhullā nāma āpatti), here the four Pārājikas are shown by way of extracting the meaning, yet only the Saṅghādisesa offense is intended. For a monk who conceals that offense, a Pācittiya offense is committed. "At the mere dropping of the responsibility" (dhuraṃ nikkhittamatta) means at the moment the effort is abandoned. Even if one informs another after dropping the responsibility, one is not released from the offense; it means the Pācittiya offense is committed at the mere dropping of the responsibility. If one drops the responsibility and informs another monk solely for the purpose of concealing it, and that monk informs another, in this way, as long as the connection is not broken, even a hundred monks or a thousand monks will incur the offense. When is the connection broken? First, the Elder Mahāsumma says— "A monk who has fallen into an offense..."
135:
(Mahāsumatthera) said: "He informs another monk; that monk turns back and informs that very same (offending) monk; in this way, the link is broken." Mahāpadumatthera, however, said: "This (returning) person is just the owner of the matter. In fact, the monk who committed the offense informs another monk; this (second) monk informs another (third) monk; that (third) monk turns back and informs that very (second) monk who informed him; in this way, when the third person informs the second person, the link is broken."

"Adullullaṃ āpattiṃ" refers to the remaining five groups of offenses. In the phrase "anupasampannassa duṭṭhullaṃ vā aduṭṭhullaṃ vā ajjhācāraṃ," the acts of emission of semen and physical contact by an unordained person (novice) are called "duṭṭhullajjhācāra" (grave misconduct). The rest of the words here are clear. This training rule has the origination of dhuranikkhepasamuṭṭhāna (laying down the burden). It arises from body, speech, and mind. It is associated with inaction (akiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), intentionality (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Fourth Training Rule on Grave Offenses is finished.

## 5. Description of the Training Rule on One Under Twenty Years

In the fifth training rule: "Aṅguliyo dukkhā bhavissanti" means (the parents) thought that the fingers of (Upāli) who was learning to write would become painful. "Urassa dukkho" means one who learns arithmetic has to think a lot; because of such much thinking, they thought that (Upāli's) chest would become painful (distressed). "Akkhīni dukkhā bhavissanti" means one who learns the art of examining coins (rūpasutta) has to turn and look at the kahāpaṇas (coins) repeatedly; because of such looking, they thought that (Upāli's) eyes would become painful. Among the words starting with "ḍaṃsa," "ḍaṃsā" refers to gadflies with a variegated color. "Dukkhānaṃ" means those difficult to endure. "Tibbānaṃ" means thick (numerous). "Kharānaṃ" means sharp. "Kaṭukānaṃ" means harsh, or similar to a bitter taste because of being unpleasant. "Asātānaṃ" means not sweet. "Pāṇaharānaṃ" means those that take away life (referring to painful feelings).

"Sīmaṃ sammannati" means establishing a new boundary (sīmā). In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said that even in the water-throwing boundary (udakukkhepa), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "Paripuṇṇavīsativasso" means one who has completed twenty years starting from the time of conception. Even one who is twenty years old including the period spent in the mother's womb (gabbhavīsa) is counted as having completed twenty years. The Blessed One taught as follows:
136:
At that time, the Venerable Kumārakassapa was ordained at twenty years including the period in the womb. Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Kumārakassapa: "The Blessed One has laid down a rule that a person under twenty years of age should not be ordained. I was ordained at twenty years including the period in the womb. Am I truly ordained, or am I not truly ordained?" They reported this matter to the Blessed One. "Monks, the first mind that arises in the mother's womb, the first consciousness that appears, starting from that rebirth-linking, is his birth (jāti). Monks, I allow the ordination of one who is twenty years old including the period in the womb."

In that Pali text, if a child stays in the mother's womb for twelve months and is born on the full moon day of Mahāpavāraṇā, he should be ordained on the first day after the full moon (the 1st waning day) after passing the Mahāpavāraṇā day of his nineteenth year, counting from that birth day. In this way, the decrease and increase of years should be understood. Ancient Elders, however, would ordain a nineteen-year-old novice on the day after the full moon of Sāvaṇa (Nikkhamanīya-puṇṇamāsī). Why is that? It is said: In one year, there are six Uposatha days of fourteen days. Thus, in twenty years, four months are lost. Kings add an intercalary month (adhimāsa) every three years. Thus, in eighteen years, six months are added. If the four months lost due to Uposatha days are removed from those six added months, two months remain. By including those two months, they ordain on the first waning day of Sāvaṇa without doubt, considering the twenty years to be complete. Here, the term "nineteen years old" is used referring to one who will be twenty years old after performing Pavāraṇā. Therefore, if a person stayed in the mother's womb for twelve months, he is twenty-one years old (when he reaches twenty after birth). If a person stayed in the mother's womb for seven months, he is twenty years and seven months old. One born after staying only six months in the womb cannot survive.

Regarding the statement "no offense for one who ordains someone under twenty years thinking they are a full twenty years old," although there is no offense for the one ordaining (the preceptor), the person remains unordained (not a true monk). If that unordained person ordains another after ten years, and if the quorum is complete even without him, then that candidate is truly ordained. As long as that unordained person does not know he is not a monk, there is no obstacle to heaven or nibbāna for him. However, if he realizes he is not a monk, he must be ordained again.
138:
## 8. Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule: They are called "Gaddhabādhi" because they harm and kill vultures. He is called "Gaddhabādhipubba" because he had ancestors who formerly harmed and killed vultures. It refers to the monk Ariṭṭha, who was born into that family of vulture-killers.

They are called "Antarāyika" (obstructive) because they create obstacles to heaven and liberation. These obstructive states (antarāyika-dhamma) are of five kinds: obstacles of action (kammantarāyika), obstacles of defilement (kilesantarāyika), obstacles of result (vipākantarāyika), obstacles of disparagement (upavādantarāyika), and obstacles of transgressing commands (āṇāvītikka-mantarāyika). Among these five, the five heinous crimes (pañcānantariya-kamma) are called obstacles of action. Likewise, the act of violating a nun is also an obstacle of action. However, that act only creates an obstacle to liberation, not to heaven. States of fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) are called obstacles of defilement. The rebirth-results of eunuchs (paṇḍaka), animals (tiracchāna), and hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka) are called obstacles of result. Disparaging the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is called an obstacle of disparagement. These disparagements create an obstacle only as long as one does not ask for forgiveness from the Noble Ones; after asking for forgiveness, they no longer create an obstacle. Offenses committed intentionally are called obstacles of transgressing commands. These offenses also create an obstacle only as long as one still claims to be a monk, or has not yet emerged [from a Saṅghādisesa offense], or has not yet confessed [lesser offenses]; after doing so, they no longer create an obstacle.

In this context, the monk Ariṭṭha was a learned Dhamma-preacher and knew the other obstructive states, but because he was not skilled in the Vinaya, he did not know the obstructive state of transgressing the [Buddha's] regulations. Therefore, when he was in a secluded place, he thought: "These laypeople living in houses can become Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners even while enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure. Monks also see delightful forms cognizable by the eye... touch tangible objects cognizable by the body, and use soft rugs, robes, and so forth. All this is allowable. Why is it that only a woman's form... a woman's touch is not allowable? These things should also be allowable."

In this way, by comparing and mixing the flavor of the [blameless] use of the four requisites with the flavor of the [blameworthy] enjoyment of sensual pleasures, and by making the enjoyment with lustful desire and the enjoyment without lustful desire into one and the same, he was like one connecting an extremely delicate thread with a coarse hemp rope, or like one placing Mount Sineru alongside a mustard seed. Having given rise to a wicked wrong view, he thought, "Why did the Blessed One, with great effort as if damming the great ocean, prescribe the first Pārājika? There is no fault in this [sexual intercourse]." Thus, opposing the Buddha's Omniscience, cutting off the hopes of those capable of attaining the paths and fruits, he struck at the Wheel of Command of the Conqueror. Therefore, it was said: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One..." and so forth.
139:
In the passage beginning with "Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā," the simile of the skeleton is used because of the meaning of providing little gratification. The simile of the piece of meat is used because it is common to many (creatures). The simile of the grass torch is used because of the meaning of burning continuously. The simile of the pit of glowing coals is used because of the meaning of great burning. The simile of a dream is used because of the meaning of appearing only for a moment. The simile of borrowed goods is used because of the meaning of being temporary. The simile of the fruit of a tree is used because of the meaning of breaking all limbs and parts. The simile of the butcher's knife and block is used because of the meaning of being cut up. The simile of the sword stake is used because of the meaning of piercing through. The simile of the snake's head is used because of the meaning of being accompanied by fearful danger. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation should be taken from the Majjhima Commentary named Papañcasūdanī (M. Ni. 1.234 etc., 2.42 etc.). "Evaṃ byā kho" means "just as one knows thus." The remaining words are clear as stated previously.

The origin of formal admonition (samanubhāsana) arises from body, speech, and mind; it is an act of omission (akiriya), with release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Eighth Training Rule: Ariṭṭha Sikkhāpada.

## 9. Commentary on the Ukkhittasambhoga Training Rule

424-5. In the ninth rule—"akaṭānudhammena": "anudhamma" refers to the restoration (osāraṇā) performed after seeing the compliant conduct of a monk who was expelled (ukkhitta) in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's Dispensation, either for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for an offense, or for not relinquishing a harmful view. One for whom this anudhamma, known as restoration, has not been performed is called "akaṭānudhamma." It means "together with such a person." Therefore, in the word-analysis, it is said: "akaṭānudhammo nāma ukkhitto anosārito" (akaṭānudhamma means one who is expelled and not yet restored).

Whether giving or receiving, for one who gives or receives much material goods with a single effort, there is one pācittiya. For one who gives or receives by repeatedly breaking (the action), there are pācittiyas according to the number of efforts. The rest is clear. There are three origins (tisamuṭṭhāna): an act of commission (kiriya), with release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), a fault of prescription (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedanā).

## The Ninth Training Rule: Ukkhittasambhoga Sikkhāpada.

## 10. Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule

428. In the tenth rule—"diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ": this means that just as with the monk Ariṭṭha, a wrong view arose in the novice Kaṇṭaka while he was thinking improperly. In the term "nāsetu," destruction (expulsion) is of three types: expulsion from communal living (saṃvāsanāsanā), expulsion from the outward form (liṅganāsanā), and expulsion as a punishment (daṇḍakammanāsanā). Among these three, expulsion due to not seeing an offense etc. is called saṃvāsanāsanā (destruction of the communion). "A corrupt novice should be destroyed (made to disrobe)"; "Destroy the bhikkhunī Mettiyā"—this type of destruction is called liṅganāsanā (destruction of the outward form). "From this day forth... apadisito"—this type of destruction is called daṇḍakammanāsanā (destruction by way of punishment). In this Kaṇṭaka training rule, this daṇḍakammanāsanā is intended. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Thus, monks, he should be destroyed... perish." In that Pali, "cara" means "go." "Pire" refers to one who is outside the Dispensation, who does not cherish the Triple Gem. "Vinassa" means "perish," meaning "go to a place where we do not see you."

429. "Upalāpeyya" means to support (or win over). "Upaṭṭhāpeyya" means to have that novice perform services for oneself. The remaining meanings and the origins (samuṭṭhāna) etc. should be understood in the same way as stated in the Ariṭṭha training rule.

## The Tenth Training Rule: Kaṇṭaka Sikkhāpada.

## The Seventh Chapter, Sappāṇaka Vagga, is finished according to the order of commentary.
140:
## 10. Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule

In the tenth training rule—"diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ": this means that just as with the monk Ariṭṭha, a wrong view arose in the novice Kaṇṭaka while he was thinking and bringing it forth improperly. In the term "nāsetu," destruction (expulsion) is of three types: expulsion from communal living (saṃvāsanāsanā), expulsion from the outward form (liṅganāsanā), and expulsion as a punishment (daṇḍakammanāsanā). Among these three, expulsion due to not seeing an offense etc. is called saṃvāsanāsanā (destruction of the communion in major and minor acts). "A corrupt novice should be destroyed (made to disrobe)"; "Destroy the bhikkhunī Mettiyā"—this type of destruction is called liṅganāsanā (destruction of the outward form). "Friend novice... from this day forth, that Blessed One should not be referred to as our teacher"—this type of destruction is called daṇḍakammanāsanā (destruction by way of punishment). In this training rule, this daṇḍakammanāsanā is intended. Therefore, He said: "Thus, monks, he should be destroyed... perish." In that Pali, "cara" means "go." "Pire" refers to one who is outside the Dispensation, who does not cherish the Triple Gem. "Vinassa" means "perish," meaning "go to a place where we do not see you."

"Upalāpeyya" means to support (or win over). "Upaṭṭhāpeyya" means to have that novice perform services for oneself. The remaining meanings and the origins (samuṭṭhāna) etc. should be understood in the same way as stated in the Ariṭṭha training rule.
