## 8. Sahadhammika Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Sahadhammika Training Rule

In the first training rule of the Sahadhammika Vagga—"in this training rule": this means "I will not yet train in what is stated in this training rule." In the phrase "there is an offense of pācittiya," it should be understood that there is an offense for every single word. "Monks, a monk who is training in the training": this means one who has the desire to train, accepting the advice on his head, and thus he should know, and if he does not know, he should ask, and after asking, he should investigate and reflect. The remaining word-meanings should be understood in the same way as stated in the Dubbaca training rule. The decision is clear.

There are three origins (tisamuṭṭhāna): an act of commission (kiriya), with release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The First Training Rule: Sahadhammika Sikkhāpada.
141:
## 2. Commentary on the Vilekhana Sikkhāpada

In the commentary on the second Vilekhana Sikkhāpada—talk that is connected with what is allowable and what is unallowable, offenses and non-offenses, the factors of restraint and the factors of abandonment, is called Vinayakathā; he speaks such talk connected with the Vinaya. He speaks the praise of the Vinaya in detail means—having laid down the Mātikā (matrix) according to the divisions of the five classes of offenses or the seven classes of offenses, the explanation through the Padabhājanī (word-analysis) is called Vinayassa vaṇṇa; he speaks that Padabhājanī which explains in detail. He speaks the praise of the benefits of learning the Vinaya means—he speaks of the virtues, qualities, and benefits that have the learning of the Vinaya Piṭaka as their root for those individuals who learn the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Indeed, a Vinayadhara (one who bears the Vinaya) can obtain five benefits, six benefits, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven benefits which have the learning of the Vinaya Piṭaka as their root; the meaning is that he speaks of all those benefits. What are the five benefits he can obtain? He can obtain such things as the good protection of his own aggregate of virtue (sīla). Regarding this, the Blessed One has said:

“Monks, there are these five benefits for a person who bears the Vinaya: his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected; he becomes a refuge for those who are troubled by remorse; he speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha; he skillfully restrains opponents with the Dhamma (in accordance with the Vinaya); and he is one who practices for the longevity of the True Dhamma.” Thus it is stated (in the Parivāra).

How is the aggregate of virtue of that Vinayadhara well-guarded and well-protected? In this Dispensation, when a certain monk falls into an offense, he does so through six ways. They are: shamelessness, ignorance, being prone to remorse, perceiving the unallowable as allowable, perceiving the allowable as unallowable, and lapse of mindfulness.

How does one fall into an offense through shamelessness? Even while knowing it is unallowable, he tramples upon and violates the regulation. This has also been stated thus:

“He falls into an offense intentionally, he conceals the offense he has committed, and he goes the wrong way (through favoritism); such a person is called a shameless (alajjī) person.” Thus it is stated (in the Parivāra).

How does one fall into an offense through ignorance? Indeed, an ignorant person is dull and deluded; not knowing what should and should not be done, he does what should not be done and fails to do what should be done. Thus he falls into an offense through ignorance.
142:
How does one fall into an offense through being prone to remorse and doubt? When remorse or doubt arises concerning what is allowable and unallowable, and after asking a Vinayadhara, he learns that if it is allowable it should be done, and if it is unallowable it should not be done; yet, this person, thinking "it is permissible," tramples upon and violates the regulation anyway. Thus he falls into an offense through being prone to remorse.

How does one fall into an offense by perceiving the unallowable as allowable? He eats bear meat with the perception that it is pork; he eats leopard meat with the perception that it is venison; he consumes unallowable food with the perception that it is allowable food; he eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time; he drinks an unallowable beverage with the perception that it is an allowable beverage. Thus he falls into an offense by perceiving the unallowable as allowable.

How does one fall into an offense by perceiving the allowable as unallowable? He eats pork with the perception that it is bear meat; he eats venison with the perception that it is leopard meat; he eats allowable food with the perception that it is unallowable food; he eats at the right time with the perception that it is the wrong time; he drinks an allowable beverage with the perception that it is an unallowable beverage. Thus he falls into an offense by perceiving the allowable as unallowable.

How does one fall into an offense through lapse of mindfulness? He falls into an offense through lapse of mindfulness due to such reasons as sleeping together (with an unordained person), being away from his robes, and exceeding the time for medicine or robes. Thus, in this Dispensation, a certain monk falls into an offense through these six ways.

However, a Vinayadhara does not fall into an offense through these six ways. How does he not fall into an offense because of being conscientious (having shame)? That Vinayadhara, guarding against the criticism of others such as, "Look, sirs, this monk violates the regulation even while knowing what is allowable and unallowable," does not fall into an offense. Thus he does not fall into an offense because of being conscientious. Even if he falls into an offense unexpectedly and suddenly, if it is an offense that can be cleared by confession (desanāgāminī), he confesses it; if it is an offense that requires a period of penance (vuṭṭhānagāminī), he emerges from it and remains in a state of purity. Therefore—

“He does not fall into an offense intentionally, he does not conceal an offense, and he does not go the wrong way; such a person is called a conscientious (lajjī) person.” (As it is stated), he remains in such a state of being conscientious.

How does he not fall into an offense because of having knowledge and understanding? He knows what is allowable and what is unallowable; therefore, he does only what is allowable and does not do what is unallowable. Thus he does not fall into an offense because of having knowledge.

How does he not fall into an offense because of not being prone to remorse? When remorse or doubt arises concerning what is allowable and unallowable, he examines the case (vatthu), the Mātikā, and the Padabhājanī...
143:
By observing intermediate offenses, offenses, and non-offenses, if something is allowable, he does it; if it is unallowable, he does not do it. In this way, being naturally free from remorse, he does not fall into an offense.

How does he not fall into an offense through the perception of what is unallowable and so forth? Indeed, that Vinaya expert knows what is allowable and what is unallowable. Therefore, he does not perceive the unallowable as allowable, nor the allowable as unallowable. His mindfulness is well-established. He performs the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for what should be determined and the formal assignment (vikappanā) for what should be assigned. Thus, through these six ways, he does not fall into an offense. One who does not fall into an offense is one whose virtue is unbroken and pure. In this way, his aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is well-guarded and well-protected.

How is he a refuge for those who are remorseful? Monks in other countries and provinces who have developed remorse, hearing that "a Vinaya expert resides in such and such a monastery," come to him even from afar and ask about their remorse. That Vinaya expert, having examined the basis of the act committed by those monks and having noted the distinctions such as offense, non-offense, grave, or light, makes them confess the offenses that are cleared by confession (desanāgāminī) and makes them emerge from the offenses that require emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī), thus establishing them in purity. In this way, he is a refuge for those who are remorseful.

"He speaks confidently in the midst of the Sangha" means that when one who is not a Vinaya expert speaks in the midst of the Sangha, fear and hesitation arise. For a Vinaya expert, this does not happen. Why? Because he speaks knowing, "Speaking in this way is a fault; speaking in this way is not a fault."

In the phrase "He well-subdues opponents with the Dhamma," there are two kinds of opponents (paccatthika): personal opponents and opponents of the Sasana. Among them, the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka, and the Licchavi prince Vaḍḍha, accused [the Elder Dabba Mallaputta] with a groundless charge of the ultimate offense (pārājika); these are called personal opponents (attapaccatthika). Furthermore, all others who are immoral and of evil nature are also personal opponents. Those with wrong views, such as the monk Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī, and those belonging to the Mahāsaṅghika sect and others who hold views such as parūpahāra, aññāṇa, kaṅkhā, and paravitāraṇa, who claim what is not the Buddha's teaching to be "the Buddha's teaching" and promote it, are called opponents of the Sasana (sāsanapaccatthika). He well-subdues all of them with Dhamma-consistent and reasoned speech so that they cannot establish that false Dhamma.
144:
"He is one who practices for the stability of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma)." In this context, the True Dhamma is threefold: Pariyatti, Paṭipatti, and Adhigama. Among these, the word of the Buddha, the Tipiṭaka, is called Pariyatti-saddhamma. The thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga), the fourteen duties in the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two great duties (fulfillment of virtue and development of meditation) are called Paṭipatti-saddhamma. The four paths and the four fruits are called Adhigama-saddhamma.

Among those three types of Saddhamma, some Elders, based on the Sutta: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and laid down shall be your teacher after my passing," say that "Pariyatti is the root of the Sasana." Some Elders, based on the Sutta: "Subhadda, if these monks live rightly, the world will not be empty of Arahants," say that "Paṭipatti is the root of the Sasana," and further state: "As long as five monks who practice rightly exist, the Sasana will remain." Other Elders say: "If Pariyatti disappears, even for one who practices rightly, there can be no realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths." If there are five monks who guard the four Pārājikas, they can ordain sons of good family who have faith, perform higher ordinations in the border regions, and thus complete a group of ten (dasavagga). Then they can perform higher ordinations even in the middle regions. In this way, by completing a Sangha group of twenty, they can perform their own rehabilitation (abbhāna) and cause the Sasana to reach growth, increase, and prosperity. Thus, this Vinaya expert is one who practices for the long-term stability of all three types of Saddhamma. Therefore, it should be understood that this Vinaya expert first obtains these five benefits.

What are the six benefits he obtains? The performance of Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, Sangha-kamma, Pabbajjā (going forth), and Upasampadā (higher ordination) are in the hands of that Vinaya expert. Furthermore, he can give dependence (nissaya) and have novices attend to him.

The nine types of Uposatha—namely, the fourteenth-day Uposatha, the fifteenth-day Uposatha, the harmony (sāmaggi) Uposatha, Uposatha in the Sangha, Uposatha in a group (gaṇa), Uposatha for an individual, the recitation of the Sutta (Pātimokkha), the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi), and the Uposatha by determination (adhiṭṭhāna)—are matters that concern only the Vinaya expert.

The nine types of Pavāraṇā—namely, the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā, the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā, the harmony Pavāraṇā, Pavāraṇā in the Sangha, Pavāraṇā in a group, Pavāraṇā for an individual, the three-word Pavāraṇā, the two-word Pavāraṇā, and the Pavāraṇā of those with equal years (samānavassika)—are also matters that concern only the Vinaya expert. These Pavāraṇās belong to the Vinaya expert, and the Vinaya expert is the master of these Pavāraṇās.
145: The four Sangha-kammas (legal acts of the Order), namely Apalokanakamma, Ñattikamma, Ñattidutiyakamma, and Ñatticatutthakamma, exist; these Sangha-kammas also pertain only to the Vinayadhara (expert in the Vinaya). Acting as a preceptor (Upajjhāya) to confer novicehood (pabbajjā) and the procedure for reaching the noble state of a monk (upasampadā) upon sons of good families also pertains only to the Vinayadhara. Even a person who has mastered two Pitakas, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma, but is not a Vinayadhara, is not entitled to act as a preceptor in this way. Only such a Vinayadhara can give dependence (nissaya) and have a novice (sāmaṇera) attend to him. No other person is entitled to give dependence or have a novice attend to him. A person desiring the service of a novice may take a preceptor from a Vinayadhara and be allowed to enjoy the practice of duties. Here, giving dependence and having a novice attend are considered as a single factor (in counting the benefits). Thus, among these six benefits, together with the previous five, there are six; with two, seven; with three, eight; with four, nine; with five, ten; and with all these, eleven. Thus, it should be understood that a Vinayadhara can obtain five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven benefits. It should be understood that the Blessed One, in showing these benefits, spoke in praise of the learning of the Vinaya (Vinayapariyatti). 'Ādissa ādissa' means repeatedly defining and doing so separately from others. Speaking in praise of the Venerable Upāli means that based on the learning of the Vinaya, He spoke of the virtues of the Elder Upāli, extolling and praising him. Why? (With the thought:) 'Perhaps upon hearing my praise, the monks will think that the Vinaya should be heard and learned from Venerable Upāli; in this way, this Sāsana will be long-lasting and will endure for five thousand years.' Upon hearing this praise from the Blessed One, many monks—elders, juniors, and those of middle standing—thinking, 'Indeed, neither those who master the Suttanta nor those who master the Abhidhamma obtain these benefits,' and being filled with zeal to attain the proclaimed benefits, learned the Vinaya from Venerable Upāli. This is the meaning. The word 'idha' is merely a particle. 439-440. 'Uddissamāne' means when being recited by a teacher to a student. Because that Pātimokkha, whether the teacher recites it of his own accord or...

When a pupil requests a teacher to recite and causes him to recite, or when a monk who has memorized [the Pātimokkha] performs a rehearsal (sajjhāya), it is called "being recited" (uddissamana). Therefore, it is stated in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanī): "whether reciting, causing to recite, or performing a rehearsal." "Khuddānukhuddakehi" means by minor rules and even lesser rules. The word "yāvadeva" is a term defining the limit of the occurrence of that remorse (kukkucca), etc.

The meaning is this: For those monks who recite, cause to recite, or rehearse these minor and lesser rules, remorse (kukkucca) known as dissatisfaction (vippaṭisāra), bodily and mental fatigue (vihesā), and mental perplexity (manovilekha) known as doubt (vicikicchā) certainly arise. It means they arise until that remorse, fatigue, and perplexity occur. Or, in another way, "yāvadeva" is an extreme distinction. That word is connected with the term "saṃvattanti" (lead to). It means they lead extremely to the occurrence of remorse, fatigue, and mental perplexity. "Criticizes the Vinaya of a monk" means, desiring to cause doubt in that monk regarding that training rule in his presence, one criticizes, blames, and disparages the Vinaya. The rest is clear.

There are 3 origins (samuṭṭhāna): action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Striking (Pahāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the fourth training rule—the phrase 'pahāraṃ denti' (they give a blow) refers to the monks of the group of seventeen (sattarasavaggī) who, after saying such things as, "Friends, prepare the seat, bring the water for washing the feet," give a blow to those who do not do as they were commanded.

In this statement, 'pahāraṃ denti āpatti pācittiyassa' (giving a blow is an offense of pācittiya), if a blow is given with the desire to strike, even if it causes death, it is only an offense of pācittiya. Even if a hand or a foot is broken because of the blow, or if the head is broken, it is only an offense of pācittiya. However, if one cuts off an ear or a nose with the intention of disfiguring, thinking, 'I will make it so that this monk cannot shine in the midst of the Saṅgha,' it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

'Anupasampannassa' (to one not ordained) means that if one gives a blow to a layperson, to a non-monk such as a novice (sāmaṇera), to a woman, to a man, or even finally to an animal, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, if one strikes a woman with a mind of lust, it is an offense requiring a formal meeting of the Order (saṅghādisesa).

'Kenaci viheṭhiyamāno' means being harassed by either a human or an animal. 'Mokkhādhippāyo' means desiring one's own escape from such a harasser. 'Pahāraṃ denti' means giving a blow with the body, an object connected to the body, or a weapon that is thrown; in such cases, there is no offense. If, while on a journey, one sees a thief or an enemy who wishes to harass them and says, "Lay follower, stay right there, do not come forward," and if that person continues to come without heeding the words, and one strikes them with a club or a small knife while saying, "Go away!" and then proceeds, even if that person dies because of that blow, there is no offense. The same method applies to fierce wild animals. The remaining words in this training rule are clear. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details of this training rule are similar to the first pārājika training rule. Specifically, this training rule involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Fourth Training Rule on Striking (Pahāra-sikkhāpada).

## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Raising the Hand (Talasattika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the fifth training rule—'talasattikaṃ uggiranti' means raising the body or an object connected to the body, showing the manner of striking. 'Te pahārasamuccitā rodanti' means that those young monks (of the group of seventeen), being accustomed to being struck, cry out thinking, "We have been struck before, and now they are going to strike us again." Some also recite 'pahārassa muccitā', which in that context means "they are afraid of being struck."

In this training rule, 'uggirati āpatti pācittiyassa' (raising [the hand] is an offense of pācittiya), if one raises the hand and then accidentally strikes because they are absolutely unable to hold back, and the blow falls suddenly, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because it was not given with the desire to strike. Even if a limb such as a hand is broken or damaged because of that blow, it is still only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

In the phrase 'mokkhādhippāyo talasattikaṃ uggirati', regarding the cases of thieves, enemies, etc., mentioned previously, there is no offense for a monk who raises his palm with the desire to escape, following the previous method. Even if he accidentally strikes them, there is no offense. The remaining origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are the same as the previous training rule.

## 2. Commentary on the Ratana Training Rule

502-3. In the commentary on the second training rule (Ratana Sikkhāpada)—'vissaritvā' means having forgotten. 'Puṇṇapatta' refers to a reward given at the rate of five kahāpaṇas per hundred. 'Kyāhaṃ karissāmi' means "What shall I do?" (i.e., what benefit will there be?). 'Ābharaṇaṃ omuñcitvā' means having removed the Mahālatā ornament worth nine crores.

'Antevāsī' means an attendant (disciple).

'Aparikkhittassa upacāro'—here, 'upacāra' (precinct) for a monastery (ārāma) is the distance of two clod-throws. For a house (āvasatha), the Mahāpaccari states that the precinct is the place where a winnowing basket or a pestle falls. 'Uggaṇhāti āပတ္တိ pācittiyassa'—here, if one picks up gold or silver for oneself or has another pick it up, one incurs an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya). If one picks it up for the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, a cetiya, or for new construction (navakamma), one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). For other jewels such as pearls, if one picks them up or has them picked up for oneself or for the Saṅgha etc., one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Whether it is an allowable object or an unallowable object, even down to a mother's ear-ornament made of palm leaf, a monk who stores laypeople's property as if he were a treasurer incurs only an offense of confession (pācittiya).

However, if the property of one's parents is an allowable item that must definitely be stored, it should be taken and stored as if it were one's own property. But if they say, "Please store this for us," one should refuse, saying, "It is not allowable." If they drop it and leave, saying, "Please store it," it becomes a concern (palibodha), and thus it is allowable to store it. If carpenters and others working in the monastery, or those close to the king, say, "Please store our tools or bedding," one must not do so out of either affection or fear; however, it is allowable to show them a secure place. If they leave after forcibly dropping the items, it is allowable to store them.

'Ajjhārāme vā ajjhāဝသထေ ဝါ'—here, if it is a large monastery like the Mahāvihāra, one should pick it up or have it picked up and stored only in a place within the fenced compound where there is a suspicion that "monks or novices might take it." In places where many people pass by, such as the Mahābodhi gatehouse or the Ambangaṇa area, it should not be picked up, as there is no concern (palibodha). In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said: "If a monk traveling on a journey sees some property in a deserted place, even if it becomes crowded with people, the people..."
153:
...will suspect only that monk; therefore, he should sit down away from the path. When the owners arrive, he should inform them of that property. If he does not see the owners, he should act appropriately (so it is said).

"Having made a mark by appearance or by sign"—here, 'appearance' (rūpa) refers to the goods inside the bundle. Therefore, one should note it by opening the bundle and counting, "There are this many kahāpaṇas or pieces of gold and silver." 'Sign' (nimitta) refers to seals and so on. Therefore, one should note everything, such as whether the sealed bundle has a clay seal or a lac seal, or whether the bundle is made with blue cloth or white cloth, and so on.

'Suitable monks' means monks who are shameful and scrupulous. It is not permissible to place [the property] in the hands of those who are frivolous by nature. If a monk neither leaves that residence nor sees the owners, he should not use it for the price of his own robes etc.; rather, he should have a permanent structure such as a dwelling, a cetiya, or a pond constructed. If the owner arrives after a long time has passed, he should be told, "Lay follower, this [structure] has been built with your property; please rejoice in it." If he rejoices, that is good. If he does not rejoice and demands, "Give me my money," one should encourage others [to donate] and give it to him.

"Taking property designated as jewels out of trust"—in such phrases, it is said with reference only to touchable (āmāsa) objects. It is not at all allowable to take untouchable (anāmāsa) objects. The rest of the text here is clear. The six origins (samuṭṭhāna) are: action (kiriya), not being exempt through perception (no-saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a breach of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three thoughts (ticitta), and three feelings (tivedana).

## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Entering a Village at the Wrong Time

In the third training rule—'tiracchānakathā' (animal talk) means talk that is contrary to the Noble Path. 'Rājakathā' means talk related to kings. The same method applies to talk about thieves and so on.

'A monk who is present'—the decision to be stated here has already been mentioned in the Cāritta training rule. If many monks enter a village for some business, all the monks should inform one another, saying, "I inform you of entering the village at the wrong time." If they go to another village because that business is not finished in the first village, there is no need to inform again, even if there are a hundred villages. However, if they have ceased the effort to enter a village and, while going to the monastery, wish to enter another village in between, they must inform again. If, after finishing the meal business at a family's house or in a refectory, one wishes to wander about to ask for oil or ghee, one should inform a monk if one is nearby and then go. If there is no monk, one should go with the thought that there is none. If one meets a monk after reaching the road, there is no need to inform; one may wander about even without informing.
154:
“I ask permission” (āpucchāmi)—all monks must ask one another. If the business in that village is not completed and they go to another village, even if it be a hundred villages, there is no need to ask permission again. However, if they cease their effort to enter the village and return to the monastery, but then wish to enter another village on the way, they must ask permission again.

Whether in a family house or in a refectory, after finishing the meal, if one wishes to go around for alms of oil or alms of ghee, if there is a monk nearby, one must go after asking permission. If no monk is present, one should go with the thought that there is no one. If one sees a monk only after descending to the road, there is no need to ask; one may go around even without asking. For a monk traveling on a road through the middle of a village, if the thought arises, “I will go around for alms of oil and so on,” if there is a monk nearby, he must ask before going around. For a monk who goes around for alms without leaving the road, there is no need to ask. The precinct (upacāra) of an unfenced village should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada.

Regarding the words “antarārāmaṃ” and so on, there is no offense for a monk who goes without asking, without tying the waistband (kāyabandhana), and without wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). “Āpadāsu” (in emergencies) means when a lion or a tiger comes, or when it rains, or when any other danger arises; in such cases, there is no offense. In such emergencies, it is allowable to enter from outside the village into the village. The remaining explanation here is clear.

The Kathina-origination (samuṭṭhāna) arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind; it is action and non-action (kiriyākiriyam); it is not released by perception (nosannāvimokkham); it is unconscious (acittakam); it is a breach of a conventional regulation (paṇṇattivajjam); it is bodily action (kāyakammam); it is vocal action (vacīkammam); it involves three types of consciousness (ticittam) and three types of feeling (tivedanam).

For it was said there: “Bhikkhus, I authorize a sitting cloth for the protection of the body, for the protection of the robes, and for the protection of the lodgings” (Mahāvagga, 353). “Like an old leather-worker” means, for example, just like an old leather-worker. Just as a leather-worker pulls and stretches the hide here and there to make it wide, so too did that monk [Udāyī] with that sitting cloth. Because of that pulling, the Blessed One, referring to that monk Udāyī, said: “A sitting cloth is said to be with a fringe (sadasa).”

“A sitting cloth is said to be with a fringe” means that after spreading it out like a rug, at one end, in a place measuring one span of the Sugata (Sugata-vidatthi), it is split in two places to make three fringes; because it is with those fringes, it is called “sadasa”. The remaining explanation here is clear. It has six originations (samuṭṭhāna).

## 6. Pāṭidesanīya Section
## 1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
Immediately after the Khuddaka training rules, those training rules called Pāṭidesanīya have been placed; now, this is the commentary on those Pāṭidesanīya training rules.

In the first Pāṭidesanīya training rule, first, "paṭikkamanakāle" means at the time of returning after wandering for alms. "Sabbēva aggahesi" means that he took all the alms food. "Pavedhentī" means trembling. "Apehi" means go away.

553-5. The words beginning with "gārayhaṃ āvuso" indicate the manner in which the confession should be made. "Rathikā" means a carriage road (main road). "Byūha" means a short road (cul-de-sac) where one must return the same way one came without passing through. "Siṅghāṭaka" means a junction where four roads or three roads meet. "Ghara" means the house of the four classes of people. For a monk who stands and accepts [food] in any of these mentioned places, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of accepting, and a pāṭidesanīya offense for every swallow according to the number of swallows. The same rule applies to a monk who stands and accepts [food] in places such as elephant stables. If a bhikkhunī stands on a carriage road and gives, even if the monk stands and accepts in places such as the monastery grounds, an offense is still incurred. Because it was taught, "having entered within a house" (antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāya), it should be understood that in this training rule, an offense is incurred only because the bhikkhunī stands and gives within the village; the place where the monk stands is not the primary factor. Therefore, if a monk standing in a place such as a main road accepts from a bhikkhunī who stands and gives in a place such as the monastery grounds, there is no offense.

If one accepts yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika for the purpose of food, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. The statement "an offense of wrong-doing is incurred for every swallow" is taught with reference to yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, and yāvajīvika that are not mixed with material food (āmisa) such as alms food; however, if they are mixed with alms food and become of one taste, it is only a pāṭidesanīya offense. "Ekatō upasampannā" refers to a bhikkhunī who has attained the status of a nun only in the presence of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. If one accepts from a bhikkhunī who has attained the status of a nun in the presence of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, a pāṭidesanīya offense is incurred according to the case.

"Dāpēti na dēti" means an unrelated bhikkhunī does not give herself but has someone else give; there is no offense for the monk who accepts such a gift. "Upanikkhitvā dēti" means placing it on the ground and saying, "Venerable sir, I offer this food to you"; after accepting such an offered food by saying "Very well, sister," it is allowable to have that bhikkhunī or someone else offer it and then consume it.

...this food brought in large quantities is also considered "leftovers of notified food" (paṭisaṃviditasesaka) and is allowable for all. If there is an excess, food that has been set aside to avoid the offense of storing up (sannidhi) is allowable even on the second day. The same method applies to the leftovers of food brought for a sick monk. As for food brought without any notification, it should be sent back outside the monastery, and after having the notification made, it should be brought back. Also, if people passing through the middle of the monastery or forest-dwellers (hunters, etc.) bring food from the forest and offer it, notification should be made according to the previous method. This training rule has the Kathina origin (kathinasamuṭṭhāna). It occurs through action and non-action (kiriyākiriya), not released by perception (nosanyāvimokkha), without thought (acittaka), prohibited by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness, and three types of feelings.

## 7. Sekhiya Section
## 1. Explanation of the Parimaṇḍala Group

The Buddha, who has practiced the three trainings through the four paths and is endowed with the quality of *tādi*—being unshakable by worldly conditions—taught these Sekhiya training rules. Now, the sequence of the explanation of those Sekhiya training rules will be presented.

Among those rules, 'parimaṇḍala' means wearing [the robe] in a circular manner all around. 'The navel-circle and the knee-circle' means that while covering the navel-circle above and the knee-circle below, the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) should be worn hanging down about eight finger-breadths from the shinbone starting from below the knee-circle. It is stated that for a monk who wears it hanging lower than those eight finger-breadths, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It is stated in the Mahāpaccari Commentary that when sitting, it should cover about four finger-breadths below the knee-circle. For a monk wearing it thus, the inner robe should be of the proper measurement.

The measurement of that inner robe is five cubits (measured by fists) in length and two and a half cubits in width. If such an inner robe is not available, an inner robe with a width of two cubits is also suitable for the purpose of covering the knee-circle. The navel-circle, however, can also be covered with the upper robe (*cīvara*). Among those robes, a single-layered inner robe, even when worn this way, tends not to stay in place; however, a double-layered one stays.

In this rule, 'If one wears it hanging down, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' it is not only for a monk who wears it hanging down in the front and the back that there is a *dukkaṭa*. For a monk who wears it with the faults regarding wearing mentioned in the Cullavagga Khandhaka, such as: 'At that time, the Chabbaggiya monks wore [the robe] like laypeople, in the elephant-trunk style, the fish-tail style, the four-cornered style, the palmyra-leaf-fan style, and the many-folds style,' there is also a *dukkaṭa*. All those faults do not occur for a monk who wears it evenly (*parimaṇḍala*) according to the method already stated. This is just a summary here; the details will become clear in that very Cullavagga Khandhaka.

'Unintentionally' means without the intention: 'I will wear it hanging down either in the front or the back.' Indeed, there is no offense for a monk who intends to wear it evenly but, through a slip, wears it unevenly. 'Mindlessly' means there is no offense for a monk who wears it that way because his mind is occupied with something else. In this word 'unknowingly,' there is no exemption from the offense for a monk who does not know the training regarding wearing the inner robe. This is because the training regarding wearing must be well-learned; the failure to learn that training is itself his disrespect (*anādariya*). That disrespect is appropriate only for a monk who does not learn because he has no intention to learn. Therefore, for a monk who has learned the training but does not know that it has slipped up or down...
162:
...there is no offense for him. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated: 'There is no offense for one who does not know how to wear it evenly.' For one whose shins are thin or whose calf muscles are very large, it is allowable to wear the inner robe hanging lower than eight finger-breadths from the knee-circle for the sake of propriety (*sāruppa*).

'A sick person' means if there is a sore on the shin or on the foot, it is allowable to wear [the robe] either by lifting it up or by letting it down. 'In times of danger' means times such as when wild beasts or robbers are pursuing; in such dangers, there is no offense. The rest of the words here are quite clear.

[The origins are] like the origins of the first Pārājika: action, release by perception, intentional, worldly fault (*lokavajja*), bodily action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling. Elder Phussadeva, however, said: 'unintentional (*acittaka*), disciplinary fault (*paṇṇattivajja*), and the three feelings.' Elder Upatissa, because it is stated 'on account of disrespect,' said: 'worldly fault, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.'

'Should be robed evenly' means: 'At that time, the Chabbaggiya monks robed themselves as laypeople do.' Without robing in the various ways of laypeople as thus stated (in the Cullavagga), a person who fulfills the training of robing by making both edges even according to the method stated here should be robed evenly. These two training rules are stated without distinction (generally). Therefore, both in the monastery and in the inhabited area, one must wear [the inner robe] evenly and robe [the upper robe] evenly. The origins and so on should be understood according to the method stated in the first training rule, along with the views of the Elders.

'Opening the body' means opening the collarbone and the chest (one should not go). 'Well-covered' means not by robing including the head; rather, one should go into the inhabited area having fastened the button, covering the neck with the border, making both edges even, and rolling it up to cover as far as the wrists. In the second training rule (the training of sitting): one should sit having exposed the head from the throat-pit, the hands from the wrists, and the feet from the calf muscles.

'For one who has entered a residence' means there is no offense for one who, having entered for the purpose of residing, sits with the body exposed during the night or during the day.

'Well-restrained' means staying without playing with the hands or the feet; it means one who is well-behaved.

'With downcast eyes' means having eyes directed downwards (one should go). In this 'looking a yoke's length,' I shall further reveal the hidden meaning. A well-trained noble horse yoked to a carriage looks at the ground for a distance of four cubits, which is one yoke's length in front of itself. This monk also should go looking at a place about four cubits in extent, which is that much measurement.

'If a monk, out of disrespect, goes looking here and there, or at a palace, or at a gabled house, or at the road, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for that monk.' However, it is allowable to stand in one place and look to see whether there are dangers such as elephants or horses. A monk who is sitting should also sit only with downcast eyes.

'By lifting up the robe' means (one should not go) by lifting up the robe. This word 'ukkhittakāya' is a word with the instrumental case ending in the sense of a characteristic attribute (*itthaṃbhūtalakkhaṇa*). Whether on one side or on both sides...
163:
"Okkhittacakkhu" means having downcast eyes. "Yugamattaṃ pekkhamāno" means that just as a trained thoroughbred horse harnessed to a yoke looks at the ground for a distance of four cubits ahead, so too should this monk walk looking ahead for about the same distance of four cubits. If a monk walks looking here and there at directions, palaces, gabled houses, or streets out of disrespect, he commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa). However, it is permissible to stop in one place and look to see if there are dangers such as elephants or horses. Even while sitting, one should sit with downcast eyes.

"Ukkhittakāyā" refers to [walking] by lifting up [the robe]. Here, the word "ukkhittakāyā" is used in the instrumental case to indicate a characteristic state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). It means having the robe lifted on one side or both sides. One should not walk in this manner from the inner threshold onwards. When sitting, even a monk who is taking out a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa) should do so without lifting the robe.

## 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Loud Laughter (Ujjagghikavagga-vaṇṇanā)

"Ujjagghikāyā" means [walking] while laughing loudly. In this word, the instrumental case is used in the same manner as previously mentioned.

Regarding the training rule "Appasaddo antaraghare" (being quiet in inhabited areas), how much sound is considered "quiet"? In a house twelve cubits long, if the senior elder (Saṅghatthera) sits at the beginning, the second elder in the middle, and the third elder at the end, and the senior elder consults with the second elder, the second elder hears the sound and can distinguish the words. The third elder, however, only hears the sound but cannot distinguish the words. A sound of this volume is called "quiet." If the third elder can distinguish the words, it is called "loud."

"Kāyaṃ paggahetvā" means keeping the body steady and walking or sitting with an upright body and a calm posture.

"Bāhuṃ paggahetvā" means keeping the arms steady [while walking or sitting].

"Sīသံ paggahetvā" means keeping the head steady and upright [while walking or sitting].

165: The Elder (Cūḷasumana) said, "How wonderful! Cūḷanāga has fallen away from the Dispensation. While I was teaching the Vinaya to this Cūḷanāga seven times, I never spoke like this. From which teacher did this Cūḷanāga receive this to speak in such a way?" The monks requested the Elder, "Venerable Sir, please speak now; by what is it delimited?" The Elder said, "Friends, it is delimited by Yāvakālika (temporary) items." Therefore, any Yāvakālika item of the nature of material food, such as gruel, rice, or various fruits, should be accepted only level with the rim of the bowl. And that Yāvakālika item should be accepted with a bowl that is suitable for determination (adhiṭṭhāna). However, with other bowls, it is allowable to accept Yāvakālika items even when they are heaped up (thūpīkata). As for Yāmakālika, Sattāhakālika, and Yāvajīvika items, they are allowable even if heaped up in a bowl suitable for determination. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that it is allowable to receive rice in two bowls, fill one, and send it to the monastery. When putting items into the bowl, if cakes, pieces of sugarcane, various fruits, etc., slide down, such sliding Yāvakālika items are not called 'heaped up' (thūpīkata). If one offers alms-food by placing a cake on top like a crest-ornament, it is indeed 'heaped up' (thūpīkata). However, items offered by placing on top things like flower-crests, cinnamon leaves, or Kaṭuka fruits are not called 'heaped up' because they are not edible. If one accepts by placing a small bowl or a leaf-cup on top of the rice and filling it, it is not called 'heaped up'. It is also stated in the Kurundī: "If they offer by putting it in a bowl or a leaf and placing that bowl or leaf on top of the alms-bowl, it is allowable as it is a separate vessel." In the section on non-offense (anāpatti) of this training rule, the sick are not included; therefore, it is not allowable even for a sick monk to accept heaped-up Yāvakālika items. In all cases of heaped-up Yāvakālika items, it is only the act of accepting that is not allowable; however, what has been accepted is indeed well-accepted and is allowable to be consumed. ## Tatiyo Vaggo. ## 4. ## 6. Surusuru-vagga-vaṇṇanā

Surusurukāraka refers to eating while repeatedly making the sound "suru-suru". "Davo" refers to jesting words; it means that one should not, through any form of disregard or jest, make remarks concerning the Triple Gem such as, "What Buddha? A stone Buddha? An awakened Buddha?", "What Dhamma? Cattle-dhamma? Goat-dhamma?", or "What Saṅgha? A herd of deer? A herd of beasts?"

Hattanillehaka means eating while repeatedly licking the hands. A monk who is eating should not lick even a single finger. However, it is allowable to pick up thick gruel (yāgu), molasses, milk-rice, and the like with the fingers and put the fingers into the mouth to eat. In the training rules of pattanillehaka (licking the bowl) and oṭṭhanillehaka (licking the lips), the same method applies. Therefore, one should not scrape the bowl with even one finger, nor lick a lip with the tongue. It is allowable to take food with the lips alone and bring it inside the mouth.

Kokanada refers to the palace of this name. A lotus is called "kokanada", and because that palace was shaped like a lotus, they named it "Kokanada". The training rule stating "one should not hold a water vessel with a hand soiled with food (āmisa)" was prohibited because it is repulsive. Therefore, whether it is communal property, personal property, the property of laypeople, or one's own, one must not hold a conch, a small water cup, or a drinking vessel with soiled hands; for a monk who does so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, if a part of the hand is not smeared with food, it is allowable to hold it with that part.

Uddharitvā vā means picking out the grains of rice from the water, piling them in one place, and then throwing the water away. Bhinditvā vā means breaking the grains of rice to make them like water and then throwing it away. Paṭiggahe vā means throwing it into a waste-water receptacle provided by those receiving it. Nīharitvā means taking it outside and throwing it away. For a monk who discards it in these ways, there is no offense.

Setacchatta refers to a white parasol wrapped in cloth. Kilañjacchatta refers to a parasol made of bamboo strips. Paṇṇacchatta refers to a parasol made of any kind of leaf, such as palm leaves. The phrase "maṇḍalabaddhaṃ salākabaddhaṃ" is mentioned to show the frame of all three types of parasols. Those parasols may be bound by a circular frame or bound by ribs. A single-leaf parasol (ekapaṇṇacchatta) made with a stalk from a tree is also considered a parasol. If any of these parasols is in the hand of a person listening to the Dhamma, that person is called "chattapāṇi" (parasol-in-hand). If that person is holding the parasol, or has it on their shoulder, or on their lap, as long as they do not let go of it with their hand, it is not allowable to teach the Dhamma to them. For a monk who teaches, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If another person holds the parasol for them, or if the parasol is on a stand, since it is separate from the hand...
168:
...as soon as it is away from the hand, they are no longer called "chattapāṇi". It is allowable to teach the Dhamma to such a person. The definition of Dhamma in this context should be understood exactly as stated in the Padasodhamma training rule.

In the term "daṇḍapāṇi", "daṇḍa" (staff) refers to a staff the size of four cubits of an average man. The condition of being "daṇḍapāṇi" (staff-in-hand) should be understood in the same way as explained for "chattapāṇi".

The same method applies to "satthapāṇi" (weapon-in-hand). One who has a sword fastened or slung on the body does not fall under the designation of "satthapāṇi".

In the term "āvudhapāṇi", although it is said that "arms (āvudha) means a cāpa bow or a kodaṇḍa bow", it should be understood as all types of bows along with all types of arrows. Therefore, it is not allowable to teach the Dhamma to a person, whether standing or sitting, who is holding a bow with an arrow, a bow alone, an arrow alone, a strung bow, or an unstrung bow. However, if the bow is slung around the neck, as long as it is not held by the hand, it is indeed allowable to teach the Dhamma.

## Sixth Chapter.

## 7. Pādukavagga-vaṇṇanā

Akkantassa means standing while treading on a sandal without inserting the toes into the thongs. Paṭimukkassa means standing while wearing them. The same method applies to shoes (upāhanā). In this context, omukko refers to standing while wearing heel-covering footwear.

Yānagatassa: In this context, whether one is carried by two people with joined hands, or placed in a cloth and carried with a bamboo pole, or sitting in a covered carriage and the like that is not hitched to oxen or horses, or even sitting on a dismantled bicycle—all are counted as "yānagata" (one in a vehicle). If both the teacher and the listener are sitting in the same vehicle, it is allowable to teach the Dhamma. Among those sitting in separate vehicles, a monk sitting in a higher vehicle is allowed to teach one sitting in a lower vehicle. It is also allowable to teach one sitting in a vehicle of equal height. A monk sitting in a front vehicle is allowed to teach one in a rear vehicle. However, a monk sitting in a higher vehicle at the rear is not allowed to teach the Dhamma to one in the front vehicle.
169:
Whether in a vehicle, or even on just a wheel [of a vehicle] that has been dismantled and set down, one who is sitting is still reckoned as 'one who has gone in a vehicle'. If both the teacher and the listener are sitting in the same vehicle, it is allowable to teach the Dhamma. When sitting separately, it is allowable for a monk sitting in a high vehicle to teach someone sitting in a low vehicle; it is also allowable for one sitting at an equal height. A monk sitting in a front vehicle may teach a person sitting in a rear vehicle. However, if the rear vehicle is higher, it is not allowable for the monk sitting in that vehicle to teach the Dhamma.

One who is 'lying down' (sayanagata) means, at the minimum, even for a person lying on a mat or on the bare ground, it is not allowable for one who is standing or sitting on a high couch, stool, or on the ground to teach the Dhamma. A monk who is lying down may teach a person who is lying down, whether on a higher bed or one of equal height. A monk who is lying down may teach one who is standing or sitting; one who is sitting may also teach one who is standing or sitting. A monk who is standing may only teach one who is standing.

It is not allowable to teach the Dhamma to one who is not ill and is sitting with knees bound (pallatthikā), whether bound with a meditation strap (āyoga), with the hands, or with a cloth.

One with a 'wrapped head' (veṭhitasīsa) refers to one whose head is wrapped with a cloth or a turban, etc., such that the hair-line is not visible.

One with a 'covered head' (oguṇṭhitasīsa) refers to one who is covered including the head.

A monk sitting on the ground should not teach the Dhamma to one who is not ill and is sitting on a seat, even if it is just a cloth or grass spread out.

Sapaka means a Caṇḍāla (outcaste). Sapaki means a female Caṇḍāla. 'Nilīno' means being hidden. It means 'the king who learns [unrighteously]'. Saying 'All these deeds are very base,' and right there saying, 'This whole world has fallen into confusion and has no boundaries,' he fell from the tree between the two of them. After falling, he stood before the two of them and recited this verse:

"Both do not know the meaning,
They do not see the Dhamma;
It will be like a pot smashed by a stone."

In that verse, 'Both do not know the meaning' means both people do not understand the meaning of the Pali. 'They do not see the Dhamma' means they do not see the Pali text. Who are those two? Saying 'He who...', he designated both the king and the brahmin as unrighteous.
170:
"He teaches the mantra, and he who learns unrighteously." Thus, he established both the brahmin and the king in the state of being unrighteous.

Then the brahmin recited the verse beginning with "Sālīnaṃ". The meaning of that verse is: "Sir, I know that this (teaching mantras from below) is unrighteous. However, for a long time, I, along with my wife, children, and attendants, have eaten the king's property, the hill-paddy rice." "Sucimaṃsūpasecano" means hill-paddy rice mixed with pure meat prepared in various ways; thus it is called sucimaṃsūpasecano. "Therefore, I cannot stand in the Dhamma" means because I have eaten the king's rice and received many other gains, I cannot stand in the Dhamma because I am bound by my stomach (livelihood); it is not because I do not know the Dhamma. I know that this Dhamma is praised and extolled by the Noble Ones.

Then the Caṇḍāla addressed the brahmin with two verses beginning with "Dhiratthu". The meaning of those verses is: "Brahmin, whatever gain of wealth and gain of fame you have received, let that gain of wealth and fame be loathsome. Why? Because this gain received by you is the cause of falling into the states of misery (apāya) in the future, and at present, it is called living by unrighteous conduct." What benefit is there in such a livelihood that results in falling into misery in the future and unrighteous conduct in this life? Therefore, he said:

"Brahmin, woe to that gain of wealth and gain of fame;
That livelihood which is by falling [into misery] or by unrighteous conduct."

"Paribbaja mahābrahme" means: "Great Brahmin, flee quickly from this place." "Pacantanyepi pāṇino" means: "It is not only you and the king who cook and eat; other beings also cook and eat." "Mā tvaṃ adhammo ācarito asmā kumbhamivābhidā" means: "If you do not flee from here and continue to practice this unrighteousness, that unrighteousness so practiced will break you just as a stone would break a water-pot." Therefore, we say to you:

"Great Brahmin, wander away to another place; other beings also cook and eat;
Let not the unrighteousness practiced by you break you as a stone breaks a water-pot."

"Ucce āsane" means it is not allowable to teach the Dhamma to one sitting in a high place, even if it is just an elevated part of the ground.
171:
Regarding the phrase "na ṭhito nisinnassa" (not [teaching] while standing to one who is sitting): if a Great Elder (Mahāthera) sitting on a seat asks a question to a junior monk who has come and is standing before him, it should not be answered. However, out of respect, it is not possible to say to the Elder, "Please stand up and ask." Therefore, it is allowable to answer while thinking, "I am answering the monk standing by my side."

Regarding the phrase "na pacchato gacchantena" (not [teaching] while walking behind): if one walking in front asks a question to one walking behind, it should not be answered. It is allowable to answer while thinking, "I am answering the monk who is behind." However, it is allowable to recite together the Dhamma that has been learned together. It is also allowable to answer one who is walking side-by-side.

Regarding the phrase "na uppathena" (not [teaching] while off-path): here too, if both the teacher and the listener walk side-by-side on a cart track, whether on separate wheel tracks or on a non-path, it is allowable.

"Asañcicca" (unintentionally) means that if excrement or urine is released suddenly while going to a secluded place, it is done without intention and there is no offense.

Regarding the phrase "na harite" (not on green plants): here, whether it is the root of a living tree visible on the ground or a branch touching the ground, all are called "harita" (greenery). It is allowable to sit on the trunk of a tree and discharge onto a spot where there is no greenery. It is also allowable if it happens suddenly while looking for a spot without greenery, or if one is in a state of illness. "Appaharite kato" (done on a spot with little greenery) means that if a spot without greenery cannot be found, it is allowable even if one places a grass-ring or a straw-ring and discharges, even if greenery eventually covers it later. In the Mahāpaccari, it is stated that phlegm is also included along with saliva in this training rule.

"Na udake" (not in water) is said with reference only to water fit for use. There is no offense for discharging in unusable water such as in latrine pits or in the ocean. If there is a flood all around due to rain and it happens while looking for a spot without water, it is allowable. It is stated in the Mahāpaccari: "In such a time, if a spot without water is not found, it is allowable to do so." In all the remaining training rules, the meaning is clear.

## Sattamo Vaggo

To clarify the origins (samuṭṭāna) and so forth, this miscellaneous decision is stated: the four rules connected with laughing and loud noise, the one rule on speaking with a mouthful of food, and the five rules connected with teaching Dhamma while on the ground, on a low seat, standing, following behind, or walking off-path—these ten training rules, like the origin of formal admonishment (samanubhāsana), arise from body, speech, and mind. They are of the nature of actions (kiriya).
172:
They involve release from offense through perception (saññāvimokkha), are with intention (sacittaka), are worldly faults (lokavajja), are bodily and vocal actions, arise with unwholesome mind, and have painful feeling.

The training rule on requesting curry or rice (sūpodanaviññatti) arises from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind, like the origin of a thief traveling with a caravan (theyyasattha). It is an action (kiriya), involves release through perception, is with intention, is a worldly fault, is a bodily and vocal action, arises with unwholesome mind, and has painful feeling.

The eleven training rules named: holding a parasol, holding a staff, holding a knife, holding a weapon, wearing shoes, wearing sandals, riding in a vehicle, lying on a bed, sitting clasping the knees (pallatthika), wearing a turban, and being veiled (oguṇṭhita)—these have the origin of Dhamma teaching (dhammadesanā). They arise from speech and mind. They are actions and non-actions (kiriya-akiriya), involve release through perception, are with intention, are worldly faults, are vocal actions, arise with unwholesome mind, and have painful feeling.

The remaining fifty-three training rules have the origin of the first Pārājika.

In all Sekhiya training rules, there is no offense due to the reason of illness. However, in these three training rules: the rule on almsfood heaped up (thūpīkata), the rule on covering with curry or bean-sauce (sūpabyañjanena paṭicchādana), and the rule on looking [at others' bowls] with a critical mind (ujjhānasaññī), there is no exemption for the sick.

## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Pārājika Section (Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)
Immediately following the collection (recitation) of the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, there is the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. The sequence of its commentary has now arrived. Therefore, in order to provide the commentary for the words not previously explained in that Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, this commentary will first be given for the Pārājika section.

## 1. Commentary on the First Pārājika Training Rule
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī... etc. In the phrase "Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra," *Sāḷha* is his name. He was the grandson of Visākhā, who stood in the position of mother to the merchant Migāra; therefore, he is called "the grandson of Migāra."

"Navakammikaṃ" means one who manages or oversees new construction works. "Paṇḍitā" means being endowed with innate wisdom that discerns cause and effect. "Byattā" means being endowed with sharp intelligence. "Medhāvinī" means being endowed with wisdom preceded by mindfulness in learning the Pāḷi text, and mindfulness preceded by wisdom in learning the meaning. "Dakkhā" means skilled, one who habitually performs what should be done quickly and without error. "Analasā" means one who is free from laziness. "Tatrupāyāya" means being an expedient (or knowing closely) in various works. "Vīmaṃsāya" means with investigative wisdom regarding the work to be done. "Samannāgatā" means associated with (or endowed with). "Alaṃ kātuṃ" means capable of performing various works oneself. "Alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ" means capable of organizing, saying, "Let this work be done in such and such a way." "Katākataṃ jānituṃ" means to know what has been done and what is yet to be done. "Te" refers to both of them, namely Sundarīnandā and Sāḷha. "Bhattagge" means in the place where food is served (the refectory). "Nikūṭe" means in a deep, secluded place made to resemble a corner. "Vissaro me bhavissati" means "My voice will be distorted (abnormal)"; my distorted...
174:
...voice will occur, meaning an abnormal sound will occur. "Patimānentī" means looking for (waiting for). "Kyāhaṃ" means "What kind of 'I' am I?" "Jarādubbalā" means weak due to old age. "Caraṇagilānā" means being endowed with a foot disease (having sore feet).

657-8. "Avassutā" means wet with the lust of physical contact; it means moistened or oozing. In the word analysis (Padabhājana), however, taking that very lust of physical contact from the word *avassuta*, it is said "sārattā," etc. There, "sārattā" means being intensely impassioned by the lust of physical contact, just as cloth is dyed with dye. "Apekkhavatī" means being endowed with longing (desire) for that man through the power of that lust. "Paṭibaddhacittā" means having a mind as if bound to that man by that lust. This method is the same in the analysis of the second word as well. "Purisapuggalassa" means of the individual known as a man. "Adhakkakaṃ" means below the collarbones. "Ubbhazāṇumaṇဍalaṃ" means above the kneecaps. In the word analysis, it is stated according to the sequence of words as "below the collarbones, above the kneecaps." In this training rule, the area above the elbow is also included by the term "above the kneecaps" (ubbha-jāṇumaṇḍala). The remaining points should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga. "Purimāyo upādāya" means taking the four Pārājikas shared with the Bhikkhus. The term "Ubbhazāṇumaṇḍalikā" is merely the name of this Pārājika, and therefore it is not analyzed in the word analysis.

Having thus analyzed the training rule presented according to the sequence of words, he now said "ubhatovassute," etc., to show the classification of offenses by way of the classification of being "wet with lust" (avassuta), etc. There, "ubhatovassute" means both are oozing; it means when there is the state of both the bhikkhunī and the man being wet with the lust of physical contact. "Kāyena kāyaṃ āmasati" means if the bhikkhunī touches any part of the man's body with her defined body, or if the man touches the defined body of the bhikkhunī with any part of his body—in both ways, a Pārājika offense is incurred by the bhikkhunī. "Kāyena kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ" means touching an object connected to the man's body with one's own body in the manner described. In this word "āmasati," whether she touches it herself or consents to his touching, only a Thullaccaya (grave offense) is incurred. "Kāyapaṭibaddhena kāyaṃ" means touching the man's body with an object connected to one's own body in the manner described. Here too, whether she touches it herself or consents to his touching, only a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. In the remaining words also, the decision should be understood by this very method.
175:
If it is both a monk and a nun, and in that situation the nun touches [him] and the monk remains still but consents mentally, the monk should not be dealt with by an offense. If the monk touches [her] and the nun remains still but accepts and consents only with her mind, even if she does not move her limbs, she should be dealt with by a Pārājika offense in a Pārājika-field, by a Thullaccaya offense in a Thullaccaya-field, and by a Dukkaṭa offense in a Dukkaṭa-field. Why? Because it was said, "should she consent to physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggā)." This is the decision in the Commentaries. In this decision, although the origination of action (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna) is not evident, it should be understood that it is stated according to the method of preponderance (tabbahulanaya).

"Ubbhakkhaka" means above the collarbones. "Adhojāṇumaṇฎala" means below the kneecaps. Here, the area below the elbows is also included within "adhojāṇumaṇฎala."

In the term "ekatovassuta" (oozing on one side), although it is stated generally as "ekato" without specification, it should be understood that this classification of offenses is stated when only the nun is "oozing" with the lust for physical contact.

Regarding this classification of offenses, the decision from the beginning is as follows: If the nun is "oozing" with the lust for physical contact and the man is likewise, and there is consent to physical contact in the part of the body below the collarbones and above the kneecaps, the nun incurs a Pārājika offense. If the nun has the lust for physical contact and the man has either sexual lust, or household-based affection (gehassitapema), or a pure mind (suddhacitta), she incurs only a Thullaccaya offense. If the nun has sexual lust and the man has lust for physical contact, sexual lust, household-based affection, or a pure mind, she incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. If the nun has household-based affection and the man has any one of the four aforementioned states, she incurs only a Dukkaṭa offense. If the nun has a pure mind, no matter what mind the man has, there is no offense.

If it is both a monk and a nun and both have the lust for physical contact, the monk incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense and the nun incurs a Pārājika offense. If the nun has the lust for physical contact and the monk has sexual lust or household-based affection, the nun incurs a Thullaccaya offense and the monk incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. If both have sexual lust or household-based affection, both incur only a Dukkaṭa offense. For whoever has a pure mind, there is no offense (anāpatti) for that person. If both have a pure mind, there is no offense for both.
176:
In the sections on non-offense such as "unintentional" (asañcicca), there is no offense for a nun who touches by mistake, or a nun whose mind is elsewhere while touching, or a nun who touches without knowing "this is a man" or "this is a woman," or a nun who, though touched by that man, does not consent to that touch. In all sections, the remaining words are clear.

The origination (samuṭṭhāna) of the first Pārājika is: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and two feelings (dvivedanā).

## The First Pārājika.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika Training Rule

In the second Pārājika—"kacci no sā" means asking "is that [Sundarīnandā] (pregnant)?" "Avaṇṇo" means a fault, the opposite of virtue. "Akittī" means being reproached. "Ayaso" means the ruin of followers or backbiting.

"Vajjapaṭicchādikā" (concealer of a fault) is also just a name for this Pārājika; therefore, it is not analyzed in the Word-for-Word Analysis (padabhājanī). Here, the remaining words are clear.

"Sā vā āroceti" means the nun who has fallen into a Pārājika offense reports it herself. "Aṭṭhannaṃ pārājikānaṃ aññataraṃ" means any one of the eight Pārājikas, consisting of the four shared with monks and the four specific [to nuns]. This second Pārājika training rule was laid down last, which is why it is said "among the eight" in the Vibhaṅga. However, it should be understood that it is placed in this position because it forms a pair with the preceding first [Pārājika]. "Dhuram nikkhippamatte" means as soon as the responsibility is laid down (she is no longer a nun). The detailed explanation here should be understood according to the method stated in the training rule on concealing a gross offense (duฎฎhullāpatti-paฎicchādana) in the Sappāṇaka Vagga. For in that rule, it is a Pācittiya offense, while here it is a Pārājika offense; this is the only distinction. The rest of the procedure is the same as that training rule. "Vajjapaฎicchādikā" is also just a name for this Pārājika; therefore, it is not analyzed in the Word-for-Word Analysis. Here, the remaining words are clear.

The origination of laying down the responsibility (dhuranikkhepa-samuฎฎhāna) arises from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (akiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Second Pārājika.

## 3. Tatiya-pārājika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the third Pārājika training rule—'Dhammena' means by a true matter or fact. 'Vinayena' means by accusing and reminding of the fault. In the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanī), however, it is said 'yena dhammena yena vinayena' (by which Dhamma, by which Vinaya) merely to show the meaning that 'a monk who is expelled by such Dhamma and such Vinaya is well-expelled.' 'Satthusāsanena' (by the Teacher's instruction) means [expulsion] by a complete motion (ñatti) and a complete proclamation (kammavācā). In the Padabhājanī, only the synonyms of that term, 'Jinasāsanena' and 'Buddhasāsanena', are mentioned. In the phrases beginning with 'saṅghaṃ vā gaṇaṃ vā', it means that one does not accept, does not follow, and does not show respect toward the Saṅgha that performed the formal act, or the group (gaṇa) consisting of many individuals therein, or a single person, or that formal act itself. 

In the passage 'Samānasaṃvāsaka monks are called companions; that [communion] does not exist with them,' first of all, 'saṃvāsa' (communion) is defined as having a single formal act, a single recitation of the Pātimokkha, and equality in training. Those who have such common communion are called 'samānasaṃvāsaka'. Such monks are called 'sahāya' (companions) of that monk because of their state of 'going together' in that communion. Now, the communion because of which those monks were called 'samānasaṃvāsaka' no longer exists for that expelled (ukkhittaka) monk together with them. Since that communion does not exist for him together with those monks, those monks are not made his companions. Therefore, it is said: 'Monks of common communion are called companions; that communion does not exist with them; therefore he is called one who has not made companions (akatasaahāya).'

The rest of the procedure is clear in meaning, following the method already stated in the Saṅghabheda training rule and others.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of formal admonition (samanubhāsana) arises from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (akiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## Tatiya-pārājikaṃ.

## 4. Catuttha-pārājika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the fourth Pārājika training rule—'Avassutā' (lustful/oozing) means soaked with the lust of physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggarāga) due to the power of making friends with worldly desire. The same method applies to the second term. In the phrases beginning with 'purisapuggalassa hatthagahaṇaṃ vā', the taking of the hand by a male person is called 'purisapuggalassa hatthagahaṇaṃ'. The same method applies to 'saṅghāṭikaṇṇagahaṇa' (taking the corner of the outer robe). In this term 'hatthagahaṇaṃ', taking the hand and taking in another place that is not a Pārājika field...
179:
(Pārājika) does not occur. Therefore, if a certain bhikkhunī, having reached one case, relinquishes the responsibility and confesses, and then again falls into it by the power of defilements, and confesses again—even if she completes the eight cases in this manner, she does not become a Pārājika.

However, if a bhikkhunī, having fallen into an offense, confesses with the exertion of thinking, "I will reach another case again," that offense of hers does not count towards the number of confessions; even though it is confessed, it is not considered confessed. It does not reach the count of being confessed and remains merely a factor of Pārājika. Upon the mere completion of the eighth case, she becomes a Pārājika. The rest of the words are clear.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of relinquishing the responsibility (dhura-nikkhepa) arises from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya), a release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), a bodily action (kāya-kamma), a verbal action (vacī-kamma), an unwholesome mind (akusala-citta), and has two feelings (dvi-vedanā).

## The Fourth Pārājika.

"Ladies, the eight Pārājika rules have been recited"—this means the four common Pārājikas prescribed starting with the monks and these four (specific to bhikkhunīs); thus, in the sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation, the meaning should be understood as "Ladies, the eight Pārājika rules have been recited." The rest of the sequence of words is just as stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
