## 2. Saṅghādisesa Section (Explanation of the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga)

## 1. Explanation of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

Immediately following the Pārājika section, I shall now state the explanation of the meanings that are not clear in this Saṅghādisesa section.

"Udositam" means a storehouse for goods (warehouse). "Māyyā evam avaca" means "Lady, do not say so." "Apināyyā" is "api nu ayyā." "Accāvadatha" means speak overwhelmingly, meaning revile.

"Ussayavādikā" is one who disputes by the power of conceit or by the power of anger. Since that bhikkhunī is, in meaning, one who brings a lawsuit, it is said in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanī): "Ussayavādikā means a litigant (aḍḍakārikā)." Here, "aḍḍa" refers to the decision of the judges, which the monks also call a "legal issue" (adhikaraṇa). If she seeks a second witness or a companion, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If she goes—whether it be a bhikkhunī monastery or a path for alms-round—at whatever place she stands and the thought "I will bring a lawsuit" arises, for that bhikkhunī who goes from that place to the presence of the judges, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) at every step. If she informs one person, it means someone informs the judges of the words of either one of two people. In informing the second person, the method is the same.

The detailed explanation here for the sake of clarity is: at the very least, if a bhikkhunī sees the judges who have come to the bhikkhunī monastery and informs them of her own words, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If a lay follower (upāsaka) informs them of her words, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya). If first the lay follower informs them of his own words, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Then, if that bhikkhunī informs them of her own words, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya). If the bhikkhunī says to the lay follower, "You yourself inform them of my words and your words," and that lay follower informs them first of either his own words or the bhikkhunī's words, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for the first informing, and a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the second informing. In the case where the lay follower says to the bhikkhunī, "You yourself inform them of my words and your words," the method is the same.
181: A bhikkhunī causes a kappiyakāraka to speak. In doing so, whether the kappiyakāraka speaks the bhikkhunī's words first, or the other person (a lay follower) speaks their own words first, or the kappiyakāraka speaks for both, or the other person speaks for both—however it is spoken—the bhikkhunī incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the first speech and a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the second speech. Regardless of how it is spoken, when the judges make a decision after hearing both sides, it is called the conclusion of the lawsuit (aḍḍapariyosāna). At the conclusion of that lawsuit, whether the bhikkhunī wins or loses, she incurs an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Order (saṅghādisesa). If, however, the case has already reached successive courts and the judges are already familiar with it, and upon seeing the bhikkhunī and the plaintiff, they decide the case themselves, saying, "There is no need for you to speak; we know the facts of this case," then there is no offense for the bhikkhunī at such a conclusion of the lawsuit.## Because this offense is reached at the very first instance, it is called "paṭhamāpattika." This means it is an offense to be committed at the very moment of transgression. In the Word-for-Word Analysis (padabhājanī), however, to show the mere meaning, it is stated: "It is incurred simultaneously with the transgression of the matter, without formal admonition (samannubhāsana)." The meaning here is: the offense that the bhikkhunī incurs simultaneously with the transgression of the matter is not due to the third formal admonition; because this offense must be incurred first, simultaneously with the transgression of the matter, it is called paṭhamāpattika. Because it causes expulsion from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, it is called "nissāraṇīya." In the Word-for-Word Analysis, to show the mere meaning, it is stated: "She is expelled from the Saṅgha." In that context, it should be understood that the bhikkhunī who has committed such an offense is expelled from the Saṅgha, and that offense is called nissāraṇīya. It is not that someone expels that specific Dhamma (offense) from the Saṅgha; rather, the bhikkhunī is expelled because of that offense. Therefore, because that offense causes expulsion, it is called nissāraṇīya.## "Being pulled, she goes" means she goes to the judges when summoned by the plaintiffs, either in person or by messenger, saying, "Please come." Thereafter, even if the plaintiff speaks his own words first or the bhikkhunī's words first, there is no offense of wrong-doing for the first speech, nor a grave offense for the second speech. Even when the lawsuit is concluded by the decision of the ministers, there is no offense. If the plaintiff says to the bhikkhunī, "You yourself speak both my words and your words," and the lawsuit is concluded after hearing the words of the bhikkhunī who speaks thus, there is no offense.
182: "Seeking protection" (rakkhaṃ yācati) means requesting lawful protection, and there is no offense. To show how the requested protection is lawful, it is said: "Reporting without specifying" (anodissa ācikkhati). In this regard, there is specifying and not specifying concerning the past, and specifying and not specifying concerning the future.## How is there specifying concerning the past? In the bhikkhunīs' monastery, village boys or rogues and the like behave improperly, cut down trees, take fruits, or seize requisites. Then the bhikkhunī approaches the judges and says, "Such and such an act was committed in our monastery." When asked, "Who did it?", she reports by specifying, "This person and that person did it." Such specifying concerning the past is not allowable. If the judges hear that and punish those people, the entire liability (gīvā) falls upon the bhikkhunī. Even if she merely intends that they will be punished, she is liable. If she directly says, "Punish that person," and a fine worth five māsakas is taken, she incurs an offense of defeat (pārājika).## When asked, "Who did it?", she should say, "It is not allowable for us to say 'this person did it'; you yourselves will know. We only seek protection; please grant it to us, and have the stolen goods returned." Reporting without specifying in this manner is allowable. When spoken thus, even if the judges search for the perpetrators and punish them, or if all the stolen property is recovered, there is no liability and no offense for the bhikkhunī.## Seeing someone taking requisites and shouting "Thief! Thief!" with the desire for their harm is also not allowable. If they are punished because of such shouting, the entire liability falls upon the bhikkhunī. However, it is allowable to say to someone who will listen to her words (a judge), "This person took my requisites; please have that property returned, but do not punish him." Engaging in a lawsuit for the sake of male slaves, female slaves, or ponds and the like is called an unallowable lawsuit (akappiya-aḍḍa) and is not allowable.## How is there specifying concerning the future? In the same manner as mentioned, when others behave improperly and so on, the bhikkhunī says to the judge, "They are doing such and such in our monastery; please give us protection so that they cannot do it in the future." When asked, "Who is doing this?", she says, "This person and that person..."
183: Thus, reporting with reference to what is yet to come occurs; that too is not allowable. If they are punished, all responsibility lies on the neck of the Bhikkhunī (the Bhikkhunī alone is responsible), just as in the previous method. The rest is the same as before. However, if the authorities have made a proclamation by beat of drum, saying, "We will impose such-and-such a punishment on those who commit such misconduct in the Bhikkhunīs' quarters," and they search for and punish those who do not abide by the order, there is no responsibility for the Bhikkhunī, nor is there an offense. This method stated for Bhikkhunīs is the same for Bhikkhus. For a Bhikkhu as well, reporting with reference [to a person] is not allowable. If they are punished because of such reporting, all responsibility lies with the Bhikkhu. For a Bhikkhu who causes punishment to be taken in the manner stated, there is a Pārājika offense. However, if one speaks without referring to a specific person, even knowing that "they will punish," and the authorities search and punish them, there is no fault. It is not allowable to take the knives, axes, etc., of those who cut trees, etc., within the monastery boundary and strike them with stones. If the blade is damaged, it must be repaired and given back. One should not run after them and take their requisites; because the mind changes quickly, if a thievish intent arises, it could lead to the cutting of the root (Pārājika) in the Dispensation. The rest is clear. The Kathina-origination (Kathinasamuṭṭhāna) is: action, not-perception-exemption, without thought, regulation-transgression, bodily action, vocal action, three thoughts, and three feelings. ## Sattarasake Paṭhama-sikkhāpadaṃ. ## 2. Dutiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā In the commentary on the second training rule: "Varabhaṇḍa" refers to precious goods such as pearls, gems, and lapis lazuli. "Anapaloketvā" means without asking (without consulting). "Gaṇa" refers to groups such as the Malla group or the Bhaṭiputta group; "Pūga" refers to a Dhamma-group (an assembly of righteous people); "Seṇi" refers to guilds such as the perfumers' guild or the cloth-merchants' guild. In whatever places kings have handed over villages or towns to groups (gaṇa), etc., saying, "You yourselves govern here," they alone are the authorities in those places. Therefore, this is said with reference to those governing groups, etc. In this matter, even after asking the king or the group, etc., the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha must still be asked. "Ṭhapetvā kappaṃ" means among the sectarians...
184:
...or among other bhikkhunīs, who were previously ordained as ascetics and have reached a suitable state (kappagatika). The rest of the explanation is clear.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the training rule on ordaining a female thief (corīvuṭṭhāpana) is: for a female preceptor who ordains [a candidate] together with her own group of disciples at the place where she is seated, without going to a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) while other bhikkhunīs have departed for some business, the offense arises from speech and mind. For a preceptor who goes to a partial boundary or a river and ordains, the offense arises from body, speech, and mind. Due to ordaining without asking, it involves action and non-action, perception-release, with thought, a breach of regulation, bodily action, vocal action, three thoughts, and three feelings.

## Second Training Rule.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

In the third training rule: regarding the phrase "crossing the enclosure (parikkhepa)," a bhikkhunī who crosses with one foot incurs a Thullaccaya offense; as soon as she crosses with the second foot, it is a Saṅghādisesa. In the case of the precinct (upacāra) of an unenclosed village, if she crosses the area where a stone's throw would reach (which is worthy of being an enclosure) with one foot, it is a Thullaccaya offense; as soon as she crosses with the second foot, it is a Saṅghādisesa. Furthermore, in this training rule, there is no offense yet for a bhikkhunī who is just leaving her own village because of the reason of [going to] another village. However, for a bhikkhunī who has left her village and is going to another village, there is a Dukkaṭa offense for every step. As soon as she crosses the enclosure or precinct of the other village with one foot, it is a Thullaccaya offense; as soon as she crosses with the second foot, it is a Saṅghādisesa. The same method applies to a bhikkhunī who leaves that other village and enters her own village again.

If it is possible to enter directly into the bhikkhunī monastery grounds through a broken wall or a hole in the fence, a bhikkhunī entering in this way is said to have entered allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi), and therefore it is permissible. If she enters by means of an elephant's back and so forth, or by psychic power, it is also permissible. This is because in this training rule, only travel by foot is intended. For that very reason, [the Buddha] said, "crossing with the first foot," and so forth.

Suppose two villages have fences connected by a bhikkhunī monastery. In the village where the bhikkhunī monastery is located, if after wandering for alms and re-entering the monastery, there is a path through the middle of the monastery to the other village, it is permissible to go. However, she must return from that village by that same path. If she leaves through the village gate and returns, the different types of offenses should be understood according to the method previously stated. From her own village...
185:
If a bhikkhunī who has gone out with other bhikkhunīs for some business, upon returning, finds that an elephant has broken loose or there is a crowd pushing through, and the other bhikkhunīs enter the village quickly, she should wait outside the village gate until another bhikkhunī arrives. If no other bhikkhunī arrives, the companion is considered to have departed, and it is allowable for her to enter the village.

In the past, there was a large village with a bhikkhunīs' monastery in the center. Later, if four people acquire that village and divide it by erecting fences, it is allowable to go from the monastery to one village. It is not allowable to enter another village from that village through a gate or a gap in the fence. She must return to the monastery first. Why? Because the monastery is common to all four villages.

"The inner robe is wet" means: in whatever river, if one wears it such that the three circles—the two knees and the navel—are covered, and a bhikkhunī dressed in this way descends into the water during the rainy season, whether at a landing place or not, and upon ascending anywhere, the inner robe becomes wet even by one or two finger-breadths. The remaining characteristics of a river will be clarified in the discussion on the signs of a river (Nadīnimitta-kathā). When descending into such a river and ascending, for a bhikkhunī who lifts the first foot and places it on the bank, there is a Thullaccaya offense. Upon lifting the second foot, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. If she goes by a bridge, there is no offense. If she descends by foot but ascends by climbing onto a bridge to reach the bank, there is no offense. However, if she goes by a bridge but descends to go by foot when ascending, there is indeed an offense. The same method applies to traveling by vehicle, boat, or through the air. If she steps directly from this bank to the other bank, there is no offense. If two or three bhikkhunīs go for the purpose of dyeing or collecting firewood and wander along both banks, it is allowable. However, if while wandering, one bhikkhunī quarrels and goes to the other bank, there is an offense. If two are crossing together and one quarrels in the middle of the river, turns back, and returns to this bank, there is an offense. For the other bhikkhunī, since the returning one is in the position of one who has departed, there is no offense even if she goes to the other bank. If she descends to bathe or drink and ascends back to the same bank, there is no offense.

Regarding the phrase "at the rise of the dawn": if while reciting, practicing meditation, or doing some other work, she intends, "I will go to the companion bhikkhunī before dawn," and even though she intends so, the dawn rises without her realizing it, there is no offense. However, if she stays in a part of the monastery thinking, "I will stay here until dawn," or without any such intention, [and does not come] within the reach (hatthapāsa) of the companion bhikkhunī...
186:
...does not enter [the hatthapāsa], there is a Saṅghādisesa offense at the rise of dawn. For in this case, the measure is only the hatthapāsa (two and a half cubits). If she exceeds the hatthapāsa, even being within the same room does not protect her from the offense.

In the phrase "agāmake araññe" (in a village-less forest), "forest" refers to the area defined as "everything outside the gate-post (indakhīla) is forest." It is called "agāmaka" (village-less) simply because of the absence of a village, not because it resembles the Vinjhā forest. Having entered such a forest, if the visual range (dassanūpacāra) is abandoned, even if the auditory range (savanūpacāra) remains, there is an offense.

Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "If, while bhikkhunīs are entering the courtyard of the Mahābodhi, one stays outside, there is an offense for her as well. The same method applies when entering the Lohapāsāda or the precinct. While they are venerating the Mahācetiya, if one goes out through the north gate, there is an offense for her as well. While they are entering the Thūpārāma, if one stays outside, there is an offense for her as well."

Here, "visual range" (dassanūpacāra) means being in a place where the companion can see her. If she is separated by a curtain, she is said to have abandoned the visual range. "Auditory range" (savanūpacāra) means being in a place where she can hear the voice of one calling "Lady!" like the voice of one who has lost their way or a voice announcing the time for hearing the Dhamma. In an open space, the visual range can exist even at a distance. If such a visual range is abandoned, the auditory range does not protect her; by the mere act of abandoning it, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

If one is left behind while traveling on a road, but she makes an effort and follows, thinking "I will catch up now," there is no offense. If those in front go by another road, they are considered to have departed, and there is no offense. Among two traveling together, if one stays behind thinking "Let this lady go," and cannot follow, or if the other goes thinking "Let this lady stay behind," both incur an offense. However, if while traveling, the one in front takes another road and the one behind also takes another road, since each is in the position of having departed from the other, there is no offense for either.

"Pakkha-saṅkantā vā" means going over to the residence of non-Buddhists (titthiyas). The rest is clear. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) is the same as the first Pārājika: action, perception of release, with intention, a breach of regulation, bodily action, three states of mind, and three feelings.

## The Third Training Rule.
187: ...Among bhikkhunīs, if one is unable to follow and thinks, 'Let this bhikkhunī ahead go on,' and stays behind, and the other bhikkhunī also thinks, 'Let this bhikkhunī following behind stay behind,' and goes on, both incur an offense. However, among the bhikkhunīs who are going, if either the one in front or the one behind enters another path and one remains at the place where the other departed, both do not incur an offense. 693. 'Pakkhasaṅkantā' means moving to the residence or monastery of the sectarians (titthiya). The rest is the same as the third training rule. ## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 694-8. In the commentary on the fourth training rule: 'Pādapīṭha' refers to a small stool for placing washed feet. 'Pādakaṭhalikā' refers to a small stool for placing unwashed feet. 'Ananyāya gaṇassa chandaṃ' means (acting) without even knowing the consent of the group performing that act. 'Vatte vattantiṃ' refers to a bhikkhunī who is practicing the duties that lead to emergence from the forty-three types of offenses. The rest is clear. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) is 'dhuranikkhepa' (laying down the burden), arising through body, speech, and mind; it involves action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriyā), release of perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). ## The Fourth Training Rule. ## 5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule In the commentary on the fifth training rule: Regarding the phrase 'ekato avassute', the Mahāpaccari states, 'The state of the bhikkhunī being wet with lust should be understood.' However, this is not stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā; this omission agrees with the Pāḷi. The rest is clear. The origin is the same as the first Pārājika; it involves action (kiriya), release of perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and two types of feelings (dvividanā). ## The Fifth Training Rule. ## 6. Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 705-6. In the commentary on the sixth training rule: 'Yato tvaṃ' means 'because you'. Regarding the offenses starting from 'uyyojeti āpatti dukkaṭassa' and ending with Saṅghādisesa, to whom do they occur? They occur to the 'uyyojikā' bhikkhunī who incites or urges. This point is also stated in the Parivāra: 'She does not give, she does not receive, therefore there is no receiving. She reaches a grave offense (garuka), not a light one (lahuka), and that occurs because of use (paribhogapaccaya). This problem has been considered by the wise.'
188:
Indeed, this verse was spoken with reference to this exhorting bhikkhunī. However, the classification of the offense for the other bhikkhunī who is exhorted has already been explained in the first training rule. The rest is clear.

This training rule has three origins. It is an action (kiriya), it is released by perception (saññāvimokkha), it is with intention (sacittaka), it is a worldly fault (lokavajja), it is bodily and vocal action (kāyakamma, vacīkamma), it is unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and it has three feelings (tivedana).

## Sixth Training Rule.

## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

In the seventh training rule, the meaning of the term 'yāvatatiyaka' (until the third time) should be understood in the same way as explained in the Bhikkhu Mahāvibhaṅga. The rest is clear.

It has the origin of formal warning (samanubhāsanasamuṭṭhāna). It is an action, it is released by perception, it is with intention, it is a worldly fault, it is bodily and vocal action, it is unwholesome consciousness, and it has painful feeling (dukkhavedana).

## Seventh Training Rule.

## 8. Commentary on the Eighth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, 'in a certain legal issue' means in one of the four types of legal issues. In the word-for-word commentary (padabhājana), however, the statement "Legal issue means the four legal issues," etc., was said merely to show the classification of legal issues. The rest, along with the origins and so forth, is clear.

## Eighth Training Rule.

## 9. Commentary on the Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

In the ninth training rule, 'saṃsaṭṭhā' means associated or mingled. 'Ananulomikena' means by way of bodily and vocal actions that are inappropriate for those who have gone forth. 'Saṃsaṭṭhā' means they are mingled with laypeople through bodily actions such as pounding grain, cooking, grinding perfumes, and stringing garlands, or through vocal actions such as carrying messages, carrying messages back, or acting as a go-between. 'Pāpa kittisaddo' means they have a bad reputation...
189:
'Pāpasaddā' means they are called 'of bad sound' because they have a bad reputation. 'Pāpasilokā' means they are called 'of bad fame' because they have a bad reputation regarding their livelihood. The rest, along with the origins and so forth, is clear.

## Ninth Training Rule.

## 10. Commentary on the Tenth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

In the tenth training rule: 'Evācārā' means of such behavior. The meaning is: 'Just as your behavior is seen to be, such are the bhikkhunīs of that behavior.' This method applies everywhere. 'Uññāya' means by knowing with contempt, by making [someone] low. 'Paribhavena' means by knowing with disrespect, thinking, 'What can these bhikkhunīs do?' 'Akkhantiyā' means by intolerance; the meaning is by anger. 'Vebhassiyā' means by the state of having powerful/harsh speech; the meaning is by frightening [others] through the display of one's own power. 'Dubbalyā' means by the state of your weakness. In all instances like 'uññāya' and 'paribhavena,' the conjunctive sense (samuccaya) of the word 'ca' should be understood. 'Viviccatha' means live separately. The rest, along with the origins and so forth, is clear.

## Tenth Training Rule.

"Venerable ladies, the seventeen Saṅghādisesas have been recited." In this statement, after the six offenses of immediate commission (paṭhamāpattika), the three training rules—one on acting as a go-between (sañcaritta) and two on corrupting with malice (duṭṭhadosa)—are included from the Mahāvibhaṅga, making nine offenses of immediate commission. After the four offenses involving formal warning (yāvatatiyaka), four more are included from the Mahāvibhaṅga, making eight offenses involving formal warning. Thus, all offenses are recited in the order of the Pātimokkha; "Venerable ladies, the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules have been recited"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. The rest of the procedure is clear, except for the fortnightly penance (pakkhamānatta). That pakkhamānatta will be explained in detail in the Khandhaka.

## 3. Nissaggiya Kaṇḍa (Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)
## Commentary on the First Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
There are thirty Nissaggiya (forfeiture) rules declared for the bhikkhunīs. Now follows the sequence of the commentary on these Nissaggiya rules.

In the term "āmattikāpaṇa," "amatta" refers to vessels or pots. Those who sell these vessels are called "āmattika." The shop of these vessel-sellers is called "āmattikāpaṇa." It means they will spread out or display the shop of these vessel-sellers.

"Pattasannicayaṃ kareyya" means one would make a hoard of bowls. It means keeping a bowl for even a single day without determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā). The rest of the procedure should be understood in the same way as stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga. This is the only distinction: in the Mahāvibhaṅga, there is a ten-day allowance, but here in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, there is not even a single day. The rest is identical.

This training rule also has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Kathina rule: it arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind; it is an act of omission (akiriya); it is not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha); it can occur without intention (acittaka); it is a violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja); it involves bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The First Training Rule.
## Commentary on the Second Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the second rule: "duccoḷa" means those with ugly or worn-out clothes. "Apayyāhi" means "O noble ladies (is it obtained?)."

"Ādisse dinna" refers to a robe given after saying, "Let the arriving nuns divide it," or a robe given after saying, "I give this to the group" or "I give this to you noble ladies," or a robe placed at the feet with the desire to give. All such robes are "akālacīvara" (out-of-season robes). However, a robe obtained by saying "I give to the noble lady" should be applied exactly as it was given. The rest is clear.

It has three origins: it is an act of commission (kiriya); it is released by perception (saññāvimokkha); it occurs with intention (sacittaka); it is a worldly fault (lokavajja); it involves bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with unwholesome consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Second Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Third Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
743-5. In the third training rule: "handa" means "take." "Sayaṃ acchindati" means for a nun who, after giving one robe, takes it back, there is one Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense; if there are many robes, there are many offenses. If she takes back robes that are folded and kept together at once, the offenses are according to the number of items. However, for robes that are tied in a bundle, there is only one offense. The rest of the explanation is clear.

This training rule has three origins: commission (kiriya), release by perception (saññāvimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.

## The Third Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Fourth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the fourth training rule: "kayena" means by price or value. "I have no use for ghee, I have use for oil"—it is said that the nun spoke this thinking she would receive oil after having already given the ghee that was brought. "Viññāpetvā" means having made it known, or having requested, "Bring such and such an item."

"Taññeva viññāpeti" means requesting the same item again because the item requested first was too little and insufficient. "Aññañca viññāpeti" means if ghee was requested first, but because the doctor said, "A combination of ghee and oil should be cooked," and she needs oil, she requests another item saying, "I also have a need for oil." "Ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā" means showing the benefit, such as saying, "If ghee worth one kahāpaṇa is brought, double the amount of oil can be obtained for this price, and the medical purpose can be fulfilled with that oil; therefore, bring only oil." The rest of the explanation is clear.

This training rule has six origins: commission (kiriya), not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), without intention (acittaka), violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Fourth Training Rule.
192:
## Commentary on the Fifth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule

In the fifth training rule: "na me sikkhamāne"—it is said that the laywoman spoke this thinking, "If this trainee (sikkhamānā) is told this, she will leave this oil and bring ghee for me from her own family home." "Cetāpetvā" simply means "having made it known." In all other parts, it is the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Fifth Training Rule is finished.

## Commentary on the Sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule

In the sixth training rule: "chandaka" is the name for requisites collected after generating the desire and wish of others by saying, "Let us perform such and such a meritorious deed; give whatever (requisite) you are able to." "Aññadatthikena" means with (a requisite) given for another purpose. "Aññuddisikena" means with (a requisite) given designated for another person. "Saṅghikena" means with (a requisite) dedicated to the Saṅgha.

"Sesakaṃ upaneti" means after purchasing (exchanging) the requisite for the purpose it was given, she applies the remaining value for another purpose. "Sāmike apaloketvā" means she applies it after asking permission, saying, "This was given by you for the sake of robes; we have robes, but we have a need for oil and so on." "Āpadāsu" means in such dangers where nuns abandon the monastery and leave; in such dangers, it is allowable to purchase (exchange) any item. The rest of the explanation is clear.

The six origins are: commission and omission (kiriyākiriya), not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), without intention (acittaka), violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Sixth Training Rule is finished.

## Commentary on the Seventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule

In the seventh training rule: "saññācikena" means with (a requisite) requested by oneself. This (term "saññācikena") is the only distinction in this training rule. The rest is the same as the sixth training rule.

## The Seventh Training Rule is finished.

In the eighth training rule—the term "mahājanikena" means with the requisites that have been relinquished to the group of bhikkhunīs. In this training rule, this term alone is the point of distinction.

## The Eighth Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the ninth training rule—this term "saññācikena" (by asking for it oneself) is an additional specific term beyond the eighth training rule.

## The Ninth Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Tenth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the tenth training rule—the phrase "pariveṇaṃ undriyatī" means the enclosure is destroyed or it falls down. This phrase and the phrase "puggalikena saññācikena" (by asking for it oneself for personal use) are the only points of distinction. The rest is exactly the same as the previous training rule.

## The Tenth Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Eleventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the eleventh training rule—"garupāvuraṇaṃ" refers to a garment (a heavy cloak) to be worn during the cold season. Regarding the term "catukkaṃsaparamam," here a "kaṃsa" is worth four kahāpaṇas; therefore, in the Padabhājanī, it was stated as "worth sixteen kahāpaṇas."

## The Eleventh Training Rule.

## Commentary on the Twelfth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the twelfth training rule—"lahupāvuraṇaṃ" refers to a garment (a light cloak) to be worn during the hot season. The remaining points in both training rules are quite clear.
194:
The six origins (samuṭṭhāna) are: action (kiriya), not being released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), being without thought (acittaka), being a violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), having three thoughts (ticitta), and having three feelings (tivedana).

## The Twelfth Training Rule.

Regarding the passage, "Ladies, the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules have been recited," the meaning is as follows: From the Cīvara Vagga of the Mahāvibhaṅga, the two training rules—the Dhovana training rule and the Paṭiggahana training rule—are removed. Then, by resolving "akalacīvaraṃ kālacīvaraṃ" (out-of-season robe, in-season robe), the first Vagga is completed by substituting them with the Bhājita training rule and the Acchinna-cīvara training rule. Again, from the beginning of the Eḷakaloma Vagga, seven training rules are removed, and by inserting the seven Aññadatthika training rules, the second Vagga is completed. From the third Vagga, these three—the first Patta training rule, the Vassikasāṭika training rule, and the Āraññaka training rule—are removed, and the third Vagga is completed with the Pattasannicaya training rule, the Garupāvuraṇa training rule, and the Lahupāvuraṇa training rule. Thus, there are twelve training rules laid down for bhikkhunīs only (ekatopaññatta) and eighteen training rules laid down for both sides (ubhatopaññatta). In this way, according to the sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation, the meaning here should be understood as "Ladies, the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules have been recited." The remaining points are as previously explained.

## 4. The Pācittiya Chapter (Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)
## 1. The Garlic Chapter (Lasuṇa Vagga)
## 1. Commentary on the First Garlic Training Rule

Immediately after the thirty [Nissaggiya] rules, there are one hundred and sixty-six rules collected and chanted; now follows the commentary on those rules as well.

Among those rules, in the first training rule of the Lasuṇa Vagga—"dve tayo bhaṇḍike" means two or three bundles; this is a designation for garlic that has full cloves/segments. "Na mattaṃ jānitvā" means not knowing the measure, she had many garlic bulbs taken while the field guard was forbidding it.

"Aññataraṃ haṃsayoniṃ" means being born in the golden goose species. That goose was one who could remember past lives, and out of past affection, he would come and give them one feather each; that feather was pure gold that could withstand heating in fire, striking, and cutting.

"Māgadhakaṃ" means garlic grown in the Magadha country. For in this training rule, only garlic grown in the Magadha country is intended as "lasuṇa," and that too must be garlic with many cloves, not garlic with one, two, or three cloves. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, without mentioning the place of origin, it is stated that "māgadhaka" means garlic with many cloves. Regarding the phrase "ajjhohāre ajjhohāre" (for every swallow), if she chews and swallows two or three bundles of multi-cloved garlic all at once, it is one Pācittiya offense. But for a bhikkhunī who breaks them and eats the cloves one by one, there are as many Pācittiya offenses as there are efforts (payoga).

The differences among onions (palaṇḍuka) and others should be known by color or by clove. By color, the palaṇḍuka onion is pale/yellowish in color. The bhañjanaka is red in color. The haritaka is the color of a green leaf. By clove, the palaṇḍuka has one clove, the bhañjanaka has two, and the haritaka has three. The cāpa-garlic has no cloves, having only a sprout. In the Mahāpaccarī and other commentaries, however, it is stated: "palaṇḍukassa tīṇi miñjāni, bhañjanakassa dve, haritakassa ekaṃ"—that the palaṇḍuka has three cloves, the bhañjanaka has two, and the haritaka has one.
196:
It is stated in the Commentary: These onions such as *palaṇḍuka* are allowable by their nature (even without being added to salads or curries). However, in the case of cooking curries well by adding garlic, even garlic from the Magadha region is allowable. Indeed, that Magadhan garlic is allowable to be added to green gram soup and the like while they are being cooked, or to specially prepared fish or meat, or to oils and the like, or to jujube jam and the like, or to sour-tasting leafy vegetables and the like, or to salads, or to any unspecified food, at the very least even to rice gruel. The remaining words in this training rule are clear.

The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the *Eḷakaloma* training rule is: it is an action, not released by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, a bodily act, having three thoughts, and having three feelings.

## 1. Lasuṇa Sikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Garlic).

## 2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule

In the second training rule: "In a confined place" (*sammādhe*) means in a concealed area. For the purpose of showing the divisions of that confined place, the Blessed One said, "the two armpits and the urinary organ." "Even a single hair" (*ekampi lomaṃ*) means for a bhikkhunī who has one hair or many hairs removed by means of scissors, tweezers, a razor, or any unspecified object, through a single effort or various efforts, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of efforts, not according to the number of hairs.

"By reason of an illness" (*ābādhapaccayā*) means there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who has [hair] removed because of a reason such as an itch or a scab. The rest is clear. There are four origins: it arises through the body, through the body and speech, through the body and mind, and through the body, speech, and mind. It is an action, not released by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, a bodily act, a vocal act, having three thoughts, and having three feelings.

## Second Training Rule.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule

803-4. In the third training rule: "Striking with the palm" (*talaghātake*) means striking the surface of the urinary organ. In this passage, "at the very least even with a lotus leaf," the leaf itself is still large; there is an offense even for a bhikkhunī who strikes with a lotus filament.
197:
"By reason of an illness" means it is allowable to strike a boil or a wound. The remaining sequence of words is very clear. The origin of this training rule is like the origin of the first *pārājika*, being the same in terms of: action, release by perception, with thought, a breach of worldly convention (*lokavajja*), a bodily act, an unwholesome thought, and the three feelings.

## Third Training Rule.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule

In the fourth training rule: "A former concubine of a king" (*purāṇarājorodhā*) means a woman who was a king's concubine in her former lay life. "Goes after a long, long time" means she goes only after a long interval. "Can you maintain it?" means "Are you able?" When asked, "Whose deed is this?", even if she remains silent without speaking, she thinks, "These bhikkhunīs will have doubts and suspicions about me," and thus says, "This deed is mine."

"A lac-stick" (*jatumuṭṭhaka*) means a smooth rod made of lac. This was spoken only by way of the specific case; in fact, there is an offense for a bhikkhunī who inserts any kind of rod. Therefore, it was said, "at the very least, she inserts even a lotus leaf into the urinary organ." Even this lotus leaf is very large; in fact, there is an offense even for a bhikkhunī who inserts even a lotus filament. The rest is very clear. The origins and so forth are exactly as stated in the *Talaghātaka* training rule.

## Fourth Training Rule.

## 5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule

In the fifth training rule: "Performing purification with water too deeply" means performing washing with water by inserting it into a very internal place.

"Exceeds even by a hair's breadth" means, in detail, for a bhikkhunī who inserts [water] more than three or four finger-breadths in width, or more than two finger-joints in depth, even by a hair's breadth, there is a *pācittiya* offense. This is stated in the *Mahāpaccari* Commentary: "It is not allowed to insert three joints of one finger; it is not allowed to insert even one joint each of three or four fingers..."
198:
"...not allowed" means (it is not allowed to insert the joints of three or four fingers). The rest is very clear. The origins and so forth are also exactly as stated in the *Talaghātaka* training rule.

## Fifth Training Rule ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule

In the sixth training rule: "Meal service" (*bhattavissagga*) means the business of eating a meal. "Standing nearby with drinking water and a fan" means standing nearby while fanning, holding a drinking water cup in one hand and a fan in the other. "Speaks excessively" means she speaks household-related talk, transgressing the conduct of a renunciant, saying, "In the past, you used to eat like this, and I used to serve you like this."

"Any kind of drinking water" means whether it is pure water or any one of buttermilk, whey, meat or fish broth, milk, and so forth—any kind of drinkable liquid. "Any kind of fan" means even the corner of a robe is called a fan at the very least. In this training rule, "If she stands within an arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*), there is a *pācittiya* offense," the *pācittiya* is stated only because of the reason of standing. However, because of the reason of striking (fanning), a *dukkaṭa* offense has been prescribed in the *Bhikkhunī Khandhaka*.

"Gives or causes to be given" means if she gives drinking water or curry and the like, saying, "Drink this water, eat with this curry," or if she gives a palm-leaf fan, saying, "Eat while fanning with this palm-leaf fan," or if she causes another to give both, there is no offense. "Commands one who is not ordained" means if she commands a *sāmaṇerī* to stand nearby and serve, there is no offense. The rest is very clear.

This training rule, like the *Eḷakaloma* origin, has: action, not released by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, a bodily act, three thoughts, and three feelings.

## Sixth Training Rule ends.

## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule

In the seventh training rule: "If she accepts, thinking 'I will eat,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)"—this is called an offense of wrong-doing by effort (*payoga-dukkaṭa*). Therefore, it does not occur only in the act of accepting (it also occurs in taking away or drying).
199:
After receiving raw grain, for all preliminary efforts—such as bringing it from the forest, drying it, preparing the stove for roasting on a rainy day, preparing the baking pan, preparing the ladle, taking wood and lighting the fire, putting the grain into the baking pan, roasting it with the ladle, preparing the mortar and pestle for pounding, pounding, winnowing, and washing the rice—up until placing it in the mouth and chewing it with the teeth for the purpose of swallowing, there are offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). At the time of swallowing, there are offenses of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of swallows.

In this training rule, requesting and eating are the essential factors. Therefore, a nun who requests it herself and has another person roast, pound, or cook it, and then eats it, also commits an offense. A nun who has another person request it and then roasts it herself, etc., and eats it, also commits an offense.

In the Mahāpaccari Commentary, it is stated: "For a nun who requests this raw grain even from her mother and eats it, there is only an offense of expiation. For a nun who eats raw grain obtained without requesting, whether she roasts it herself or has another do it, there is an offense of wrongdoing. For a nun who eats raw grain obtained through another's request, whether she roasts it herself, has the requester do it, or has someone else do it, there is also only an offense of wrongdoing." Again, it is said: "For a nun who eats raw grain obtained through another's request and roasts it herself, there is only an offense of expiation. But for a nun who has it roasted and then eats it, there is an offense of wrongdoing." This statement is contradictory, because there is no difference between doing the roasting oneself or having it done. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated generally without distinction: "For a nun who eats raw grain requested by another, there is an offense of wrongdoing."

"Ābādhapaccayā" means there is no offense in requesting grain for the purpose of medical treatment, such as for a sweat-treatment. In the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "It is allowable to accept raw grain obtained without requesting for the purpose of new construction (navakamma)." "Aparaṇṇaṃ viññāpeti" means that, excluding the seven types of grain, there is no offense for a nun who requests mung beans, black grams, etc., or gourds, pumpkins, etc., or any other kind from relatives or those who have given an invitation. However, it is not allowable to request raw grain even from relatives or those who have given an invitation. The remaining words are clear.

This training rule arises from four origins: body, body and speech, body and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It is an action, not released by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, bodily action, vocal action, having three thoughts and three feelings.

## Sattamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 8. Explanation of the Eighth Training Rule

In the eighth training rule: "A royal servant who has received his wages" (nibbiṭṭharājabhaṭo) refers to a royal servant who remains established by the taxes paid to the king; it means one who has taken a specific position through taxes and obtained profit from that place. It refers to a brahmin who goes with the intention of requesting that same position again after having paid the tax to the king, thinking, "I will request that same servant's path." "Paribhāsī" means scolding and threatening those nuns, saying, "Do not do this again in the future."

"Sayaṃ chaḍḍeti" means that for a nun who throws all four substances with a single effort, there is only one offense; if she throws them separately, there are offenses according to the number of objects. The same method applies to commanding. In throwing away a tooth-stick (dantakaṭṭha) as well, there is only an offense of expiation for a nun. For a monk, there is an offense of wrongdoing in all these matters. The rest is clear.

This training rule has six origins: action and non-action, not released by perception, without thought, a breach of regulation, bodily action, vocal action, three thoughts, and three feelings.

## Aṭṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 9. Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule

830-2. In the ninth training rule: For a nun who throws these substances, such as excrement, in any cultivated green area used by people, whether it be a field or a coconut grove, etc., the distinction of offenses should be understood according to the previous method. If she throws waste-water, sugarcane dregs, etc., in a green area while sitting and eating in a field or grove, or while walking and chewing sugarcane, etc.—even if she just throws a coconut shell with the top cut off after drinking the water—there is an offense of expiation. For a monk, there is an offense of wrongdoing.

In a ploughed area, as long as the sprouts have not yet emerged even if seeds have been sown, there is an offense of wrongdoing for all monks and nuns. It is allowable to throw in fields where seeds have not yet been sown, or in the corners of fields where cultivated plants have not yet grown well, or on the embankments of fields, etc. It is also allowable to throw in places where people throw rubbish. "Chaḍḍitakhetta" refers to a field from which people have harvested and removed the crops; it is allowable to throw there. However, in a field where, although harvested, it is guarded with the expectation that beans, etc., will grow again, if one throws there, there is an offense according to the object. The rest is clear. The six origins are the same as the previous method, from action and non-action... up to three feelings.

## Navamasikkhāpadaṃ.
201:
## 10. Dassamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the tenth training rule: 'Whatever kind of dancing' refers to dancing by actors and such, or dancing by drunkards, or even dancing by animals such as peacocks, parrots, and monkeys (including the dancing of snakes in a snake-charmer's show). All such dancing is indeed 'dancing' (nacca). 'Whatever kind of singing' refers to the songs of actors and such, or the songs of the virtuous associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the Parinibbāna of Noble Ones (Ariyas), or the singing of unrestrained monks while preaching the Dhamma. All such singing is indeed 'singing' (gīta). 'Whatever kind of instrumental music' refers to the playing of stringed instruments and the like, or the beating of drums, or even the beating of water-drums. All such playing is indeed 'instrumental music' (vādita).

'If she goes to see, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)' means that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for every single step taken. 'Standing in whatever place she sees or listens' means if she sees with a single effort of looking, and also hears their singing and music, only one pācittiya offense is incurred. However, if she looks in one direction and sees dancing, and then looks elsewhere and sees those who are singing, or elsewhere sees those who are playing music, separate offenses are incurred. A bhikkhunī must not dance, sing, or play music herself. She must not tell others, 'Dance, sing, play music.' She must not say, 'Lay devotees, make an offering to the cetiya,' nor should she accept by saying 'Very well' when people say, 'We shall perform a service to your cetiya.' It is stated in all commentaries that in all such efforts, a pācittiya offense is incurred. For a monk (bhikkhu), it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, when people say, 'We shall perform a service to your cetiya,' it is proper to say, 'Performing a service is indeed good.'

'Standing in the monastery (ārāma)' means if she stands within her own monastery and watches or listens to dancing and so on, whether it is inside the monastery or outside the monastery, there is no offense. 'If there is a duty' means if she goes for the sake of food distributed by tickets (salāka-bhatta) or for any other duty, and watches or listens at the place she has arrived, there is no offense. 'In times of danger' means if she enters a place of public entertainment while fleeing from such dangers as fire or thieves; if she watches or listens while having entered thus, there is no offense. The rest is clear.

This rule has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the Eḷakaloma training rule: it is an action (kiriya), not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and involves three feelings (tivedana).

## Dassamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 1. Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Andhakāra Chapter: 'In the dark (appadīpe)' means in a place not illuminated by any one of these: a lamp, the moon, the sun, or fire. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājana) of that term 'appadīpe', the Blessed One said 'in the absence of light (anāloke)'. 'Or should converse (sallapeyya vā)' means speaking talk related to the household.

'Seeking privacy, being distracted (araho-pekkha aññavihitā)' means not seeking the enjoyment of privacy, but having a mind directed toward an object other than the enjoyment of privacy, such as asking about relatives or consulting about gifts or offerings. It is an action (kiriya), released by perception (saññāvimokkha), intentional (sacittaka), a worldly fault (lokavajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), a verbal action (vacīkamma), an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and involves two feelings (dwivedana).

850-3. In the fourth training rule: 'In the ear (nikaṇṇikaṃ)' refers to the base of the ear. It means 'she should whisper at the base of the ear'. ## 5. Pañcamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule: "While they were cleaning the house" means it occurred to those householders, "No transgression of body or speech is seen in the Elder Nun; let us also clean the house." Then, while cleaning the house, they saw that bedding.

Regarding "to a bhikkhunī who passes beyond a rain-free (sheltered) place": if she passes beyond with the first step, there is a dukkaṭa; if she passes beyond with the second step, there is a pācittiya offense. The same method applies to passing beyond the precinct (upacāra).

"To a sick bhikkhunī" refers to a bhikkhunī who is unable to ask permission due to such illness. "In times of danger" means when a fire has broken out in the house or there is danger from thieves; in the presence of such an accident, if she departs without asking permission, there is no offense. The rest here is clear.

Like the Kathina origin (samuṭṭhāna), it arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind. It is an action and non-action (kiriya-akiriya), not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), a verbal action (vacīkamma), involves three types of mind (ticitta), and three feelings (tivedana).

## Pañcamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 6. Chaṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule: "Should sit down (abhinisīdeyya)" means she sits. For a bhikkhunī who goes away after sitting down, there is one offense; for one who goes away after lying down without sitting, there is one offense; for one who goes away after both sitting and lying down, there are two offenses.

"Permanently prepared (dhuva-paññatte)" means a seat that is constantly set out for the sake of bhikkhunīs. The rest is clear. The origin is like the Kathina origin... up to... three feelings.

## Chaṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 7. Sattamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule also: everything should be understood in the same manner as stated in the sixth training rule.

## Sattamasikkhāpadaṃ.
204:
## 8. Aṭṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the eighth training rule, everything is clear. The three origins (samuṭṭhāna) are: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusala-citta), and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## Aṭṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 9. Navamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule: "Shall curse" (abhisapeyya) means one shall make an oath or a curse. Cursing by means of hell (niraya) means reviling in this manner: "May I be reborn in hell, may I be reborn in Avīci; may that person be reborn in hell, may that person be reborn in Avīci." Cursing by means of the holy life (brahmacariya) means reviling in this manner: "May I become a laywoman, may I become a white-robed woman, may I become a female wanderer, or may another person become like this." For every word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Excluding hell and the holy life, for a bhikkhunī who reviles in this manner: "Bitch, sow, blind woman, cripple," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) for every word.

"Prioritizing the benefit" (atthapurekkhārāya) refers to a bhikkhunī who is explaining the commentary (aṭṭhakathā). "Prioritizing the Dhamma" (dhammapurekkhārāya) refers to a bhikkhunī who is teaching the Pali text. "Prioritizing instruction" (anusāsanipurekkhārāya) means there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who speaks while established in instruction, saying: "Even now you are like this; refrain well. If you do not refrain, surely by performing such deeds again, you will be reborn in hell, you will be reborn in the animal realm."

The rest of the text is clear. The three origins are: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusala-citta), and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## Navamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 10. Dasamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the tenth training rule, everything is clear. The origin of relinquishing responsibility (dhuranikkhepasamuṭṭhāna) arises from body, speech, and mind. It consists of: action (kiriya), release through perception (saññā-vimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome action (akusala-kamma), and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## Dasamasikkhāpadaṃ.

## 3. Naggavagga
## 1. Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
883-6. In the first training rule of the Naggavagga— "Brahmacariyaṃ ciṇṇena" means "by the practiced holy life" or "by the practicing of the holy life"; thus, the accusative case (upayogavacana) should be understood in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa) or the possessive (sāmī). "Acchinnacīvarikāya" is said with reference to the water-cloth (udakasāṭika), not any other robe. Therefore, there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who bathes naked if her water-cloth has been snatched away or is lost. Even if the water-cloth robe is very expensive and she is unable to go outside wearing it, it is also allowable to bathe naked. The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

According to the origin of sheep's wool (eḷakalomasamuṭṭhāna)—it consists of: action (kiriya), no release through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), three minds (ticitta), and three feelings (tivedanā).

## The first training rule is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule
In the tenth training rule: 'Āhundarikā' means narrow.

'Just as the responsibility is laid down' (Dhuraṃ nikkhittamatta) means that if she departs after having abandoned the responsibility to go, it is indeed an offense. For a nun who goes up to five yojanas after having performed Pavāraṇā, there is no offense. Regarding six yojanas, there is no question of no offense (an offense is incurred). If she goes three yojanas and returns by that same path, it is not allowable. It is allowable to return by another path.

'In danger' (Antarāye) refers to the ten kinds of danger. If she has set out thinking 'I will go to another place,' but the river overflows, or there are robbers on the path, or it rains, it is allowable to turn back. The rest is clear in meaning. (This training rule) has the origin like the first Pārājika (paṭhama-pārājika-samuṭṭhāna): non-action, release through perception, with intention, worldly fault, bodily action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.

## 5. Cittāgāra-vagga

## 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule
In the first training rule of the Cittāgāra Chapter: 'King's house' (Rājāgāra) means the king's pleasure house (palace). 'Picture gallery' (Cittāgāra) means an ornately constructed house for people's enjoyment (picture gallery). 'Park' (Ārāma) means a park within the city for people's enjoyment. 'Garden' (Uyyāna) means a pleasure grove outside the city for people's enjoyment. 'Lotus pond' (Pokkharaṇī) means a pond for people's enjoyment. Therefore, in the word analysis (padabhājana), it is said, 'Wherever the king's pleasure place is,' and so on. In the phrase 'If she goes to see, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa),' the wrongdoing is by the number of steps. In the phrase 'Standing in whatever place she sees,' if she stands in one place without lifting her feet and sees all five (the king's house, etc.), there is only one pācittiya offense. However, for a nun who turns and looks in various directions, there are separate offenses. For a monk, there is an offense of wrongdoing in all instances of looking.

'Standing in the park' means if they build a king's house and so on within the park, there is no offense for a nun who sees them. 'Whether going or coming' means if it is on the path of a nun going for alms-food and so on, and she sees those king's houses, etc., there is no offense. 'Going because there is business to be done' means if she goes to the king's presence for some business and sees them, there is no offense. 'In times of danger' means if she enters and sees them while being oppressed by some danger, there is no offense. The rest is clear. This training rule is like the origin of the sheep's wool rule (eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna): action, not released through perception, without intention, worldly fault, bodily action, unwholesome mind, and three feelings.

## The First Training Rule.

In the fourth training rule: For all preliminary efforts starting from pounding rice for gruel and the like, a *dukkaṭa* offense is committed according to the number of efforts. Regarding gruel and meals, *pācittiya* offenses are committed according to the number of vessels; regarding snacks and the like, according to the number of items.

*Yāgupāna* means that when people prepare gruel or a meal for the Saṅgha, there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who cooks anything as their assistant. Regarding the phrase "for one's own attendant": even if parents come to the monastery, if she has them perform a task such as making a fan or a broom handle and places them in the position of an attendant, it is allowable to cook something for them. ## 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule

In the third training rule, regarding the phrase "to give the agreement on training" (sikkha-sammuti), why is it caused to be given? It is because women are said to be fickle; if they fulfill the virtues for two years without training in the six rules, they become exhausted. However, if they train first, they will not be exhausted later and will be able to carry out the fulfillment of virtue. Seeing this, [the Buddha] caused it to be given.

The meaning of "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life, not transgressing it for two years" is: having made the undertaking not to transgress for two years the training rule prescribed as "abstaining from taking life" (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), I undertake it. This method applies to all training rules. These six trainings must be given even to a woman who has gone forth as a novice at the age of sixty. One who has not trained in these should not be ordained as a bhikkhunī.

## 8. Kumāribhūta Vagga

## 1-2-3. Commentary on the First, Second, and Third Training Rules

The three training rules—the first, second, and third—of the Kumāribhūta Vagga are similar to the three Gihigata training rules (found in the Gabhini Vagga). It should be understood that the two Mahāsikkhamānās, who are the very first of all sikkhamānās, are those who have passed the age of twenty. Whether those Mahāsikkhamānās are formerly married (gihigatā) or not formerly married (agihigatā), they should be called only "sikkhamānā"; they should not be called "gihigatā" or "kumāribhūta." For a formerly married woman (gihigatā), the agreement of training (sikkhāsammuti) should be given when she is ten years old, and higher ordination (upasampadā) should be performed when she is twelve years old. If given at the age of eleven, it should be performed at the age of thirteen. If the agreement is given at the age of twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, or eighteen, the higher ordination should be performed at the age of twenty. From the age of eighteen onwards, however, it is proper to call this sikkhamānā either "gihigatā" or "kumāribhūta." But a maiden (kumāribhūta) should not be called "gihigatā"; she should be called only "kumāribhūta." A Mahāsikkhamānā should not be called either "gihigatā" or "kumāribhūta"; by virtue of the granting of the agreement of training, it is proper to call all three types of sikkhamānās simply "sikkhamānā."

## 10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule

In the tenth training rule, "anāpucchā" means without having asked permission (from parents, husband, etc., to ordain the sikkhamānā). Bhikkhunīs must ask permission twice: at the time of going forth (pabbajjā) and at the time of higher ordination (upasampadā). For monks, however, asking once is sufficient.

"Ajānantī" means not knowing that the mother or others are present (and ordaining her). The rest is clear. This training rule has a head of origin not previously mentioned (apubbasamuṭṭhāna). It has four origins: it arises from speech, from body and speech, from speech and consciousness, and from body, speech, and consciousness.

How? While sitting in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) for some business such as the rehabilitation (abbhānakamma) ceremony, if one says, "Call the sikkhamānā, we will ordain her right here," and then ordains her, it thus arises from speech. For a nun who, starting from the nunnery, says, "I will ordain her," and goes to the khaṇḍasīmā, it arises from body and speech. For a nun who, in both places, knows that there is a regulation but still commits the transgression, it arises from speech and consciousness, and from body, speech, and consciousness. Because of ordaining without asking permission, it is an act of commission and omission (kiriyākirya) (the act of ordaining is commission, the failure to ask is omission); it is not release from offense through perception; it is without consciousness, a fault of regulation, bodily action, verbal action, having three types of consciousness, and three types of feelings.

## The Tenth Training Rule.

## 11. Commentary on the Eleventh Training Rule

1167-8. In the eleventh training rule, "pārivāsikachandadānena" means by giving consent that has been set aside (to ordain someone). In that context, there are four kinds of pārivāsiya: parisapārivāsiya, rattipārivāsiya, chandapārivāsiya, and ajjhāsayapārivāsiya. Among those four, parisapārivāsiya means that monks have assembled for some business, and then if rain falls, or if people are cleared away, or if a crowd of people comes overwhelming them...
225:
Monks assemble for some business to be done. At that time, due to rain, or because people are being cleared away, or because a crowd is pushing in, they think, "We have no opportunity here; let us go elsewhere," and they depart without giving up their intention (chanda) to perform the legal act. This is called parisapārivāsiya (interruption by the assembly). Although it is parisapārivāsiya, because the intention has not been given up, it is proper to perform that legal act (at another place).

Furthermore, monks assemble at night, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha and so forth," and saying, "We shall listen to the Dhamma until everyone has assembled," they invite one monk to preach the Dhamma. While that monk is preaching the Dhamma, dawn breaks. If they were sitting with the intention, "We shall perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha," it is proper to perform it as the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If they were sitting to perform the fifteenth-day Uposatha, but (at dawn) it becomes the first day of the next fortnight, which is not an Uposatha day, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha; however, it is proper to perform other Sangha business. This is called rattipārivāsiya (interruption by the night).

Furthermore, monks are sitting, thinking, "We shall perform some Sangha act such as abbhāna (rehabilitation)." Among them, a monk who is an expert in astrology says, "Today the constellation is harsh; do not perform this act." Based on his words, they give up their intention and remain sitting right there. Then another monk arrives and says, "The benefit bypasses the fool who waits for the stars (constellations)," and asks, "What will you do with the stars?" This is known as chandapārivāsiya and ajjhāsayapārivāsiya. In such an interruption, it is not proper to perform the act without again bringing the declaration of purity (chanda-pārisuddhi).

"Vuṭṭhitāya parisāya" means the assembly has risen after giving up the intention, whether by body, by speech, or by the mere act of giving up the intention.

"Anāpatti avuṭṭhitāya parisāya" means there is no offense if the assembly has not yet risen and the intention has not been given up (when, for example, ordaining a sikkhamānā). The remaining words are clear. This training rule has three origins (ti-samuṭṭhāna): action (kiriya), release from perception (saññā-vimokkha), with intention (sacittaka), prohibited by regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāya-kamma), verbal action (vacī-kamma), three types of consciousness (ti-citta), and three types of feeling (ti-vedanā).

## 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule

In the commentary on the first training rule of the Chattu-pāhana Chapter—"sakimpi dhāreti āpatti pācittiyassa" means that while traveling on a journey, even if one carries [an umbrella] all day with a single effort, there is only one offence. If, upon reaching mud and so forth, she removes her sandals and walks while only carrying an umbrella, she incurs an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, if seeing bushes and so forth, she removes the umbrella and walks only wearing sandals, she also incurs an offence of wrong-doing. If she removes the umbrella and also takes off the sandals, and then carries or wears them again, she incurs another pācittiya offence. Thus, the offences should be understood by the number of efforts (payoga). The rest is clear. Like the origin of the sheep's wool rule—it consists of: action, no release through perception, without consciousness, prescriptive fault, bodily action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## Explanation of the Training Rules for Confession

Immediately after the minor training rules are those called Pāṭidesanīya,
These eight rules have been included in the summary of the rehearsal,
This commentary on those Pāṭidesanīya rules proceeds in brief.

In these training rules for confession, whatever items such as ghee, oil, and so forth are specified in the Pali—a nun who requests and eats those very items mentioned in the Pali incurs an offence of confession (pāṭidesanīya). However, for all items not directly included in the Pali, it is an offence of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). The rest here is clear. These eight types of confession rules also arise from four originations: from the body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. They are actions (kiriya), not released by perception (no-saññāvimokkha), unintentional (acittaka), regulatory faults (paṇṇattivajja), bodily acts, vocal acts, and are associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

How the five generals (powers: faith, wisdom, energy, etc.) govern within my own body:

General of Faith (Saddhā-bala): I truly believe in past kamma. All the benefits in this life are due to past kamma. Being born in Thayaing village, relying on good teachers, and having wisdom and energy are all due to past kamma. This faith is a firm general that no one can shake.

General of Wisdom (Paññā-bala): The Buddha's teachings learned since childhood increase the knowledge of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), thus being the opposite of ignorance (avijjā). This wisdom will surely be the true general capable of destroying ignorance to the end.

General of Energy (Viriya-bala): When faith and wisdom are firm, energy also becomes steadfast without retreating. Therefore, even at the age of over 60, I can teach and write scriptures with agility. This general of energy stands tall, suppressing laziness.
